x: Digital Health Guide A practical handbook of best practices for delivering digital services in health and social care organizations # This book is written for the people who lead and run digital delivery in health and care: chief executives and senior leaders, directors of digital and transformation, product and delivery leads, clinical and care professionals moving into digital roles, programme and portfolio managers, and the operational managers who make services work every day. Its centre of gravity is the UK's National Health Service (NHS) and social care system, but its principles transfer to any publicly-accountable, safety-critical, partnership-dependent health organization anywhere. The premise is simple: in health and care, how you work is a clinical-safety, equity, and public-trust issue, not merely an efficiency one. Good ways of working get safe, equitable services to people faster and waste less public money. Poor ones cause harm. This book collects the best available practice — from the NHS and GOV.UK service standards, from portfolio, programme and product disciplines, from change and improvement science, and from the health-and-care workforce evidence base — into one coherent operating playbook. How to use this guide # The topics are ordered but self-contained; each ends with a maturity model and a checklist so you can assess where you are and decide what to do next. Read Part I first to fix the vocabulary and the non-negotiables — safety, regulation, data, ethics, and inclusion — then jump to whichever part answers your current problem. x: Preface Digital health and care is now delivered by organizations that must be, all at once, safe like a hospital, iterative like a start-up, accountable like a government department, and collaborative like a coalition. No single existing playbook covers that combination. Software teams have agile and product management; the public sector has the GOV.UK and NHS service standards; large change has programme and portfolio management; the health system has improvement science and a deep workforce evidence base. Each is excellent in its lane. The problem leaders actually face is that their work spans all the lanes at once, every day. This book is an attempt to assemble those disciplines into one coherent set of ways of working for a digital health and care organization — and to do it honestly, naming trade-offs rather than selling a method. Why "ways of working" deserves a book # In most industries, how you organize work is an efficiency question. In health and care it is also a safety question (bad process harms patients), an equity question (services designed narrowly exclude the people who need them most), a public-money question (the funding is taxpayers' and finite), and a trust question (people share their most sensitive data with you). That raises the stakes on ordinary decisions — how work gets in the door, how it is triaged and prioritized, how teams are shaped, how change is led — to a level that justifies treating them as a discipline. What this book covers # The topics move from foundations (what ways of working means, the operating model, evidence-driven decisions), through the flow of work (intake, triage, prioritization) and the delivery lifecycle (discovery, and the discovery→alpha→beta→live path), into the modes you deliver in (product, project, programme, portfolio, and the ERP backbone), then the people who do the work (team structures, workforce planning, workforce strategy, and organizational development), the disciplines of change and innovation, the realities of partnership and government, and finally measurement and the visibility senior leaders need. Every topic is built the same way — thesis, why it matters in health and care, core concepts, best practices, a worked health example, failure modes, a maturity model, a checklist, and real sources — so you can assess where you are and decide what to do next without reading cover to cover. How to read it # Read Part I to fix the shared vocabulary, then treat the rest as a reference. If your problem is "too much work, no way to choose," start at Part II. If it is "our transformation keeps stalling," start with change ( Topic 8.5 ) and phasing innovation ( Topic 8.4 ). If it is "the board can't see what's really happening," start with Topics 10.3 and 10.4. The cross-references will pull you to the neighbouring topics you need. A note on grounding and scope # The centre of gravity is the UK's NHS and social care system, because that is where much of the best public guidance on these ways of working has been written and tested — the NHS Digital Service Manual, the GOV.UK Service Manual, NICE's Evidence Standards Framework, and the health-and-care workforce strategies among them. The principles, though, are not parochial: safety-critical, publicly-accountable, partnership-dependent health organizations everywhere face the same forces. Where the book cites frameworks, statistics or documents, it cites real, checkable ones; where the evidence is thin, it says so rather than inventing certainty. The aim throughout is a handbook you can act on, not admire. Edit this page on GitHub — the book is the source of truth; this site renders it.

x: Topic 1.0 — Ways of Working in Digital Health & Care In one sentence: Ways of working are the deliberate, shared habits — how you organize teams, make decisions, manage risk, and deliver value — that let a health and care organization turn intent into safe, equitable, evidence-based outcomes for patients and citizens. Why this matters in health and care # Every organization has ways of working, whether chosen or inherited. In digital health and care, the ones you inherit are usually wrong for the job: they were built for construction-style projects with fixed scope, not for adaptive services that touch clinical safety, statutory duty, and public money. Getting them right is not a back-office nicety; it is the difference between a shared care record that clinicians trust and one that sits unused. Health and care is distinctive in ways that shape every practice in this book. Safety is non-negotiable — a defect in a digital service can harm a patient, so clinical risk management (see Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management) is woven through delivery, not bolted on. Equity matters because a service that works only for the digitally confident widens health inequalities ; the Core20PLUS5 populations and people with limited digital access must be designed for, not designed out. Statutory duties — the NHS commitment to comprehensive care, data-protection law, the duty of confidentiality — constrain what you may do with data and how you must consult. Public money demands proportionate spend control and demonstrable value. And almost nothing is delivered by one body alone: partnership across integrated care systems (ICS), local authorities, social care providers, and suppliers is the default operating condition. These four pressures — safety, equity, duty, money — are why you cannot simply copy a consumer-tech playbook. You need ways of working that are agile and accountable, fast and safe, user-centred and population-fair. Core concepts # Ways of working operate at three levels. At the team level they are the daily practices: stand-ups, user research, iterative delivery, pairing. At the organizational level they are the operating model — how strategy becomes value streams, capabilities, funding, and decision rights (see Topic 1.1 — The Operating Model). At the system level they are how independent organizations align: shared standards, interoperability, and common governance across an ICS. This book moves deliberately across all three. User-centred design means starting from the needs of the people who use a service — patients, carers, clinicians, administrators — rather than from an assumed solution. The UK Government Digital Service (GDS) and the NHS codified this in service standards: understand users and their needs before you build, and keep testing with real users throughout. Agile, iterative delivery means getting a working service in front of real users early, learning, and adapting — rather than specifying everything up front. The NHS digital service manual is explicit that agile, user-centred ways of working reduce the risk of building the wrong thing. Agile here is a risk-management strategy as much as a delivery method. Multidisciplinary teams (MDTs) bring together, in one empowered team, the mix of skills a service needs: product and delivery management, user research and design, engineering, clinical and information-governance expertise, and operational knowledge. The NHS service standard requires teams that include multidisciplinary skills and perspectives — including access to specialist clinical, legal, or policy input. The MDT is the atom of digital delivery; most failures trace back to a missing discipline at the table. Product over project. A project has a start, an end, and a hand-off; a product is funded and stewarded for its whole life. The shift from project to product thinking (see Topic 1.1 and Topic 5.0 — Product-Led Work) changes funding, teams, and accountability, and it fits health services — which are long-lived and continuously evolving — far better than one-off projects do. Best practices # Start from user needs, evidenced by research. Before committing to a build, understand who the users are, what they are trying to do, and where the current service fails them. Fund a discovery (see Topic 3.4 — Discovery Phases) and treat "we assumed" as a red flag. User needs, not internal preferences, are the anchor for every later decision. Build multidisciplinary, empowered, and stable teams. Assemble the full mix of skills — including clinical safety and information governance — and give the team authority to decide within clear guardrails. Keep teams together around a service rather than disbanding them at each project boundary; stable teams accumulate the domain and safety knowledge that health services demand. Work in the open and iterate in small steps . Ship thin slices, measure, and adjust. Small, frequent releases are safer than big-bang launches because problems surface while they are still small, and they let clinical-safety and information-governance review keep pace with change rather than becoming a gate at the end. Make safety and equity first-class from day one. Run clinical risk management (DCB0129/DCB0160) and equality/health-inequalities analysis alongside delivery, not as end-stage sign-offs. Ask early who could be excluded or harmed, and design for the hardest cases — assisted digital routes, accessibility ( WCAG ), and offline fallbacks. Decide with evidence, and record the decision. Distinguish clinical evidence (does it work and is it safe?) from delivery evidence (are we building it well and being used?), and keep a lightweight decision log so the reasoning survives staff turnover (see Topic 1.3 — Evidence-Driven Decisions). Evidence beats the highest-paid person's opinion. Design for interoperability and reuse. Health and care data must flow safely between organizations; build to open standards ( HL7 FHIR , SNOMED CT ) and reuse platforms rather than re-inventing them (see Topic 1.1 's "thinnest viable platform" and Topic 4.3 — Interoperability & Data Standards). A service that cannot share data is a silo waiting to become a risk. Govern proportionately. Match the weight of assurance to the level of risk. High-risk clinical changes deserve deep scrutiny; low-risk content changes should not wait weeks for a board. Proportionate governance keeps you both safe and fast. Work in the open. Share plans, decisions, roadmaps and — where safe — code, so partners, clinicians and the public can see how and why choices are made. Openness builds trust, cuts duplication across a fragmented system, and invites challenge before mistakes harden into live services. In health and care, being transparent about what a service does with data, and why, is itself a trust and safety practice. Design for the long term and for handover. Digital services in health outlive the teams and contracts that build them, so capture decisions, avoid undocumented "hero" knowledge, and design for the people who will run and change the service for years (see Topic 10.3 — Knowledge Management & Documentation). Treat sustainability — of the team, the technology and the funding model — as a first-class constraint, not an afterthought. Questions to discuss with your team # Where are our current ways of working inherited rather than chosen, and which inherited habit is costing us the most in safety, equity, or wasted spend? This question forces an honest audit of the practices no one decided but everyone follows — fixed-scope programme funding, disband-and-rebuild project teams, governance consulted only at go-live. It matters because inherited habits are usually invisible until named, and in health and care they carry real cost: a shared record clinicians do not trust, a service that excludes Core20PLUS5 populations, or a rebuild of the same login plumbing on public money. The tension to debate is that inherited ways often feel safe precisely because they are familiar and auditable, so retiring them looks like taking on risk rather than removing it. Ground the discussion in concrete artefacts — look at your last three business cases, your team turnover between projects, and when clinical safety was first engaged — rather than trading opinions. A good answer names one or two specific habits with evidence of their cost, distinguishes the ones worth keeping from the ones actively harming outcomes, and commits to a change that a senior leader will be accountable for. Do our teams genuinely have the full multidisciplinary skill mix — including clinical safety and information governance — sitting inside the team, or are those disciplines still bolted on as end-stage gates? The topic argues the MDT is the atom of digital delivery and that most failures trace to a missing discipline at the table, so this question tests whether that principle is real in your organization or merely aspirational. It matters because a clinical safety officer or Caldicott Guardian engaged only at go-live forces either rework or unsafe shortcuts, whereas one embedded from week one keeps a live hazard log that paces delivery. The trade-off worth surfacing is cost and scarcity: specialist clinical, legal, and IG time is genuinely limited, so "embed everyone in every team" collides with real resourcing constraints, and the team must decide where fractional or shared roles are acceptable and where they are not. Look at a current service and map who is actually in the standing team versus who is consulted as an external sign-off, and check whether the team has authority to decide within guardrails or must escalate constantly. An honest, good answer is specific about which disciplines are missing or borrowed, acknowledges the resourcing tension frankly, and proposes a concrete model — full-time, fractional, or on-call — for closing the gap without pretending scarcity away. When have we treated a digital service as a project with a hand-off rather than a product stewarded for its whole life, and what did that cost us in lost domain and safety knowledge? Product-over-project is one of the topic's load-bearing shifts, and this question makes the team confront where they still fund and staff for closure rather than continuity. It matters because health services are long-lived and continuously evolving; a team disbanded at the project boundary takes with it exactly the accumulated clinical and operational knowledge that keeps a service safe, and "pilot purgatory" is the recurring symptom. The real tension is financial and structural: product funding requires standing budgets and challenges the annual-bid, time-boxed model that finance and governance are built around, so this is as much a conversation about money and accountability as about delivery. Consider a specific service that went through a hand-off — trace what happened to its hazard log, its user research, and its team — and weigh that against the discipline product funding demands. A good answer identifies a concrete case, quantifies or at least characterizes the knowledge lost, and is candid about which organizational barriers (funding cycles, resourcing rules, governance structures) would have to move for persistent product teams to become the norm. Who is most likely to be excluded or harmed by the services we build, and can we point to where we designed for them first rather than last? The topic insists that equity is non-negotiable and that a service which works only for the digitally confident widens health inequalities, so this question tests whether "design for the hardest cases" is a live practice or a slogan. It matters because exclusion in health and care is not an inconvenience but a safety and access harm: the Core20PLUS5 populations, people with limited digital access, low health literacy, or no smartphone are precisely the people whose needs are greatest, and a service that designs them out concentrates harm where it is least affordable. The tension worth surfacing is that designing for the margins costs time and money up front — assisted-digital routes, accessibility to WCAG, offline and non-digital fallbacks, translation — and those costs are easy to defer when a delivery date looms and the confident majority can already use the thing. Look at a real service and ask who is in its user research sample, whether an equality and health-inequalities analysis actually shaped a design decision, and what happens to someone who cannot or will not go online. An honest answer names the specific groups at risk for this service, shows at least one concrete design choice made for them, and is candid about where the team traded inclusion away under pressure and how it would defend that trade next time. Where are we re-inventing plumbing that already exists, and where would building to open standards and reusing shared platforms actually change what we ship? Designing for interoperability and reuse is one of the topic's best practices, and this question makes the team confront the pull to build bespoke rather than reuse — the login, the notifications, the record integration that a dozen other teams have also built. It matters because in a fragmented system every re-invented component is public money spent twice and a new silo that cannot exchange data safely; conversely, building to HL7 FHIR and SNOMED CT and reusing the thinnest viable platform is what lets a service clear procurement and share data across an ICS at all. The real trade-off is that reuse means dependency: a shared platform may be slower, less tailored, or governed by someone else's roadmap, so the team must weigh the drag of a shared component against the long-term cost and risk of a bespoke silo. Examine a current build and list what is genuinely novel versus what duplicates an existing platform, standard, or open component, and check whether "we cannot reuse that" is an evidenced constraint or an untested assumption. A good answer distinguishes the parts worth building from the parts worth reusing, is honest about the maturity and governance of the platforms on offer, and commits to open standards for anything that must exchange data. How do we match the weight of our governance to the level of risk, and where is assurance currently either too heavy for low-risk change or too light for high-risk change? Proportionate governance is a load-bearing idea in this topic — high-risk clinical changes deserve deep scrutiny while low-risk content changes should not wait weeks for a board — and this question tests whether the organization calibrates assurance to risk or applies one blunt process to everything. It matters because mis-set governance harms both ways: a heavy one-size-fits-all gate makes teams batch up changes and slows the very iteration that keeps services safe, while a uniformly light touch lets a genuinely high-risk clinical change through without the clinical-safety and information-governance scrutiny it needs. The tension is that proportionality requires judgement, and judgement is uncomfortable for boards and auditors who find a single mandatory checklist easier to defend than a risk-tiered route. Look at how your last dozen changes were assured, sort them by actual clinical and data risk, and see whether the effort spent tracked the risk or the calendar. An honest answer identifies concrete examples of both over- and under-governance, proposes clear criteria for tiering change by risk, and names who holds the authority to decide the tier and to be accountable for it. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system wants to give clinicians across three acute trusts, community services, and local authority social care a shared care record . The old way would commission a fixed-scope programme, specify every screen up front, and integrate late. Instead the ICS forms a multidisciplinary team: a product manager, delivery manager, user researcher, interaction designer, two engineers, a clinical safety officer, and an information governance lead, with access to a caldicott guardian and a social-care practitioner. They run an eight-week discovery, observing how a district nurse, an A&E consultant, and a social worker actually try to find information today. They discover the real pain is not "no data" but "data they cannot trust the currency of." The team ships a narrow alpha: read-only access to allergies, medications, and current care-plan status for one clinical pathway, with a visible "last updated" stamp. Clinical safety runs in parallel; a hazard log is maintained from week one. They measure whether clinicians stop phoning other teams to confirm information. Only once that thin slice proves valuable and safe do they widen the record — funded as a continuing product, not a closed project. Sector lenses # The same four pressures — safety, equity, duty, money — bear on every organization, but the ways of working that answer them shift with scale, funding, and accountability. Startup # A small digital-health company lives or dies by focus, so its ways of working are lean by necessity: one multidisciplinary team, flat decision-making, and daily contact with users. The constraint is runway, not headcount rules, so discovery is measured in weeks and evidence is gathered cheaply — a handful of clinical interviews, a clickable prototype, an honest hazard log kept by a fractional clinical safety officer. The danger is skipping safety and information-governance rigour to hit an investor milestone; the discipline that survives scrutiny is treating DCB0129 and a data-protection impact assessment as entry criteria for a pilot, not paperwork deferred until a trust asks. Interoperability from day one (FHIR, SNOMED CT) is also a commercial asset, because a startup that cannot exchange data will never clear NHS procurement. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home or domiciliary-care agency, a single-site clinic, or a modest health-tech supplier past the pre-revenue stage — carries the same safety, equity, duty and money pressures as a large trust but with a fraction of the capability to meet them. Ways of working here have to be radically proportionate: there is rarely a dedicated digital or IG team, so the "multidisciplinary team" is often a handful of people wearing several hats plus a shared or outsourced clinical-safety and data-protection resource. The trap is assuming the statutory duties scale down with the organization — they do not, so DCB0129/DCB0160 clinical safety, a data-protection impact assessment, and accessibility still apply in full even when a single practice manager is accountable for all of them. The practical discipline is to lean hard on reuse rather than build: adopt accredited off-the-shelf systems, insist suppliers meet DTAC and open standards (FHIR, SNOMED CT), and use national and ICS-provided platforms so that safety, interoperability and information governance are inherited rather than reinvented on a shoestring. Enterprise # An NHS trust or ICS has the opposite problem: abundant process and fragmented ownership. Ways of working here are as much about unlearning — retiring fixed-scope programme habits, standing down disband-and-rebuild project teams — as about adopting new practices. Accountability is formal and personal (a senior responsible owner, a Caldicott Guardian, board-level clinical safety sign-off), so the win is embedding those roles inside the delivery team rather than bolting them on as gates. A large health-tech or pharma supplier faces the mirror image: strong engineering maturity but distance from frontline clinical reality, which multidisciplinary teams with real clinician time exist to close. Government # A national or local public body — NHS England, DHSC, UKHSA, a local authority — sets the standards everyone else works to, so its ways of working ripple outward. x: Topic 1.1 — The Operating Model In one sentence: A target operating model (TOM) is the deliberate design of how your organization's strategy flows through value streams, capabilities, teams, governance, technology, data, and suppliers to deliver digital health and care outcomes — and getting its shape right determines whether everything downstream is fast and safe or slow and brittle. Why this matters in health and care # Most digital health organizations do not fail for lack of talent or technology; they fail because their operating model fights them. Funding is tied to time-limited projects, decision rights are ambiguous, and every team rebuilds the same login, integration, and audit plumbing. The result is duplicated cost on public money, inconsistent clinical safety, and services that cannot share data across an integrated care system (ICS). An operating model is distinctive in this domain because it must reconcile competing goods. It has to be federated enough to respect the autonomy of sovereign organizations — trusts, local authorities, GP practices — yet coherent enough to give a patient one safe experience across them. It must balance run (keeping clinical systems safely available) against change (improving them), when downtime can affect care. And it must spend proportionately: assurance heavy enough for public accountability and clinical safety, light enough not to strangle iteration. The TOM is where those trade-offs are made explicit rather than left to accident. Core concepts # The layers of an operating model . A useful TOM is a stack, each layer serving the one above: Strategy and outcomes — the measurable population and service outcomes you exist to improve (often expressed as OKRs ; see Topic 1.3 — Evidence-Driven Decisions). Value streams — the end-to-end flows that deliver value to a user, e.g. "refer, triage, and treat a patient" — organized around the citizen's journey, not the org chart. Capabilities — the things you must be able to do (identity, appointment booking, clinical documentation, analytics). Capabilities are stable even as solutions change. Teams — the people organized to deliver capabilities and value streams (see Team Topologies below). Governance and decision rights — who decides what, and how assurance is applied. Technology and data — the platforms, standards, and data architecture the teams build on. Suppliers — the market you buy from and how you manage it. Designing top-down (strategy → value streams → capabilities) keeps teams and technology aligned to outcomes rather than to legacy structures. Centralized vs federated vs platform models. A centralized model concentrates delivery in one team or arms-length body: consistent and cheap to standardize, but a bottleneck and often remote from local need. A federated model devolves delivery to trusts and places: responsive and locally owned, but prone to duplication and divergence. A platform model is the reconciling pattern: a central team provides shared, reusable capabilities (identity, interoperability, hosting, design system) as a platform , and federated teams build on top at speed. Most mature health systems converge on "platform plus federation." Team Topologies. This framework names four team types — stream-aligned (owning a value stream), platform (providing self-service capabilities), enabling (coaching others up a capability), and complicated-subsystem (deep specialist work such as an algorithm) — and stresses low-friction interaction between them. It maps cleanly onto the platform model: platform teams reduce the cognitive load on stream-aligned teams so they can focus on user and clinical value. Run vs change. Run is keeping live services safe and available; change is improving or building them. Product teams that both build and run a service ("you build it, you run it") close the feedback loop and improve safety, but the balance must be funded honestly — starving run to fund change is how clinical systems degrade. The thinnest viable platform (TVP). From Team Topologies: a platform should be the smallest set of shared services that genuinely reduces friction for stream teams — no more. An over-built platform becomes its own bottleneck and its own legacy. Start with the few capabilities every team truly needs (authentication, an interoperability layer, hosting, a design system) and grow only on evidenced demand. Best practices # Design the model from outcomes down, not the org chart up. Begin with the population and service outcomes you must move, derive the value streams that deliver them, and only then design teams and technology. A TOM anchored in the existing hierarchy just automates the current silos. Adopt a platform-plus-federation shape. Provide shared capabilities centrally as a self-service platform, and let stream-aligned teams in trusts and places build on top. This gives you national consistency on safety and interoperability with local speed and ownership — the reconciliation the domain demands. Fund products, not projects. Move money from time-boxed projects to persistently funded product teams aligned to value streams. Project funding forces teams to disband at exactly the point they have learned the domain; product funding sustains the safety knowledge and iteration that health services need (see Topic 5.0 — Product-Led Work). Make spend control proportionate and staged. Use staged funding tied to evidence — release money at discovery, alpha, beta, and live gates rather than approving a whole programme up front. GDS -style spend controls and the NHS assurance route exist to prevent large sunk costs on unproven ideas; apply them as thresholds scaled to risk and value, not blanket bureaucracy. Make decision rights explicit with a RACI or RAPID map. Ambiguous authority is the commonest cause of stalled delivery. Name, for each significant decision type, who is Responsible/Accountable/Consulted/Informed ( RACI ) or who Recommends, Agrees, Performs, has Input, and Decides (RAPID). Publish it so teams stop escalating decisions they are empowered to make. Keep the platform thin and demand-led. Build shared capabilities only when two or more teams demonstrably need the same thing, and treat the platform as a product with its own users (the internal teams). Resist the urge to pre-build a grand platform; the thinnest viable platform earns its scope through adoption. Manage suppliers as part of the model, not outside it. Decide deliberately which capabilities are strategic (build/own) and which are commodity (buy), avoid single-supplier lock-in on core clinical data, and require open standards and exit rights in contracts. Your suppliers are a layer of your operating model, and their ways of working must be compatible with yours. Make decision rights explicit. An operating model only works if people know who decides what — which choices sit with a product team, which with a clinical-safety authority, and which must reach a board. Map decision rights and push each decision to the lowest level that can safely hold it, so delivery is not throttled by needless escalation. Ambiguous authority is one of the most common causes of slow, defensive delivery. Treat the operating model as a product you evolve. A target operating model is not set once and framed on a wall; inspect it as demand, technology and partnerships change, and adapt it on evidence. Watch a few signals — flow of work, time-to-decision, rework, and team health — and change structures when they are demonstrably getting in the way, not in response to reorganization fashion. Questions to discuss with your team # Is our operating model designed from outcomes and value streams down, or has it simply automated our existing org chart and its silos? This question goes to the topic's central warning that a TOM anchored in the current hierarchy just entrenches the silos you already have, so it is worth putting on the table before any reorganization. It matters in a health and care setting because value streams follow the citizen's journey — refer, triage, treat — across sovereign organizations, while org charts follow institutional boundaries, and a model built on the latter will keep producing fragmented, non-interoperable services on public money. The tension to debate honestly is that designing top-down from outcomes is genuinely disruptive: it cuts across departmental ownership, budgets, and reporting lines that senior people have built careers around, so there is real political cost to doing it properly. Test yourselves concretely by naming your top three outcomes and tracing whether your actual team boundaries and funding lines follow those value streams or the departments; if teams map cleanly to departments, that is your answer. A good, honest response admits where the model is org-chart-shaped, identifies at least one value stream that is currently split across silos to its detriment, and is realistic about which structural boundaries the organization is willing to redraw. What belongs in our thinnest viable platform, and how will we stop it from either being over-built into a bottleneck or under-built so every team rebuilds the same plumbing? The platform-plus-federation shape only works if the platform stays thin and demand-led, and this question makes the team confront both failure modes the topic names — the grand platform that becomes its own legacy bottleneck, and the absence that forces every team to rebuild login, integration, and audit. It matters because in an ICS the platform is effectively shared infrastructure (identity, a FHIR interoperability layer, hosting with safety baselines, a design system) and getting its scope wrong multiplies either cost or friction across every stream team. The trade-off to debate is timing and evidence: build too early and you guess wrong and create a bottleneck; build too late and duplication has already calcified — so the "two or more teams demonstrably need the same thing" test is the crux, and the team should stress-test whether they actually apply it or just build what seems obviously central. Look at what you currently treat as platform versus what teams rebuild, and ask whether the platform is run as a product with its own internal users and SLAs or as a queue everyone waits behind. An honest answer names the specific capabilities that pass the two-team test today, resists the temptation to pre-build the rest, and commits to treating the platform team's internal users as real customers with real service levels. Where are our decision rights genuinely ambiguous, and what are teams escalating today that they should be empowered to decide themselves? Ambiguous authority is called out as the commonest cause of stalled delivery, so this question surfaces the everyday friction that a published RACI or RAPID map is meant to remove. It matters acutely in a federated health system where place teams, an ICS digital board, clinical safety, and information governance all have legitimate claims on a decision, and unclear boundaries mean either everything escalates or, worse, no one owns a call until it goes wrong. The tension worth exploring is that devolving decisions requires trusting teams within guardrails, which senior leaders and boards often resist precisely where clinical safety or public money is involved — yet withholding that trust is what creates the escalation gridlock in the first place. Make it concrete by listing the last five decisions that escalated and asking, for each, who should have decided and what guardrail would have let them; the pattern usually reveals a small number of recurring ambiguous decision types. A good answer produces a specific, publishable statement of who decides what — distinguishing platform standards, service design, and clinical-safety sign-off — and is honest about which decisions the organization is genuinely willing to devolve versus which it will keep central and why. Are we funding run and change honestly, or are we quietly starving live-service operations to pay for new features? The topic is blunt that starving run to fund change is how clinical systems degrade, and this question forces the balance into the open before an outage or a safety incident makes it for you. It matters in health and care because "run" is not back-office overhead — it is the availability of systems clinicians depend on at the point of care, so a degraded run budget shows up as downtime that can affect patients, not merely inconvenienced users. The trade-off is uncomfortable because change is visible and celebrated while run is invisible until it fails, so boards and roadmaps naturally bias toward the new; a "you build it, you run it" model helps by keeping the feedback loop closed, but only if the team's run time is genuinely protected rather than notionally allocated and then raided. Make it concrete by looking at what proportion of each product team's capacity actually went to keeping services safe and available last quarter versus what was planned, and whether run work is tracked and valued or treated as interruption. An honest answer names where run is being under-funded today, protects a realistic run allocation as a first charge rather than a residual, and is candid about which live services are carrying accumulated operational risk. Which capabilities are we deliberately choosing to build and own versus buy, and are we accepting lock-in on our core clinical data without meaning to? Best practice here is to decide build versus buy deliberately, avoid single-supplier lock-in on core clinical data, and treat suppliers as a layer of the operating model rather than something outside it — this question tests whether those choices are actually being made or defaulting. It matters because in digital health the most consequential lock-in is around the clinical record and its data, where a proprietary store with no realistic exit can trap a whole system for a decade and dictate what every downstream service can do. The tension is speed versus optionality: buying is faster and often cheaper today, especially for a stretched team, but each convenient buy without open standards or exit rights quietly narrows tomorrow's choices, and the cost only becomes visible when you try to leave. Make it concrete by listing your core capabilities, marking each as strategic (build/own) or commodity (buy), and checking whether the contracts behind the commodity ones actually require open standards (HL7 FHIR, SNOMED CT) and enforceable exit rights. A good answer distinguishes the few genuinely strategic capabilities from the many that are safely bought, is honest about where the organization is already locked in on clinical data, and commits to open standards and exit rights in the contracts that matter most. How will we know when our operating model needs to change, and what signals would tell us — rather than reorganizing on fashion or on a new leader's arrival? The topic frames the operating model as a product you evolve on evidence, not a diagram framed on a wall, so this question asks the team to define in advance what evidence would justify reshaping it. It matters in health and care because reorganization is disruptive and expensive — it disbands hard-won domain and clinical-safety knowledge — yet the sector is prone to structural churn driven by policy cycles and new appointments rather than by whether the current model is actually getting in the way. The tension is between stability and adaptation: change the model too readily and you never let teams settle or accrue safety expertise, change it too rarely and calcified structures throttle flow long after they stopped fitting the work. Make it concrete by choosing a small set of signals to watch — flow of work, time-to-decision, rework, and team health — and agreeing what movement in them would trigger a deliberate redesign versus a smaller adjustment. An honest answer commits to a few leading indicators, distinguishes evidence-led change from reorganization theatre, and is clear about who is accountable for inspecting the model and acting when the signals say it is impeding delivery. In practice: a health & care example # An ICS covering five places has each trust building its own patient-facing appointment tools. Costs duplicate, experiences diverge, and none share data cleanly. The ICS redesigns its operating model. It defines three outcomes (reduce did-not-attends, cut avoidable admissions, improve access equity) and the value streams behind them. It stands up a small platform team owning four thinnest-viable capabilities: a shared identity/login, a FHIR -based interoperability layer, common hosting with security and clinical-safety baselines, and a design system. Each place keeps a stream-aligned team but now builds on the platform instead of from scratch. Funding shifts from annual project bids to standing product budgets for each stream, released through discovery/alpha/beta gates. A published RAPID map makes clear that place teams decide their own service design within platform and clinical-safety guardrails, while the ICS digital board decides platform standards. Within a year, three places share one booking capability, the design and safety baseline is consistent, and new features that once took a project cycle ship in weeks — because the platform absorbed the undifferentiated heavy lifting. Sector lenses # An operating model is sized to the organization it serves; the same layers — value streams, capabilities, teams, governance, platform, suppliers — are drawn very differently by a startup, an enterprise, and a government body. Startup # In a small digital-health company the operating model is mostly implicit and that is fine: one or two stream-aligned teams, a founder holding most decision rights, and no platform team because there is nothing yet to platform. The discipline is to make the few real decisions explicit early — build versus buy for the clinical data store, which open standards to commit to — so today's shortcut does not become tomorrow's lock-in. Run and change sit in the same hands, so the risk is that keeping the lights on for early customers starves the roadmap; a simple, honest split of engineering time is the lightweight equivalent of a protected run budget. Suppliers are chosen for speed, but a startup should still refuse core-clinical-data lock-in, because its future NHS buyers will demand exit rights. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home or domiciliary-care provider, a single-site clinic, or a small health-tech supplier past the pre-revenue stage — has real patients and ongoing operations but no platform team, no dedicated digital or IT capability, and little slack in cash or staff. Here the operating model is largely a set of bought capabilities stitched together, so the decisive choices are supplier ones: insisting on open standards and exit rights in the clinical systems you procure, because you carry the same interoperability and clinical-safety duties as a large trust without its buying power or in-house expertise. Run and change collapse onto the same handful of people who also deliver care, so the honest discipline is protecting a little time to keep systems safe and up to date rather than only firefighting. Decision rights are simple — usually a partner or owner-manager decides — but that makes it easy to defer digital decisions indefinitely, so the value is naming the few that matter (which clinical record, which shared regional platform to join) and making them deliberately. Where an ICS or national body offers a shared identity, interoperability, or design platform, the small business's best move is often to build on it rather than reinvent, borrowing the capability it cannot staff itself. Enterprise # An NHS trust or ICS is where the platform-plus-federation shape earns its keep: sovereign organizations that must feel like one service to a patient.

x: Topic 1.2 — Digital Strategy & Roadmapping A digital strategy is a small set of deliberate, defensible choices about where you will invest scarce capacity to improve care — and a roadmap is how you sequence those choices under uncertainty, so that direction survives contact with reality instead of gathering dust as shelfware. Why this matters in health and care # In most sectors a weak digital strategy costs money and momentum. In health and care it also costs safety, equity, and public trust. When there is no shared direction, every trust, place, and team optimizes locally: one buys a booking tool, another builds a portal, a third digitizes a paper form. The estate fragments, data cannot flow across an integrated care system , clinicians juggle a dozen logins, and patients fall through the gaps between systems that were never designed to talk to each other. A strategy is how you convert scattered activity into coherent direction that a board, a clinician, and a citizen can all recognize. The domain makes this harder in three specific ways. First, you are spending public money under intense scrutiny, so your choices must be explicit and defensible, not merely plausible. Second, you inherit a deep, safety-critical legacy system estate that cannot simply be switched off — strategy here is as much about what you keep running safely as about what you build next. Third, the constraint is rarely ambition and almost always capacity: clinical time, engineering capacity, information-governance headroom, and change tolerance in the workforce. A strategy that pretends everything is a priority quietly prioritizes nothing, and in a health setting that means the safety-critical and the equity-critical get starved alongside the merely interesting. The uncomfortable truth is that most digital strategies fail not at the whiteboard but in the gap between the deck and the delivery. A beautifully argued vision that no team can act on next Monday is worse than no strategy at all, because it consumes credibility. This topic treats strategy as a live instrument of direction, tightly coupled to your operating model and your portfolio, rather than a document you refresh once a year and file. Core concepts # Digital strategy versus organizational and clinical strategy. A digital or technology strategy is not a separate thing that sits alongside the organization's clinical and corporate strategy — it is strategic planning applied to how digital, data, and technology will help deliver the organization's actual goals. The test is simple: every material line in your digital strategy should trace to a clinical, operational, or population-health outcome the organization already cares about. If it traces only to a technology aspiration ("move to cloud", "adopt AI"), it is an activity, not a strategy. Vision and target state. A vision statement describes the idealized future you are working towards — what care feels like for a patient, a carer, and a clinician when the strategy has landed. The target state (or target architecture) is the more concrete, testable description of the estate, capabilities, and data flows that vision implies. Vision inspires; target state lets you measure the gap. You need both, and you need them written in language a clinician recognizes, not only in language an architect recognizes. Digital maturity assessment. A maturity model gives you an honest, repeatable read on where you are today across dimensions such as infrastructure, workforce capability, safe practice, and citizen empowerment. Maturity assessment matters because strategy is a vector: it needs a starting point as much as a destination. In the NHS, the What Good Looks Like framework (below) is the most widely used shared reference for this. What Good Looks Like (WGLL). Published by NHS England's Transformation Directorate (originally NHSX) in 2021, WGLL sets out seven success measures for digital transformation across health and care: Well Led, Ensure Smart Foundations, Safe Practice, Support People, Empower Citizens, Improve Care, and Healthy Populations . It is a shared vocabulary and self-assessment framework, not a mandate or a maturity score you are ranked against — its value is giving boards and integrated care systems a common definition of "good" so that local strategies point in a compatible direction. Use it to structure your maturity assessment and to sense-check the breadth of your strategy, but treat it as a lens, not a checklist to game. Who Pays for What. Published alongside WGLL, Who Pays for What describes the funding context: over time, moving away from national teams centrally funding frontline technology and instead allocating digital funding directly to integrated care systems — initially weighted towards "levelling up" less digitally mature systems, then moving towards a fair-shares basis. Accurately understood, it is a direction of travel for where digital money is decided, not a fixed formula, and the balance of central versus local funding has continued to evolve. Its practical implication for your strategy is that you increasingly make and defend your own investment choices locally, which raises the bar on having a defensible strategy in the first place. Roadmap and sequencing. A technology roadmap turns strategy into time-phased intent. The most durable format in fast-moving contexts is now / next / later : what is in delivery now, what is committed next, and what is a direction for later — with confidence and detail deliberately decreasing as you look further out. This is honest about uncertainty in a way that a fully-dated three-year Gantt chart never is. Gap analysis and strategic choices. Gap analysis is the disciplined comparison of current maturity against target state; the gaps become your candidate investments. Strategy is then the act of choosing among them — including the strategic build/buy/partner posture for each major capability, and the equally strategic choice of what to stop or decommission. A Wardley map — plotting capabilities in a value chain against how commoditized they are — is a useful tool here: it helps you see which capabilities are genuinely differentiating (worth building) and which are utilities (worth buying), so build/buy is a reasoned position rather than a habit. Strategy, operating model, and portfolio. Strategy sets direction; the operating model (see Topic 1.1 — The Operating Model) is the machine that delivers it; the portfolio is where money and capacity are actually committed (see Topic 5.3 — EPPM). A strategy that is not wired into portfolio decisions and enterprise architecture has no hands. This wiring is what separates digital transformation that changes care from digital transformation that changes only slide decks. Best practices # Anchor every strategic aim to a clinical, operational, or population outcome. Start from the outcomes the organization already owns — reduce did-not-attends, cut avoidable admissions, close an inequity in access — and derive digital aims from them. Express the aims as measurable objectives (see Topic 10.0 — OKRs & KPIs) so progress is visible. An aim that cannot name the outcome it serves is a candidate for the cutting-room floor. Assess maturity honestly before you set direction. Run a structured maturity assessment using WGLL's seven measures as your frame, and involve clinicians, operational leaders, and information-governance colleagues, not only the digital team. The point is not the score; it is the shared, evidenced picture of where you genuinely stand, which prevents a strategy built on flattering assumptions. Repeat it annually so you can see the vector, not just the position. Write a target state clinicians and citizens can recognize. Describe the future in terms of what changes for the people using and delivering care, then translate that into the target architecture and capabilities. If your target state reads only as a technology diagram, it will not survive a board conversation or earn clinical buy-in. Pair the inspirational vision with a concrete, testable target so the gap is measurable. Sequence with now / next / later, and decrease certainty with distance. Commit in detail to what is in delivery now, hold "next" as a firm but adjustable queue, and keep "later" as direction rather than dates. This format tells the honest truth that the future is less certain than the present, and it lets you re-sequence as evidence arrives without every change looking like a failure to plan. Resist pressure to fully date the whole multi-year horizon; false precision is the enemy of credibility. Make build / buy / partner an explicit strategic posture, capability by capability. For each major capability, decide deliberately whether it is differentiating (build), a commodity (buy), or best delivered with others (partner) — a Wardley map or simple value-chain view makes this defensible rather than habitual. Buy commodities and open-standard platforms; reserve scarce engineering for what genuinely differentiates care in your context. Require open standards and exit rights so a buy decision today does not become lock-in tomorrow (see Topic 4.0 — Technical Architecture, Cloud & Legacy). Wire the strategy into the portfolio and spend control. A strategy only bites when it governs where money and capacity go, so connect it directly to portfolio prioritization and staged funding (see Topic 5.3 — EPPM). Every significant investment should be traceable to a strategic aim, and proposals that trace to nothing should be visibly harder to fund. This is the single most effective defence against strategy-as-shelfware. Prioritize ruthlessly on a constrained estate, and decide what to stop. Capacity, not ambition, is your binding constraint, so an honest strategy names what you will not do and what you will decommission. Protect capacity for running safety-critical systems and for reducing the legacy and technical-debt burden, not only for shiny new builds. A strategy that only adds, never subtracts, will collapse under its own weight. Treat the strategy as a living instrument on a review cadence. Set direction firmly, then review it against evidence on a regular rhythm — quarterly for the roadmap, annually for the strategy itself — rather than treating it as fixed for three years. Base changes on evidence (see Topic 1.3 — Evidence-Driven Decisions), and communicate re-sequencing as learning, not failure. Direction under uncertainty means holding the destination steady while adjusting the route. Questions to discuss with your team # Can we trace every major line of our strategy to an outcome a clinician or citizen would recognize — and where can't we? This question tests the topic's central discipline: that a digital strategy is organizational strategy expressed through technology, not a parallel technology wish-list. It matters in health and care because public money and clinical attention are scarce, and anything that cannot name the care outcome it serves is competing for that scarcity on weak grounds. The honest work is to take your current strategy line by line and ask, for each, "which outcome does this move, and how would we know?" — and to sit with the discomfort when several lines trace only to a technology aspiration like "adopt cloud" or "use AI". Those orphaned lines are not necessarily wrong, but they need either a real outcome attached or a demotion. Watch for the subtler failure too: aims that trace to an outcome on paper but that no one is actually measuring. A good discussion ends with a shorter, clearer strategy in which the survivors each have an owner and a measure. Where are we being dishonest about our current maturity, and what would an outsider using WGLL see that we don't? Strategy is a vector, so a flattering read of the starting point quietly corrupts everything downstream, and teams have every incentive to overstate maturity to leadership and to national bodies. This question invites the team to name the areas — often smart foundations, safe practice, or genuine citizen empowerment — where the gap between the narrative and the reality is widest. It matters because building an ambitious "improve care" or "healthy populations" strategy on shaky foundations is how you end up with clinical-safety incidents and stalled delivery. Ground the conversation in evidence: incident logs, infrastructure age, adoption data, and inequity in who actually uses your digital services. Bring in voices from outside the digital team, because clinicians and operational leaders often see the foundations differently from the people who built them. An honest answer identifies two or three areas where the strategy must first shore up the foundations before it can chase the more exciting aims. What are we choosing not to do, and what are we willing to stop or decommission to make room? The topic argues that capacity, not ambition, is the binding constraint, so a strategy that only adds is not really a strategy at all. This question forces the trade-off into the open: with finite clinical, engineering, and change capacity, every "yes" is a "no" to something else, and pretending otherwise means the safety-critical and equity-critical work gets silently starved by whatever is loudest. It is politically hard, because stopping a project or decommissioning a beloved legacy system has named owners and real feelings attached, whereas starting things wins applause. Make it concrete by listing what would have to be dropped or delayed to fund your top three aims, and by naming at least one system you will actively retire. Discuss how you will protect capacity for running safety-critical services and paying down technical debt, not just for new builds. A mature answer treats "what we will stop" as a first-class part of the strategy, published alongside "what we will start", rather than an awkward footnote. For each major capability, have we made a deliberate build / buy / partner choice — and are we sure today's "buy" will not become tomorrow's lock-in? This question probes the posture the topic treats as strategic rather than technical: deciding, capability by capability, what is differentiating enough to build, what is a commodity to buy, and what is best delivered with others. It matters acutely in health and care because scarce engineering capacity spent re-building a commodity is capacity stolen from the work that genuinely improves care, while an unconsidered purchase can trap safety-critical data behind a proprietary format your successors cannot escape. The honest work is to lay out your major capabilities — the shared record, interoperability, identity, analytics — and name the posture and the reasoning for each, ideally against a value-chain or Wardley view so the choice is defensible rather than habitual. Interrogate every "buy" for exit rights, open standards, and data portability, because lock-in in this sector is measured in decades and paid for in clinician workarounds. Watch for the two symmetrical failures: building by default because the team enjoys it, and buying by default because procurement is easier. A good answer leaves you able to explain, to a board and to a future buyer, why each capability sits where it does. How will we hold direction steady while re-sequencing the roadmap as evidence arrives — and can we do that without every change looking like failure? The topic insists that certainty should decrease with distance and that now / next / later is more honest than a fully-dated multi-year plan, but living that discipline is culturally hard when boards and funders reward the appearance of a fixed plan. This question surfaces the real tension between the credibility that comes from commitment and the credibility that comes from adapting to what you learn. It matters in health and care because the ground genuinely shifts — national policy, funding allocations, clinical priorities and safety incidents all move faster than a three-year Gantt chart can absorb. Discuss the concrete mechanics: what review cadence you hold for the roadmap versus the strategy, what evidence would trigger a re-sequence, and how you will communicate changes as learning rather than as a plan that failed. Name the "later" items you are deliberately refusing to date, and be honest about the pressure to over-commit to keep a stakeholder happy. An honest answer describes a strategy that holds its destination firm while treating the route as revisable, and a team that has rehearsed how it will explain a change of route without losing trust. Does our strategy actively close the digital-access gap, or does it quietly widen it for the people with the greatest need? The topic warns that in health and care a weak strategy costs equity and public trust, not only money, and that the people least likely to use digital services are often those with the greatest clinical need. This question asks whether "empower citizens" is a genuine aim with a measure attached or a slogan that assumes a confident, connected, digitally literate patient. It matters because every channel you digitize can improve access for the many while silently removing it for the few — the housebound, the digitally excluded, those without data, language, or trust — and a strategy that averages these together will look successful while care becomes less fair. Ground the discussion in who actually uses your services today, segmented by deprivation, age, language and disability, and in what non-digital or assisted routes you are committing to preserve. Discuss the trade-off between the efficiency case for "digital by default" and the equity duty to leave no one behind, and who at the board owns that tension. A good answer names inclusion as an explicit strategic aim with its own measure, not a caveat buried in the delivery detail. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system covering four places has no shared digital strategy. Each trust invests independently: one has a modern electronic patient record, another runs on ageing systems held together by heroics, and a community provider still faxes referrals. A citizen moving between services re-tells their story every time, and the ICS board cannot answer a simple question from its region: are we spending digital money where it improves care the most? The new chief digital information officer resists the urge to write a grand three-year plan. Instead, over eight weeks, the team runs a maturity assessment structured around the seven What Good Looks Like measures, involving clinicians and operational leaders in every place. The assessment is deliberately unflattering: smart foundations are weak in two providers, safe practice varies, and "empower citizens" scores low because the people least likely to use digital services are also those with the greatest need. The board sees, for the first time, an evidenced picture rather than four separate optimistic narratives. From the gap analysis, the team frames three strategic aims, each tied to an outcome the board already owns: stabilize safety-critical foundations, give clinicians one shared view of the patient across places, and close the digital-access gap for underserved groups. They set these on a now / next / later roadmap. Now : shore up the weakest infrastructure and stand up a shared interoperability layer. Next : a single sign-on and a shared record view. Later : population-health analytics — held as direction, not dated. For each major capability they take an explicit build/buy/partner posture: buy the commodity infrastructure, partner on interoperability using open standards, and reserve their small engineering capacity for the access-equity work that genuinely differentiates their population's needs. Crucially, the strategy is wired into the portfolio. The ICS agrees that funding — now allocated to the system rather than bid for centrally, in the spirit of Who Pays for What — follows the three aims, and that proposals
