x: Topic 1.7 — Information Governance, Data Protection & Cyber Security In health and care, protecting information is inseparable from delivering care: the same data that saves a life can, if mishandled, break the trust that makes treatment possible — so how you govern, share, and secure it is a clinical, ethical, and public-trust obligation, not a compliance afterthought. Why this matters in health and care # Health and care data is among the most sensitive information a person will ever create. It records diagnoses, medications, mental-health episodes, sexual health, immigration-linked entitlements, and the intimate details of frail and vulnerable lives. People disclose these things to clinicians on an implicit promise: that the information will be used to help them and will not be spread carelessly. When that promise breaks — through a leak, a ransomware outage, or an unexplained data-sharing deal — patients withhold information, opt out of records, or avoid care altogether. That is not an abstract harm; it degrades clinical safety and population health directly. The stakes are also operational. A modern hospital cannot function without its electronic systems: order communications, results, e-prescribing, imaging, and patient administration are all digital. When those systems go down, ambulances divert, operations cancel, and clinicians revert to paper in ways that introduce their own errors. Information governance and cyber security are therefore continuity-of-care disciplines. They belong beside clinical safety ( Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management), not in a separate compliance silo. Finally, there is a genuine and unavoidable tension at the centre of this topic. The public rightly expects the health service to use data to improve care, plan services, and support research that finds tomorrow's treatments. It also expects confidentiality and control. These goals pull against each other, and your job as a leader is not to pretend the tension away but to manage it openly — enabling legitimate use while making the safeguards, and the choices patients have, visible and honest. Get that balance wrong in either direction and you lose: either you starve care and research of data, or you erode the trust the whole system depends on. Core concepts # Underpinning this field is the discipline of information governance — the framework of rules, roles, and controls through which an organization handles information legally, securely, and ethically. In the United Kingdom, the primary legal foundations are the UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR), the domestic version of the EU regulation retained after Brexit, and the Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA 2018), which supplements it. Together they require that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently, and that every processing activity rest on a lawful basis . Health information is special category data , which needs both a lawful basis under Article 6 and an additional condition under Article 9 — for direct care, typically the provision of health or social care by a professional under a duty of confidence. Data protection law is not the only constraint. The common law duty of confidentiality is a separate, older obligation: information given in confidence may not be disclosed without either consent, a legal requirement, or an overriding public interest. You can be fully compliant with UK GDPR and still breach confidentiality, so both must be satisfied. Two health-specific frameworks translate these duties into practice. The Caldicott Principles — a set of principles (now eight) for handling confidential patient information, first set out in the 1997 Caldicott Report — are upheld inside each organization by a Caldicott Guardian , a senior person responsible for protecting patient confidentiality and enabling appropriate information sharing. Nationally, the National Data Guardian for Health and Social Care (NDG) is an independent statutory voice advising on how patient data should be used and safeguarded. The national data opt-out gives patients a mechanism to prevent their confidential information being used for purposes beyond their direct care, such as planning and research, and organizations must honour it. Operationally, a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) is the structured assessment you complete before processing that is likely to be high risk — which most new health data projects are — to identify and mitigate privacy risks. Each organization must appoint a Data Protection Officer (DPO), an independent role responsible for advising on and monitoring compliance. In England, the Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT) is the annual self-assessment through which health and care organizations demonstrate they meet the data-security and information-governance standards required to handle NHS data. On the security side, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) provides authoritative UK guidance and, through its Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF), a structured way to measure cyber resilience. Sound practice rests on well-established fundamentals: defence in depth , layering multiple controls so no single failure is catastrophic; the principle of least privilege , granting people and systems only the access they genuinely need; disciplined patching and tested backups; and preparedness for ransomware , the malware that encrypts systems for extortion. Because prevention alone never holds, mature organizations also invest in operations: a security operations centre (SOC) — a capability, whether in-house or shared, that monitors logs and telemetry to detect and contain intrusions — and a practised incident response process to move quickly from detection to recovery. The 2017 WannaCry ransomware attack , which disrupted around a third of NHS trusts in England and caused an estimated £92 million in impact, remains the defining cautionary example — its damage flowed largely from unpatched systems, not exotic hacking. Best practices # Start every data project with a DPIA, and treat it as design, not paperwork. Before you build or procure anything that processes personal data, work through a Data Protection Impact Assessment with your DPO and Caldicott Guardian. Done early, it shapes the design — minimizing the data collected, choosing pseudonymization, tightening access — rather than rubber-stamping decisions already made. A DPIA parked until go-live is a warning sign that governance is theatre. Name your lawful basis and confidentiality basis explicitly, and write them down. For every flow of health data, state the Article 6 lawful basis, the Article 9 special-category condition, and how the common law duty of confidentiality is satisfied — consent, a statutory gateway, or public interest. Ambiguity here is where projects stall or get pulled after launch. Being explicit also lets you explain the processing to patients in plain language, which is itself a legal requirement. Apply least privilege and role-based access everywhere. Grant clinicians, administrators, researchers, and systems only the access their role requires, and review it regularly as people move and leave. Log access to sensitive records and audit it, because the credible threat of detection deters inappropriate curiosity as much as any technical control. Most real-world breaches are mundane — the wrong person seeing the wrong record — not sophisticated intrusions. Get the cyber fundamentals right before buying advanced tools. The NCSC's guidance is unglamorous and effective: patch promptly, especially internet-facing and clinical systems; enforce multi-factor authentication; segment networks so an infection cannot spread freely; and maintain offline, tested backups. WannaCry spread through unpatched Windows systems, and the lesson endures — basic hygiene prevents the majority of incidents. Spend on fundamentals first; buy sophisticated detection once the basics are solid. Assume you will be attacked, and rehearse your response. Maintain and exercise an incident-response and business-continuity plan that assumes systems will be unavailable, including clinical fallback to paper and a communications plan for staff and patients. Test your backups by actually restoring from them, because a backup you have never restored is a hope, not a control. Run tabletop exercises so that the first time your team handles a ransomware outage is not during a real one. Complete the DSPT honestly and use it as a real assessment. The Data Security and Protection Toolkit is a requirement for handling NHS data, but its value comes from treating it as an honest yearly stocktake rather than a box-ticking ritual. Where you cannot meet a standard, record the gap and a credible improvement plan rather than overstating your position. An inflated DSPT return gives your board false assurance, which is worse than none. Make information sharing a designed capability, not an obstacle. Across an integrated care system (ICS), good care depends on data crossing organizational boundaries between trusts, GP practices, social care, and community providers. Put clear information sharing agreements (ISAs) and data sharing agreements in place, agree the lawful and confidentiality bases jointly, and design shared records so the right professional sees the right information at the point of care. The goal is safe sharing, not no sharing — withholding data that a clinician needs is itself a patient-safety failure. This connects directly to Topic 4.3 — Interoperability & Data Standards. Honour patient choice and be transparent about secondary uses. Respect the national data opt-out in every secondary-use flow, and publish clear, accessible information about how data is used for planning and research. When data is shared with commercial partners or used to train models, disclose it proactively rather than letting it surface through a leak — hidden arrangements have repeatedly triggered public backlash and opt-out surges. Transparency is not a courtesy; it is what keeps the data flowing at all. Manage records across their whole lifecycle. Apply retention schedules based on the NHS Records Management Code of Practice, disposing of records securely when their retention period ends and keeping them accessible and intact while it lasts. Poor records management creates both risk (holding data you no longer need) and harm (losing data clinicians rely on). Migration between systems is a high-risk moment — plan for data quality, mapping, and archiving deliberately. Build governance into procurement and supplier management. Bake data protection and security requirements into contracts: data processing terms, DSPT or equivalent certification, breach-notification timelines, and the right to audit. A supplier's weak security becomes your incident and your headline, so assess the supply chain, not just your own perimeter. Work this jointly with commercial colleagues as covered in Topic 6.3 — Procurement & Commercial, and demand clear answers about where data is hosted and who can access it. Invest in detection, not just prevention. Assume some attacks will get through your defences, and build the capability to see them: centralized logging, monitoring of key systems, and a security operations centre — in-house, shared across an ICS, or drawing on national services such as the NCSC and NHS England's cyber operations — so that suspicious activity is spotted and contained rather than discovered weeks later. Pair this with continuous vulnerability management and threat detection, so you patch the weaknesses attackers actually exploit. Detection buys you the time to contain an incident before it becomes an outage. Treat a serious cyber attack as a clinical-continuity event. Write, resource, and rehearse a cyber incident response plan that names who declares an incident, who leads technical response, and who owns clinical safety and external communications while systems are down. Wire it directly into your business continuity and disaster recovery arrangements (see Topic 3.9 — Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery) and your major-incident and EPRR processes (see Topic 3.10 — Emergency Preparedness, Resilience & Response), so a ransomware outage is handled with the same discipline as any threat to patient care. A plan that lives only in the IT department will fail the moment an attack becomes a clinical crisis. Questions to discuss with your team # Where in our services are we sharing too little, and where are we sharing too much — and how would we even know? Information governance failures run in both directions. Over-sharing shows up as breaches and eroded trust; under-sharing shows up quietly, as a clinician who could not see an allergy, a safeguarding concern that fell between agencies, or a discharge that went wrong because community teams lacked context. Discuss concrete cases from your own setting. Do you have a bias — often defensive — that treats withholding as automatically safe? What signals would tell you a sharing boundary is harming patients, and who is accountable for noticing? A mature team can name examples of both failure modes and has a route to escalate each. If a ransomware attack took our clinical systems offline tomorrow morning, what would actually happen in the first hour? Move past the plan on paper to the lived reality. Who declares the incident, and how do staff find out when email and the intranet may be down? What is the clinical fallback for prescribing, results, and patient identification, and have frontline staff ever practised it? How long can each service run on paper before patient safety degrades, and how do you decide to divert or cancel? When did you last restore from backup to prove it works? The honesty of this conversation — especially the gaps people are reluctant to admit — is a better measure of resilience than any framework score. How would we explain our data uses to a sceptical patient, and would they feel we had been straight with them? Public trust is earned in plain language, not legal notices. Pick a real secondary use of data in your organization — service planning, a research partnership, a supplier arrangement, an AI tool — and try to explain it to an ordinary person: what data, for what purpose, who benefits, what safeguards, and what choice they have. Where does the explanation get uncomfortable or evasive? That discomfort usually marks something you should either change or communicate more openly. Consider how the national data opt-out and your transparency materials would look to someone predisposed to distrust, and connect this to the governance of AI in Topic 8.4 — AI & Emerging Technology Governance. When a supplier or partner holds our patients' data, whose incident is it — and are we sure we could find out in time? Most health and care organizations now depend on a chain of third parties: the EPR vendor, a cloud host, a managed-service provider, a pathology or imaging partner. A breach or outage anywhere in that chain becomes your clinical crisis and your headline, yet the contract, the certification, and the breach-notification clock often get far less scrutiny than your own perimeter. Discuss what you actually know about where your data is hosted, who can access it, and how quickly a supplier is contractually bound to tell you when something goes wrong. Have you ever tested that notification path, or seen a supplier's DSPT or equivalent assurance rather than taken it on trust? What happens if a critical supplier is themselves hit by ransomware on a Friday night? An honest answer names the suppliers you cannot currently hold to account and connects this to Topic 6.3 — Procurement & Commercial. Who genuinely owns information-governance risk here — and would they hear about a problem before it became a crisis? On paper, a DPO and a Caldicott Guardian own confidentiality and data-protection risk, and the board owns cyber resilience. In practice these roles are often under-resourced, consulted late, or treated as a sign-off rather than a voice, so risks are neither surfaced nor escalated until they surface as incidents. Talk honestly about whether your Caldicott Guardian and DPO are actually pulled into decisions early, whether they can say no and be heard, and whether cyber risk reaches the board as something they understand and own rather than a technical report they nod through. Would a frontline clinician who spotted inappropriate access, or an engineer who found an unpatched critical system, know how to raise it and trust that something would happen? The test of ownership is not the org chart but whether uncomfortable news travels upward quickly, and this links to the safety culture discussed in Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management. How do we decide what data to keep, what to delete, and who still needs access — and when did we last actually do it? Governance attention concentrates on collecting and sharing data, but retention, disposal, and access review are where quiet risk accumulates: records held long past their lawful retention period, dormant accounts that still open live systems, and access rights that followed people as they changed roles but were never taken away. Every record you no longer need is liability you are storing, and every stale credential is a route in for an attacker or a curious insider. Discuss whether your retention schedules follow the NHS Records Management Code of Practice in reality or only in policy, when access rights were last reviewed and pruned, and how you handle the high-risk moment of migrating or decommissioning a system. Who is accountable for pressing delete, and is anyone measured on it? An honest answer usually reveals an accumulation of data and access that no one has owned for years. In practice: a health & care example # Meadowford Integrated Care System is standing up a shared care record so that hospital clinicians, GPs, community nurses, and social workers can see a unified view of each person. The programme is popular with clinicians and politically visible, and the temptation is to move fast. The programme director insists on sequencing governance alongside build rather than behind it. A DPIA is opened at the outset, led jointly by the DPO and the lead Caldicott Guardian drawn from the partner organizations. It forces early, useful decisions: the record will show a curated clinical summary rather than every historical document; social care records with third-party information will be handled under tighter rules; and access will be role-based, with a legitimate-relationship check so a professional can only open a record for someone in their care. Every access is logged and audited, and staff are told so plainly. The partners agree a single information sharing agreement covering the common law duty of confidentiality and the lawful bases — direct care under Article 6(1)(e) and Article 9(2)(h) — and they confirm the shared record is used only for direct care, so the national data opt-out does not restrict it. When a separate proposal arrives to use the same data for population-health analytics, the team treats it as a distinct flow with its own DPIA, its own lawful basis, opt-out compliance, and public communications, rather than quietly extending the existing agreement. Six weeks before go-live, the security lead runs a tabletop ransomware exercise. It exposes that the shared record has no clinical fallback if it becomes unavailable and that backups have never been test-restored. Go-live slips by a month while the team adds an offline read-only copy refreshed nightly, proves the restore works, and briefs frontline staff on paper fallback. The delay is unpopular, but when a supplier patching error takes the main system offline for a morning three months later, care continues on the fallback and no appointments are lost. The programme's credibility — and clinicians' trust in the record — survives intact. The trade-off was

x: Topic 1.8 — Data Ethics, Consent & Public Trust In health and care, the law tells you what you can do with data, but public trust depends on whether you should — and once people believe their information is being used behind their backs, they withhold it, opt out, or avoid care, so ethics and honest engagement are not soft extras but the conditions under which data can be used at all. Why this matters in health and care # Topic 1.7 — Information Governance, Data Protection & Cyber Security covers the law and the technical controls: lawful bases, the UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR), the Data Security and Protection Toolkit, encryption, and access control. This topic is about everything that remains once you are legally compliant. You can satisfy every statute and still lose the public's trust, because trust is not granted by lawyers — it is granted by patients and citizens who decide, individually and collectively, whether they believe you are handling their information in a way they would recognize as fair. That distinction matters more in health and care than almost anywhere else. People disclose things to clinicians — mental-health crises, substance use, sexual health, abuse, immigration-linked entitlements — on an unspoken understanding that the information exists to help them, not to be traded, published, or repurposed without their knowledge. When that understanding breaks, the harm is measurable: patients lie to clinicians, decline to share history, or stay away from services. Those are clinical-safety and equity failures, and they land hardest on the people who already trust institutions least. The system also depends, genuinely, on using data beyond the single consultation — to plan services, run population health management, detect safety signals, and support the research that produces tomorrow's treatments. So you sit inside a permanent tension: withhold data and you starve care and research; use it carelessly and you forfeit the consent of the public whose data it is. This topic is about holding that tension honestly. The recent history of the health service contains at least one large, expensive lesson in what happens when an organization answers only the legal question and never the ethical one. Core concepts # The governing discipline here is data ethics — the systematic study of right and wrong conduct in the collection, use, and sharing of data, especially personal data. Its central move is to separate two questions that organizations routinely conflate: can we do this lawfully, and should we do this given what people reasonably expect and what harms might follow. A lawful basis answers the first. Only deliberate ethical reasoning, transparency, and engagement answer the second. Consent is more layered than everyday usage suggests. Informed consent — a person agreeing to something with adequate understanding of what it involves — is the gold standard for direct care and most research. But at population scale, individual explicit consent is often impractical or would itself bias the data, so the system relies on other models: implied consent for direct care (you accept that the clinician treating you will read your record), and opt-out models for some secondary uses, where data is used unless a person actively objects. In England the principal instrument is the NHS national data opt-out , which lets a person prevent their confidential patient information being used for planning and research beyond their own care. Knowing which model applies, and being honest that opt-out is not the same as active consent, is a core competence. Alongside data-protection law sits an older and separate obligation: the common law duty of confidentiality , under which information shared in confidence may not be disclosed without consent, a legal requirement, or an overriding public interest. From it flows the reasonable expectations or "no surprises" principle: you should not use someone's data in a way that would genuinely surprise them if they found out. This is a practical ethical test that often bites well before the law does. Two health-specific institutions carry the ethical load. The Caldicott principles — upheld in each organization by a Caldicott Guardian — famously insist that the duty to share information can be as important as the duty to protect it , correcting the reflex that treats withholding as automatically safe. Nationally, the National Data Guardian for Health and Social Care (NDG) is the independent statutory voice on how patient data should be used and safeguarded. Around these sits the idea of a social licence : the ongoing, informal acceptance from the public that legitimizes how an institution uses data — earned through transparency and engagement, not granted by statute, and quickly withdrawn when trust is broken. For secondary uses — analytics, planning, and research rather than direct care — the technical bridge between usefulness and privacy is de-identification : reducing the identifiability of data through pseudonymisation (replacing identifiers with artificial tokens, reversible with separately held keys) or anonymisation (removing identifiers so a person can no longer be identified). Both have limits: rich health data can often be re-identified by linking it with other datasets — the "mosaic effect" — so "anonymized" is a claim to be tested, not assumed. Finally, where data drives automated or model-based decisions, you inherit questions of algorithmic bias — systematic unfairness that disadvantages some groups — and algorithmic accountability , the allocation of responsibility for those outcomes. The deep governance of AI belongs to Topic 8.4 — AI & Emerging Technology Governance; here it matters only as one more use of data that must earn public trust. Best practices # Ask "should we?" as a distinct, minuted decision — not a footnote to "can we?". For any non-obvious use of data, run the ethical question separately from the legal one and record the answer. Name who benefits, who might be harmed, what people would reasonably expect, and whether you would be comfortable explaining the use on the front page of a newspaper. A use that is lawful but fails the reasonable-expectations test is a use to redesign or explain openly, not to proceed with quietly. Match the consent model to the use, and be honest about which one you are using. Direct care runs on implied consent; most research needs explicit informed consent or an approved legal route; some planning uses rely on the opt-out. Do not dress an opt-out up as if it were active agreement, and do not lean on "consent" language when the real basis is a statutory power. Clarity here protects both the patient's autonomy and your own credibility when the arrangement is scrutinized. Honour the national data opt-out reliably, and treat it as a floor, not a ceiling. Apply the NHS national data opt-out to every secondary-use flow it covers, and be able to demonstrate that you do. But recognize that legal compliance with the opt-out is the minimum; a use that technically respects opt-outs while blindsiding the public will still cost you trust. Where a use is novel or sensitive, consider going beyond the baseline with clearer notice or a more active choice. Apply the reasonable-expectations test before every new data flow. Ask plainly: if the people whose data this is knew exactly what we were doing, would they be surprised, and would they feel misled? Surprise is an early-warning signal that arrives long before a legal breach. When the honest answer is "yes, they would be surprised", you have three choices — change the use, obtain meaningful consent, or explain it so thoroughly and so early that it stops being a surprise. Remember that the duty to share can be as vital as the duty to protect. The Caldicott principles exist partly to counter defensive over-caution, which quietly harms patients when a clinician cannot see an allergy, a safeguarding concern falls between agencies, or a discharge fails for want of context. Ethical data handling is not the same as data hoarding. Weigh the harm of not sharing as deliberately as the harm of sharing, and connect this to the safe-sharing design in Topic 1.7 — Information Governance, Data Protection & Cyber Security and the safety consequences in Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management. Treat de-identification as risk reduction, not a magic eraser. Pseudonymize or anonymize secondary-use data, but assess re-identification risk realistically, especially for rare conditions, small populations, or richly linked datasets where the mosaic effect bites. Control the environment as well as the data: prefer accredited Secure Data Environments, where analysts work on data that never leaves a governed setting, over shipping "anonymized" extracts out of the building. Document the residual risk and who accepts it. Run an ethics review for uses that law alone does not settle. Establish a route — a data ethics committee, an existing research ethics process, or a standing function — to scrutinize novel, sensitive, or commercially entangled uses before they proceed. Give it independent and lay membership so it is not merely the organization reassuring itself, and require it to consider fairness and differential impact on groups, not only privacy. Make transparency proactive, specific, and human-readable. Publish, in plain language, what data you hold, what you use it for, who you share it with (including commercial partners), and what choices people have. A dense privacy notice written for regulators is not transparency; a clear public register of data uses is. Disclose new or commercial arrangements before they start, because a use that surfaces through a journalist's leak is read as a cover-up regardless of its merits. Involve patients and communities in decisions about their data — early and for real. Public and patient engagement is not a communications exercise bolted on at launch; it shapes what you build and whether it earns a social licence. Bring patients, carers, and community representatives — especially from groups with good historical reason to distrust institutions — into design and governance, and show how their input changed decisions. This connects directly to Topic 3.0 — User Research & Service Design and to Topic 8.2 — Communications & Engagement. Own fairness and accountability when data drives decisions. Where data feeds risk scores, prioritization tools, or models, ask whose data trained them, which groups may be under-represented, and who is answerable when the output is wrong or discriminatory. Keep a human in the loop for consequential decisions and monitor outcomes across demographic groups over time. Hand the detailed model governance to Topic 8.4 — AI & Emerging Technology Governance, but do not treat "the algorithm decided" as an escape from responsibility. Questions to discuss with your team # For our most sensitive or novel data use, what is the honest gap between what is legally permitted and what our patients would actually expect — and how would we close it? This is the core question of the topic, so make it concrete rather than abstract: pick a real use in your organization — a research partnership, a supplier arrangement, a population-health dashboard, a model. Walk through what the law permits, then ask separately what an ordinary, moderately sceptical patient would assume was happening, and name the gap between the two. The gap is where trust is won or lost, and it is invisible if you only ever ask the legal question. A good discussion surfaces at least one use where the team is relying on "it's lawful" to avoid a harder conversation, and produces a decision to either change the use, seek meaningful consent, or explain it far more openly. Watch for the tell-tale defence "but we're allowed to" — it usually means the ethical question has never been asked. Where are we harming patients by not sharing data, and are we as honest about that harm as we are about the risk of a breach? Data ethics is routinely mistaken for data minimization, and defensive over-caution wears the costume of safety while doing real damage. Discuss concrete cases from your own setting: a missed allergy, a safeguarding concern that fell between agencies, a discharge that went wrong because community teams lacked context, a researcher blocked from data that could have found a safety signal. The Caldicott principle that the duty to share can be as important as the duty to protect exists precisely because organizations find withholding psychologically safer, even when it is not actually safer for the patient. A mature team can name failures in both directions and has a route to escalate each, rather than treating "no" as the risk-free default. Consider, too, whether your incentives reward the person who refuses to share far more than the one who shares appropriately. If a national newspaper reported one of our data-sharing arrangements tomorrow — accurately but unsympathetically — would we survive it, and what does the answer tell us to fix now? The care.data programme was not brought down by illegality; it was brought down by the public feeling that something was being done to them without a real explanation or a real choice. Run the test against your own arrangements, especially any involving commercial partners, model training, or secondary uses that patients have not been told about clearly. Where does the story get uncomfortable — is it the partner, the lack of an opt-out, the vagueness of the public notice, the absence of any community involvement? That discomfort is a precise map of where your social licence is thin. A good answer is not "we'd manage the press"; it is a list of things you will make more transparent, more consented, or simply stop doing, and it connects to the engagement discipline in Topic 8.2 — Communications & Engagement. When we call data "anonymized", how confident are we that it could not be re-linked to a person — and who has actually tested that claim? De-identification is treated as a finish line far more often than it deserves, and "anonymized" is frequently asserted rather than assessed. Pick a real secondary-use dataset and ask precisely what was done to it — pseudonymization with a separately held key, or genuine anonymization — and then ask how it would fare against the mosaic effect if someone linked it to other data, especially for rare conditions, small populations, or richly detailed records. Ask, too, where the data physically lives: is it analysed inside an accredited Secure Data Environment that never lets it leave, or shipped out as an extract on the assumption that the label makes it safe? An honest discussion names the residual re-identification risk explicitly, records who has accepted that risk, and distinguishes what has been tested from what has merely been hoped. If no one in the room can say who last stress-tested the claim, that absence is the finding. Where data feeds a risk score, a prioritization tool, or a model, whose data trained it, who might it disadvantage, and who answers when it is wrong? Fairness is easy to endorse in principle and easy to neglect in practice, because bias hides in data that looks complete but under-represents exactly the groups who already fare worst. Take a concrete example — an admissions-risk model, a triage tool, a caseload-prioritization score — and ask which populations are thin in the training data, how a wrongly flagged or wrongly overlooked person would be affected, and whether anyone monitors outcomes across ethnicity and deprivation over time rather than only at launch. Press on accountability: when the output is challenged, is there a named human who owns the decision, or does "the algorithm decided" quietly absorb the responsibility? The deep model governance belongs to Topic 8.4 — AI & Emerging Technology Governance, but the ethical ownership sits here. A mature answer pairs a specific fairness-monitoring commitment with a clear line of accountability, not a reassurance that the maths is neutral. How do we involve the people whose data this is — particularly the communities with the best reason to distrust us — and can we point to a decision their involvement actually changed? Engagement is the part most easily reduced to decoration: a consultation held after the design is fixed, or a panel drawn only from people who already trust the institution. The harder and more valuable question is whether patients, carers, and community representatives — especially from groups historically let down by the health service — are in the room early enough to alter what gets built, and whether you can name a concrete change that resulted. Discuss who you are not hearing from and why, and whether your engagement reaches the seldom-heard or simply reconfirms the comfortable. This connects to Topic 3.0 — User Research & Service Design and Topic 8.2 — Communications & Engagement. An honest answer distinguishes genuine co-design that shifted a decision from a communications exercise that merely announced one, and is candid about which of the two you are currently doing. In practice: a health & care example # Riverbourne Integrated Care System wants to use linked patient data to reduce emergency admissions among people with multiple long-term conditions. The analytics team has a strong case: bring hospital, GP, community, and social-care data together, build a risk model, and offer proactive support to the people most likely to deteriorate. Legally, the route is workable. The programme director, however, remembers care.data, and insists the ethical and trust questions are answered before a line of the model is built. The team separates the two questions deliberately. Can we? is handled with the Data Protection Officer and Caldicott Guardian: a lawful basis, a Data Protection Impact Assessment, and confirmation that the national data opt-out applies to this secondary use. Should we? goes to a newly convened data ethics group with independent and lay members, including two patient representatives from communities with historically low trust in the health service. The group asks harder questions than the lawyers did: who might a risk score disadvantage, what happens to someone wrongly flagged, and would patients be surprised to learn their social-care data was feeding a hospital model? Those questions change the design. The analysis runs inside an accredited Secure Data Environment, so analysts work only on pseudonymized records that never leave the governed setting. The model's outputs are reviewed by a clinician before anyone is contacted, not acted on automatically. The team commits to monitoring whether the model performs equally well across ethnic groups and deprivation levels, having found that under-representation in the training data could otherwise entrench inequity. And the ICS publishes a plain-language description — what data, what purpose, who benefits, what safeguards, and how to opt out — before the programme starts, rather than waiting to be asked. When a local journalist does ask, months later, the story is uneventful: the arrangement is already public, the opt-out is honoured, patients helped shape it, and the safeguards are real. Opt-out rates barely move. The programme reduces admissions modestly in its first year, but the more durable win is that Riverbourne can now propose its next data initiative from a position of trust rather than suspicion. The trade-off was explicit: engagement and ethics review added three months and some awkward redesign, and bought a social licence that a faster, quieter launch would have gambled away. x: Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility In health and care, a digital service that excludes some people is not a neutral technical choice — it withholds care from those who often need it most, so inclusion and accessibility are matters of clinical safety, equity, and public trust, not optional polish. Why this matters in health and care # In most sectors, an inaccessible website loses a sale. In health and care, it can mean a person misses a screening invitation, cannot book an urgent appointment, cannot understand their discharge instructions, or cannot see the medication warning that would have kept them safe. Digital exclusion here is not an inconvenience; it is a route to harm and to widening inequality, delivered with public money under statutory duty. The people most likely to be digitally excluded — older people, disabled people, people in poverty, people with low literacy, people whose first language is not English, people in areas with poor connectivity — are very often the same people who carry the greatest burden of ill health. This is the uncomfortable core of the topic: digital exclusion maps almost exactly onto health inequality. When you digitize a service without a plan for those who cannot use the digital route, you can actively move resource and attention towards those already best served, and call it progress — the "inverse care law" in a new medium. Accessibility is also a legal duty, not a nicety. Public sector bodies in the United Kingdom must meet accessibility standards in law, and health and care organizations carry additional statutory obligations to meet the communication needs of disabled patients and carers. Access to digital services is itself increasingly a wider determinant of health — connectivity, a device, and the confidence to use them now shape whether a person can reach care at all. Treating inclusion as a bolt-on is how organizations end up in breach of the law, of trust, and of their own equity commitments. Inclusion and accessibility must be designed in from the first discovery conversation (see Topic 3.4 — Discovery Phases) and measured as a first-class outcome (see Topic 10.0 — Objectives & Key Results (OKRs)). Core concepts # The digital divide and digital exclusion. The digital divide is the gap between those who can access and use digital technology and those who cannot. Digital exclusion is usually driven by five interacting factors: access (a device and a reliable connection), affordability (data and hardware cost money), skills (the confidence and ability to use digital tools), motivation and trust (believing digital is safe and worthwhile), and design (whether the service is usable at all). A person is rarely excluded by one factor alone; an older person on a low income in a rural area with poor broadband faces several at once, which is why simplistic fixes fail. Who is excluded, and the equity link. Exclusion clusters by age, disability, income and poverty, literacy, language, and connectivity. Because these same characteristics predict poorer health, digital exclusion compounds existing health equity gaps. The mental shift required is to stop treating "digital access" as a background utility and start treating it as one of the social determinants of health — a factor that shapes health outcomes as surely as housing or income. Core20PLUS5. NHS England's Core20PLUS5 is a national framework for reducing health inequalities. It focuses effort on the most deprived 20% of the population (the "Core20"), plus locally identified inclusion groups experiencing poorer access or outcomes (the "PLUS"), and five clinical areas of particular focus. It gives you a ready-made lens for asking who is your service failing , and a shared vocabulary with clinical and public-health colleagues for targeting inclusion work where the inequality is greatest. Web accessibility and WCAG 2.2. Web accessibility is the practice of removing barriers that stop disabled people using digital services. The recognized technical standard is the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), currently version 2.2, organized around four principles — content must be perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust — at three conformance levels, A, AA, and AAA. UK public sector services are expected to meet WCAG 2.2 level AA. The Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations 2018. The Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) (No. 2) Accessibility Regulations 2018 make WCAG conformance a legal requirement for most public sector websites and apps, and require a published, accurate accessibility statement. This sits alongside the Equality Act 2010 duty to make reasonable adjustments. Accessibility is a compliance floor with legal consequence, not an aspiration. The Accessible Information Standard. The NHS Accessible Information Standard (data standard reference DCB1605) is a mandatory standard requiring health and adult social care providers to identify, record, flag, share, and meet the information and communication needs of patients, service users, and carers with a disability, impairment, or sensory loss — for example, providing information in easy-read, braille, large print, or via a British Sign Language interpreter. It is a statutory duty, not guidance. Inclusive design and universal design . Universal design aims to make products usable by as many people as possible without adaptation; inclusive design is the process of deliberately designing with and for people who are usually excluded, on the principle that solving for the edges improves the service for everyone — the "curb-cut effect". Assistive technology . Assistive technologies — screen readers, magnifiers, voice input, switch access, alternative keyboards — are how many disabled people use digital services. Accessible design is what lets these technologies work; an inaccessible interface silently breaks them. Assisted digital and offline routes. "Assisted digital" describes support for people who cannot use a digital service independently — by phone, in person, through a trained helper, or via an intermediary. Offline and analogue routes (post, telephone, face-to-face) are not legacy debt to be switched off; for some people they are the only safe route to care. Treat them as first-class channels with their own service levels. Plain language , readability , and health literacy . Plain language is writing that a reader can understand the first time they read it. Readability is measurable — reading-age formulas estimate how hard text is. Health literacy is a person's ability to find, understand, and use health information; a large share of adults find standard health materials too complex, so clear content is a safety intervention, not a stylistic one. Best practices # Design for inclusion from discovery, never as a retrofit. Bring accessibility and inclusion into the first discovery conversations, user research, and design decisions (see Topic 3.0 — User Research & Service Design and Topic 3.4 — Discovery Phases). Retrofitting accessibility onto a finished product is more expensive, less effective, and often impossible without rebuilding. Make "who might this exclude?" a standing question at every design review. Meet WCAG 2.2 level AA as a floor, and test with real assistive technology. Treat WCAG 2.2 AA conformance as the minimum, not the target, and verify it with automated tools and manual testing using screen readers, keyboard-only navigation, and magnification. Automated checkers catch perhaps a third of issues; the rest need human testing, ideally including disabled users. Publish an honest, specific accessibility statement and keep it current, as the regulations require. Meet the Accessible Information Standard as an operational reality, not a policy on a shelf. Ensure your systems can capture a person's communication needs, flag them, share them across settings, and actually deliver information in the required format — easy-read, large print, braille, BSL. This is a legal duty and a safety issue: a deaf patient who cannot understand appointment changes, or a person with a learning disability given only dense text, is a patient at risk. Make assisted digital and offline routes first-class channels. Resource, monitor, and improve the telephone, in-person, and paper routes with the same seriousness as the app. Never decommission an analogue route until you have evidence that everyone who relied on it has a genuine, tested alternative. "Digital by default" must never become "digital only" in a service where exclusion means missed care. Write in plain language and test readability. Aim health and care content at a reading age around 9 to 11 years, use short sentences and common words, expand or avoid jargon, and structure content so the most important information comes first. Test with readability tools and, better, with people who have low literacy or English as an additional language. Offer easy-read and translated versions where your population needs them. Use Core20PLUS5 to target inclusion effort where inequality is greatest. Rather than spreading inclusion work thinly, use Core20PLUS5 and local population data to identify who your service is failing and concentrate improvement there. This connects your digital delivery to the organization's health-inequalities strategy and gives clinical and public-health colleagues a shared frame for prioritization. Design with excluded people, not just for them. Recruit research and testing participants who are older, disabled, digitally unconfident, on low incomes, or speak other languages — the people usually absent from convenience samples — and pay them properly. Co-design and lived-experience input surface barriers no checklist predicts, and build the empathy that sustains inclusion work under delivery pressure. Measure inclusion, not just averages. Headline metrics hide exclusion: a service used successfully by most people can be quietly failing exactly the groups most in need. Segment your data by the characteristics that predict exclusion, track completion and drop-off for each, and watch the gap between groups, not just the mean (see Topic 1.3 — Evidence-Driven Decisions and Topic 10.0 — Objectives & Key Results (OKRs)). Questions to discuss with your team # Who does our service currently exclude — and have we actually looked, or are we reassured by an average? This question forces the team past comfortable headline figures to the distribution underneath them. In health and care it matters acutely because the people a digital service is most likely to shut out — older, disabled, poorer, less literate, non-English-speaking, poorly connected — are disproportionately those with the greatest health needs, so exclusion and inequality reinforce each other. The tension to surface is that segmenting your data may reveal an uncomfortable truth that a strong overall completion rate was hiding, and that fixing it costs money and slows the roadmap. Look concretely at drop-off rates by age band, by device, by whether an assisted route was used, and by any inclusion groups your organization tracks under Core20PLUS5. Consider whether you even collect the data needed to see exclusion, or whether your analytics are blind to it by design. A good, honest answer names specific groups the service is failing, admits where you lack the data to know, and commits to measuring the gap between groups rather than celebrating the mean. Are our non-digital routes genuinely first-class, or are we quietly starving them so we can declare a digital success? Digital transformation programmes are often incentivized on digital uptake, which creates a subtle pressure to let telephone, paper, and face-to-face routes wither — or to close them before a safe alternative exists. This matters because for some patients the analogue route is not a preference but the only safe way to reach care, and withdrawing it can cause real harm while the dashboard shows progress. Debate the honest trade-off: maintaining multiple channels costs money and effort, and there is legitimate value in moving willing users to efficient digital routes, but "digital by default" must never slide into "digital only". Look at whether your offline routes have proper service levels, funding, and monitoring, or whether they are treated as legacy debt. Examine what evidence you would need before decommissioning any route, and whether you have it. A strong answer treats assisted-digital and offline channels as first-class services with owners and standards, and sets an explicit, evidence-based bar that must be cleared before any route is closed. When we say we meet our accessibility and Accessible Information Standard duties, is that a tested reality or a statement of intent? Many organizations have an accessibility statement and a policy referencing the Accessible Information Standard, yet fail in practice — the screen reader breaks on the booking flow, or the deaf patient still gets an unreadable letter. This question matters because these are legal duties with real consequences, and because the gap between paper compliance and lived experience is where patients actually get harmed. The tension is that genuine assurance requires manual testing with assistive technology and disabled users, capturing and acting on recorded communication needs across systems, and ongoing effort — all harder than publishing a statement once. Probe specifics: when did a real screen-reader user last complete your core journey; can your systems flag and share a communication need from one setting to another; who is accountable when an easy-read version does not exist. Consider that automated accessibility tools miss most issues, so a green automated report proves little. A good answer distinguishes clearly between what has been tested with real users and assistive technology and what is merely asserted, and owns the gaps with a plan and an accountable owner rather than a reassuring form of words. Do we design and test with excluded people, or only for them — and are we willing to pay for that involvement? It is easy to build an idea of the excluded user from personas, assumptions, and checklists, and much harder to put a screen-reader user, a person with a learning disability, or someone with English as an additional language in the room and act on what they show you. This matters because lived experience surfaces barriers no automated tool or well-meaning designer predicts, and because inclusion work loses momentum under delivery pressure unless the team has met the people it affects. The tension is practical: recruiting excluded participants takes longer, costs more, requires paying people properly for their time, and sometimes returns findings that force an uncomfortable rework late in a sprint. Probe whether your research samples reach beyond the confident, able, connected users who are easiest to find, and whether procurement and delivery timelines leave room for genuine co-design rather than a token consultation. Consider who holds the budget for participant payment and whether "no budget" is quietly excluding the very people you most need to hear. An honest answer shows excluded people shaping decisions, not merely validating them, and treats their involvement as a funded, recurring practice rather than a one-off exercise. How will digitizing this service change the equity picture — could we widen the gap even as the headline improves? Digitizing a service redistributes effort, attention, and convenience, and it rarely does so neutrally: the people quickest to adopt a new digital route are often those already best served, so a service can improve on average while the most excluded fall further behind. This is the "inverse care law" playing out in a new medium, and in health and care it maps almost exactly onto existing health inequality, which is why it deserves explicit scrutiny rather than optimistic assumption. The trade-off to name is that the efficiencies and savings that justify a digital programme are real, but banking them can mean withdrawing resource from the slower, costlier routes that keep the most excluded connected to care. Look concretely at your population through Core20PLUS5 and local data: which cohorts carry the highest need, how do they currently reach the service, and what happens to them under the new design. Ask whether your success measure is "more people use digital" or "no group is worse off and the most excluded improve" — the two can point in opposite directions. A good answer sets equity as an explicit design goal from the outset, models the effect on the most excluded before build, and commits to monitoring the gap after go-live rather than assuming digitization lifts everyone. When digital and non-digital budgets compete, how do we decide — and who is accountable for the people a cut would exclude? Inclusion is ultimately a resourcing decision, and it is usually made implicitly, through where money and management attention flow rather than through an explicit, owned choice. This matters because the assisted-digital and offline routes that protect the most excluded are the easiest line to trim when budgets tighten, and their users are often those least able to complain loudly or visibly. The real tension is that every pound spent maintaining a telephone or paper route is a pound not spent on new digital capability, and the savings case for a programme frequently depends on eventually reducing those routes — so the pressure to cut is structural, not accidental. Examine whether inclusion has a named senior owner with actual budget authority, whether inclusion metrics reach the board alongside financial and clinical ones, and whether anyone is formally accountable when a cut re-excludes a group the organization is statutorily committed to reaching. Consider how a proposed saving would be scrutinized: is there an equity impact assessment, or does the number simply get banked. An honest answer places accountability for the excluded with a specific, senior person, makes the trade-off visible at the level where money is allocated, and refuses to treat inclusion funding as a discretionary extra to be raided when times are hard. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system (ICS) is rolling out a new online route for patients to book and manage outpatient appointments, aiming to cut the volume of phone calls to booking teams and reduce missed appointments. The first business case is framed entirely around digital uptake and call-centre savings. The digital inclusion lead intervenes early, during discovery. She maps the outpatient population against Core20PLUS5 and finds that a large share of the highest-need patients are older, live in the most deprived neighbourhoods, or have a recorded communication need under the Accessible Information Standard. She reframes the success measure: not "percentage of bookings made online" but "no group is worse off than before, and the most excluded groups improve." User research deliberately recruits older patients, a blind man who uses a screen reader, a woman with a learning disability, and a family who speak Sylheti at home, paying them for their time. The research is sobering. The prototype booking flow breaks under keyboard-only navigation; the confirmation letter is written at a reading age far above most patients; there is no route at all for someone who cannot use the app. The team fixes the flow to meet WCAG 2.2 level AA, verified by manual testing with the same assistive technology real patients use. Content designers rewrite letters in plain language, tested for readability and available in easy-read and translated versions, with communication-need flags carried through from the shared record. x: Topic 1.10 — Safeguarding in Digital Services In health and care, a digital service that reveals where a woman lives, lets a controlling partner read her messages, or gives an abuser access to a child's record has caused harm as real as a clinical error — so safeguarding must be designed in, not bolted on. Why this matters in health and care # Safeguarding is the set of statutory duties to protect children and adults at risk from abuse, harm and neglect. In England these duties flow from the Children Act 2004, the Care Act 2014 and multi-agency guidance such as Working Together to Safeguard Children . They are not optional add-ons to a digital programme; they are legal obligations that follow your service wherever it touches a vulnerable person. Digital services change the safeguarding picture in two directions at once. They create new opportunities — a young person may disclose self-harm through a messaging channel they would never raise face-to-face, and a shared record can surface a pattern of missed appointments that flags neglect. They also create new risks. An appointment reminder text, a repeat-prescription notification, or a proxy-access grant can leak a person's location, diagnosis or whereabouts to exactly the person they are hiding from. The people most exposed to these risks are often the same people who are hardest to reach. Victims of domestic abuse, children in care, adults who lack capacity, and people experiencing coercion tend to have less control over their own devices, accounts and post. When you design a patient app or a shared care record, you are quietly making decisions about who can see what — and for someone living with an abuser, that decision can be a matter of physical safety. This is why safeguarding sits alongside clinical safety (see Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management) and information governance (see Topic 1.7 — Information Governance, Data Protection & Cyber Security) as a core condition of a service being safe to run at all. Core concepts # Safeguarding is the umbrella term for protecting people's health, wellbeing and human rights so they live free from abuse, harm and neglect. It splits into two related but distinct regimes: child protection for anyone under 18, and adult safeguarding for adults with care and support needs who cannot protect themselves — the latter grounded in the Care Act 2014 . Both operate through multi-agency working : health, social care, police, education and the voluntary sector share information and act together, because no single organization sees the whole picture. The Mental Capacity Act 2005 governs decisions made for adults who lack the capacity to make a particular decision themselves. It matters intensely for digital access: capacity is decision-specific and can fluctuate, so "granting a carer full access to the app" is rarely a single, permanent choice. Proxy and delegated access — a parent acting for a young child, a carer for an older adult, an attorney under a lasting power of attorney — must be justified, proportionate, and reviewed, especially as a child approaches the age at which they gain their own confidentiality rights. Several forms of harm are amplified by digital design. Domestic violence and controlling behaviour in relationships — coercive control — turn ordinary features into weapons: a shared login becomes surveillance, a location-revealing notification becomes a tracking beacon. Stalking exploits any data point that discloses routine or whereabouts. "Safeguarding by design" is the discipline of anticipating these harms and building in the ability to hide, redact, suppress or delay information for people at risk. Two more concepts complete the picture. Authentication and identity verification determine whether the person accessing a service is who they claim to be — the front line against impersonation, and the mechanism through which a strong digital identity either protects or endangers. Where a service hosts peer support, forums or messaging, content moderation and the duties under the Online Safety Act 2023 govern how you keep people safe from harmful content and from each other. Best practices # Treat safeguarding as a design requirement, not a policy document. Write safeguarding scenarios into your discovery and user research from the first sprint, alongside clinical and accessibility needs (see Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility). Ask, for every feature that shows or sends information: "What if the wrong person sees this?" A safeguarding-by-design review should be a named gate in your delivery lifecycle, with a clinician or safeguarding lead signing it off, not a box ticked at go-live. Make sensitive data hideable, suppressible and redactable by default capability. Every notification, reminder, letter and shared-record view should have a documented way to be suppressed, made generic, or redirected for a person at risk. A woman fleeing an abuser may need appointment reminders switched off, her address flagged as sensitive, and specific record entries hidden from proxy viewers. Build these controls once, centrally, so a frontline worker can apply them in minutes rather than filing a change request that takes weeks. Design proxy and delegated access to be granular, time-bound and reviewable. Proxy access is a genuine good — carers and parents need it — but "all or nothing, forever" is dangerous. Support partial access (e.g. bookings but not clinical notes), automatic review points (notably when a child turns 11 and again at the age they gain confidentiality rights, commonly 16), and one-click revocation. Anchor every grant in a capacity or best-interests judgement consistent with the Mental Capacity Act, and record who authorized it and why. Verify identity proportionately, and defend against impersonation. Weak verification lets an abuser register as, or link to, their victim; heavy verification excludes the very people who most need care. Match assurance to risk: booking a routine appointment needs less than granting proxy access to a teenager's mental-health record. Use recognized identity assurance approaches (NHS login, GOV.UK One Login patterns) and watch for the tell-tales of coercion — the same phone number or device linked to many accounts, or a "carer" who resists any direct contact with the patient. Build clear escalation and referral into the service, not around it. When a member of staff — or an automated signal — spots a safeguarding concern through a digital channel, the path to a referral must be obvious, fast and logged. Integrate with local authority multi-agency safeguarding hubs (MASH) and named safeguarding leads, and make sure a concern raised at 2am through a messaging service reaches a human who can act. Never let a digital service become a place where disclosures are received but not routed. Moderate hosted spaces actively and lawfully. If your service hosts peer support, forums or user-to-user messaging, you have both a duty of care and, under the Online Safety Act 2023, legal duties around illegal and harmful content. Combine automated filtering with trained human moderators, clear reporting tools, and escalation routes for disclosures of abuse, self-harm or suicidal intent. Publish the rules, respond to reports within a stated time, and preserve evidence appropriately when you refer on. Train staff to recognize and respond to risk through digital channels. Recognizing abuse over chat, video or a portal message is a different skill from recognizing it in a clinic. Give frontline and contact-centre staff scenario-based training on digital disclosure, coercion signs, and the mechanics of applying record redaction and notification suppression. Safeguarding leads should understand the system's controls well enough to direct their use under pressure. Remember that digital exclusion concentrates among people at risk. The groups most likely to be excluded — people experiencing abuse, those with cognitive impairment, care leavers, people in poverty — overlap heavily with those the service most needs to protect. A "digital by default" channel can cut them off from help, or force them onto a device an abuser controls. Always keep a safe non-digital route, and treat exclusion itself as a safeguarding risk (see Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility and Topic 3.3 — Patient & Citizen-Facing Digital Services). Log, audit and review access to catch misuse. Maintain tamper-evident access logs, run proactive audits for anomalous access (a proxy viewing far more than expected, staff looking up records without a care relationship), and give patients transparency over who has seen their data. Auditability both deters insider abuse and provides evidence when a concern is investigated. Feed patterns back into design so recurring risks are engineered out. Questions to discuss with your team # For every piece of information our service shows or sends, who could be harmed if the wrong person saw it — and can a frontline worker stop that within minutes? This question forces you past the "happy path" user and onto the person living with an abuser, the teenager whose parent still holds proxy access, the adult whose whereabouts must stay hidden. The tension is between convenience for the majority and safety for a vulnerable minority: default-on reminders and rich shared records help most people and endanger a few. Walk through concrete flows — an appointment SMS, a repeat-prescription notification, a proxy view of clinical notes — and ask who holds the device and the account in each case. A good answer names the specific controls (suppression, redaction, sensitive-address flagging), confirms a non-technical worker can apply them quickly, and admits honestly where today the only option is a slow manual workaround that leaves people exposed in the meantime. How do we handle proxy and delegated access as capacity, age and relationships change over time? Proxy access is rarely wrong at the moment it is granted and often wrong later — the child grows up, the carer relationship breaks down, capacity fluctuates. The debate should surface how you detect and act on these transitions rather than leaving stale access in place. Consider the eleven-year-old whose parent still sees everything, the adult whose attorney's interests have diverged from their own, the person whose capacity returns after a crisis. Ground the discussion in the Mental Capacity Act's principle that capacity is decision-specific and presumed. A strong answer describes automatic review triggers, granular access levels, easy revocation, and a clear record of who authorized each grant and on what basis — and is honest about how much of this is currently manual or missing. When someone discloses harm or abuse through a digital channel, what exactly happens next — and how do we know it worked? Digital channels invite disclosures that never surface in a clinic, which is a genuine opportunity, but only if the disclosure reaches someone who can act. The discussion should trace the full path from a chat message at 2am, a portal note, or an automated risk flag, through to a logged referral to a multi-agency safeguarding hub or named lead. Debate the hard edges: out-of-hours cover, the boundary between the service's duty and statutory services, and what happens when a moderated forum surfaces a suicidal post. Look at your own incident and referral data — are disclosures being received but not routed? A good answer shows a tested, logged, human-backed escalation route, names who owns it, and can point to evidence that referrals actually complete rather than assuming they do. How would we know if our own service were being used to abuse, stalk or coerce someone — and who is watching for it? The dangerous cases rarely announce themselves; the abuser looks like a legitimate proxy, a caring relative, or the account holder themselves. This question shifts the team from designing controls to actively detecting misuse: the shared device linked to a dozen accounts, the proxy who reads far more than the child's care requires, the "carer" who blocks every direct contact with the patient. Debate what signals you could surface from access logs and registration data, who is accountable for reviewing them, and how a suspicion becomes a safeguarding action rather than a note nobody reads. Weigh the privacy cost of proactive monitoring against the harm of staying blind. An honest answer names the anomalies you would look for, says who owns the audit, and admits where today misuse would simply go unnoticed until someone is hurt. When safety and privacy pull in opposite directions, how do we decide — and who is in the room? Safeguarding is not a clean win for data protection: hiding a record from a proxy, sharing a concern with the police, or overriding a person's stated wishes can all sit in tension with confidentiality and the person's own autonomy. This question forces the team to name the trade-offs explicitly rather than letting whichever discipline shouts loudest decide by default. Consider the adult with fluctuating capacity who asks you to grant access their best interests may not support, or the multi-agency share that protects a child but breaches an adult's expectation of privacy. Ground the debate in the Mental Capacity Act, the Caldicott principles and the lawful bases for sharing to prevent serious harm. A good answer describes who adjudicates these calls — safeguarding, clinical-safety and information-governance leads together — how the reasoning is recorded, and how you avoid both reflexive over-sharing and paralysed under-sharing. How do we keep safeguarding working as the service, its suppliers and the threats around it change? Safeguarding controls decay: a new release quietly re-enables a default notification, a third-party messaging supplier changes its moderation, a platform update breaks a suppression rule, and a new coercion tactic emerges that nobody designed for. This question makes the team treat safeguarding as a living property of the running service, not a one-time gate passed at go-live. Discuss how change control, supplier assurance and post-incident learning feed back into the controls, and who re-tests the at-risk configuration after each significant change. Look at whether regression testing covers safeguarding scenarios at all. An honest answer points to a named owner, a review cadence, evidence that controls are re-checked after changes, and a mechanism for folding new threats and near-misses back into design rather than rediscovering them through harm. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system (ICS) rolls out a shared care record and a companion patient app across its acute, community, mental-health and social-care partners. Early adoption is strong, and proxy access is enabled so parents can manage children's care and carers can support older relatives. Three months in, a community midwife raises a concern. A pregnant woman has quietly asked whether her partner, who has proxy access to their toddler's record, can see her appointments and address. He can: the proxy relationship was set up at registration and grants broad visibility, and her antenatal appointment reminders are sent by default SMS to a phone he sometimes checks. The woman is being controlled and is planning to leave; the service, as configured, is helping her abuser track her. The safeguarding lead convenes the digital, clinical-safety and information-governance leads. In the short term they apply a sensitive-address flag, suppress her SMS reminders in favour of a phone call to a safe number, and revoke the partner's ability to see her records while preserving his legitimate access to the child's. They discover this took a day of manual effort across three systems — far too slow to be safe at scale. The lasting fix is a design change. The ICS builds a single "at-risk" configuration a frontline worker can apply in minutes: it suppresses or genericizes notifications, hides the sensitive record from named proxies, and routes future correspondence to a safe channel. They add an eleven-and-sixteen review trigger to all child proxy grants, tighten identity checks on new proxy links, and train contact-centre staff to recognize coercion signals. The change is logged as a clinical-safety and safeguarding improvement, reviewed at the ICS assurance board, and shared with neighbouring systems using the same platform. Sector lenses # Startup # A small digital-health company building, say, a teen mental-health app carries safeguarding risk that far outweighs its headcount — its users are minors disclosing self-harm and abuse. With limited resources, the temptation is to defer moderation and escalation to "later", but a single unhandled disclosure of suicidal intent is an existential and ethical failure. Prioritize a lean but real safeguarding stack from day one: a trained on-call responder or a contracted crisis-escalation partner, clear content rules, and identity checks proportionate to risk. Bake safeguarding acceptance criteria into your definition of done, and be ready to evidence them for buyers under DTAC and for the Online Safety Act 2023. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home or a domiciliary-care agency — carries the same safeguarding duties as a large trust but has no dedicated digital or IT team to apply them. It typically runs supplier-provided systems it cannot reconfigure, so the practical task is knowing which safeguarding controls those systems already offer and how to use them fast: suppressing an appointment reminder, flagging a sensitive address, hiding a record from a proxy. Nominate a named safeguarding lead and make sure at least one person knows how to apply notification suppression and proxy revocation without waiting on the supplier. Because cash and time are tight, lean on shared resources — CQC expectations, local authority MASH contacts, and NHS England proxy-access guidance — rather than building your own, and press suppliers to make at-risk controls quick and obvious. Keep a safe non-digital route open, since your patients cannot fall back on an internal helpdesk you do not have. Enterprise # An NHS trust or ICS runs many systems, many proxies and millions of records, so the challenge is consistency and speed at scale. The risk is fragmentation — each system with its own, slow, inconsistent way to hide data — which leaves gaps an abuser can exploit and workers who cannot act fast enough. Invest in centralized, reusable safeguarding controls (sensitive flags, notification suppression, proxy governance) that apply across the estate, backed by named safeguarding leads, MASH integration, and proactive access audits. Governance and assurance boards (see Topic 6.4 — Governance & Assurance) should treat safeguarding-by-design as a standing gate, not a one-off. Government # A national body — NHS England, DHSC, or a devolved government — sets the standards, platforms and identity infrastructure that everyone else builds on, so its design decisions ripple across the whole system. Choices about NHS login, GOV.UK One Login, proxy-access rules and record-sharing defaults determine what safeguarding controls are even possible downstream. The accountability is to Parliament and the public, and the failure mode is a national default that quietly exposes at-risk citizens at scale. Government should mandate safeguarding-by-design in service standards, fund shared components (safe-address handling, sensitive-record suppression), and legislate and regulate — via the Online Safety Act 2023 and Ofcom — with vulnerable users explicitly in scope. Common failure modes # Bolt-on safeguarding. Treating safeguarding as a policy PDF rather than a design requirement, so controls are missing when the risk arrives and workers improvise slow manual fixes. Default-on, no way off.
