x: Topic 3.1 — Content Design & Health Literacy In health and care, the words and structure you put in front of a person are part of the treatment, so content that confuses, excludes, or misleads is a clinical-safety and equity failure, not a cosmetic one. Why this matters in health and care # Most of the digital health service a person actually experiences is content: a letter, a screen of instructions, an appointment reminder, a consent form, a set of medication directions, an error message when a booking fails. People do not experience your architecture, your data model, or your governance board. They experience the words, and whether those words help them do the thing they came to do — book, cancel, understand a result, prepare for a procedure, take a medicine safely, decide whether to seek help. The stakes are high because the audience is, by definition, often unwell, anxious, tired, in pain, grieving, or in crisis. Comprehension drops under stress. A sentence that reads fine to a policy author in a quiet office can be unreadable to a frightened person at 2am. And the gap between how content is written and how people actually read is large. In England, around four in ten working-age adults struggle with health information that includes both text and numbers; that proportion rises sharply when numbers are involved. Much clinical content is written several reading ages above what a large part of the population can comfortably use. This is not a minor usability point. Poor comprehension is linked to missed appointments, medication errors, avoidable admissions, failure to attend screening, and worse outcomes overall — and those harms fall hardest on people already facing disadvantage, deepening health inequalities rather than narrowing them. If someone cannot understand how to prepare for a colonoscopy, the clinical procedure is compromised before it begins. If a safety-netting message ("come back if you notice these symptoms") is buried in jargon, the safety net has holes. Content design is therefore inseparable from Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management, from Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility, and from the research practice in Topic 3.0 — User Research & Service Design. Core concepts # Content design is a discipline, popularized by the UK Government Digital Service (GDS) and adopted by NHS Digital and NHS England, that treats writing as design: you decide what a person needs to complete a task, then choose the words, order, and format that meet that need in the simplest way — which is sometimes prose, but often a list, a table, a step-by-step, or no content at all. It starts from evidence about user needs rather than from what an organization wants to say. Plain language — in English, plain English — is writing whose wording, structure, and design let the intended reader find what they need, understand it, and use it, on first reading. It is not "dumbing down"; it is precision that respects the reader's time and effort. Readability is how easily a text can be understood, and it can be estimated with formulas such as the Flesch–Kincaid readability tests , which translate sentence length and word complexity into an approximate reading age or grade. These formulas are a useful signal, not a verdict — they measure surface difficulty, not whether the content is correct, findable, or usable. Health literacy is a person's ability to find, understand, and use health information and services to make decisions and act. It is not a fixed trait of the person; it is a relationship between the demands your content makes and the skills, context, and state the person brings. Numeracy — the ability to reason with numbers, risks, doses, and dates — is a distinct and often weaker skill, which matters enormously when you communicate probabilities, results, or medication amounts. Accessible content is content that works for people regardless of disability or communication need. It is governed by the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) for digital products, and in the NHS by the Accessible Information Standard, which is a legal requirement to identify, record, and meet the communication needs of patients and carers. Accessible formats include easy read (short sentences paired with images, for people with a learning disability), translations, large print, audio, and British Sign Language (BSL) video for Deaf people whose first language is BSL, not English. Health equity is the principle that everyone has a fair opportunity to be as healthy as possible; content that only works for confident, digitally included, English-reading users actively widens the gap and is therefore an equity issue, tying this topic to web accessibility obligations that apply to all public sector bodies. Best practices # Start from the user need and the task, not the message. Before writing anything, be able to state, in one sentence, what the person is trying to do and what they need to know to do it. Content that exists to protect the organization, list every caveat, or reproduce a policy is content that fails the person. Design the smallest thing that lets them succeed, and cut everything that does not serve that task. Write in plain language and check the reading age. Aim for short sentences, common words, active voice, and one idea per sentence. Use readability tools such as Flesch–Kincaid or SMOG as a quick signal, targeting roughly a reading age of nine to eleven for general public content, lower for high-stakes or crisis content. Treat the score as a smoke alarm, not a certificate — a text can score well and still be wrong, ambiguous, or missing the one thing the reader needed. Front-load, chunk, and structure for scanning. People do not read health content linearly; they scan for the part that applies to them. Put the most important information first, use clear and honest headings, break content into short chunks, and prefer lists and step-by-steps over dense paragraphs. Structured content — content broken into consistent, reusable components — also makes information easier to translate, reuse across channels, and keep clinically accurate in one place. Design numbers as carefully as words. Numeracy is weaker than literacy in the population, and numbers carry the highest-consequence content: doses, frequencies, risks, and results. Use natural frequencies ("about 1 in 10 people") rather than bare percentages where you can, keep denominators consistent, show absolute as well as relative risk, and never make the reader do arithmetic to stay safe. Test numerical content specifically, because a mis-read dose is a direct patient-safety harm. Adopt a single content style and reuse content patterns. A shared style guide — the NHS digital service manual content style guide is the reference standard in this sector — settles thousands of small decisions (how to write dates, phone numbers, medication names, "GP" vs "doctor") so authors do not reinvent them and readers get consistency. Reusable content patterns for common situations (appointment reminders, results, safety-netting) raise quality and safety at scale and reduce the cost of getting each new page right. Meet accessibility and the Accessible Information Standard by default, not on request. Build to WCAG 2.2 AA, and treat easy read, translations, BSL video, large print, and audio as part of the service, not an afterthought bolted on when someone complains. Under the Accessible Information Standard you must identify, flag, and meet communication needs and share those needs across care settings — so accessible content is a legal and clinical obligation, not a nice-to-have. Machine translation can help triage but is not safe for clinical content without human checking. Write for people in stress, distress, or crisis. Someone reading about a cancer result, a mental health crisis, or a bereavement has less working memory and less patience for tone that is cheerful, bureaucratic, or vague. Use calm, direct, human language; say what is happening and what to do next; make the path to urgent help unmissable; and remove anything that adds cognitive load. Kind, plain content in these moments is a form of clinical care. Test content with real and excluded users, and iterate. Content is a hypothesis about what helps until you watch real people use it. Run comprehension and task-based testing — ask people to tell you what a page means and what they would do — with a sample that deliberately includes people with low health literacy, low digital confidence, learning disabilities, and English as an additional language. This connects directly to Topic 3.0 — User Research & Service Design; content that has only been signed off by clinicians and lawyers has not been tested. Questions to discuss with your team # Do we actually know the reading age and comprehension of our highest-stakes content, or are we guessing? Most organizations cannot say what reading age their appointment letters, consent forms, or medication instructions are written at, let alone whether patients understand them. Pick your ten highest-consequence pieces of content — the ones where misunderstanding causes real harm — and measure them: run readability scores, but more importantly run comprehension testing with real users. Ask people to explain, in their own words, what the content means and what they would do next. You will usually find gaps between what the content says and what people take from it. Decide who owns closing those gaps, and how you will know they are closed. This is a clinical-safety exercise, not a copy-editing one. Who is allowed to publish content, and what stops unsafe or inaccessible content going live? In many services, content is written by whoever happens to own the system — a developer, a clinician, an administrator — with no content design skill, no style guide, and no accessibility check. Discuss where content sits in your delivery lifecycle: is there a content designer involved, is there a shared style guide, is there a review step that checks plain language and accessibility before publish? Consider what your equivalent of a clinical-safety sign-off is for content, and whether it exists at all. Talk honestly about the trade-off between speed and safety, and about who is accountable when content causes harm. The goal is a repeatable path to good content, not heroics from individuals. How do we serve the people our content currently fails, and are we measuring that? Averages hide exclusion: content that works for 80% of users can be completely failing the 20% who most need the service. Discuss which groups your current content excludes — people with low literacy or numeracy, Deaf BSL users, people who do not read English, people with learning disabilities, people in crisis — and whether you provide easy read, translations, BSL video, and alternative formats as standard. Ask whether you are meeting the Accessible Information Standard in practice, not just on paper. Consider how you would even detect that a group is being excluded, given they may simply drop out silently. Agree what you will measure and who represents these users when decisions are made, linking this to Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility. When content and clinical accuracy pull in opposite directions, how do we decide? Plain language and clinical precision are usually allies, but sometimes they conflict: a clinician insists on a technical term for exactness, legal wants a caveat that lengthens and clouds the message, or a safety-netting instruction has to name a symptom the reader may not understand. If you always defer to the clinician or lawyer you will publish content people cannot use; if you always simplify you risk stripping out a distinction that keeps someone safe. Discuss how you resolve these tensions in practice — who is in the room, what evidence settles it, and whether comprehension testing is allowed to override an expert's preference. Consider concrete cases: rewording a medication instruction, softening a threatening non-attendance warning, or explaining a risk figure. An honest answer names a decision-making process, not a default winner, and shows that both comprehension and clinical correctness are treated as safety requirements rather than one being a nice-to-have. Who owns content after it is published, and how do we keep it accurate as clinical guidance changes? Content is often treated as done at launch, but a medication direction, a screening interval, or a referral route can become dangerously wrong when clinical guidance or a pathway changes and nobody updates the words. Discuss whether every high-stakes piece of content has a named owner, a review cycle, and a way to find and fix all the places a fact appears — or whether the same statement is copied across letters, portals, and leaflets with no single source of truth. Ask what happens when a guideline changes: who is told, how quickly the content follows, and how you would even know a page had gone stale. Consider whether structured, reusable content would let you change something once rather than hunting for every copy. An honest answer confronts the unglamorous reality that most content decays silently, and sets out how you detect and prevent that decay. Are we treating AI-generated and AI-translated content with the caution that patient safety demands? Teams are increasingly tempted to draft patient content, summarize clinical information, or translate at scale using large language models, because it is fast and cheap. The danger is that fluent, confident output masks errors that a stressed reader will act on — a wrong dose, an invented reassurance, a mistranslated instruction — and the English-speaking team never sees the mistake. Discuss where, if anywhere, you allow generated or machine-translated content, and what human clinical and linguistic checking is mandatory before it reaches a patient. Consider the difference between using AI to triage or draft internally and using it to publish unreviewed content that tells someone what to do about their health. An honest answer sets a clear line, names who is accountable for checking, and treats an unverified machine output the same way you would treat an unqualified person writing clinical instructions. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care board is rolling out a digital service that lets patients book their own follow-up appointments after a hospital outpatient clinic. The first version is built quickly. The confirmation screen reads: "Your appointment request has been submitted and is pending clinical validation. Please note DNA policy applies." The reminder text message says: "You have an appt with the Ambulatory Care Unit re your recent attendance. Non-attendance may result in discharge per Trust policy." Within weeks, the team notices a pattern. Attendance for this cohort is worse than for letters, not better. User researchers and a content designer sit with fifteen patients, deliberately including two people with a learning disability, one Deaf BSL user, one person who reads little English, and several older patients with long-term conditions. The findings are stark. Almost no one knows what "DNA" or "ambulatory" means; several assume "DNA" refers to a genetic test. "Pending clinical validation" makes people think the appointment is not confirmed, so they do not put it in their calendar. The threat about discharge frightens people without telling them what to do. The Deaf patient never engaged with the service at all, because there was no BSL video explaining it and the text assumed fluent written English. The content designer rewrites against the NHS content style guide and tests each version. The confirmation becomes: "Your appointment is booked. We will send a reminder. If you need to change it, tap 'Change appointment' or call 0300 000 0000." The reminder becomes: "Reminder: your appointment is on Tuesday 12 August at 2pm at St Mary's Hospital, Clinic 4. If you cannot come, please tell us so we can offer the time to someone else: [link]." The reading age drops from around fifteen to around nine. The team adds an easy read version, a set of translated versions checked by human translators, and a short BSL video explaining how booking works. They add a clinical-safety review step for any content that tells a patient what to do about their health. Three months on, non-attendance in the cohort has fallen below the letter baseline, complaints have dropped, and the Deaf patient has used the service independently for the first time. The clinical safety officer records the content changes as a risk control in the service's safety case. The words were the intervention. Sector lenses # Startup # A health-tech startup can build content quality into its DNA cheaply, because it has no legacy content to unpick and can hire or contract a content designer early. The risk is that founders treat content as marketing copy — persuasive, on-brand, benefit-led — rather than as task-focused design for people who may be unwell. Adopt the NHS content style guide from day one, set a reading-age target, and put comprehension testing into your usability sessions from the first prototype. If you are pursuing NHS or public sector contracts, WCAG 2.2 AA and the Accessible Information Standard are entry requirements, not differentiators, so build to them now rather than retrofitting under procurement pressure. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home, a domiciliary-care agency, a single-site clinic, or a small health-tech supplier past the startup stage — has real patients and the same legal duties as a hospital trust, but no content designer, no style guide, and often one person doing IT alongside another job. The practical risk is that letters, consent forms, texts, and website content are written by whoever has time, in local jargon, and that easy read, translations, and BSL are simply not offered, quietly breaching the Accessible Information Standard. You do not need to build capability from scratch: adopt the free NHS content style guide and reuse its ready-made patterns rather than writing from a blank page, and use the NHS reading-age and accessibility guidance as your checklist. Prioritize your handful of highest-stakes items — medication instructions, appointment and safety-netting messages — and get those into plain language and accessible formats first, using community or voluntary-sector translators for your local languages rather than unchecked machine translation. Enterprise # A large provider or supplier has thousands of pieces of content spread across letters, portals, apps, leaflets, and third-party systems, written by many hands over many years with no shared style. The enterprise problem is consistency and governance at scale: the same medication or condition described five different ways, translations done ad hoc, easy read produced reactively. Invest in a single content style, a reusable content pattern library, a content design capability that supports delivery teams, and a publishing workflow with accessibility and clinical-safety checks built in. Treat high-stakes content — consent, medication, results, safety-netting — as a managed asset with named owners, version control, and a review cycle, the same way you would treat clinical protocols. Government # National and system bodies set the standards that everyone else inherits, so their content decisions are leveraged across millions of interactions. The GDS and NHS lineage — the service manual, the content style guide, the Accessible Information Standard, WCAG obligations under the Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations — exists precisely so that quality and equity are baked into public services rather than left to chance. Government's job is to maintain these shared standards, provide reusable patterns and components, mandate accessible formats, and hold service

x: Topic 3.2 — Design Systems & Prototyping A design system turns good design decisions into shared, reusable infrastructure — so that accessibility, clinical safety, and consistency are built in once and inherited everywhere, instead of being re-argued and re-broken on every screen. Why this matters in health and care # In health and care, the interface is often the last few centimetres between a clinical decision and a patient. A confusing medication field, an inaccessible date picker, a button that means "cancel appointment" in one service and "cancel and lose your data" in another — these are not cosmetic problems. They are patient-safety problems, equity problems, and trust problems. When every team designs its own components from scratch, defects multiply and safety guarantees become impossible to reason about across a portfolio. A design system is how you stop paying for the same mistakes repeatedly. When an accessible, well-tested component is built once and reused across dozens of services, you fix an accessibility defect or a safety ambiguity in one place and every service inherits the fix. The alternative — bespoke front-ends everywhere — means unknown, uneven quality: some services meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) and some quietly exclude the very people who most depend on public health services. Consistency is also a comprehension issue. Patients and staff move between services — a National Health Service (NHS) app, a trust's outpatient portal, a general practice booking tool — and every unfamiliar pattern imposes cognitive load. In a population that includes people who are unwell, anxious, older, digitally excluded, or using assistive technology, that load is not evenly distributed. Shared patterns lower it for everyone. This topic is about the machinery — components, patterns, tokens, prototypes, and design operations — that makes safe, accessible, consistent design the path of least resistance rather than an act of heroism. Core concepts # A design system is a single source of truth for the reusable components, patterns, styles, and guidance used to build a set of digital services. It is more than a style guide: it pairs working, coded components with the design rationale, accessibility notes, and usage guidance that tell you when and how to use each one. The two most relevant public examples are the NHS design system (maintained by NHS England, built on NHS.UK front-end) and the GOV.UK Design System , maintained by the Government Digital Service (GDS). Both are open, freely available, and battle-tested across millions of interactions. A component library holds the discrete building blocks — buttons, form inputs, headers, error summaries — while a pattern library holds the higher-order solutions to recurring problems: how to ask for a date of birth, how to structure a page of questions, how to report an error, how to ask a user their NHS number. Components are the vocabulary; patterns are the sentences. Both draw on component-based software engineering , where systems are assembled from loosely coupled, independently testable, reusable parts. Design tokens are the smallest shared decisions expressed as named variables — a colour, a spacing unit, a font size, a focus-state outline. Because tokens are referenced by name rather than hard-coded, a change to a token (say, increasing minimum touch-target size or contrast) propagates consistently to every component that uses it. Tokens are the mechanism that keeps a system coherent as it scales, and that makes it possible to theme a shared system for local use without forking it. A single source of truth is the governing idea: each design decision is mastered in exactly one place, so it cannot drift out of sync across services. When the design and the code and the guidance for a component all live in one authoritative library, you eliminate the class of bugs where the picture and the product disagree. Software prototyping is the practice of building deliberately incomplete versions of a service to learn something before you commit to building the real thing. Prototypes range from low-fidelity (paper sketches, greyscale wireframes) to high-fidelity (interactive, realistic, often built in code). The GDS principle is prototype to learn, not to keep : a prototype's job is to answer a question through usability testing with real users, after which it is thrown away — this is throwaway (or "rapid") prototyping, distinct from an evolutionary prototype you intend to harden into production. DesignOps (design operations) is the discipline of running design at scale — the people, workflows, governance, contribution model, and tooling that keep a shared design system healthy, funded, and trustworthy across an organization or integrated care system (ICS). It is to design what platform engineering is to code: mostly invisible when it works, painfully obvious when it does not. Prototyping is done in design tools such as Figma or directly in code using the front-end of a design system, which brings us to front-end web development — the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript layer where reuse actually reduces duplication, cost, and risk. This topic deliberately does not re-cover what users need (see Topic 3.0 — User Research & Service Design) or how words are written (see Topic 3.1 — Content Design & Health Literacy). Those disciplines feed the design system; this topic is about the reusable machinery that carries their conclusions safely into production. Best practices # Adopt before you build. Start from the NHS design system and the GOV.UK Design System rather than inventing your own. They already encode years of accessibility testing, content design, and real-world use across health and government services. Reinventing a date picker or an error summary is not a good use of scarce, expensive design and engineering capacity, and a home-grown version will almost always be less accessible. Extend and theme these systems for local needs; do not fork them without a deliberate, documented reason. Build accessibility and clinical safety into the shared components, not the individual screens. The whole economic and safety case for a design system is that you fix something once and inherit it everywhere. An accessible, keyboard-navigable, screen-reader-tested date-of-birth component, built and assured once, protects every service that uses it. Bake WCAG conformance, sensible error handling, and safety-relevant behaviours (clear confirmation of destructive actions, unambiguous units for doses and measurements) into the component itself, so teams cannot easily get them wrong (see Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility, and Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management). Prototype to learn, not to keep. Treat prototypes as disposable experiments that answer a specific question — "can a patient with low health literacy complete this referral?" — cheaply and fast. Match fidelity to the question: use low-fidelity sketches to test flow and comprehension early, and high-fidelity coded prototypes to test realistic interaction, accessibility, and edge cases later. Resist the pull to promote a prototype straight into production; prototype code optimized for speed of learning is rarely safe, secure, or maintainable enough for a live clinical service. Prototype in the real front-end when interaction and accessibility are the question. Design-tool prototypes (Figma and similar) are excellent for exploring layout, flow, and content quickly and collaboratively. But they cannot faithfully test keyboard navigation, screen-reader behaviour, focus management, or performance on old NHS estate hardware. When those are the risks, prototype in code using the design system's front-end, so you are testing something close to what real users will actually experience with real assistive technology. Test prototypes with real users before you build. A prototype that is never put in front of representative users is just an expensive opinion. Test with people who reflect your actual population — including older people, people with disabilities, people with low digital confidence, and staff working under time pressure. Even five participants will surface most of the serious usability and comprehension problems, and finding them in a prototype is orders of magnitude cheaper than finding them in production (see Topic 3.7 — Testing & Quality Assurance). Manage tokens as the contract for consistency. Express colours, spacing, typography, and interaction states as named design tokens, and treat changes to them with the seriousness of a shared dependency change. Tokens let you enforce minimum contrast, touch-target size, and focus visibility system-wide, and let a local team re-theme for their brand without breaking the underlying accessibility guarantees. When a national standard shifts, you want to change one token, not audit ten thousand screens. Run a contribution model, not a walled garden. A design system that only accepts input from a central team will always lag behind real service needs and will be resented by delivery teams. Publish a clear route for teams to propose new components and patterns, with criteria for what gets accepted, who reviews it, and how accessibility and safety are assured before anything is promoted to the shared library. This is core DesignOps work: it balances the tension between local flexibility and shared consistency without letting the system rot or fragment. Version, document, and communicate changes. Treat the design system as a product with users (your delivery teams), a roadmap, release notes, and a support channel. Semantic versioning, changelogs, and clear deprecation notices let teams adopt improvements safely and on their own schedule. Undocumented breaking changes destroy the trust that makes teams choose the shared system over rolling their own. Measure adoption and quality, not just existence. A design system delivers value only when it is used. Track which services use the shared components, where teams have had to build bespoke alternatives (and why), and whether accessibility conformance improves as adoption rises. High rates of local workarounds are a signal that the system is missing something real — treat them as backlog, not as disobedience. Questions to discuss with your team # Where should the line sit between shared consistency and local flexibility, and who gets to decide? This is the central governance tension of any design system. Too rigid, and delivery teams feel blocked, build shadow components, and route around the system — fragmenting the very consistency you were trying to protect. Too loose, and the "system" becomes a loosely related pile of one-offs with no shared safety or accessibility guarantees. In a health and care context the stakes are specific: some variation is legitimate (a mental-health crisis service has genuinely different needs from a routine appointment booker), while some variation is dangerous (inconsistent ways of confirming a destructive clinical action). A good answer names which decisions are non-negotiable (accessibility, safety-critical patterns, core interaction behaviours) and which are open to local theming, and it defines an explicit, humane process for a team to request an exception or contribute a new pattern rather than just forbidding divergence. How will accessibility and clinical safety actually be assured inside our components — and who signs it off? It is easy to claim that accessibility and safety are "baked in"; it is hard to guarantee it. This question forces you to be concrete about the assurance pipeline: who tests each component against WCAG, with which assistive technologies, and with which disabled users; how safety-relevant behaviours are reviewed against your clinical safety process (DCB0129/DCB0160); and what evidence is attached to a component before it is published as "safe to reuse". The debate should surface honest gaps — perhaps you have automated contrast checks but have never tested with a real screen-reader user, or your Clinical Safety Officer has never reviewed the shared component library. A strong answer produces a named owner, a defined test regime, and a rule that no component enters the shared library without documented accessibility and safety evidence, because a defect inherited by fifty services is fifty times the harm. Who funds, staffs, and maintains the design system once the initial enthusiasm fades? Design systems are frequently created in a burst of energy and then quietly abandoned when the founding team moves on, leaving a stale library that teams no longer trust. This is fundamentally a DesignOps and funding question, not a design question. Debate honestly whether you have a standing, funded team responsible for the system as an ongoing product — with capacity for support, contribution review, versioning, and keeping pace with the upstream NHS and GOV.UK systems — or whether you are relying on goodwill that will evaporate. In an ICS this is sharper still: is the system owned by one dominant organization, jointly governed, or orphaned between them? A good answer treats the design system as long-lived infrastructure with a named owner, a running budget, and a clear relationship to the national systems it builds on, rather than a project that "finishes". What is our relationship to the upstream NHS and GOV.UK systems — and how will we stay in step with them as they change? Adopting a national design system is not a one-off download; it is an ongoing dependency on infrastructure you do not control. This question forces you to decide, deliberately, where you sit on the spectrum from "theme lightly and track upstream closely" to "fork and diverge". Each choice has a cost: staying close means absorbing upstream changes (a new accessibility fix, a revised pattern) on someone else's schedule and occasionally reworking local customizations; forking means you own every future accessibility and safety fix the national team would otherwise have given you for free. In health and care the pull to diverge is real — clinical workflows and local branding create genuine pressure — but every divergence is a standing liability. A good answer names who watches the upstream release notes, how local extensions are structured so they survive an upstream update, and the explicit test a proposed divergence must pass before it is allowed, so that "we needed it to look different" never quietly becomes "we now maintain a stale, less-accessible fork of the NHS date picker". How will we actually hold the line between "prototype to learn" and "build to keep"? Everyone agrees in principle that throwaway prototypes should not become production services; the failure happens under deadline pressure, when a convincing high-fidelity prototype is sitting right there and shipping it looks like a shortcut. This question makes the boundary concrete rather than aspirational. Debate what practically stops prototype code — optimized for speed of learning, not for security, resilience, or maintainability — from being promoted into a live clinical service: is it a technical separation (prototypes built in a sandbox that cannot reach production), a governance gate (no clinical safety sign-off, no go-live), or merely a shared good intention that evaporates the first time a delivery date slips? The health and care stakes are specific, because unassured code in a clinical pathway is a patient-safety exposure, not just technical debt. An honest answer admits where the pressure will come from, names who is empowered to say no, and defines what "rebuild for production from assured components" actually requires so the boundary holds when it is tested. How will we know whether the design system is actually working — and what will we do when the metrics are uncomfortable? A design system can exist, be beautifully documented, and still deliver little value if teams quietly route around it. This question pushes past "we have a design system" to "is it earning its keep". Decide what you will measure: adoption across services, the rate and reasons for bespoke workarounds, whether accessibility conformance actually improves as adoption rises, and how much time teams save by reusing rather than rebuilding. The hard part is not collecting the numbers but agreeing in advance how you will read them — because a high rate of local workarounds is a signal that the shared system is missing something real, not evidence that delivery teams are being disobedient. A good answer commits to treating uncomfortable adoption data as backlog and roadmap input, defines who reviews it and how often, and resists the temptation to measure only the flattering thing (existence, download counts) instead of the thing that matters (safer, more accessible, more consistent services actually shipped). In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system covering three acute trusts, a mental-health trust, and a community provider decides to consolidate its patient-facing digital estate. Today each organization runs its own outpatient portal; between them they have four incompatible date pickers, three different ways of asking for an NHS number, and wildly varying accessibility conformance. An internal audit finds that only one of the four portals passes a basic screen-reader test of its appointment-booking flow — a clear equity and clinical-safety exposure. The ICS stands up a small, jointly funded design system team. Rather than build from scratch, they adopt the NHS design system as their foundation and define a thin local layer of design tokens for ICS-specific branding, plus a handful of genuinely local patterns (for example, a shared pattern for booking interpreter support, which none of the national systems cover). Every shared component carries documented WCAG evidence and a sign-off from the ICS Clinical Safety Officer under the DCB0129 process before it is published. Before rebuilding the outpatient booking flow, the team prototypes. They start low-fidelity, testing a paper-and-greyscale version of the new flow with twelve participants recruited to reflect the local population — including two screen-reader users, three people over 75, and several with low digital confidence. The prototype exposes a serious comprehension problem: patients cannot tell a "reschedule" action from a "cancel" action. The team fixes the pattern, then builds a high-fidelity coded prototype using the design system front-end and retests, this time confirming keyboard and screen-reader behaviour on the actual hardware used in a partner trust's outpatient clinics. Only then do they build for real, assembling the production service largely from assured, reusable components. Eighteen months later, a WCAG update tightens focus-visibility requirements. Because focus styling lives in a single design token, the team ships one change and every ICS service inherits it in the next release — a fix that, under the old fragmented estate, would have meant five separate remediation projects and, realistically, at least one service left broken. Sector lenses # Startup # A small digital-health startup should almost never build its own design system from zero — it cannot afford the accessibility testing overhead, and investors are paying for clinical validation, not bespoke buttons. Adopt the NHS or GOV.UK front-end where you are building for NHS users, and treat prototyping as your core competitive advantage: cheap, fast, throwaway prototypes tested with real patients let you learn faster than better-funded incumbents. The risk is the opposite one — promoting a slick high-fidelity prototype straight into production to hit an investor demo, carrying unassured, insecure code into a live clinical service. Keep a hard line between "prototype to learn" and "build to keep", even under funding pressure. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy,

x: Topic 3.3 — Patient & Citizen-Facing Digital Services A patient-facing digital service is a public health intervention in its own right: it can widen access and confidence for millions, or quietly exclude the very people who need care most, and how you build it decides which. Why this matters in health and care # When you put a service directly into the hands of the public, you change the relationship between a person and the system that cares for them. A staff-facing system is used by trained people inside a controlled environment; a patient-facing service is used by a frightened parent at 2am, an 84-year-old sharing a phone with a neighbour, someone with no fixed address, someone who reads little English, someone in crisis. You do not get to choose your users, train them, or stand beside them. The service has to work — safely, clearly, and fairly — for everyone the health system is obliged to serve, not merely for the confident and connected. That obligation is what makes this different from consumer technology. In retail, a confusing checkout loses a sale. In health and care, a confusing online triage form, an unclear medication instruction, or a "book an appointment" flow that silently fails can lead to a missed diagnosis, a wrong dose, or a person who gives up and presents later and sicker. The stakes are clinical (see Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management), legal (equality and accessibility duties bind public bodies), and financial, because public money is spent whether or not the service actually helps anyone. There is also a trust dimension that consumer products rarely carry. People bring their health data, their fears, and a lifetime of experience with the NHS to every screen you show them. If the service feels extractive, opaque, or unsafe, they will not simply churn — they will lose confidence in the institution behind it (see Topic 1.8 — Data Ethics, Consent & Public Trust). And because the people least able to navigate a poor digital service are disproportionately older, poorer, disabled, or digitally excluded, badly designed patient-facing services actively widen health inequalities. Doing this well is not a matter of polish. It is a matter of equity, safety, and public confidence. Core concepts # A patient-facing service is the "digital front door": the online entry point through which a person finds information, proves who they are, and starts a task. In England the two national platforms most people meet are the NHS App and NHS login. The NHS App, developed by NHS England, lets people in England book and manage GP appointments, order repeat prescriptions, view their GP-held record, access NHS 111 online, and set data-sharing and organ-donation preferences. NHS login is the separate identity and authentication service that verifies who a person is (to a proportionate level of assurance) so that they can safely reach their own record across many different NHS and partner services — much as GOV.UK Verify once aimed to do for central government. It is important to describe these accurately: the NHS App is a front door and an app, while NHS login is the identity layer that many apps and websites, not just the NHS App, can use. Behind the front door sit records and tools. An electronic health record (EHR) is the clinician-maintained record held by a provider. A personal health record (PHR) is a record that the patient can see, add to, and sometimes control, giving them a fuller view of their own care. A patient portal is the web or app interface through which people view results, messages, letters, and records, and communicate with their care team. "Patient access to records" — the right to read your own GP and increasingly hospital record — is now a default expectation in England, not a favour. Several service types run on top. Online consultation and online triage let a person describe a problem digitally so it can be routed and prioritized without a phone queue. Shared decision-making in medicine is the practice of clinician and patient reaching care decisions together, supported by clear information and decision aids — captured in the NHS phrase "no decision about me, without me". Self-management tools help people manage long-term conditions day to day. Remote patient monitoring and telehealth extend care into the home through devices, video, and asynchronous messaging. The concepts that decide whether any of this works are about people, not features. Adoption is whether people start using a service; activation is whether they reach the point of getting value from it; and sustained engagement is whether they keep using it when it matters. The Patient Activation Measure (PAM) is a validated instrument for a related idea — a person's knowledge, skills, and confidence to manage their own health. Set against all of this is the digital divide : the gap in access, connectivity, and confidence that means a purely digital health service will leave some people behind unless assisted-digital and non-digital routes are deliberately preserved (see Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility). Best practices # Design the whole front door, not one app. Decide deliberately which channels a person can use to reach each task — app, website, phone, in person, via a carer or proxy — and make them consistent rather than competing. A patient-facing service is a set of routes to a need, not a single download. Map where the digital route hands off to a human one and make that seam graceful, because most real journeys cross it. Treat channel choice as the user's to make, not yours to force. Use national platforms rather than rebuilding them. Where NHS App and NHS login already provide identity, records access, appointments, and prescriptions, integrate with them instead of building a parallel front door that fragments the experience and the security model. This gives users one trusted identity and one place to look, and it inherits assurance work you would otherwise repeat. Reserve bespoke build for genuinely local needs the national platforms do not meet, and feed those needs back to the national teams (see Topic 9.0 — Collaborating with Partner Organizations). Give people real access to their own records, and make it legible. Access to records builds trust and supports self-management, but a record dumped on screen in clinical shorthand can confuse or frighten. Invest in content design so results, letters, and coded entries are understandable, and think carefully about sensitive information, safeguarding, and how a proxy or carer sees another person's data (see Topic 1.10 — Safeguarding in Digital Services). Patient access is a design problem, not just a switch to turn on. Preserve assisted-digital and non-digital routes as a permanent feature. For every online task, keep a supported and a fully offline way to complete it, and resource them properly rather than treating them as legacy overhead. "Digital by default" must never mean "digital only", because a meaningful proportion of the population cannot or will not use the digital route, and they are disproportionately those in greatest need. Design the assisted route — a phone line, a receptionist, a library helper, a family proxy — with the same care as the app (see Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility). Make online triage clinically safe by design. Any tool that asks about symptoms and routes people must be built and governed as a clinical-safety activity, with clear escalation for red-flag symptoms and a bias toward safe over-triage. Apply the relevant clinical-risk-management standards, keep a named clinical-safety officer involved, and monitor outcomes for missed or delayed care (see Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management). A triage flow that fails silently is not a usability defect; it is a patient-safety incident. Support shared decision-making, not just transactions. The highest value in patient-facing digital is helping people understand options and make choices that fit their lives, not merely booking slots. Offer decision aids, plain-language information, and prompts that invite questions, and design so a person can pause, involve family, and return. Measure whether people feel more informed and more in control, because that is the point of the tool. Transactions are necessary; deliberation is where outcomes improve. Instrument for outcomes and experience, not vanity metrics. Downloads and registrations tell you almost nothing; a service can have millions of registered users and change no one's health. Measure activation and sustained, meaningful use, task completion, and — where you can — real clinical outcomes and patient-reported experience and outcome measures (PREMs and PROMs). Publish these alongside adoption numbers so the organization cannot mistake reach for value (see Topic 10.0 — Objectives & Key Results (OKRs)). Build trust through clarity, consent, and safety. Tell people plainly what a service does, what it does not do, who sees their data, and how to get help or reach a human. Make consent and data-sharing choices genuine and reversible, and never dark-pattern people into sharing more than they intend (see Topic 1.8 — Data Ethics, Consent & Public Trust). In health, trust is the platform everything else runs on; one breach of it costs far more than any feature earns. Design for interoperability from the start. A patient-facing service that cannot read from and write to the underlying records is a silo that creates double-keying and error. Use open standards so bookings, messages, and observations flow to and from the systems clinicians actually use, and so a person's data follows them across a fragmented care landscape (see Topic 4.3 — Interoperability & Data Standards). The public experiences interoperability as "I don't have to repeat myself" — and its absence as danger and frustration. Close the loop with continuous research and live operations. Keep researching with real, diverse users after launch, not just before it, and route what you learn back into the backlog (see Topic 3.0 — User Research & Service Design). Run the service as a live product with proper support, monitoring, and incident response, because a patient-facing service that is down or broken erodes trust instantly (see Topic 3.8 — Service Management & Live Operations). Adoption is earned continuously, not captured once. Questions to discuss with your team # Who cannot use this service the way we have designed it, and what happens to them? Every patient-facing service embeds assumptions — that people have a smartphone, data, an email address, a fixed identity to verify against, the literacy and confidence to complete a form, and the sight, dexterity, and language to do so. Name the groups your current design excludes or disadvantages, and be specific: people with no NHS-verifiable identity, people sharing one device, people fleeing abuse who cannot risk a digital trail, people with cognitive impairment. For each, decide what the assisted or non-digital route actually is, who resources it, and how you will know it works. A good, honest answer does not claim to serve everyone through the app; it names the excluded, quantifies them where possible, and shows a funded, dignified alternative rather than a token phone number nobody answers. This is where equity is won or lost, and it connects directly to Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility. How will we know this service actually improves health, not just that people signed up? It is easy to celebrate registrations and downloads because they are countable and they rise; it is much harder, and far more important, to show that anyone is better off. Discuss what outcome you are actually trying to move — fewer missed appointments, better-controlled long-term conditions, earlier presentation, more informed decisions — and how you would detect a change in it. Debate the trade-off between metrics you can gather cheaply now and the harder measures of activation, sustained use, and clinical outcome that tell the truth. Consider who is accountable if adoption is high but outcomes are flat, and whether you are willing to change or stop the service if the evidence says it is not helping. A strong answer ties the service to a small number of honest outcome and experience measures, admits what you cannot yet measure, and refuses to let vanity metrics stand in for value (see Topic 1.3 — Evidence-Driven Decisions and Topic 10.0 — Objectives & Key Results (OKRs)). Where does digital convenience trade off against clinical safety, and who decides? Patient-facing tools create real tensions: faster access can mean less clinical oversight; self-service triage can miss the subtle presentation a clinician would catch; showing people their raw results can inform or alarm; letting people book directly can undermine prioritization. Work through where your service leans toward convenience and where it must lean toward caution, and make those choices explicit rather than emergent. Ask who owns the clinical-safety case, how red-flag symptoms escalate, and how you monitor for harm that only shows up in aggregate over time. Consider the safeguarding angle too — a service that assumes the person on screen is who they say they are, and is safe, is not always right (see Topic 1.10 — Safeguarding in Digital Services). A good answer treats safety as a design input from day one, with a named clinical-safety officer and live monitoring, not as a compliance sign-off at the end. When the digital route hands a person over to a human one, how graceful is that seam — and who catches what falls through it? Almost every real patient journey crosses from the app to a person and sometimes back again: an online triage that routes to a call-back, a booking that needs a receptionist to resolve, a proxy request that needs verifying, a result that prompts a worried message. These handoffs are where services quietly fail, because each side assumes the other has the person and the context. Map the specific transitions your service creates and ask what information travels across them, how long the person waits, and what happens if neither side picks them up. Debate whether the digital route is genuinely reducing load on staff or merely moving it somewhere less visible, and whether frontline teams were designed with, not just handed, the new flow (see Topic 3.0 — User Research & Service Design). An honest answer can trace a person end to end across every seam, names who owns the handoff, and shows the fallback for when the automated route cannot finish the job — rather than assuming the digital front door closes the loop by itself. What is the total cost of running this well for years, and are we honestly resourced to meet it? Patient-facing services are often funded as projects — a build, a launch, a headline — when they are in truth live products that must be supported, monitored, researched, and improved indefinitely, alongside the assisted-digital and non-digital routes they can never fully replace. Discuss what it actually costs to keep the phone line staffed, the content current, the accessibility maintained, the clinical-safety case live, and the integrations working as national platforms change beneath you. Surface the uncomfortable trade-off that a genuinely inclusive service is more expensive than a digital-only one, and decide whether the business case is built on real recurring funding or on optimistic savings that assume everyone switches channel. Consider what you will stop doing to pay for this, and who is accountable when year-two funding evaporates but the service and its users remain. A strong answer treats sustainability and support as first-class costs from the outset (see Topic 3.8 — Service Management & Live Operations and Topic 6.1 — Health Economics & Value), not as an afterthought once the launch budget is spent. Who owns this service once the launch is over, and do they have the mandate to keep changing it? A patient-facing service that no one owns as a living product drifts: content goes stale, accessibility regresses, the integration breaks quietly, and research stops the day the project team disbands. Discuss who holds the service after go-live, whether they are a genuine product team with the authority to prioritize, change, and even switch off features, or merely a maintenance function that can only keep the lights on. Examine how decisions get made when clinical, operational, information-governance, and communications stakeholders all have a stake and a veto, and whether that decision path is fast enough to fix a safety issue or slow enough to protect one. Consider how feedback from users and frontline staff actually reaches the people who can act on it, and whether the organization will keep funding a team to improve something that already appears to work. An honest answer names the accountable owner, describes their real mandate and how live learning feeds the backlog, and admits where governance either protects or paralyses the service (see Topic 5.0 — Product-Led Work). In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system (ICS) covering a mixed urban and coastal population wants to reduce pressure on GP phone lines and improve access, and proposes rolling out an online consultation and triage tool integrated with the NHS App and NHS login. The temptation is to measure success by the number of registrations and the fall in call volumes, and to declare victory within a quarter. The delivery lead insists on framing it differently. In discovery, the team researches with a deliberately broad group: confident app users, but also an older woman on the coast with intermittent broadband, a man with low literacy who has never used email, a carer managing appointments for her mother as a proxy, and a woman in a refuge who cannot risk her whereabouts being logged. They find that the triage form's red-flag handling is sound but that its language defeats the low-literacy user, that the proxy journey is confusing, and that the identity verification in NHS login excludes people with no passport or driving licence. Crucially, they find that when the phone line is de-prioritized in favour of the app, the coastal and vulnerable users simply drop out of contact rather than switching channel. So the ICS resets its plan. It keeps the phone line fully staffed as the assisted-digital route, not a legacy cost, and funds a community "digital health helper" scheme through libraries and pharmacies. It works with the national NHS App team on the proxy journey rather than building a workaround, and appoints a clinical-safety officer to own the triage risk case with monitoring for cases where digital triage under-routed a patient who later presented acutely. It also changes its measures: alongside adoption, it tracks task completion by user group, sustained use, patient-reported experience, and a small set of clinical outcomes. Six months in, downloads are lower than a pure app-first push would have produced, but access has improved across every group including the most excluded, and the triage tool has safely escalated several serious presentations. The board accepts the slower adoption because the service is demonstrably fairer and safer. Sector lenses # Startup # A small digital-health company lives or dies on adoption and retention, so it will instrument engagement obsessively and iterate fast — a genuine strength the wider system can learn from. The danger is optimizing for the metrics that impress investors (downloads, monthly active users) rather than health outcomes, and designing for the confident early adopters who are cheapest to acquire. A startup selling into the NHS must show it meets the Digital Technology Assessment Criteria (DTAC), integrates with NHS login and open standards rather than trapping users in a silo, and has a credible clinical-safety case. x: Topic 3.4 — Discovery Phases In one sentence: Discovery is the disciplined, time-boxed effort to understand your users and the real problem before you commit money, clinical risk, or reputation to building a solution. Why this matters in health and care # In most sectors, building the wrong thing wastes money. In health and care, it can also waste clinical time, entrench health inequalities, and — at the extreme — harm patients. A digital service that assumes every user has a smartphone, reliable broadband, and confident English quietly excludes the frail, the poor, and the digitally marginalised : precisely the people the NHS and social care exist to serve. Discovery is where you find that out for the price of a few weeks of research, rather than after a national rollout. Health and care spending is public money held in trust, and much of it flows through statutory duties: the NHS Constitution , the public sector equality duty under the Equality Act 2010 , and the Caldicott principles for handling confidential patient information. Discovery is the phase where you test whether a proposed service is needed , lawful , safe , and equitable — before those questions become expensive to answer. Skipping it does not remove the questions; it merely defers them to a point where the honest answer is politically impossible to accept. The NHS Digital Service Standard and the GOV.UK Service Manual both make discovery the mandatory first phase of any user-facing digital service for exactly this reason. It is not bureaucratic theatre. It is the cheapest insurance you will ever buy. Core concepts # Discovery, defined. Discovery is a short (typically 6–10 week) phase whose goal is to understand a problem space: who the users are, what they are trying to do, what stops them, what already exists, and whether there is a problem worth solving at all. Its output is understanding and evidence , not a product. A good discovery can validly conclude "do nothing" or "this is a policy problem, not a digital one." The double diamond. The Design Council's double diamond (2005) frames design as two linked diamonds. The first — Discover then Define — diverges to explore the problem widely, then converges to frame it precisely. The second — Develop then Deliver — diverges to explore solutions, then converges to build one. Discovery, as a delivery phase, lives almost entirely in the first diamond. The recurring failure is teams sprinting into the second diamond before the first is finished. User need versus stakeholder want. A user need is something a person is trying to accomplish, expressed from their point of view ("I need to know my appointment is confirmed so I don't take a day off work for nothing"). A stakeholder want is a feature or solution someone has already decided on ("we need an app"). Discovery's core discipline is translating wants back into needs, because needs are stable and solutions are cheap and interchangeable once the need is clear. Problem framing. How you state a problem constrains every solution you will consider. "Patients miss appointments" invites a reminder app. "Patients cannot easily rearrange appointments that no longer suit them" invites self-service rebooking. Same symptom, different problem, radically different service. Discovery earns its keep largely in the quality of the problem statement it produces. Assumptions, hypotheses, and evidence. Every project rests on assumptions. Discovery makes them explicit, ranks them by risk, and tests the riskiest ones with real users. The goal is not certainty — that is unattainable — but reduced uncertainty on the things that would sink the project . Best practices # Start from a problem, not a solution. Write the problem statement before anyone names a technology. If the funding bid, the board paper, or the supplier pitch already specifies "an app" or "a portal," treat that as an assumption to test, not a decision to implement. Solutions arrived at before the problem is understood are almost always someone's habit, not the user's need. Do real user research with real users. Interview and observe the actual people who will use the service — patients, carers, receptionists, community nurses, social workers — in their real context, not a workshop of managers speaking on their behalf. Aim for depth over volume; a dozen well-chosen contextual interviews reveal more than a thousand-response survey. Recruit deliberately for the users who are hardest to reach, because they are the ones a service most often fails. Map the whole service, not the digital sliver. Users experience an end-to-end service — a referral, an assessment, a treatment, a follow-up — of which your digital component is one step. Map the current journey across every channel and organization, including the paper, phone, and face-to-face parts. Digital changes routinely fail because they optimize one step and break the two on either side of it. Frame the problem explicitly and get it agreed. Produce a written problem statement and the evidence behind it, and secure explicit agreement from your senior sponsor. This artefact is your contract: it defines what "done" means for the next phases and gives you the standing to say no to scope that does not serve the agreed problem. Size the opportunity and the risk honestly. Estimate how many people are affected, how badly, and what it costs the system today. Pair this with the risks a solution would introduce — clinical, information governance, equity, delivery. Leaders fund discoveries; they decide on the basis of a defensible opportunity-and-risk picture, so give them one. Design for the edges from day one. Recruit research participants across the digital-inclusion spectrum, test against Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.2 AA) expectations early, and treat assisted-digital and offline routes as first-class, not afterthoughts. In health and care, the excluded user is often the high-need user; a service that works only for the confident and connected widens inequality. Keep it multidisciplinary and time-boxed. Staff discovery with a user researcher, a service designer, a product person, a technical architect, and — for anything touching care — clinical and information-governance input. Time-box it hard (weeks, not quarters) to force convergence. An open-ended discovery is a warning sign that the team is avoiding a decision. Write down what would make you stop. Agree, at the start, the conditions under which the honest recommendation would be "do not proceed": no genuine user need, an insurmountable IG or safety barrier, a better non-digital fix, or a problem owned by another team. A discovery that cannot recommend stopping is not a discovery; it is a pre-justified build. Questions to discuss with your team # What would we have to see in discovery to honestly recommend "do not proceed", and does anyone in this room have the standing to say it? Stop conditions are worthless if they cannot be exercised, and in health and care the pressure not to exercise them is intense: a director has announced the app, a supplier contract is half-signed, or a funding window closes if the team hesitates. This question forces a team to name the specific evidence — no genuine user need, an insurmountable information-governance or clinical-safety barrier, a better non-digital fix, a problem owned by another service — that would flip the recommendation to stop, and to write it down before the research begins so it cannot be quietly redefined later. The tension worth debating is between sponsor confidence and researcher independence: a discovery that structurally cannot say no is a pre-justified build wearing discovery's clothes. Consider who protects the researcher's findings from editing, whether an outsider reviews the evidence, and what the last discovery your organization actually stopped was — if there isn't one, that is itself a finding. An honest answer identifies the real reasons "no" is hard here and a concrete mechanism (agreed stop criteria, an independent challenge, a sponsor who has publicly blessed the possibility of stopping) that makes it sayable. Who are the users we are most likely to exclude, and how will we get them into the research rather than deferring them to beta? In health and care the excluded user — the frail, the digitally marginalized, the person with low confidence in English, the carer juggling three systems — is disproportionately the high-need user the service exists to serve, so sampling for convenience quietly designs inequality into the architecture. The trade-off to debate is depth and inclusion versus the schedule and recruitment cost: reaching the hardest-to-reach takes time, community partners, incentives, and assisted or offline research methods that a rushed discovery is tempted to skip "for now". Concrete angles include mapping the digital-inclusion spectrum explicitly, recruiting through voluntary-sector and clinical gatekeepers rather than a mailing list, and treating assisted-digital and non-digital routes as first-class findings rather than afterthoughts. It is worth naming the public sector equality duty and the Caldicott context so inclusion is understood as a legal and ethical obligation, not a nicety. A good answer produces a named recruitment plan that deliberately over-samples the edges, and a clear statement of which users the team will treat as the design's centre of gravity. Have we framed a problem, or have we smuggled a solution into the problem statement? How a problem is stated silently constrains every solution the team will consider — "patients forget appointments" invites a reminder app, while "patients cannot easily rearrange appointments that no longer suit them" invites self-service rebooking and a slot-policy review — so the wording of the problem statement is where discovery earns most of its keep. The debate is whether the funding bid, board paper, or supplier pitch has already fixed the answer ("an app", "a portal", "an AI triage tool") and dressed it as a need, and whether the team has the discipline to translate that want back into the underlying user goal. Useful angles include banning solution nouns from the problem statement, mapping the whole end-to-end service across every channel and organization so the digital sliver is seen in context, and checking each stated need is expressed from the user's point of view rather than the organization's. Evidence matters here: a framing should be traceable to what real users said and did, not to a habit or a strategy slide. An honest answer either confirms the statement names a stable user need with evidence behind it, or admits a solution has been assumed and reopens the framing before any alpha is scoped. Do we have the right disciplines in the room, and are clinical safety and information governance shaping the work rather than signing it off at the end? A discovery staffed only by a product manager and a delivery lead will find product and delivery problems; the users, clinicians, and legal duties it never invites into the room become the risks that surface expensively in alpha or, worse, after go-live. The tension is that a genuinely multidisciplinary team — user researcher, service designer, technical architect, clinical safety officer, information-governance and Caldicott expertise — is scarce, competed-for, and slow to convene, so teams are tempted to "borrow" a clinician for an hour or bolt IG on as a final gate. That sequencing is the trap: clinical safety and IG are cheap to design in during framing and ruinously expensive to retrofit once an architecture assumes data will flow across organizational boundaries. Concrete angles include naming a clinical safety officer from week one for anything touching care, treating a data protection impact assessment as a live discovery artefact rather than a later formality, and checking whether the people who understand the frontline workflow are contributors or merely consultees. An honest answer names who is actually in the team, which duties are represented by a person versus a checkbox, and where the discovery would be blind because a discipline is missing. How will we know discovery is finished, and what stops it drifting for months or being cut off after a fortnight? Discovery has two opposite failure modes and both are about time: the unbounded study that maps everything and decides nothing, and the truncated fortnight that rushes to a foregone conclusion because a delivery date was fixed before the research began. The discipline the double diamond demands is convergence — knowing when the problem is understood well enough to make a defensible decision, not when every question has been answered, because certainty is unattainable and the goal is reduced uncertainty on the things that would sink the project. The trade-off worth debating is depth versus momentum: a hard time-box of weeks forces the team to prioritize the riskiest assumptions, but a box set too tight starves the inclusive, hard-to-reach research that this domain most needs. Useful angles include agreeing the decision the discovery must inform and the artefacts a sponsor needs to make it, ranking assumptions so the box is spent on what matters, and naming a decision point rather than letting the phase dribble into an unacknowledged alpha. An honest answer states how long the box is, what "understood enough" looks like for this problem, and who calls the end. When discovery ends, can we hand a funding board a defensible picture of the opportunity and the risk — or only a story? Leaders do not fund understanding; they fund decisions, and a discovery that produces rich insight but no board-legible account of how many people are affected, how badly, what it costs the system today, and what a solution would put at risk leaves the decision to whoever tells the most confident story. The tension is between the researcher's nuanced, caveated findings and the board's need for a sized, comparable, defensible case — compress too hard and you lose the equity and safety subtleties that were the point; refuse to compress and the evidence never reaches the people who allocate money. In health and care the picture must pair opportunity with the risks a solution introduces — clinical, information-governance, equity, delivery — because a board that sees only upside is being set up to make a bad bet. Concrete angles include sizing the affected population from real data rather than a hopeful estimate, making findings traceable so a sceptic can follow them back to what users said, and framing the recommendation (including "do not proceed" or "alpha this narrower thing") in terms the next phase can act on. An honest answer shows the team can move from evidence to a recommendation a funding board could scrutinize in the open without it falling apart. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system (ICS) is under pressure to reduce did-not-attend (DNA) rates at outpatient clinics. A supplier has pitched an AI-powered reminder app, and a director is keen to fund it. Instead of buying, the ICS runs an eight-week discovery. The user researcher interviews eighteen patients who recently missed appointments, plus receptionists and two clinic managers. A pattern emerges that the reminder theory missed: many "no-shows" had tried to rearrange but hit an engaged phone line for days, or had been given an appointment during working hours they could not take without losing pay. A subset had died or been admitted elsewhere and were still on the list. Reminders would not touch any of these causes. The team maps the end-to-end booking journey and finds three organizations, two patient administration systems, and a fax machine in the loop. They reframe the problem from "patients forget appointments" to "patients cannot easily reach us to rearrange appointments that no longer work for them." They quantify it: roughly 40% of DNAs at the sampled clinics involved a failed prior contact attempt. They flag an information-governance question (a shared rebooking tool would cross organizational boundaries) and an equity finding (the highest DNA rates were among patients in the most deprived postcodes, for whom the working-hours slot was the barrier). The discovery recommends against the app, and for an alpha exploring self-service rebooking plus a review of slot-scheduling policy. The reframed problem is agreed by the sponsor, a clinical safety officer is named for the alpha, and a data protection impact assessment is commissioned. The ICS has spent eight weeks and avoided funding a solution that would have failed measurably in public. Sector lenses # Startup # A digital-health startup runs discovery on a shoestring and against the clock — often the "discovery" is the founders' own lived experience plus a fortnight of user interviews squeezed between investor meetings. The funding pressure is to show traction, which tempts founders to skip straight to a demo; the discipline that matters most is naming the riskiest assumption and killing the idea cheaply if it fails, because a startup cannot afford to build the wrong thing even once. Accountability runs to investors and early adopters rather than a statutory board, so stop conditions are commercial (no willingness to pay, no reachable market) as much as clinical. The upside is speed and the freedom to pivot; the risk is mistaking a compelling founder narrative for evidence of a real user need. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home, a domiciliary-care agency, a single-site clinic, or a small health-tech supplier past the pre-revenue stage — has real patients and running operations, but rarely a spare user researcher or service designer to staff a formal discovery. Here discovery is lightweight and opportunistic: the "research" is the receptionist who already knows why patients cannot get through on the phone, the care workers who see the paperwork duplication daily, and a handful of deliberate conversations with the users a change would affect. The trap is that the same statutory duties — Caldicott, UK GDPR, the equality duty, clinical safety — apply in full whether or not there is anyone in-house who owns them, so the discipline that matters most is framing the problem honestly and testing the riskiest assumption before committing scarce cash to a supplier's product. Because ongoing operations cannot pause, a small provider often runs its discovery around a single concrete pain point rather than a broad problem space, and its most valuable stop condition is recognizing when the fix is a process change or a shared regional platform rather than a system to buy. Enterprise # An NHS trust or large health-tech supplier can staff a proper multidisciplinary discovery — user researchers, service designers, clinical safety, information governance — but must fight organizational gravity: an incumbent supplier contract, a board that has already announced "the app", or a business case that pre-decided the solution. Here discovery's hardest work is political — reframing a sanctioned solution back into a user need without losing sponsor support. Funding is annual and committee-bound, so discoveries compete for slots and must produce board-legible artefacts. Risk appetite is low and accountability broad (regulators, auditors, the public), which makes an honest "do not proceed" both more valuable and harder to say aloud. Government # A national or local public body — NHS England, DHSC, a devolved government, a local authority — runs discovery under the full weight of the Service Standard, spend-control gates, and public scrutiny, where the discovery report itself may be published and challenged. The user base is enormous and the duty to include the marginalized is a legal, not optional, concern, so inclusive recruitment and assisted-digital routes are mandatory from the first week.
