x: Topic 3.9 — Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery In health and care, a major system outage is a patient-safety event before it is an IT problem, so your ability to keep delivering care while a system is down — and to recover it fully and quickly — is a core clinical and public-trust capability, not a technical footnote. Why this matters in health and care # Care does not stop when the technology does. When an electronic patient record, an e-prescribing platform, or a laboratory results system fails across a hospital, clinicians do not get to pause treatment while engineers work. They must keep seeing patients, prescribing medicines, and making decisions — often without the allergy alerts, dose checks, and prior history that the failed system normally provides. That is why an outage is not measured only in downtime hours and service credits; it is measured in delayed diagnoses, missed interactions, cancelled operations, and the additional risk carried by every clinician working blind. Business continuity is the discipline of making sure that when the worst happens, care stays as safe as it can be. The stakes are national and well-documented. The 2017 WannaCry ransomware attack disrupted around a third of NHS trusts in England, forced the cancellation of thousands of appointments and operations, diverted ambulances, and locked staff out of the very devices — including some imaging and pathology equipment — that they needed to treat people. It cost the NHS an estimated £92 million and, more importantly, showed that a cyber-attack on health infrastructure lands as a clinical crisis, not merely a data-security incident. Since then, resilience has moved from the server room to the board table, and rightly so. This topic extends the operational discipline of Topic 3.8 — Service Management & Live Operations, but shifts the focus from everyday running to major disruption: the fire, flood, cyber-attack, supplier collapse, or regional outage that threatens to take a critical service down for hours or days. It connects tightly to Topic 1.7 — Information Governance, Data Protection & Cyber Security (because ransomware recovery is now a central continuity scenario), to Topic 4.0 — Technical Architecture, Cloud & Legacy (because resilience is designed in, not bolted on), and to Topic 6.4 — Governance & Assurance (because someone must own, test, and be accountable for the plan). Get this right and disruption becomes a bad day; get it wrong and it becomes a public inquiry. Core concepts # Business continuity and disaster recovery. Business continuity planning (BCP) is the capability to keep delivering products or services — in your case, safe care — at pre-defined acceptable levels during and after a disruptive incident. IT disaster recovery (DR) is the narrower, technical subset concerned with restoring the systems, data, and infrastructure that underpin those services. Business continuity is the wider promise ("patients keep being treated"); disaster recovery is one of the means ("the results system is back within four hours"). You need both, and you must not confuse a restored server with a restored service. Business continuity management and business impact analysis. Business continuity management (BCM) is the ongoing management process — not a one-off document — that identifies threats and builds organizational resilience. Its foundation is the business impact analysis (BIA): a structured assessment of each service that asks how quickly its loss causes unacceptable harm, what it depends on, and how far back in time you can afford to lose data. The BIA is where clinical judgement enters engineering: clinicians, not just technologists, must define what "unacceptable" means for a maternity system versus a staff intranet. Recovery time objective and recovery point objective. Two numbers anchor every recovery plan. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable time to restore a service after failure. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, expressed as time — an RPO of fifteen minutes means you can tolerate losing at most the last fifteen minutes of entries. For a critical clinical system these may be minutes; for a reporting warehouse they may be days. Setting them honestly, per service, is the single most useful continuity decision you will make. Backups and tested restores. A backup is a copy of data stored elsewhere so the original can be restored after loss. The industry baseline is the 3-2-1 rule : three copies, on two types of media, with one held off-site (and, in the ransomware era, one held immutable or offline). Crucially, a backup you have never restored is a hope, not a control. Ransomware routinely encrypts backups that are reachable from the network, and untested restores routinely fail on the day. The discipline is not "do we back up?" but "when did we last successfully restore, end to end, and how long did it take?" High availability, redundancy, and failover. High availability (HA) is a design property that keeps a system running through component failure, usually measured in "nines" of uptime. It is achieved through redundancy — the deliberate duplication of critical components — and failover , the automatic switch to a standby component or site when the primary fails. High availability reduces the frequency of outages; disaster recovery handles the ones that get through. They are complementary, not alternatives, and confusing them leaves dangerous gaps. Single points of failure and critical dependencies. A single point of failure (SPOF) is any component whose failure stops the whole service — one network link, one authentication service, one supplier, one database, or one person who alone knows how something works. Mapping SPOFs and critical dependencies (the upstream services and third parties your service silently relies on) is the analytical heart of resilience. In modern health IT, dependencies are rarely local: a single-sign-on service, a national spine connection, or a cloud region can take down many systems at once. Clinical downtime and business-continuity procedures. Health and care has a distinctive control that generic IT lacks: the clinical downtime procedure , a rehearsed, safe fallback — usually paper — for delivering care when a digital system is unavailable, plus the re-entry process for reconciling that paper record back into the system once it returns. This is business continuity made concrete at the bedside, and it is where continuity plans most often meet reality. Ransomware and cyber-recovery. Ransomware encrypts your data and demands payment, and it has become the defining continuity threat for health systems. The WannaCry ransomware attack of 2017 is the reference case: it is why cyber-recovery — isolating, rebuilding from clean backups, and validating integrity before reconnecting — is now a first-class scenario in every serious plan. The continuity standard. ISO 22301 is the international standard for business continuity management systems. It provides a recognized structure — context, leadership, planning, support, operation, evaluation, improvement — for building and auditing continuity capability, and it is a useful backbone whether or not you seek formal certification. Best practices # Start from a business impact analysis owned by clinicians, not IT alone. Rank every service by the clinical harm caused when it fails and by how quickly that harm becomes intolerable, then assign each a specific RTO and RPO. Do this with the clinicians and operational managers who bear the consequences, because "how long can we run without this safely?" is a care question, not an infrastructure one. The output is a prioritized list that tells you where to spend your finite resilience budget first. Design resilience proportionate to criticality. Match the engineering to the impact: mission-critical systems (emergency department, patient administration, e-prescribing) warrant high availability, geographic redundancy, and automatic failover; lower-criticality systems can accept longer recovery and simpler backups. Resist both under-engineering critical systems and gold-plating trivial ones. Architecture and continuity must be designed together (see Topic 4.0 — Technical Architecture, Cloud & Legacy), because you cannot bolt resilience onto a fragile design after the fact. Hunt down single points of failure and hidden dependencies. Systematically map each critical service's dependencies — network, authentication, DNS, national connections, power, cooling, key suppliers, and key people — and identify where one failure cascades. Pay particular attention to shared services such as single sign-on or a common integration engine, whose failure takes down many systems at once. A dependency you have not mapped is a dependency you will discover during the outage. Back up to survive ransomware, and prove restores by testing them. Follow the 3-2-1 rule and keep at least one backup copy immutable or physically offline, so an attacker who reaches your network cannot encrypt your last line of defence. Then test restores on a schedule, timing them against your RTO and validating data integrity against your RPO — a restore that takes two days against a four-hour objective is a failed control you have simply not noticed yet. Treat "last successful full restore" as a metric you report, not a task you assume. Write, resource, and rehearse clinical downtime procedures. For every critical clinical system, maintain a tested paper (or offline) fallback that lets staff keep delivering safe care during an outage, plus a clear process for re-entering that data afterwards without loss or duplication. Store downtime forms where they can be reached when the network and the printers are also down. Rehearse them with frontline staff, because a procedure that lives only in a folder will not be found, understood, or trusted at 3 a.m. during a crisis. Maintain a disaster recovery plan with real site failover. Document, for each critical system, exactly how it recovers: what runs where, in what order, who decides to invoke it, and how you fail back afterwards. Where the impact justifies it, run a genuinely separate recovery site or cloud region and prove you can switch to it — recovery order matters, because systems have dependencies that dictate sequence. An untested DR site is an expensive assumption. Exercise the plan; a plan never tested is a plan that fails. Run regular exercises across a spectrum: desktop tabletop walk-throughs of scenarios, technical failover tests, and occasional full live simulations including the clinical fallback. Exercises expose the gaps — the out-of-date contact list, the recovery step that needs a password no one has, the assumption that staff know the paper process — while it is safe to find them. Capture the lessons, fix them, and re-test; an exercise with no follow-up is theatre. Extend continuity to your suppliers and cloud. Your resilience is only as strong as the third parties your critical services depend on, so make continuity a contractual and assurance matter: require suppliers to evidence their own RTO/RPO, DR testing, and cyber-recovery, and understand your cloud provider's shared-responsibility model — availability zones and regions protect against some failures but not against a mis-configuration or account compromise that you own. Plan for supplier failure itself, including the scenario where a key supplier is the one hit by ransomware (see Topic 6.3 — Procurement & Commercial). Adopt a recognized standard and put continuity under governance. Use ISO 22301 as a structured backbone and NHS and national guidance as the sector overlay, and give a named executive accountability for business continuity, reporting to the board. Continuity that no one owns, funds, or reviews decays quietly until the incident reveals it. Wire it into your assurance framework (see Topic 6.4 — Governance & Assurance) so plans are maintained, tested, and improved as a matter of routine, not rediscovered in a crisis. Questions to discuss with your team # For each of our critical clinical systems, what RTO and RPO have we actually agreed with clinicians — and can we currently meet them? This question forces the gap between aspiration and capability into the open. Many organizations have never set explicit recovery objectives, or set them in IT without clinical input, so the "acceptable" downtime is really just whatever the current architecture happens to deliver. Debate where clinical need (minutes for an emergency system) collides with what your backups and DR can actually achieve (perhaps a day), because that gap is unmanaged clinical risk you are carrying whether you name it or not. Look concretely at your last real or tested recovery: how long did it take, how much data would you have lost, and who signed off that this is safe? A good, honest answer names specific numbers per system, admits where you cannot yet meet them, and turns each gap into a funded action rather than a comfortable silence. If ransomware encrypted our core systems and our backups tonight, how would we keep patients safe tomorrow — and how long until we are fully recovered? This is the scenario that has hit real health systems, so it deserves a concrete, unflinching walk-through rather than reassurance. Explore both halves honestly: the immediate clinical continuity (are the downtime procedures rehearsed, resourced, and trusted enough to run a whole hospital on paper for days?) and the technical recovery (are backups immutable and offline, have you tested rebuilding from clean copies, and do you know the recovery order?). Surface the uncomfortable dependencies — if single sign-on, the integration engine, or a key supplier is down, how much else falls with it? Consider who declares the major incident, who talks to staff, patients, and the media, and who decides that a system is safe to reconnect. A strong answer describes a rehearsed plan with named roles and tested restores; a weak one assumes the backups are fine and the paper process will simply work. When did we last test our continuity and disaster recovery plans end to end, and what did we learn? The purpose here is to distinguish a living capability from a shelf document. A plan that has not been exercised is untested, and untested plans routinely fail on contact with reality — the contact list is stale, the recovery step needs credentials no one has, the downtime forms are stored on the system that is down. Discuss the range of exercising you actually do: tabletop scenarios, technical failover tests, and full simulations that include the frontline clinical fallback, not just the server restore. Probe whether lessons from past incidents and exercises were actually fixed and re-tested, or logged and forgotten. A good answer shows a regular exercise calendar, evidence of gaps found and closed, and honesty about which parts of the plan remain unproven. Which of our critical dependencies do we not control — and what is our plan for the day one of them fails? Modern health IT rarely fails alone; it fails through the services and suppliers underneath it. Push the team past the systems you own to the ones you merely rely on: the national spine connection, the single-sign-on provider, the cloud region, the integration engine, the outsourced data centre, the managed-service partner who holds the keys to recovery. For each, ask what happens to care if it disappears for a day, whether the contract obliges the third party to a recovery objective that matches your clinical need, and whether you have ever seen evidence of their DR testing rather than a reassuring paragraph in a bid. The uncomfortable truth is that you can carry residual risk you have never priced, because the failure sits in someone else's estate. An honest answer names the specific external dependencies of each critical service, states which are contractually assured and which are simply trusted, and identifies a fallback — even a manual one — for the dependencies you cannot make resilient. When a major incident hits, who decides what, who communicates to whom, and does everyone know their role before the day? Continuity is as much about command and communication as it is about backups, and this is where rehearsed plans and improvised chaos diverge. Work through the human choreography: who has the authority to declare a major incident and invoke the plan, who runs the operational response, who decides a system is safe to reconnect, and who speaks to staff, patients, the press, regulators, and — in a cyber-attack — law enforcement. Consider the failure of your own tools during the incident, because the outage may take down the email, phone directory, or intranet you would normally use to coordinate. Surface the tension between moving fast and moving safely, and the reputational stakes of getting the public message wrong. A strong answer points to a tested incident-command structure with named, deputized roles, out-of-band communication channels, and pre-agreed message templates; a weak one assumes the right people will simply gather and know what to do. How do we fund, own, and keep continuity alive when nothing has gone wrong for two years? Resilience decays quietly in the gap between incidents, and this question confronts the organizational discipline that keeps it from rotting. Continuity competes for money and attention against visible, urgent clinical and digital priorities, and the immature-and-lucky organization looks identical to the mature one right up until the day it does not. Debate who genuinely owns continuity at executive level, whether it has a funded line rather than borrowed goodwill, and how plans, dependency maps, and contact lists are kept current as systems and staff change. Ask what the board actually sees — tested assurance and honest gaps, or a green rating and a filed document. A good answer describes named accountability, a recurring budget and exercise calendar, and a governance rhythm that treats maintained, tested continuity as routine rather than something rediscovered in the next crisis. In practice: a health & care example # Meadowvale NHS Foundation Trust runs a 600-bed acute hospital. On a Tuesday morning, staff arrive to find their electronic patient record (EPR), pathology, and radiology systems locked by a ransom note; the attackers had entered through a supplier's remote-access account ten days earlier. The chief information officer declares a major incident within the hour, and the trust's business continuity plan activates. Because the trust had done its business impact analysis, it knew the EPR and pathology were its highest-criticality systems, with agreed recovery objectives, while its downtime procedures had been rehearsed the previous autumn. Wards switch to paper drug charts and pre-printed observation forms — stored deliberately in physical cabinets on each ward, not on a shared drive — and the emergency department reverts to its paper pathway. Elective operations for the week are postponed and communicated to patients; ambulances are diverted from the busiest periods. Care continues, degraded but safe, because staff had practised working this way. Recovery is harder than restoration. The security team isolates the network to stop the spread, then rebuilds critical systems from immutable backups held offline — copies the attackers could not reach. Those backups had been restore-tested quarterly, so the team knew the process worked and roughly how long it took; the EPR is back within its RTO of eight hours, though pathology, with more complex dependencies, takes two days. The RPO of fifteen minutes means only a short window of data was lost, and staff reconcile the paper records back into the system under a controlled re-entry process, double-checking medications and results. x: Topic 3.10 — Emergency Preparedness, Resilience & Response Emergency Preparedness, Resilience and Response (EPRR) is a statutory duty, not a nice-to-have, and in a modern health system the digital and data dimension is now part of the front line — so you must plan, train, exercise and command your technology alongside your clinicians. Why this matters in health and care # When a major incident happens — a terrorist attack, a chemical spill, a heatwave, a flu surge, or a cyber-attack that locks every clinician out of the electronic patient record — the health and care system is expected to keep functioning while everyone around it is disrupted. That expectation is written into law. Under the Civil Contingencies Act 2004 , NHS bodies and their partners have specific duties to assess risks, maintain plans, and be able to respond. Emergency Preparedness, Resilience and Response is the umbrella term the NHS uses for how it meets those duties. It is not the same as ordinary service management, and it is broader than the IT-focused disaster recovery covered in Topic 3.9 — Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery. The reason this matters more in health and care than almost anywhere else is that failure has an immediate human cost. If a supermarket's till system fails, sales stop; if a hospital's clinical system fails during a mass-casualty event, people may die who would otherwise have lived. Digital services are now so deeply woven into clinical work — ordering tests, prescribing, checking allergies, viewing images, discharging patients — that a technology outage is a clinical-safety event, and it must be treated with the same seriousness as any other threat to life. This is why the "how you work" thesis of this book is sharpest here: your preparedness is a clinical-safety, equity and public-trust issue. Emergencies also expose inequality. The people least able to cope when normal services fail — those without transport, without English, without money, without carers, with long-term conditions — are exactly the people your emergency plans must protect first. A response that quietly leaves them behind is not a successful response, however slick the command structure looks. Preparing well, and rehearsing honestly, is how you earn the public trust that a real crisis will test to destruction. Core concepts # Emergency management is the discipline of reducing a community's vulnerability to hazards and coordinating the response when they occur. It is conventionally described as a cycle — anticipate, assess, prevent, prepare, respond, recover — and health systems run that cycle continuously, not just during a crisis. EPRR is the NHS's expression of it. The Civil Contingencies Act 2004 is the legal backbone. It divides responders into two groups. Category 1 responders are those at the core of the response — emergency services, NHS trusts and boards, integrated care boards, UK Health Security Agency, and local authorities — and they carry the full set of duties: risk assessment, emergency planning, business continuity, information sharing, and warning the public. Category 2 responders — utilities, transport operators, telecommunications firms and others — are "co-operating bodies" with a lighter duty, mainly to share information and co-operate with Category 1 responders. Knowing which you are, and which duties attach, is the starting point for everything else. Responders coordinate through a Local Resilience Forum (LRF), a multi-agency partnership built around each police area. The LRF is where the NHS, councils, police, fire, ambulance and others plan together, and it maintains a community risk register — a shared, published assessment of the local hazards most likely to require a coordinated response, from pandemic influenza to flooding to industrial accidents. The register is a worked example of risk assessment : identifying hazards, judging likelihood and impact, and deciding what to plan for. Incidents are classified so that everyone shares a language for scale. A business-continuity incident disrupts your ability to deliver services but is, in principle, manageable with your own plans. A critical incident is more serious: the level of disruption threatens the organization's ability to deliver safe care and requires special measures. A major incident is one whose scale or nature demands special arrangements by one or more emergency services and usually the wider system — a mass-casualty event being the archetype. The thresholds matter because declaring an incident unlocks resources, authority and mutual aid. Command runs through the gold–silver–bronze command structure , also called strategic–tactical–operational. Gold (strategic) sets objectives and owns the big decisions; silver (tactical) decides how resources are deployed to meet them; bronze (operational) delivers the hands-on tasks. The structure is deliberately generic so that agencies who have never worked together can slot into a single command system on the day. Three more concepts complete the picture. Surge is the ability to expand capacity — beds, staff, oxygen, compute — rapidly and temporarily beyond normal limits. Triage is the process of prioritizing casualties when need exceeds capacity, and mass-casualty triage systems exist precisely for the worst days. Mutual aid is the agreement to lend staff, equipment or capacity across organizational boundaries when one responder is overwhelmed. And a pandemic — an infectious-disease outbreak spreading across a large region — is the standing worst-case that most health systems now plan against explicitly, informed hard by the COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom . Best practices # Treat major technology outages and cyber-attacks as major incidents in their own right. A ransomware attack that disables clinical systems is not merely an "IT problem" to be handled quietly by a service desk; it is a threat to patient safety across a whole organization. Wire your cyber and digital incident response into the same gold–silver–bronze command structure your organization uses for a coach crash, with a defined trigger for when a digital incident is escalated to a formal critical or major incident. The WannaCry attack of 2017 showed how a single piece of malware could ripple across dozens of trusts within hours — see Topic 1.7 — Information Governance, Data Protection & Cyber Security for the controls that prevent it, and this topic for how you command the response when they fail. Run the plan–train–exercise cycle relentlessly, and mean it. A plan that has never been tested is a hypothesis. NHS EPRR requires a rolling programme of exercises — communications tests, table-top exercises and full live exercises — and you should schedule them, resource them, and treat non-attendance by senior leaders as the red flag it is. Crucially, include your digital and data teams: rehearse losing the electronic patient record, losing the network, and losing your primary data centre, not just a fire in a ward. Design and rehearse your paper-and-downtime fallback deliberately. Every critical clinical system needs a documented, practised way of working when it is unavailable — downtime forms, printed drug charts, read-only "business continuity" copies of records, and a known process for reconciling data once systems return. These fallbacks decay silently; forms go out of date, staff who knew the drill leave, and the printer has no toner on the day you need it. Audit them as carefully as you audit the live system, and connect this work explicitly to the recovery-time objectives in Topic 3.9 — Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery. Keep command-and-control communications working when everything else fails. In a real incident, your ordinary email and telephony may be part of what has failed, especially in a cyber-attack. Maintain out-of-band communications — a way to convene gold command that does not depend on the network being attacked — along with up-to-date, offline call-out lists and a resilient method for reaching frontline staff. Test these channels during exercises; discovering that your incident bridge relies on the same single sign-on that ransomware just encrypted is a discovery you want to make in rehearsal, not at 3 a.m. Pre-agree the information-governance rules for a crisis before the crisis. In an emergency you will need to share data quickly — between hospitals, with public health, with mutual-aid partners — and staff must know they are allowed to. Work with your Data Protection Officer and Caldicott Guardian to establish, in advance, the lawful bases and standing information-sharing agreements that apply in an emergency, so that clinicians share what is needed to save life without freezing in uncertainty. Keeping a record of emergency data-sharing decisions protects both patients and staff afterwards (see Topic 1.8 — Data Ethics, Consent & Public Trust). Build surge into your digital services, not just your wards. Population-facing digital services — booking, triage, symptom checkers, vaccination systems — can be hit by demand spikes of ten or a hundred times normal during an emergency, exactly when they matter most. Load-test against realistic surge scenarios, agree how you will scale cloud capacity quickly, and decide in advance what to gracefully degrade so the core function survives. A queue that holds is better than a website that collapses under the weight of a frightened public. Feed digital and data expertise into risk assessment and the community risk register. Your organization's contribution to the Local Resilience Forum should include a clear-eyed view of digital and cyber risk, single points of failure, and dependencies on national systems and suppliers. Too often the risk register treats "IT failure" as a single vague line; break it down, quantify it, and make sure the LRF understands that a regional network or cloud outage is now a credible mass-disruption event. This is part of the governance and assurance loop described in Topic 6.4 — Governance & Assurance. Learn openly from every exercise and every real incident. The value of an exercise is the debrief, and the value of a real incident is the structured lessons that follow it. Capture what happened without blame, track the actions to completion, and — the hard part — actually close them before the next incident finds the same gap. Share learning across the system through your LRF and national channels, because the point of a resilient network is that no organization has to learn the same painful lesson twice. Look after your people through and after the response. Resilience is not only technical; a workforce that is exhausted, frightened or morally injured cannot sustain a long emergency. Plan for shift patterns, rest, psychological first aid and welfare during protracted incidents such as a pandemic, and make it legitimate to ask for help. The organizations that recovered best from COVID-19 were often those that protected their staff's wellbeing deliberately rather than treating stamina as infinite. Questions to discuss with your team # When exactly does a digital or cyber problem stop being a "service incident" and become a declared critical or major incident — and who has the authority to make that call at 2 a.m. on a Sunday? This question forces you to test the seam between the everyday service management of Topic 3.8 — Service Management & Live Operations and the statutory EPRR machinery. The tension is between over-escalating (crying wolf, exhausting your command structure) and under-escalating (letting a ransomware attack spread for hours while people debate whether it counts). A good answer names explicit, observable triggers — for example, loss of the electronic patient record across multiple sites, or confirmed malware on clinical systems — and names the on-call roles empowered to declare, without waiting for office hours. Discuss who is on that rota, whether they have been trained, and whether they can convene gold command when the normal network is down. Consider walking through a recent near-miss and asking honestly whether you would have escalated in time. The best answers also cover de-escalation: how you decide the emergency is over and return to business as usual. If our primary clinical systems went dark for 72 hours, what would we actually do — and have we ever proved it, or do we only believe it? This is a question about the gap between the plan on the shelf and the reality on the ward. The trade-off to surface is investment: maintaining and rehearsing downtime procedures costs money and clinical time that could go elsewhere, and it is easy to let them quietly rot. A strong answer distinguishes what is genuinely rehearsed from what is merely written down, and is specific about the first hour, the first shift and the second day, because the problems change over time — reconciling three days of paper records back into the system is its own major task. Probe whether frontline staff, not just managers, know the fallback, and whether recent joiners have ever seen it. Look for honesty about single points of failure, including dependencies on national infrastructure and suppliers you do not control. The most mature teams can point to a real exercise or a real outage where the fallback held, and to the lessons they closed afterwards. How do we make sure our emergency response protects the people who are hardest to reach, rather than quietly leaving them behind? Emergencies amplify existing inequality, and digital responses can make it worse: an online-only booking system, an English-only alert, or an app that assumes a smartphone and data can exclude the very people most at risk. The tension is between the speed and scale that digital channels offer and the coverage that equity demands, and there is no free lunch — you will need non-digital routes running in parallel, which cost more. A good answer connects to the community risk register and asks which vulnerable groups a given hazard threatens, then checks the response reaches them. Consider assisted digital routes, translated materials, and how you reach people who are housebound, digitally excluded or without support (see Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility). Discuss how you would know if you were failing them during an incident, not months later in a review. Honest answers admit where current plans are weakest and commit to testing them with the communities involved. Which of our critical digital dependencies do we not actually control — and what is our plan when the failure is upstream of us? Modern health and care runs on national systems, cloud regions, connectivity providers and a handful of dominant suppliers, and a great deal of your resilience is therefore in someone else's hands. The uncomfortable tension is that you carry the statutory duty and the clinical-safety consequences, yet the single point of failure may be a supplier's data centre or a shared national service you cannot inspect. A strong answer maps these dependencies explicitly — which systems are hosted where, which suppliers underpin which clinical functions, and where concentration risk means one outage takes out several services at once — rather than leaving "IT failure" as a single vague line on the risk register. It asks hard questions about contractual recovery commitments, what happens when a supplier is itself the victim of the attack, and whether a regional cloud outage is treated as the credible mass-disruption event it now is. Probe whether these upstream risks are surfaced to your Local Resilience Forum and board, and whether you have any mutual-aid or manual fallback for the dependencies you cannot influence. The honest answer usually admits that some risks can only be mitigated, not removed, and is explicit about which ones you are consciously accepting. Do our exercises tell us the truth, and do the lessons we learn actually change anything before the next incident? An exercise programme can become theatre — a scripted table-top that everyone knows will succeed, attended by juniors while senior leaders send apologies, producing a tidy report and a list of actions no one closes. The tension is between exercises that are comfortable and reassuring and exercises that are realistic enough to fail safely, which is the only kind that teaches you anything. A good answer looks at whether you rehearse genuinely hard scenarios — losing the EPR, losing the network, a supplier ransomware attack — with the people who would really be on shift, and whether senior attendance is treated as mandatory rather than optional. It is candid about the debrief culture: are lessons captured without blame, tracked to completion, and verified as closed, or do the same gaps recur incident after incident? Look for evidence that a lesson from one exercise or real event demonstrably changed a plan, a rota or a control. The most mature teams can name a failure they surfaced deliberately in rehearsal and fixed before it could hurt a patient. How will we sustain and protect our people through a response that lasts weeks, not hours? Much emergency planning implicitly assumes a sharp, short shock, but the events that test a health system hardest — a pandemic, a protracted cyber recovery, a long cold-weather surge — grind on for weeks or months, and human stamina is not infinite. The trade-off is real: rotating people for rest and welfare reduces the raw hours available at exactly the moment demand peaks, and it is tempting to lean on the willing until they break. A strong answer plans for shift patterns, hand-overs, rest, psychological first aid and welfare from the outset, and makes it legitimate for staff to ask for help rather than treating exhaustion as commitment. It considers the digital and data teams too, who often carry a recovery for days with no relief because they are few and specialized. Discuss how you would spot burnout, moral injury and attrition during a long incident, and who owns workforce welfare in your command structure. The organizations that came through COVID-19 best were frequently those that protected their people deliberately, and honest answers admit whether your plans currently do that or merely hope for heroics. In practice: a health & care example # Meadowford is a fictional integrated care system covering a mid-sized city and its rural hinterland. On a wet February morning, its acute trust's electronic patient record — hosted by a national supplier and shared with two neighbouring trusts — begins throwing errors, then fails entirely. Within twenty minutes the supplier confirms a ransomware attack. Clinicians can no longer see medications, allergies, results or care plans across three hospitals and their linked community services. The trust's on-call director declares a critical incident using a pre-agreed trigger — "loss of the EPR across multiple sites" — and, as the scale becomes clear, escalates to a major incident. Gold command convenes not by the usual Teams call, which runs through the affected single sign-on, but via a rehearsed out-of-band bridge on a separate platform, using a printed call-out list. Silver command activates downtime procedures: paper drug charts, downtime request forms, and read-only "break-glass" copies of records that were replicated to a segregated environment for exactly this scenario, as designed under the recovery objectives in Topic 3.9 . The cyber and clinical-safety leads run in parallel. The chief clinical information officer opens a clinical-safety case, treating the outage as a hazard and tracking the specific risks — missed allergies, duplicated doses, lost results — with mitigations for each (see Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management). The Caldicott Guardian and Data Protection Officer confirm the pre-agreed emergency information-sharing position so that clinicians can phone neighbouring sites for critical patient details without hesitating over lawfulness,

x: Topic 3.11 — Telehealth, Remote Consultation & Virtual Wards Moving care out of the clinic and into the phone, the screen and the home changes not just where care happens but who is accountable for it, who can reach it, and how you know it is safe — so remote care is an operating-model decision, not a technology purchase. Why this matters in health and care # Remote care used to be a fringe option; now it is a mainstream way of delivering health and social care. A patient with a long-term condition may have a video appointment with a specialist, wear a monitor that streams readings to a team miles away, and be treated for an acute illness in their own bedroom under a "virtual ward" instead of a hospital bed. Each of these is a genuine model of care, with its own clinical risks, staffing model and accountability trail — not merely a digital convenience bolted onto the old pathway. The stakes are high in three directions at once. Safety is the first: a remote clinician sees less than one in the room — no smell of ketones, no handshake that reveals a tremor, no colleague glancing over — and a monitoring stream that no one is resourced to watch is a false reassurance dressed up as a service. Equity is the second: the people who most need care are often those least able to join a video call, own a smartphone, or trust a device in their living room, so a poorly designed remote service can quietly widen the very inequalities the NHS exists to close. Public trust is the third: putting cameras, sensors and data flows into someone's home crosses a threshold of intimacy that a waiting room never did, and consent, safeguarding and privacy have to be earned there, not assumed. There is also a hard operational reason to get this right. Remote and virtual models are being asked to carry real capacity — to keep people out of hospital, to free beds, to reach rural and housebound patients — and they only deliver those benefits if the operating model behind them is sound. A virtual ward with the wrong staffing ratio, an unclear escalation route, or a triage front door that funnels the wrong patients to the wrong channel does not save capacity; it manufactures risk and rework. How you design the way of working is the clinical service. Core concepts # Telehealth is the use of electronic information and telecommunications technologies to support health care at a distance — clinical consultation, monitoring, education and administration. It is the umbrella term; "telemedicine" is often used more narrowly for remote clinical consultation specifically, and the two are frequently used interchangeably. Telehealth sits within the broader field of eHealth — health care supported by digital processes and communication — and overlaps with mHealth , the delivery of health services through mobile devices and apps. It helps to separate telehealth into three modalities , because each has a different risk and workflow profile. Synchronous consultation happens in real time by telephone or by video call , with clinician and patient present together at a distance. Asynchronous or "store-and-forward" consultation — sometimes called e-consultation — exchanges information without both parties being present at once: a patient submits symptoms, photographs or a form, and a clinician responds later. Remote patient monitoring (RPM) streams physiological readings — blood pressure, oxygen saturation, blood glucose, weight — from the patient's home to a clinical team who review and act on them. Most real services blend all three. A virtual ward — internationally often called hospital-at-home — delivers hospital-level acute care to patients in their own homes, supported by daily clinical review, remote monitoring and the ability to escalate rapidly. It is a genuine ward with a virtual footprint: a defined patient list, a named clinical lead, a multidisciplinary team, and admission and discharge criteria. NHS England has invested heavily in virtual wards to expand acute capacity, particularly for frailty and acute respiratory infection. The device fleet and clinical engineering that make monitoring possible are covered elsewhere (see Topic 4.4 — Connected Devices, IoT & Clinical Engineering); this topic owns the care model that sits on top of them. Two access concepts complete the picture. Total triage is an operating model in which every request for care — however it arrives — is assessed first and directed to the most appropriate response, rather than defaulting to a face-to-face appointment. It is triage applied to the whole front door, often described as "digital-first" access when an online form is the first step. Done well it matches need to channel; done badly it becomes a barrier that the digitally excluded cannot cross. That risk connects directly to health equity and the digital divide — the unequal access to devices, connectivity, skills and confidence that determines who can actually use a remote service. And because care now enters the home, informed consent — a person understanding what is being monitored, by whom, and to what end — becomes a live, ongoing practice rather than a one-off signature. In social care, closely related telecare — alarms and sensors that help people stay safe at home — is owned by Topic 9.3 (Digital in Adult Social Care). Best practices # Choose the modality from clinical appropriateness, not convenience or target. The first question is never "can we do this remotely?" but "should we, for this patient, this time?" Some presentations need hands, eyes and a room — a possible acute abdomen, a safeguarding concern, a frail patient whose deterioration shows in the walk from the waiting room. Build explicit criteria for when each channel is and is not appropriate, empower any clinician to convert a remote contact to face-to-face without friction or penalty, and treat "remote-first" as a default to be overridden on clinical judgement, not a quota to be hit. Design the whole access pathway, not just the front door. Total triage and digital-first access only work when every route in — online form, phone, walk-in, carer request — lands in one assessment process with consistent clinical prioritization and a guaranteed non-digital alternative. Map what happens after the form is submitted: who reviews it, in what time, with what safety-netting for the patient who deteriorates while waiting. A digital front door that quietly lengthens the path for the sickest or the least digitally confident is a safety and equity failure, however slick the interface (see Topic 3.3 — Patient & Citizen-Facing Digital Services). Make clinical accountability for monitored data explicit and resourced. The single most dangerous pattern in remote care is data that is collected but not watched. Every monitoring stream needs a named clinical owner, a defined review frequency, clear thresholds that trigger action, and an escalation route that works out of hours — and the staffing to sustain all of it. Be honest about the difference between "monitored" and "watched": a dashboard checked twice a day is a different clinical promise from continuous surveillance, and patients and referrers must know which they are getting (see Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management). Build the virtual ward's operating model before the technology. A virtual ward is a clinical service with admission and discharge criteria, a named consultant or senior clinical lead, a multidisciplinary team, daily board rounds, and a rapid-response route when a patient deteriorates. Decide the staffing model, the caseload per clinician, the visiting logistics, and the interface with the acute site — including how a patient is readmitted physically when home care is no longer safe. The monitoring kit and app are the easy part; the rota, the escalation pathway and the clinical governance are what make it a ward rather than a set of gadgets (see Topic 7.2 — Workforce Planning). Design for digital inclusion from the start, and measure who you exclude. Assume that a meaningful share of your patients lack a suitable device, reliable connectivity, data allowance, digital confidence, or the language and literacy to use your service — and that these are often the people in greatest clinical need. Offer assisted-digital and non-digital routes as first-class options, lend equipment where appropriate, and monitor uptake and outcomes broken down by age, deprivation, disability and ethnicity so you can see whether the service is widening or narrowing inequality (see Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility). An unmeasured remote service is presumed to be excluding someone; find out who. Treat consent, privacy and safeguarding in the home as continuous practice. Bringing cameras, microphones and sensors into a home changes the privacy contract profoundly: other household members are captured, the setting reveals things a clinic never would, and the patient may feel unable to refuse. Make consent specific and revocable — what is collected, who sees it, how long it is kept — and design for the reality that a video call can expose neglect, coercion or abuse that triggers safeguarding duties (see Topic 1.10 — Safeguarding in Digital Services, and Topic 1.8 — Data Ethics, Consent & Public Trust). Give clinicians a protocol for what to do when a remote contact raises a concern the patient did not intend to share. Engineer the rota and workflow for remote work as a distinct discipline. Remote consultation and monitoring are not the same job done from a different chair; they demand different skills, different fatigue patterns and different tooling. Design rotas that account for the cognitive load of back-to-back video, the vigilance load of monitoring queues, and the need to blend remote review with in-person visits for virtual-ward patients. Give staff proper kit, connectivity, quiet space, training in remote clinical assessment, and workflow that surfaces the right patient at the right moment rather than burying alerts in an unmanageable list. Evaluate against safety, experience and outcomes — not just activity. It is tempting to report a remote service by counting contacts, but volume says nothing about whether it is safe, fair or effective. Track clinical outcomes and safety incidents, patient and carer experience, equity of access and outcome across groups, did-not-attend (DNA) and technology-failure rates, escalation and readmission rates from virtual wards, and staff experience. Compare against the pathway you replaced, publish what you find, and be willing to retire or redesign a remote model that is not delivering (see Topic 8.6 — Research & Real-World Evaluation, and Topic 6.2 — Benefits Realization & Value Management). Questions to discuss with your team # For this pathway, where is the line between what is clinically appropriate to do remotely and what is not — and who is allowed to override it? This matters because the pressure to move care remotely often comes from capacity and cost, while the judgement about whether it is safe for a given patient sits with the clinician in the moment. Debate the concrete cases: which presentations, which patient groups, which risk factors should never default to remote, and what red flags should force a face-to-face conversion. Surface the tension between a "remote-first" target and a clinician's discretion — if converting to in-person is slow, penalized, or invisible in the metrics, staff will feel pressured to keep patients on the wrong channel. Consider how the decision differs for a first contact versus a follow-up, and for a patient the clinician knows well versus a stranger. A good, honest answer produces explicit appropriateness criteria, a frictionless route to escalate to face-to-face, and agreement that clinical judgement overrides operational default every time — with no one second-guessed for using it. Who is our remote service quietly excluding, and how would we even know? Digital-first and remote models risk widening inequality precisely because the people least able to use them — older, poorer, disabled, isolated, or less digitally confident patients — are often those in greatest need. Discuss how your access data is broken down: can you see uptake, DNA rates and outcomes by age, deprivation, disability, ethnicity and language, or only a single headline number that hides the gaps? Probe the assisted-digital and non-digital routes: are they genuinely equivalent first-class options, or a grudging afterthought that adds delay and stigma? Consider the hardest cases — the patient with no smartphone, no data, no English, or no private space for a video call — and whether your service reaches them at all. A good answer names the groups at risk, commits to measuring outcomes not just access, and treats an equity gap as a defect to fix rather than an acceptable cost of efficiency. What exactly is our promise about the data we monitor — and is it resourced to be true? The most dangerous gap in remote care is between what patients and referrers think is happening to their readings and what the service is actually staffed to do. Debate the precise clinical promise for each monitoring stream: is it continuous surveillance, twice-daily review, or a patient-triggered alert model — and does everyone in the chain understand which? Examine the out-of-hours reality: who watches the data at 2am, what happens when a reading breaches a threshold, and how fast can a deteriorating patient be reached or readmitted. Surface the resourcing honestly — a monitoring service without the staff to act on what it sees is not a safety net but a liability, and the incident review after a missed deterioration will ask who owned the number. A good answer states the promise plainly, matches it to a named owner and a funded rota, and closes any gap between the reassurance given and the response guaranteed. When a virtual-ward patient deteriorates at home, what exactly happens — and have we rehearsed it? A virtual ward is only as safe as its worst-case pathway, yet the escalation and physical-readmission route is often the least designed part of the model. Walk through a concrete deterioration: who is contacted, in what order, how quickly a clinician can reach the home or bring the patient back to an acute bed, and what happens if that route is saturated on a winter evening. Surface the interfaces that tend to fail — the handover between the community team and the acute site, the ambulance conveyance that competes with the wider system, the out-of-hours gap when the board round is over and the caseload is still live. Consider whether your admission criteria are honest about which patients this ward can safely hold, and whether the caseload cap protects the response time or merely the headline capacity number. An honest answer names the escalation route step by step, states the time within which a patient can be readmitted, confirms it has been tested rather than assumed, and admits which patient types the ward should not be taking at all. How do we hold consent, privacy and safeguarding as a living practice once care is inside someone's home? Putting cameras, microphones and sensors into a household crosses a threshold a waiting room never does, and the people affected include those who never consented — other residents, carers, children in the background. Discuss how consent is made specific and revocable in practice: does the patient genuinely understand what is captured, who sees it, and how to switch it off, or is it a one-off signature at enrolment that no one revisits? Probe the safeguarding reality — a video call can reveal neglect, coercion, self-neglect or a carer at breaking point that the patient did not intend to show — and whether clinicians have a clear protocol for acting on what they see rather than recording it and moving on. Weigh the tension between the clinical value of richer home data and the intrusion it represents, especially for patients who feel unable to refuse a service they depend on. A good answer treats consent as ongoing and reversible, equips staff to respond to incidental safeguarding concerns, and is explicit about the privacy of everyone the monitoring touches, not just the patient. Are we honestly willing to redesign or retire this remote model if the evidence says it is not working? Remote and virtual services are frequently launched with political and capacity momentum behind them, which makes them hard to question once activity is flowing — but volume is not value, and a service that shifts activity without improving safety, equity or outcomes is consuming resource it cannot justify. Debate what evidence would actually change your mind: which outcome, safety, experience and equity measures you would track, against what comparison to the pathway you replaced, and what result would trigger a redesign or a stop. Examine the organizational honesty this demands — publishing an equity gap that is not yet closed, admitting a virtual ward is not freeing the capacity claimed, resisting the pull to keep a funded programme alive for its own sake. Consider who owns that decision and whether the evaluation is independent enough to deliver bad news. An honest answer commits to a real evaluation plan with pre-agreed thresholds for action, names who can call time on the model, and treats the willingness to stop as a mark of a safe service rather than a failure. In practice: a health & care example # Wyvern Vale Integrated Care System runs a frailty and acute respiratory virtual ward across two acute trusts and a community provider, aiming to care for up to 200 patients at home who would otherwise occupy hospital beds. Early enthusiasm produced a pilot that looked good on an activity dashboard — hundreds of patients enrolled — but a serious incident forced a rethink: a patient's oxygen readings had drifted downward over a weekend, no one had been rostered to review the overnight queue, and the deterioration was caught late. The ICS rebuilds the service around the operating model rather than the app. It sets clear admission and discharge criteria, appoints a named consultant clinical lead per virtual ward, and defines the staffing: a daily virtual board round, a caseload cap per clinician, community nurses for in-person visits, and a rapid-response route to readmit a patient physically within a defined time when home care is no longer safe. Crucially, it makes the monitoring promise explicit — patients are told this is twice-daily structured review plus a patient-triggered alert line, not continuous surveillance — and it funds a rota that actually covers evenings and weekends, with a single clinician owning the escalation queue at all times. Access and equity get equal attention. The team finds that early enrolment skewed towards patients who already owned smartphones and lived in less deprived areas, so it introduces loaned monitoring kit with pre-paid connectivity, a telephone-only monitoring option for those who cannot use the app, and translated onboarding with carer involvement. Consent is reworked to be specific and revocable, and staff get a safeguarding protocol for when a home video reveals a concern — after a video call surfaces a carer under visible strain, the team is able to route it to the right support rather than record it and move on. Six months on, Wyvern Vale evaluates against outcomes, not counts. It reports escalation and readmission rates, patient and carer experience, safety incidents, technology-failure rates, and uptake broken down by deprivation and age — and it finds the equity gap narrowing but not closed, which it publishes rather than hides. The virtual ward is now genuinely freeing acute capacity, but the leadership is clear that it earned that outcome through the rota, the escalation pathway and the inclusion work, not through the monitoring devices, which were never the hard part. x: Topic 4.0 — Technical Architecture, Cloud & Legacy In health and care, technical architecture is a clinical-safety, security, and public-money decision made years in advance: the platforms you stand up and the legacy you leave in place quietly determine whether care can be safe, joined-up, and affordable long after the people who chose them have moved on. Why this matters in health and care # Architecture is the set of long-lived structural choices beneath your digital services: what runs where, how components connect, what you build versus buy, and what you keep alive from the past. These choices are rarely visible to patients or clinicians, and rarely exciting to boards. Yet they shape everything that sits on top. A well-architected estate lets you add a new service quickly, share data safely, and recover fast when something breaks. A poorly-architected one makes every change slow, every integration fragile, and every incident worse. In health and care the stakes are high because the systems are consequential. When an ageing patient administration system falls over, ambulances divert and clinics cancel. When an unsupported operating system is exploited, confidential records are exposed and services stop — as the NHS learned in 2017 when the WannaCry ransomware attack spread through machines running software that could no longer be patched. That disruption was not a clever, targeted assault; it was the predictable consequence of accumulated technical debt in critical systems. Architecture decisions are therefore safety decisions, whether or not anyone frames them that way. They are also equity and trust decisions. Legacy systems that cannot share data leave the most complex patients — those touching many services — with the most fragmented records. Closed platforms that lock you into a single supplier drain money that could fund care. And the public reasonably expects the NHS to run on modern, secure, well-maintained technology; the gap between that expectation and the actual estate is itself a risk to trust. Finally, this is where a great deal of public money is committed for a very long time. The most expensive part of a system is rarely its purchase; it is the decade of hosting, licensing, maintenance, and eventual replacement that follows. Leaders who treat architecture as "something the technical team handles" are delegating some of the largest and longest-lasting financial commitments the organization makes. This topic is written so you can hold those decisions to account without being an engineer. Core concepts # Enterprise architecture is the discipline of aligning an organization's business processes, information, applications, and technology so they support strategy coherently rather than growing by accident. It takes the whole-organization view: which capabilities you need, which systems provide them, and where the gaps and duplications lie. Solution architecture is the narrower, project-level discipline of designing how a specific service will be built and fit into the wider estate. Both sit within the broader idea of systems architecture — the structural model of how components, interfaces, and behaviours combine into a working whole. Leaders do not need to practise these disciplines, but they should insist they exist, because their absence is how estates become unmanageable. Architecture is guided by architecture principles: a short, agreed set of statements — such as "reuse before buy, buy before build" or "build to open standards" — that make consistent decisions possible without every choice being escalated. Principles are enforced, lightly, by a design authority: a small group that reviews significant technical decisions. The healthy version of a design authority enables rather than blocks; it exists to prevent avoidable harm and duplication, not to slow teams down or gatekeep for its own sake. Cloud computing is the delivery of computing — servers, storage, databases, networking — as an on-demand service over the internet, rather than from hardware you own in your own building. A public cloud is run by a third-party provider and shared among many customers; a private cloud is dedicated to one organization; a hybrid cloud combines the two, often keeping some workloads on existing infrastructure while moving others out. Many governments, including the UK's, have adopted a "cloud-first" policy, meaning teams should consider public cloud before other options and justify not using it. Because cloud is billed by consumption rather than bought once, controlling that spend has become its own discipline — FinOps, the practice of bringing engineering and finance together so teams have visibility of, and accountability for, what their cloud usage actually costs. At the application layer, software as a service (SaaS) delivers a finished application over the web that the supplier hosts and maintains, so you configure rather than run it. Infrastructure and hosting — where and how your systems physically run — sit beneath all of this, and increasingly carry a carbon cost that belongs in the decision (see Topic 8.5 — Sustainability & Net Zero). A legacy system is an ageing but still-relied-upon system that is hard to change, often running unsupported software for which security patches are no longer issued. Legacy accumulates as technical debt — the future cost of expedient choices made in the past. A little debt is normal and even sensible; unmanaged debt at scale becomes a safety and security liability, because the systems most people depend on become the systems no one dares to touch. Managing this is the job of application portfolio management : keeping a clear inventory of every application, its cost, condition, and business value, so you can rationalize the estate — retiring, replacing, or consolidating systems — and decommission safely rather than leaving the old thing quietly running. Modern estates are held together by application programming interfaces (APIs) : defined interfaces through which one system offers a capability to another. Well-designed APIs let you assemble platforms — reusable services that many teams build on — while keeping components loosely coupled and replaceable. A useful discipline here is the "thinnest viable platform": build only the shared capability that genuinely reduces others' work, and no more. Underpinning secure design is secure by design , the principle that security is built in from the start rather than bolted on afterwards. And the financial frame for all of it is total cost of ownership (TCO) : the full lifetime cost of a system, not its purchase price — the lens through which the build/buy/configure choice, and the risk of vendor lock-in , should be judged. Best practices # Agree a short set of architecture principles and use them to decide. Write down a handful of clear, memorable principles — reuse before buy before build, build to open standards, cloud where it makes sense, secure by design, design for the whole care pathway — and let teams make most decisions themselves by applying them. Principles work only if they are genuinely used to say yes and no, and only if there are few enough to remember. This connects directly to Topic 1.1 — The Operating Model and Topic 1.2 — Digital Strategy & Roadmapping, which set the direction the principles serve. Run a design authority that enables rather than blocks. Establish a small, senior, cross-disciplinary group to review significant technical decisions — those that are expensive, hard to reverse, affect many services, or carry safety and security risk. Give it a fast, lightweight route so routine choices are not dragged through it, and hold it to a service standard: it should help teams find a good answer, not simply refuse. A design authority that becomes a bottleneck will be routed around, and shadow architecture is worse than none. Adopt cloud deliberately, workload by workload, not as a slogan. Treat "cloud-first" as a default to be reasoned about, not an instruction to move everything. Assess each workload for suitability, data residency, resilience, cost at scale, and the effort to migrate, and be honest that lift-and-shift of an unchanged legacy application often just relocates the problem at higher cost. Weigh the carbon dimension explicitly, since where and how you host affects emissions (see Topic 8.5 — Sustainability & Net Zero), and design for portability so a future move between providers remains possible. Maintain a live application portfolio and manage technical debt as a named risk. Keep an accurate inventory of every application, its business owner, cost, supportability, and the risk it carries, and review it regularly. Put technical debt and unsupported software on the corporate risk register with the same seriousness as clinical or financial risk, because that is what it is. What you cannot see, you cannot fund, prioritize, or safely retire, and estates that are never inventoried are exactly the ones that fail without warning. Rationalize the estate and decommission safely. Actively retire duplicated, obsolete, and end-of-life systems rather than letting them linger "just in case", because every live system is an attack surface, a licence cost, and a maintenance burden. Decommissioning is a project in its own right: migrate or archive the data under clear retention rules, confirm nothing still depends on the system, communicate with users, and verify before you switch off. Done well, rationalization frees money and reduces risk; done carelessly, it destroys records or breaks a dependency no one documented. Prefer open standards, APIs, and loosely coupled components. Design so capabilities are exposed through documented, versioned APIs, so that one component can be replaced without rebuilding everything around it. This is the architectural foundation for the interoperability discussed in Topic 4.3 — Interoperability & Data Standards, and it is your main defence against lock-in. It costs a little more up front than a direct, hard-wired connection, and repays that many times over the first time you need to change a supplier or add a service. Build the thinnest viable platform, and no more. When you create a shared platform for others to build on, resist the urge to make it comprehensive from day one. Provide the smallest reusable capability that genuinely removes work for teams, prove it is used, and grow it in response to real demand. Over-built platforms become their own legacy — expensive, rigid, and resented — while a thin, well-run platform earns adoption and evolves with need. Make security architecture and secure-by-design non-negotiable. Bring security thinking into design from the first sketch, not as a pre-launch gate: minimize the attack surface, apply least privilege, segment networks, and assume components will be probed. In health and care this is inseparable from clinical safety and information governance ( Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management; Topic 1.7 — Information Governance, Data Protection & Cyber Security), because a breach is both a data harm and, when it stops systems, a patient-safety event. Unsupported, unpatchable software is a security decision you are making by default — so make it deliberately, with mitigations, or not at all. Decide build, buy, or configure on total cost of ownership, not sticker price. For each capability, compare building bespoke, buying a product, and configuring an existing platform on their full lifetime cost — hosting, licensing, integration, support, upgrades, and eventual exit — not the initial price. Favour buying or configuring for commodity needs and reserve building for genuine differentiation, and weigh the lock-in each option creates. Work this through with commercial colleagues ( Topic 6.3 — Procurement & Commercial), because the cheapest time to secure open interfaces and exit rights is before you sign. Treat cloud spend as a shared engineering-and-finance discipline (FinOps). Give teams clear visibility of what their services cost by tagging cloud resources to owners, right-size instances against real usage, and turn off idle or over-provisioned resources rather than paying for them month after month. Make the teams that run a service accountable for its running cost, so the people best placed to reduce waste are the ones who see the bill. Pay-as-you-go cloud without this discipline quietly consumes budget that should be funding care, and the drift is rarely noticed until an invoice forces the question. Architect for cost as a first-class non-functional requirement, weighed against carbon and resilience. Treat cost the way you treat performance, security, and availability: a property you design for deliberately, estimate before you build, and review as usage grows. Weigh it explicitly against carbon (see Topic 8.5 — Sustainability & Net Zero) and against resilience, because the three often move together — but never chase the lowest bill at the expense of safety, recoverability, or patient outcomes. The right answer is the lowest cost that still meets your clinical-safety and resilience obligations, not the cheapest option in isolation. Questions to discuss with your team # Which of our critical systems are unsupported or unpatchable today, and what is our actual exposure if one is attacked or fails? Start from the systems clinical and operational services genuinely cannot function without, and establish concretely which run software that no longer receives security updates or vendor support. Ask what would happen — to patients, to staff, to data — if each were hit by ransomware or simply stopped, and how long recovery would take. Distinguish systems you have consciously accepted risk on, with mitigations in place, from those whose fragility no one has assessed. Consider whether this exposure is visible on the corporate risk register or buried in a spreadsheet no board has seen. Reflect on WannaCry: the harm came not from sophistication but from known, unaddressed debt in critical systems. If you cannot answer this with evidence, that gap is itself your most urgent finding, because you cannot fund a risk you have not named. Where are we locked in, and what would it truly cost us to leave our biggest platform? Many organizations discover the real price of a closed system only when they try to change it. Work through what it would actually take to move off your largest clinical or corporate platform: whether you can extract your data in a usable, standard form, what proprietary interfaces would have to be unpicked, and what your contract says about ownership and exit. Consider whether "cloud" has quietly become lock-in of a different kind, with data and tooling so entangled in one provider that leaving is impractical. Weigh this against the openness of alternatives and any national platforms you could reuse instead. This is not an argument for churning suppliers; it is about understanding your leverage before you next negotiate, and not letting one vendor's roadmap silently become your only option. Are we investing enough in maintaining and rationalizing what we already have, or only in the new and visible? New systems attract funding and attention; the unglamorous work of patching, upgrading, consolidating, and safely retiring rarely does, which is exactly how debt accumulates. Ask what proportion of your digital budget actually goes to keeping the existing estate safe and current versus building new things, and whether anyone owns that balance deliberately. Discuss whether decommissioning is ever properly resourced, or whether old systems simply linger because switching them off is nobody's job. Consider the duplicated applications doing the same thing across the organization, and what it would take to consolidate them. Think about who, at board level, is accountable for the health of the estate as a whole rather than for individual projects. An organization that only funds the new is borrowing against its own future safety, and the repayment always comes due at the worst possible moment. Do we actually know what our cloud costs, who owns that bill, and whether the spend is under control? Pay-as-you-go cloud can quietly consume budget that should be funding care, and the drift is rarely noticed until an invoice forces the question. Ask whether cloud resources are tagged to the teams and services that own them, whether anyone right-sizes instances against real usage, and whether idle or over-provisioned resources are ever switched off. Discuss whether the people who run a service see and answer for its running cost, or whether cloud spend lands as a single unexplained line in a central budget no one can decompose. Consider whether cost is treated as a first-class non-functional requirement — estimated before you build and reviewed as usage grows — or only discovered after the fact. Be honest about the tension between engineering autonomy and financial control, and about weighing cost against carbon and resilience rather than simply chasing the lowest bill. An honest answer names who holds the FinOps discipline and shows the evidence that it is working, rather than assuming the cloud is cheaper because it is modern. When we need a new capability, how do we decide between building it, buying it, and configuring something we already have — and on what basis? The instinct to build bespoke, or to buy the product with the best demo, often wins before anyone has compared the full lifetime cost. Work through how your last few significant choices were actually made: whether hosting, licensing, integration, support, upgrades, and eventual exit were weighed, or only the initial price. Ask whether you reserve building for genuine differentiation and default to buying or configuring for commodity needs, or whether custom builds quietly proliferate because a team preferred them. Consider who is in the room for these decisions — commercial and clinical colleagues as well as engineers — and whether the lock-in each option creates is assessed before signing rather than discovered later. Reflect on whether your architecture principles ("reuse before buy, buy before build") genuinely bind these choices or are quietly ignored. An honest answer can point to real decisions where total cost of ownership, not sticker price, changed the outcome. Do we have the in-house architecture capability to hold our own decisions, or are we dependent on the suppliers we are meant to be holding to account? Architecture is where the largest and longest-lasting commitments are made, yet many organizations have hollowed out the very capability needed to make them well, relying on the vendors whose products are under evaluation to tell them what good looks like. Ask whether you have credible enterprise and solution architecture skill on your own side, and whether your design authority is staffed to enable teams or merely to rubber-stamp. Discuss whether significant, hard-to-reverse decisions are genuinely tested against agreed principles, or whether they are effectively delegated to whichever supplier is closest to the problem. Consider how you would even recognize a bad architectural recommendation if you had no independent expertise to challenge it. Weigh the cost of building and retaining this capability against the far larger cost of the lock-in and rework that its absence produces. An honest answer distinguishes the decisions you can genuinely own from those you are currently taking on trust. In practice: a health & care example # An acute hospital trust's technical estate has grown organically for two decades. At its heart sits a patient administration system running on an operating system the vendor stopped supporting eighteen months ago; around it are more than two hundred applications, many bought departmentally, several doing overlapping jobs, and no one holds a complete list.
