x: Topic 5.1 — Project-Led Work In one sentence: Project-led work is the right tool when the job has a defined scope, a finite life, and a clear end state — a temporary, controlled endeavour delivered to agreed time, cost, and quality, then closed. Why this matters in health and care # Not everything is a living service. Some of the most important work in health and care is genuinely finite: migrating from one electronic patient record to another, rolling out Wi-Fi across a hospital estate, replacing end-of-life servers, decommissioning a legacy system before a supplier contract ends, or delivering the digital element of a new hospital build. This work has a beginning, a middle, and a definite end. Managing it as an open-ended product would waste money and blur accountability; it needs the discipline of a project. Project management earns its keep here precisely because the stakes are high and the constraints are hard. A data-migration cutover has a fixed go-live weekend, a patient-safety risk if records are lost or corrupted, and a contractual cliff-edge if the old system switches off. Public money is committed against a business case, and Parliament, auditors, and boards will ask whether it was spent as approved. Project-led work provides the governance — a business case, stage gates, and a controlled close — that lets a board commit capital with confidence and stop the work cleanly if the justification falls away. The danger is using this tool for the wrong job. Project-led governance applied to an evolving digital service produces the "build it and abandon it" pathology described in Topic 5.0 — Product-Led Work. This topic explains where project-led work is the right instrument, and where its limits begin. It sits alongside Topic 5.2 — Programme-Led Work, which coordinates multiple projects, and Topic 5.3 — Enterprise Portfolio & Project Management (EPPM), which chooses between these tools. Core concepts # Project. A temporary organization created to deliver one or more defined outputs to an agreed specification, within constraints of time, cost, and quality. The defining feature is that it is temporary — it exists to reach a defined end and then disband. The iron triangle (scope, time, cost). The classic constraint model: scope, schedule, and budget are interdependent, and quality is affected by how they are balanced. Change one and you change the others; project control is largely the discipline of managing this trade-off transparently. PRINCE2 (PRojects IN Controlled Environments). The UK government's structured project method, widely used across the NHS and public sector. It is built on principles (continued business justification, defined roles, manage by stages, manage by exception, focus on products, learn from experience, tailor to the environment) and organizes work into controlled stages with a project board providing direction. PMI / PMBOK. The Project Management Institute 's Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge is the dominant international counterpart, framing project work around performance domains and principles rather than a prescribed staged process. PRINCE2 and PMBOK are complementary lenses on the same discipline. Business case . The document that justifies the project: the problem, the options appraised, the expected benefits, the costs, and the risks. In PRINCE2 the business case is living — it is checked at every stage boundary, and if continued justification disappears, the right decision is to stop. In UK public bodies this is usually structured as HM Treasury 's Five Case Model (strategic, economic, commercial, financial, management). Stage gates . A PRINCE2 project is divided into management stages separated by decision gates. At each boundary the project board makes a deliberate stop/proceed decision: it reviews progress and the business case, approves the next stage plan, and commits resources only for that stage. This is how a board keeps control and avoids throwing good money after bad. RAID log. A single register of Risks, Assumptions, Issues, and Dependencies — the project manager's core control artefact. RAID makes uncertainty visible and manageable: risks are things that might happen, issues are things that have, assumptions are what the plan relies on, and dependencies are what the plan needs from elsewhere. Best practices # Start with an honest business case and keep it alive. Use a recognized structure (the Five Case Model in UK public bodies) to appraise real options, not a single predetermined answer. Then treat the business case as a living document reviewed at every stage gate — continued business justification is the first PRINCE2 principle, and losing it is a legitimate reason to stop. Define scope precisely and control changes to it. The value of a project is a clear, bounded definition of "done". Agree the scope, baseline it, and run every proposed change through a change-control process so scope creep does not quietly consume the budget and the timeline. Manage by stages with real decision gates. Break the work into management stages and hold a genuine stop/proceed review at each boundary. A gate that always says "proceed" is theatre; the discipline only works if stopping or re-planning is a real option the board will exercise. Run a live RAID log and escalate by exception. Maintain Risks, Assumptions, Issues, and Dependencies in one place, review it regularly, and use PRINCE2's "manage by exception" — the project manager runs within agreed tolerances and escalates to the board only when a tolerance is threatened. This keeps senior time focused on genuine decisions. Assign clear, single-point accountability. PRINCE2 insists on defined roles: a project board with a senior responsible owner/executive owning the business case, a senior user representing those who will use the output, and a senior supplier. Ambiguous accountability is the most common cause of drift. Plan the transition to live service before you start. A project delivers an output; someone must operate it afterwards. Agree the receiving team, the support model, and the clinical-safety handover (DCB0160 for deployment) as part of the project, so go-live is not a cliff-edge into an ownership vacuum. Bake in clinical safety, information governance, and testing. For any system touching patient data, the clinical safety case, DPIA, and cutover/rollback testing are not optional extras — they are gating deliverables. A migration without a tested rollback plan is not ready to go live. Close the project deliberately and capture lessons. A defined end means a defined close: confirm the outputs are accepted, hand over to operations, release the team, and record lessons learned (PRINCE2's lessons log). An un-closed project leaks resources and accountability indefinitely. Questions to discuss with your team # Is the work in front of us genuinely finite with a defined end state, or are we reaching for project governance because it is the funding route we know? This is the decisive question the topic turns on, because project-led discipline is the right instrument only when the job truly has a beginning, a middle, and a definite end. In a health and care organization the pull toward project shape is strong — capital budgeting, business-case machinery, and board reporting are all built for it — so an evolving digital service can get dressed up as a project simply because that is how money is released, which then produces the build-it-and-abandon-it pathology. The debate should examine each candidate honestly: a pathology system replacement before a supplier withdraws support has a hard contractual cliff-edge and is unambiguously finite, whereas "improve the patient app" has no end state and belongs in Topic 5.0 . Consider whether there is a real go-live after which the team should disband, or whether someone will need to keep improving the thing indefinitely. A good answer resists using project governance as a habit, names the concrete end state and the event that defines "done", and is willing to say that some of what we currently run as projects should never have been projects at all. At our stage gates, would this board actually stop or re-plan a project that has lost its justification — and can we point to a time we did? Stage gates are only a control if stopping is a genuine option the board will exercise; a gate that always says "proceed" is theatre, and continued business justification is the first PRINCE2 principle precisely because losing it should end the work. The tension in health and care is acute: halting a part-built EPR migration or a laboratory-system cutover feels like admitting failure, wasting sunk cost, and disrupting clinicians who have already changed their plans, so boards rationalize pressing on even as the business case quietly evaporates. Bring a real example to the discussion — a project where testing revealed the data-mapping risk was worse than assumed, or where benefits slipped — and ask whether the gate was used as designed or rubber-stamped. Consider what tolerances trigger escalation, who at the board has the standing to call a stop, and whether sunk-cost reasoning is named and challenged in the room. An honest answer admits where gates have been formalities, describes the conditions under which the board genuinely would halt or re-scope, and treats the authority to stop before a public write-off as the discipline's real value rather than a threat. Who receives each project's output as a live service, and how do we make clinical-safety handover and ongoing ownership a gating deliverable rather than a cliff-edge? A project delivers an output; something finite ends, but the thing it produced must be operated, improved, and kept safe long after the team disbands — and the most common quiet failure is that no one owns it on the other side. In a system touching patient data this is not administrative tidiness: the DCB0160 deployment safety case, the DPIA, a tested rollback, and a named receiving team are what stand between a controlled go-live and an ownership vacuum where safety risks accumulate unmanaged. The debate should force clarity about the transition before the project starts, not at go-live weekend: which operational team takes it, what the support model is, and whether that team has the capacity and mode of work (product-led, per Topic 5.0 ) to keep improving it. Consider concrete recent go-lives and whether the handover was planned or improvised, and whether "the project is done" was allowed to mean "and now it is nobody's job". A good answer names the receiving team and support model up front, treats the safety handover as a gate the project cannot pass without, and explicitly assigns the ongoing improvement of the live service to the right mode of work rather than leaving it to drift. When the iron triangle bites and scope, time, and cost collide, which constraint do we flex, and is patient safety ever allowed to be the variable that gives? Every real project eventually hits the moment where the schedule, the budget, and the promised scope cannot all hold, and how the team resolves that squeeze reveals what it actually values. In health and care the trap is distinctive: because the end date is often a hard contractual cliff-edge — a supplier withdrawing support, a lease expiring, a data-centre closing — time frequently cannot move, so the pressure lands silently on quality, which in a clinical system means cutting testing, compressing validation, or shipping with known data-mapping defects. The discussion should name, in advance, which corner of the triangle the organization will protect and which it will sacrifice, and be explicit that clinical safety and information governance are not the release valve even when everything else is fixed. Look at a recent cutover and ask what quietly gave when the dates held: was it the rollback rehearsal, the clinical-validation window, the training? Consider who has the authority to move the go-live date rather than erode the safety margin, and whether that conversation happens openly at the board or by default on the ground. An honest answer states the priority order before the crunch, treats a slipped date or a re-planned stage as a legitimate outcome, and refuses to let unspoken schedule pressure convert into unlogged clinical risk. Is our RAID log a live instrument that changes what we do, or a document we maintain to look governed — and would it surface the risk that actually sinks the project? A RAID log earns its place only if reviewing it changes decisions; the common pathology is a register written at kick-off, presented at boards, and never genuinely acted on while the risks that matter mature unwatched. In a migration or cutover the decisive risks are often specific and knowable — historical results that will not map cleanly to new reference ranges, a dependency on another team's firewall changes, an assumption that clinical validation resource will be free when it is needed — and the question is whether the log names those concretely or hides behind generic entries like "resource constraints". The debate should test whether escalation by exception is real: does the project manager run within agreed tolerances and raise the board's attention only when one is threatened, or does everything either stay silent or become a crisis? Consider whether near-misses and materialized issues feed back into how the next stage is planned, or simply get logged and forgotten. A good answer can point to a decision the RAID log actually changed, distinguishes the two or three risks that could genuinely stop the project from the long tail of minor ones, and treats the log as a working control rather than an artefact produced for assurance. After we close and disband, does anyone check whether the benefits in the business case actually materialized — and would we know if they did not? The business case promises benefits to justify the spend, but project-led work naturally ends at go-live and team release, so the moment of truth — did the migration actually reduce risk, cut cost, or improve care — usually falls after everyone has moved on and no one is accountable for confirming it. This matters acutely in public health and care, where money is committed against a Five Case business case that Parliament, auditors, and boards were told would deliver specific outcomes, yet benefits realization is the step most often skipped because the project that would have owned it no longer exists. The discussion should decide who inherits benefits tracking when the project closes, over what period, and against which baseline measurements — which have to be captured before go-live or they are lost. Consider a recent completed project and ask plainly whether anyone has since checked its promised benefits, and whether a shortfall would ever reach the board that approved it. An honest answer assigns post-closure benefits ownership to a standing function rather than the disbanded team, captures the baseline while the project is still live, and is willing to record that a project delivered its output on time and to budget yet did not deliver the value that justified it. In practice: a health & care example # An acute trust must replace its ageing pathology laboratory information management system before the incumbent supplier withdraws support in 14 months. This is textbook project-led work: fixed end date, defined scope, a hard contractual cliff-edge, and acute patient-safety risk if results are lost in migration. The trust writes a Five Case business case appraising three options (upgrade in place, procure a new system, share a regional instance), selects procurement, and stands up a PRINCE2 project with a clear board: an executive owning the business case, a senior user (the lead biomedical scientist), and the senior supplier. The work is split into management stages — procurement, build and configuration, data migration, testing, and go-live — each ending in a decision gate. The project manager runs a RAID log. A key risk is that historical results may not map cleanly to the new system's reference ranges; a dependency is the network team's firewall changes; an assumption is that clinical validation resource will be available for testing. At the migration stage gate, testing reveals the data-mapping risk is worse than assumed, so the board uses the gate as designed: it does not blindly proceed, but approves a re-planned stage with an extended validation window and a tested rollback plan, protecting patient safety over the original schedule. Go-live happens over a controlled weekend with the rollback plan on standby and a DCB0160 clinical-safety sign-off. The system is accepted, handed to the operations team who will run it, lessons are logged, and the project is formally closed. The team disbands — correctly, because the job is genuinely done. What comes next (continuous improvement of the live service) is a different mode of work, and the trust is careful not to keep a full project team running perpetually to do it. Sector lenses # Startup # A small digital-health company rarely runs formal PRINCE2 projects, but genuinely finite work still appears — a one-off data migration onto a new cloud platform, a Cyber Essentials or DTAC certification push, pen-test remediation before a big NHS contract. The startup handles these as lightweight, time-boxed efforts with a named owner and a clear definition of done, borrowing the discipline (fixed scope, an end date, a go/no-go) without the ceremony (no formal project board, no five-stage gating). Funding is really founder attention and runway, so the risk is that finite work gets squeezed between product sprints and never actually closed. The corrective is naming a single owner and a hard deadline, and treating the certification or migration as done-and-dusted rather than perpetually "in progress". Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home, or a single-site clinic — meets project-led work as occasional but unavoidable events: switching clinical system supplier, migrating to a new practice-management platform, or replacing end-of-life devices before support lapses. The organization has real patients and ongoing operations but no dedicated project or IT function, so the "project team" is usually the practice manager or a registered manager doing this alongside the day job, often leaning on the incoming supplier to run the migration. The discipline that survives contact with this reality is the lightweight core: a clear end state, a baselined scope so the supplier does not quietly expand it, a named accountable person, and a tested rollback before any cutover that touches patient records. The trap is outsourcing not just the work but the judgement — accepting the supplier's go-live date and data-mapping assurances without independent checking — because the same clinical-safety and information-governance duties (DCB0160, a DPIA) apply regardless of how small the organization is. The corrective is to keep ownership of the go/no-go decision and the acceptance criteria in-house, even when every other pair of hands belongs to the vendor. Enterprise # A large NHS trust or integrated care system (ICS) is where project-led work is most at home: EPR replacements, estate-wide Wi-Fi, data-centre exits, and cutovers all carry hard contractual and patient-safety cliff-edges. Here the full apparatus is justified — a Five Case business case, a PRINCE2 board with a named executive/SRO, senior user and senior supplier, management stages with real gates, and a live RAID log — because the sums are large, the safety exposure is acute, and internal audit and the board will scrutinize the spend. x: Topic 5.2 — Programme-Led Work In one sentence: Programme-led work coordinates a set of related projects and products toward a strategic change that none could deliver alone, holding a clear line of sight from the work to the benefits it is meant to realize. Why this matters in health and care # The biggest changes in health and care are never a single project. Rolling out a shared care record across an integrated care system (ICS), moving a region to a single electronic patient record , transforming an urgent-and-emergency-care pathway, or delivering a virtual-ward programme across multiple trusts — each of these is a coordinated bundle of projects, product teams, workforce change, estates work, and clinical redesign, aligned to one strategic outcome. Manage the pieces in isolation and they collide: incompatible data standards, duplicated spend, contradictory clinical workflows, and benefits that never actually materialize. Programme management exists to hold that coalition together and to keep it pointed at outcomes and benefits , not just outputs. This matters acutely in health and care because system-wide change touches patient safety across organizational boundaries, commits large sums of public money over several years, and depends on many autonomous organizations choosing to move in step. A programme provides the leadership, the shared target state, and the benefits discipline to make that happen — and, just as importantly, to know whether it is working. The recurring failure it guards against is the programme that spends millions, delivers a pile of technical outputs, and yet changes nothing measurable for patients or staff. This topic uses Managing Successful Programmes (MSP), the UK public sector's dominant framework, and shows how programme-led work coexists with the project-led ( Topic 5.1 — Project-Led Work) and product-led ( Topic 5.0 — Product-Led Work) modes it coordinates. Topic 5.3 — Enterprise Portfolio & Project Management (EPPM) then explains how an organization prioritizes across many programmes. Core concepts # Programme. A temporary, flexible organization created to coordinate, direct, and oversee a group of related projects and activities to deliver outcomes and benefits aligned to strategic objectives. A programme differs from a project in that it is defined by the outcome and benefits it seeks, and it manages the uncertainty of coordinating many moving parts, rather than delivering a single fixed output. MSP (Managing Successful Programmes). The UK best-practice framework for managing transformational change through multiple related projects. It is organized around principles, themes, and a "transformational flow" of processes, and is designed for large, complex change where the end state is known in direction but the path involves many interdependent deliveries. Vision and blueprint. The vision is the compelling picture of the future the programme will create. The blueprint makes it concrete: it describes the target operating model — the future state of processes, organization, technology, information, and roles (often summarized as POTI). The blueprint is the reference point every project is steered toward, so the pieces add up to a coherent whole. Benefits realisation . The heart of programme management. Benefits are the measurable improvements that justify the investment — reduced delayed discharges, fewer duplicated tests, faster diagnosis, lower administrative burden. MSP treats identifying, mapping, measuring, and actively managing benefits across the whole lifecycle as a core discipline, because outputs only create value when they are used to change how care is delivered. Tranches. MSP breaks a programme into tranches — blocks of work ending at a major review point where a step of capability has been delivered and benefits realization can begin. A tranche is a moment to demonstrate outcomes, reassess the blueprint against reality, and decide whether to continue, adjust, or stop, rather than merely a slice of the schedule. Programme board and SRO. The Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) is the single individual accountable for the programme meeting its objectives and realizing its benefits, with enough seniority and authority to lead and to make decisions. The SRO chairs a programme board — typically a business change manager, project leads, and senior stakeholders — that provides direction across organizational boundaries. Business change manager (BCM). MSP's distinctive role: someone from the operational business (not the delivery team) accountable for embedding the change and realizing the benefits on the ground. The BCM is why programmes deliver outcomes and not just outputs — projects hand over capability, the BCM turns it into benefit. Best practices # Anchor the programme in a vision and a blueprint. Define the strategic outcome and translate it into a concrete target operating model (processes, organization, technology, information — POTI). Every constituent project and product is then steered toward the same future state, which is what stops a coalition of deliveries from fragmenting. Manage benefits, not just deliverables. Build a benefits map linking each output to the outcomes and measurable benefits it should produce, with owners and baselines. Review benefits actively across the programme, and be willing to stop work that is not going to pay back — MSP's emphasis on benefits realization is the discipline that separates a programme from an expensive to-do list. Structure the work into tranches with real review points. Deliver capability in tranches, and at each tranche boundary demonstrate the benefits realized so far, re-test the blueprint against what you have learned, and make a genuine continue/adjust/stop decision. Early tranches should target visible quick wins to build stakeholder confidence for the harder later ones. Appoint an empowered SRO and a real programme board. Name a single SRO with the seniority and authority to direct the programme and decide across organizational boundaries, and convene a board that genuinely represents the affected organizations. Programmes fail when accountability is diffuse or the SRO cannot actually make cross-boundary decisions stick. Put business change managers in the operational business. Assign BCMs from the frontline organizations to own adoption and benefit realization where care is delivered. Capability delivered but not adopted realizes no benefit; the BCM role is the mechanism that closes that gap. Coordinate — do not micromanage — the constituent projects and products. The programme sets the blueprint, the interdependencies, the standards, and the benefits; it lets projects and product teams deliver within that frame. It manages the seams — shared data standards, information governance, sequencing, and shared infrastructure — not the internal detail of each delivery. Manage cross-cutting risk, dependency, and stakeholders relentlessly. The value a programme adds over standalone projects is largely in managing what happens between them. Maintain a programme-level view of interdependencies and shared risks, and invest heavily in stakeholder engagement across autonomous organizations, since alignment is voluntary, not commanded. Close the programme when the change is embedded, and hand ongoing services to product teams. A programme is temporary. When the blueprint is achieved and benefits are being realized, close it deliberately, transfer any enduring services to durable product teams ( Topic 5.0 ), and keep tracking benefits into business-as-usual — many benefits accrue after the programme ends. Questions to discuss with your team # Does our senior responsible owner actually have the authority to make decisions stick across sovereign partner organizations, or only the accountability when they do not? Programme-led work lives or dies on cross-boundary authority, because the change spans autonomous trusts, primary care, community, mental health, and social care that cannot simply be ordered to move in step. The characteristic failure is a named SRO who carries the personal, public accountability for benefits but lacks the standing to compel a reluctant partner to adopt a shared data standard or change a clinical workflow — accountability without authority. The debate should be candid about where real power sits in the system: whether the programme board genuinely represents the affected organizations or is a reporting forum, whether the SRO is senior enough that their decisions are honoured across sovereign boundaries, and what happens when one partner declines to move. Consider a recent cross-organization decision and trace whether it actually held. A good answer names who the SRO is and tests their authority against a concrete cross-boundary conflict, is honest about the organizations that can effectively opt out, and treats a representative board and embedded business change managers as load-bearing mechanisms for voluntary alignment rather than governance decoration. How will we know this programme has realized benefits and not merely delivered outputs — and who, in the operational business, is accountable for turning capability into benefit? Output theatre is the recurring pathology the topic warns against: a programme spends millions, produces a pile of interoperability platforms and integrations, and yet nothing measurable changes for patients or staff. The distinction that prevents it is the business change manager — someone from the frontline operation, not the delivery team, accountable for embedding the change and realizing benefit where care is delivered — so the question forces the team to name those people and confirm they exist. The tension is that delivery is visible and satisfying while adoption is slow, unglamorous, and easy to assume will just happen; a shared care record buried behind an extra login realizes no benefit however well it is built. Bring the benefits map to the discussion and stress-test whether each output is linked to an owned, baselined, measurable benefit (fewer duplicated tests, reduced delayed discharges) or whether benefits are merely asserted. An honest answer names a BCM in each partner organization, admits where benefits are currently unowned or unmeasured, and accepts that some benefits accrue only after the programme closes and must be tracked into business-as-usual. Are we tranching this programme to bank early benefits and create real continue/adjust/stop points, or drifting toward a big-bang delivery that defers all the risk to one late moment? Tranches are what separate a programme from an expensive frozen plan: each tranche boundary should deliver a step of capability, demonstrate benefits realized so far, re-test the blueprint against what has actually been learned, and support a genuine decision to continue, adjust, or stop. The health and care temptation is to sequence for engineering convenience and defer visible value — connecting every trust before anyone can use anything — which loads all the risk into a single late delivery and leaves the board with no evidence to defend continued investment through fiscal and political cycles. The debate should examine whether early tranches target deliberate quick wins that build stakeholder confidence for the harder later work, and whether the review points are real decisions or schedule checkpoints. Consider what the first demonstrable benefit is, how soon it lands, and what the board would actually do at a tranche review if adoption lagged or the blueprint proved wrong. A good answer describes concrete tranches with early, measurable wins, treats each boundary as a real go/no-go with the blueprint genuinely open to revision, and is honest about any pressure to defer value to the end. Do we have a single, maintained blueprint of the target operating model, or is each project quietly optimizing toward its own version of the future? The blueprint — the concrete POTI target operating model of processes, organization, technology, and information — is what makes the pieces add up to a coherent whole rather than a collision of locally sensible decisions. Without one, each constituent project rationally optimizes for its own scope: one trust picks a data standard that suits its incumbent EPR, another designs a clinical workflow around its own staffing, and the shared care record fragments into integrations that technically connect but do not cohere. The tension is that maintaining a blueprint feels like overhead to delivery teams under pressure to ship, and it must be a living reference re-tested at every tranche rather than a document written once and shelved. The debate should establish whether the blueprint actually exists in usable form, who owns it, and whether real project decisions are being steered by it or merely reconciled to it after the fact. Consider a recent design choice in one project and ask whether the blueprint shaped it or was silently overridden. An honest answer can point to a current blueprint, names its owner, and is candid about where local optimization is already pulling the target state apart. When the programme closes, what endures — and have we named the durable product teams that will run the capability and keep tracking benefits into business-as-usual? A programme is temporary by definition, but the shared care record, the interoperability platform, and the benefits they produce are not, so closure is a design problem to be planned from the start rather than an afterthought. The recurring failure at each end of the spectrum is real: some programmes never close and harden into permanent bureaucracies long after the change is embedded, while others close abruptly and strand a live clinical service with no durable owner. The topic is explicit that enduring services should transfer to durable product teams ( Topic 5.0 ) and that many benefits accrue only after the programme ends and must be tracked into BAU — which means the receiving teams and the ongoing benefits ownership have to be identified while the programme still has the authority and funding to establish them. The debate should surface who will run each enduring capability, how it will be funded once transformation money stops, and who keeps measuring benefits when the programme board has dissolved. A good answer names the specific product teams and BAU owners, describes the funding transition honestly, and treats closure and benefit tracking as planned tranches rather than a hopeful handover. How are we managing the seams between projects — shared standards, information governance, sequencing, and shared infrastructure — rather than the internals of each delivery? The value a programme adds over a set of standalone projects lives almost entirely in the space between them: the interdependencies, the shared data standards, the information-governance and consent framework, and the common infrastructure that no single project owns but all depend on. The temptation for a programme team is to drift into micromanaging the internals of each delivery — comfortable, visible work — while the genuinely hard cross-cutting seams go unmanaged until they surface as an integration failure or an information-governance blocker at go-live. In health and care these seams are unusually load-bearing, because data flows and consent cross sovereign organizational and regulatory boundaries where alignment is voluntary and legal duties are shared but unevenly resourced. The debate should test whether there is a programme-level view of interdependencies and shared risks, who owns the shared standards and infrastructure, and whether the programme is coordinating seams or meddling in project detail. An honest answer identifies the specific seams that most threaten the outcome, names their owners, and is candid about whether the programme is adding value at the boundaries or duplicating the work of the projects it should be enabling. In practice: a health & care example # An ICS sets out to deliver a shared care record giving clinicians across acute, community, mental health, primary care, and social care a unified view of a person. No single project can deliver this: it spans multiple trusts, several source systems, information-governance agreements, clinical-workflow redesign, and public engagement. It is coordinated as an MSP programme. The SRO — an ICS executive with genuine cross-system authority — chairs a programme board with representatives from each partner organization and named business change managers in each. The programme sets a vision ("the right information, about the right person, available to the right clinician, at the point of care") and a blueprint describing the target operating model: the data-sharing architecture and standards ( HL7 FHIR -based interoperability ), the information-governance framework, the consent model, and the redesigned clinical workflows. The work is organized into tranches. Tranche one connects two willing acute trusts and delivers a read-only record, a deliberate quick win that proves the approach and lets the board demonstrate an early benefit — a measurable reduction in duplicated tests — to build confidence. At the tranche-one review, the board learns that clinician adoption lags where the record is buried in an extra login, so it adjusts the blueprint to prioritize single-sign-on integration before widening rollout. Underneath the programme, the modes coexist. The interoperability platform is run by a durable product team ( Topic 5.0 ) that keeps improving it across the whole programme and beyond. Each trust's connection is a bounded project ( Topic 5.1 ) with its own business case and go-live. The programme itself coordinates the blueprint, the standards, the interdependencies, and — through the BCMs — the benefits realization. When the blueprint is achieved and duplicated-testing and delayed-discharge benefits are flowing, the programme closes; the platform product team endures, and benefit tracking continues into business-as-usual. Sector lenses # Startup # Few startups run programmes in the MSP sense — they lack the multi-organization scope that defines one — but a scale-up deploying across several trusts effectively becomes a programme participant . Its realistic role is as a supplier inside someone else's programme: aligning its product to the programme blueprint, hitting tranche milestones, and feeding the benefits case that the SRO must evidence. Funding and survival depend on the programme continuing, so the startup treats tranche reviews as existential go/no-go points and invests in the business change managers' success, because adoption on the ground is what renews its contract. The discipline it must borrow is benefits language — framing its value as realized outcomes, not features shipped. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home, or a small health-tech supplier past the startup stage — almost never runs a programme, but is routinely swept into one as an affected participant when an ICS rolls out a shared care record or converges systems across the patch. Its practical concern is the seam the programme owns: it must adopt the mandated data standards, information-governance agreements, and consent model with thin or no dedicated IT capability and no slack to absorb workflow change, yet it carries the same legal duties as the large trusts around it. The most valuable relationship it has is with the business change manager for its locality, because a well-supported adoption — training, single-sign-on, a workflow that fits how the practice actually runs — is the difference between the programme's benefit landing and the change being quietly worked around. Its realistic ask of the programme is proportionate support and sequencing that does not assume enterprise-scale resources, and its honest contribution is early, frank feedback at tranche reviews about what is unwo

x: Topic 5.3 — Enterprise Project Portfolio Management (EPPM) In one sentence: Enterprise Project Portfolio Management is how a health and care organization chooses, balances, and steers its whole collection of change — deciding which projects, products, and programmes to fund, in what order, against finite money and people, so that scarce investment lands where it does the most good for patients and citizens. Why this matters in health and care # Every NHS body, integrated care system (ICS), and social care organization runs more change than it can afford. Digital ambitions — a shared care record, an electronic patient record (EPR), a patient-facing app, virtual wards, cyber remediation — compete for the same limited capital, the same scarce clinical-informatics staff, and the same finite tolerance of frontline teams for disruption. Without a portfolio view, each initiative is approved on its own merits, and the organization quietly over-commits: too many things start, too few finish, and the ones that matter most for safety or equity are starved by the ones that shouted loudest. The stakes are public money and public trust. NHS capital is genuinely constrained — the Capital Departmental Expenditure Limit (CDEL) is divided across ICSs as a fixed system capital envelope, and there is rarely enough to do everything (see Key sources ). Portfolio choices are therefore rationing decisions with clinical consequences: fund the cyber upgrade or the diagnostics platform; refresh ageing infrastructure or launch the new pathway. EPPM makes that rationing explicit, evidence-based, and accountable, rather than the accidental output of who has the loudest sponsor. It also protects delivery capacity: a realistic portfolio is one the workforce can actually absorb without burning out the very teams it depends on. Core concepts # Portfolio. The totality of an organization's investment in change — all its projects, products, and programmes — viewed as one managed collection rather than a list. A portfolio is bounded (a trust's, an ICS's) and aligned to strategy: every item earns its place by contributing to strategic objectives at an acceptable level of risk. EPPM vs. project, product, and programme. Topics 5.0 –11 cover the delivery constructs: a product is an enduring capability run by a stable team ( Topic 5.0 ); a project is a time-boxed effort with a defined output ( Topic 5.1 ); a programme coordinates related projects to deliver an outcome ( Topic 5.2 ). EPPM — the health-and-care application of project portfolio management — sits above all three. It does not deliver anything itself — it decides which products, projects, and programmes should exist, how they are prioritized and balanced, and whether, collectively, they add up to the strategy. Management of Portfolios (MoP). The recognized UK/AXELOS framework. MoP is built on five principles and organized into two cycles. The portfolio definition cycle decides what the portfolio should contain — understand, categorize, prioritize, balance, and plan — producing a portfolio strategy and a delivery plan. The portfolio delivery cycle keeps it on track — management control, benefits management, financial management, risk, stakeholder engagement, and organizational governance. Definition asks "are we doing the right things?"; delivery asks "are we doing them right, and still the right things?". EPMO (Enterprise Project Management Office). The standing function that runs EPPM: maintaining the portfolio, enforcing prioritization, running the stage-gates, aggregating reporting, and stewarding capacity. An EPMO differs from a project management office or programme office in altitude — it serves the executive and board, connecting strategy to execution in a closed loop, not administering a single delivery. Stage-gates. Predefined decision points in a phase-gate process (often labelled discovery, business case, build, deploy, close) at which an initiative must be revalidated to continue receiving funding. Gates convert funding from a one-off "yes" into a series of renewable commitments, so money follows evidence rather than sunk cost. Capacity vs. demand. Demand is everything the organization wants to do; capacity is what its money and people can actually deliver. Portfolio management exists precisely because demand always exceeds capacity, and the job is to hold that line honestly. Best practices # Establish a single, authoritative portfolio. Maintain one list of every change initiative above a defined threshold, with a consistent record for each — sponsor, strategic objective, cost, benefit, risk, stage, and status. Fragmented lists in separate directorates guarantee double-counting and blind spots. The single portfolio is the precondition for every other practice here. Prioritize against explicit, published criteria. Score initiatives on strategic contribution, benefit, risk, deliverability, and (in health) safety and health-inequality impact, using criteria agreed with the board and visible to all. Transparent scoring turns prioritization from a corridor negotiation into a defensible decision — and lets you say a principled "not yet" to a well-connected sponsor. Balance the portfolio, don't just rank it. A ranked list can still be undeliverable or lopsided. Balance across dimensions — capital vs. revenue, run vs. transform, quick wins vs. multi-year platforms, risk spread, and delivery load on shared teams — so the portfolio is achievable and resilient, not merely a queue of everyone's favourite. Manage capacity and demand as a hard constraint. Size the portfolio to real delivery capacity — especially the genuine bottleneck resources (clinical-informatics leads, EPR configuration specialists, cyber engineers), not just budget. Starting more than you can finish is the most common and most expensive portfolio failure; a smaller portfolio that completes beats a larger one that stalls. Gate funding in stages, and be willing to stop. Fund initiatives to the next gate, not to the end, and use each gate to revalidate the business case against latest cost, benefit, and strategic fit. The hardest, most valuable EPPM discipline is stopping or pausing work that no longer earns its place — freeing capacity for what does. Track benefits at portfolio level, not just delivery. Aggregate expected and realized benefits ( benefits realisation management ) across the portfolio so the board can see whether the whole investment is paying back, and challenge double-counted or evaporating benefits. Delivering outputs on time means nothing if the portfolio's promised outcomes never materialize (see Topic 5.2 — Programme-Led Work). Report a portfolio dashboard the board can act on. Give leaders one concise, current view — RAG status, spend against plan, capacity utilization, gate decisions due, top portfolio risks, and benefits trajectory — refreshed on a regular cadence. The dashboard is the interface between EPPM and leadership visibility (see Topic 10.4 — Visibility for the CEO & Senior Leaders); if the board cannot see the portfolio, it cannot govern it. Right-size the tooling to the maturity. Start with a disciplined spreadsheet and a clear data model; adopt a dedicated portfolio tool only when the manual overhead genuinely bites. A tool enforces nothing on its own — many organizations buy portfolio software and still lack a real portfolio because the underlying decision discipline was never built. Questions to discuss with your team # How would we decide, out loud and against agreed criteria, which two of our current digital initiatives to pause if the capital envelope were cut by a fifth next year? This question forces the abstraction of "prioritization" into a concrete rationing choice with named victims, which is where most portfolios reveal they have no real criteria at all. In a health and care organization the trade-offs are acute: a paused cyber-remediation programme carries a live safety and regulatory risk, a paused health-inequality initiative widens a gap the board has publicly committed to closing, and a paused EPR wave frees scarce integration engineers but delays a promised clinical benefit. The tension to debate is whether your published scoring weights — safety, statutory duty, benefit, deliverability, inequality impact — would actually produce a defensible answer, or whether the loudest sponsor would still win in the room. Good teams will test their criteria against a real shortlist rather than in the abstract, and will notice where two initiatives score identically yet one is politically untouchable. An honest answer names the specific initiatives, shows the working, and admits which "protected" items are protected by evidence versus by influence. It should also surface whether the organization can even stop work gracefully, or whether sunk-cost inertia and contractual commitments make "pause" a fiction. Do we actually know our true bottleneck capacity — the specific people, not the money — and are we sizing the portfolio to it or to the budget? Budget is the visible constraint and therefore the one organizations manage, but in digital health the binding limit is almost always a handful of scarce specialists: clinical-informatics leads, EPR configuration analysts, integration engineers, information-governance and cyber staff. The debate worth having is whether anyone in the room can state, with evidence, how many concurrent programmes those individuals can genuinely support before quality and safety degrade, or whether that number is simply assumed. Concrete angles include mapping every in-flight initiative against the same short list of named specialists, and asking how many of them are already committed at more than a hundred per cent across "individually approved" projects. A recurring failure mode to examine is that finance sees a balanced budget while the same three engineers appear on nine plans. A good answer distinguishes capacity for money from capacity for people, quantifies the real bottlenecks, and accepts that a smaller portfolio which finishes beats a larger one that stalls. It should also confront the workforce cost: a portfolio the teams cannot absorb burns out the very people it depends on. When a new ministerial or board priority lands mid-year, is our default reflex "add it to the pile" or "what comes out to make room" — and what would it take to make the second reflex normal? This probes whether the portfolio is a steering instrument or merely an inventory that only ever grows. Health and care leaders face genuine, non-optional demand shocks — a new national target, a regulatory must-do, an emergent cyber threat — and the honest question is whether the organization can absorb them by explicit trade-off rather than by silent over-commitment that slows everything. The tension to debate is real: refusing to displace existing work when a statutory duty arrives is not an option, yet accepting every new priority without subtraction is how portfolios quietly become undeliverable. Useful angles include recalling the last three mid-year additions and asking what, if anything, was actually stopped to accommodate them, and whether the board was ever shown the displaced cost. A mature answer describes a standing mechanism — a re-prioritization gate, a reserved contingency, a visible "what we stopped" line in the dashboard — that makes displacement routine and transparent rather than a crisis negotiation. It should also be candid about the cultural work required, since making "stop" a celebrated outcome rather than an admission of failure is as much a leadership challenge as a process one. Can we show, for the initiatives that finished last year, what benefits were actually realized — and would that survive an auditor netting out the double-counting? Portfolios are justified by benefits, yet most organizations track only the benefits they forecast at business-case time and never revisit whether they materialized, so the portfolio's promised return quietly becomes fiction. The debate worth having is whether anyone can point to a delivered initiative and state the cash-releasing saving, the clinical outcome, or the capacity freed that it genuinely produced, as opposed to the number that was written to win approval. In health and care the trap is especially sharp because the same efficiency — beds freed by a virtual ward, admin hours saved by an EPR module — is often claimed independently by three business cases, so the aggregate looks transformational while the organization's actual costs never fall. Concrete angles include picking two completed initiatives and tracing their promised benefits into the accounts or activity data, and asking who owns each benefit after the project team disbands. A recurring failure mode to surface is the evaporating benefit that had no named owner and no baseline, making realization impossible to prove either way. An honest answer distinguishes forecast from realized benefits, reconciles overlaps centrally, and admits where the organization simply does not know. It should also confront whether the board is ever shown realized-versus-promised benefit at portfolio level, or only a comforting pipeline of forecasts. Does our EPMO actually hold decision rights over prioritization and gates, or is it a well-staffed function that collects status and hopes the executive will act on it? An EPMO with no mandate is the most expensive kind of report: it aggregates beautifully and changes nothing, because every real allocation decision is still settled elsewhere by seniority and sponsorship. The question to debate is where the authority to say "not yet", to hold a gate, or to release a bottleneck resource genuinely sits — with the EPMO by delegated mandate, or with whichever director shouts loudest in the room. In health and care this matters because clinical and operational sponsors carry enormous informal weight, and an EPMO that can be overruled by a phone call cannot hold capacity as a hard constraint no matter how good its data. Useful angles include recalling the last time the portfolio function actually stopped or re-sequenced a powerful sponsor's initiative, and asking what happened next. A mature answer is explicit about the EPMO's delegated authority, the executive backing behind it, and the escalation route when a gate decision is contested. It should also be candid about the difference between influence and mandate, since a function that only advises will always be the first thing bypassed under pressure. Is our portfolio genuinely balanced — across run versus transform, capital versus revenue, quick wins versus multi-year platforms, and load on shared teams — or is it just a ranked queue of everyone's favourites? Ranking answers "which matters most", but a portfolio can be perfectly ranked and still undeliverable or dangerously lopsided, because balance is a different discipline from priority. The tension to debate is that the highest-scoring initiatives are often the exciting transform bets, and a portfolio stacked with them can starve the unglamorous "run" work — infrastructure refresh, cyber remediation, keeping the lights on — until something fails. In health and care the balance dimensions are concrete and consequential: too much capital and no revenue to operate what you build, too many multi-year platforms and no near-term wins to sustain confidence, or every major programme leaning on the same three integration engineers. Concrete angles include plotting the current portfolio across two or three of these axes and asking whether any dimension is empty or overloaded, and whether safety-critical run work is protected against shinier new pathways. A good answer treats balance as an explicit design choice the board can see and adjust, not an accidental by-product of scoring. It should also acknowledge that a balanced, resilient portfolio sometimes means funding a lower-scoring item because the mix, not the rank, demands it. In practice: a health & care example # An ICS covering three acute trusts, a mental-health trust, a community provider, and its constituent local authorities has thirty-odd digital initiatives in flight: a shared care record, two EPR deployments, a patient app, virtual wards, cyber remediation across all providers, a data platform, and a long tail of directorate projects. Each was approved separately; nobody can say what the system is spending on digital in total, and three programmes are quietly competing for the same four integration engineers. The ICS stands up an EPMO reporting to the system's digital and finance leadership. Its first act is not to buy a tool but to build one authoritative portfolio — every initiative captured with sponsor, cost split into capital and revenue, expected benefit, risk, stage, and the shared specialist resources it needs. The exercise alone is revealing: total committed spend exceeds the system capital envelope by a third, and the integration-engineer demand is triple the supply. The EPMO runs a prioritization and balancing session with system leaders against published criteria weighted toward safety, statutory duties, and health-inequality impact. Cyber remediation and the shared care record score highest and are protected; two directorate projects with thin benefit cases are paused; one EPR deployment is re-sequenced six months later to break the integration-engineer contention rather than run both in parallel and fail both. A stage-gate calendar is introduced: nothing proceeds to build without a revalidated business case. Six months on, the board sees a single portfolio dashboard each month — spend against the capital limit, capacity utilization on the bottleneck teams, gate decisions taken, and a benefits trajectory. When a new ministerial priority arrives mid-year, the conversation is no longer "add it to the pile" but "what comes out to make room?". The portfolio is now a steering instrument, not an inventory. Sector lenses # Startup # A small digital-health company's "portfolio" is really its product roadmap plus a handful of bets funded by a finite runway; burn rate, not a capital envelope, is the binding constraint. Prioritization is existential — every engineer diverted to a low-value feature shortens the time to the next funding round — so the discipline that matters most is ruthless focus, saying no to promising-but-off-strategy opportunities. Governance is deliberately light: the founders and lead investors are the portfolio board, and a weekly review can re-sequence everything without a formal stage-gate calendar. Balancing "run vs. transform" barely applies when almost everything is transform; the risk is starting three products at once and finishing none. The right move is to fund one or two things to a decisive learning milestone and kill the rest early. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a single-site clinic, a care home, or a small health-tech supplier past the pre-revenue stage — has a real but tiny portfolio: perhaps a clinical system upgrade, a cyber-remediation must-do, and one improvement everyone wants, all competing for the same handful of people and the same thin cash. There is rarely a dedicated digital or IT function, so the "EPMO" is the practice manager or an owner-director doing portfolio choices in the margins of running the service. The binding constraint is neither a startup's runway nor an enterprise's capital envelope but ongoing operating cash and the near-total absence of slack: the same person who would deliver change is also delivering care. Yet the compliance duties — information governance, clinical safety, cyber — are the same ones the big organizations carry, without the specialists to discharge them. The right move is brutal sequencing: pick the one statutory or safety-critical change that must happen this year, do it to completion before starting the next, and lean on supplier-managed and shared-se

x: Topic 5.4 — Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) In one sentence: Enterprise Resource Planning is the integrated back-office system — finance, human resources, payroll, procurement, and supply chain — that acts as the organization's system of record for money, people, and stock, and quietly underpins almost every way of working in this book. Why this matters in health and care # Digital transformation in health and care gets its attention from clinical systems — the electronic patient record , the shared care record, the patient app. But none of those run without the unglamorous back office beneath them. Staff must be recruited, rostered, and paid; suppliers must be contracted and settled; drugs, devices, and consumables must be ordered and tracked; and every pound must be accounted for against tightly constrained public budgets. ERP is where that happens, and when it fails, the consequences are immediate: unpaid staff, stalled procurement, unreconciled accounts, and a finance function flying blind. The scale is enormous. NHS Shared Business Services (NHS SBS), a joint venture created in 2004, runs a national Oracle-based finance and procurement platform that processes millions of invoices and handles a very large share of total NHS spend for over a hundred NHS organizations (see Key sources ). ERP decisions are therefore not a niche finance concern — they shape workforce management, control of public money, and the data quality that every downstream analysis depends on. For a director, ERP is both a foundational enabler and one of the highest-risk programmes an organization will ever attempt. Core concepts # What ERP is. A single, integrated enterprise resource planning suite of modules sharing one database and one set of master data, covering the enterprise's core administrative processes: general ledger and financial accounting, accounts payable and receivable, HR and workforce administration, payroll , procurement ( purchase-to-pay ), inventory and supply chain, and increasingly planning and analytics (FP&A — financial planning and analysis). The point of "integration" is that a purchase order, a goods receipt, and an invoice reconcile automatically because they are the same data, not three copies. System of record . ERP is the authoritative source for financial and resource data — the ledger that auditors trust and the payroll that staff are paid from. Other systems may hold operational copies, but the ERP is the version of truth for money and, often, for the substantive HR record. Master data . The shared reference data on which everything else depends: the chart of accounts , cost centres, supplier records, the item catalogue, and employee records. Master data is the quiet determinant of ERP success — dirty, duplicated, or inconsistent master data corrupts reporting, breaks reconciliation, and undermines every process built on top. Common platforms in health and public sector. In the NHS and wider UK public sector the main ERP platforms are Oracle (dominant, largely through NHS SBS and consortia such as NEP), SAP , Unit4 (widely chosen by trusts, universities, and local authorities), and Microsoft Dynamics 365 . Local authorities delivering adult social care run the same class of systems for their finance and procurement. The modern direction of travel is cloud ERP ( software-as-a-service ) rather than on-premise installations. Shared services . Rather than every organization running its own ERP, many share a common platform and a common back-office operation — the NHS SBS model, and NHS consortia running templated Oracle Cloud instances. Shared services trade some local flexibility for standardization, economies of scale, and a smaller collective implementation and support burden. Best practices # Treat master data as the foundation, not an afterthought. Cleanse and de-duplicate the chart of accounts, supplier records, item catalogue, and employee data before migration , and put ongoing data-governance ownership in place. The most damaging ERP failures trace back to bad master data that no amount of good software can fix; a data-quality workstream is not optional. Adopt the standard; minimize customization. Configure the ERP to the vendor's or consortium's standard template wherever the process is genuinely commodity, and reserve bespoke change for the rare true differentiator. Heavy customization inflates cost, wrecks upgradeability, and re-imports the local mess you were trying to escape — cloud ERP in particular punishes the "make it look like our old system" instinct. Design the integrations deliberately. ERP does not stand alone: it must exchange data with workforce and e-rostering systems, clinical and pharmacy systems (for stock and costing), banking, and analytics. Map every interface, own the data contracts, and test them end to end — payroll fed by a broken rostering feed pays people wrong, and that is a trust-destroying failure. Run ERP replacement as a major programme, with change management at its core. An ERP implementation is a business-change programme that happens to involve software, not an IT project. Resource it with programme discipline (see Topic 5.2 — Programme Management) and a genuine change-management effort (see Topic 8.1 — Change Management), because most ERP pain is people and process, not technology. Be honest about ERP programme risk. Large ERP implementations have a well-earned reputation for overrunning on time and cost and under-delivering on benefit; the failure literature is extensive and cross-sector. Build in contingency, avoid a big-bang go-live where a phased approach is feasible, and never let an optimistic timeline override readiness — a slipped date is recoverable, a botched payroll or ledger cut-over is not. Protect the go-live and the period after it. Plan data cut-over, parallel running, reconciliation, and hypercare support in detail, and resist pressure to shorten them. The weeks around go-live are when suppliers go unpaid and month-end breaks; a well-staffed stabilization period is the difference between a rough start and a public crisis. Use ERP as the resource-management system of record — and design ways of working around it. Let the ERP be the single source for cost centres, budgets, procurement approvals, and workforce establishment, and align your operating processes to it rather than maintaining shadow spreadsheets. Shadow systems re-introduce the fragmentation ERP exists to remove and quietly rot data quality. Weigh shared services and cloud ERP on their real trade-offs. Shared platforms (NHS SBS, NEP-style consortia) and cloud ERP offer standardization, scale, continuous upgrades, and a lighter local burden, at the cost of some local flexibility and a dependency on the provider. Choose deliberately: for most organizations the standardization gain outweighs the flexibility lost, but the decision should be made with eyes open, not by default. Questions to discuss with your team # How confident are we — with evidence, not assurance — about the quality of the master data we would carry into a new ERP, and who owns it after go-live? Master data is the quiet determinant of ERP success, yet it is routinely treated as a migration housekeeping task rather than the foundation it is, so this question tests whether the team has looked hard at the chart of accounts, supplier records, item catalogue, and employee master or is simply hoping they are clean. In a health and care setting the stakes are concrete: duplicated supplier records break purchase-to-pay reconciliation, an employee master that disagrees with ESR pays people wrong, and an inconsistent chart of accounts corrupts every downstream financial report the board and auditors rely on. The tension worth debating is the pull to migrate wholesale to hit a date versus the months of unglamorous cleansing and de-duplication that good practice demands, and whether anyone senior is willing to fund a data-quality workstream that shows no visible product. A strong answer cites actual counts — how many duplicate suppliers, how many unreconciled employee records — rather than a general sense that "the data is mostly fine". It should also name the person and governance mechanism accountable for master-data quality after go-live, because data that is cleansed once and then left ungoverned simply drifts back to disorder. Where are we genuinely tempted to customize the ERP to preserve a familiar process, and is that difference a real differentiator or just the old mess we are trying to escape? Heavy customization is the classic enterprise ERP trap: it inflates cost, wrecks upgradeability, and re-imports the very local fragmentation the programme was meant to remove, and cloud ERP in particular punishes the instinct to "make it look like our old system". This question asks the team to be specific about which processes they will insist on bending the software to fit, and to justify each against a hard test of whether it is a true differentiator or merely comfortable habit. The debate matters because in health and care almost every back-office process — general ledger, procurement approvals, payroll administration — is genuinely commodity, so the honest default should be to adopt the vendor or consortium standard template and change the process, not the software. Concrete angles include listing every requested customization and asking who benefits, what upgrade cost it locks in, and whether a neighbouring trust on the same template manages without it. A good answer distinguishes the rare legitimate exception from the many requests driven by change-aversion, and recognizes that adopting the standard is a change-management and leadership problem, not a technical one. It should also confront the long-term cost: every bespoke change is a tax paid at every future cloud release. Have we honestly resourced the human and process side of this ERP change — cut-over, parallel running, hypercare, training, and integration testing — or are we quietly running it as an IT project? The failure literature is unambiguous that most ERP pain is people and process rather than technology, so this question exposes whether the programme is genuinely a business-change effort or an IT swap wearing programme clothing. The period around go-live is when suppliers go unpaid, month-end breaks, and staff get paid late, and each of those in a public health body is not a rough start but a trust-destroying, potentially newsworthy failure. The tension to debate is the constant pressure to shorten parallel running, thin the hypercare team, and compress the timeline to hit an imposed date, against the reality that a slipped date is recoverable while a botched payroll or ledger cut-over is not. Useful angles include walking through every integration — e-rostering, ESR, pharmacy stock, banking, analytics — and asking which have been end-to-end tested versus assumed, and whether process owners in finance, procurement, and HR have actually been seconded to redesign their workflows. An honest answer shows named change-management, training, and reconciliation resource in the plan rather than a line that says "IT will handle it", and is willing to phase the go-live where a big-bang cut-over adds avoidable risk. It should also acknowledge that readiness, not the calendar, must govern the decision to proceed. On the shared-services and cloud-ERP question, have we weighed the standardization we would gain against the local flexibility we would surrender — and made that call deliberately rather than by default? Shared platforms such as NHS SBS and consortium Oracle Cloud instances, and cloud ERP more broadly, offer real prizes — economies of scale, continuous upgrades, a lighter local implementation and support burden — but they buy those with a genuine loss of local control and a hard dependency on the provider's roadmap and release cadence. This question forces the team to name what flexibility actually matters to them and test whether it is worth the cost of running, patching, and separately supporting their own back office. The tension in a health and care setting is sharpened by the fact that most back-office process is commodity, so the standardization gain usually outweighs the flexibility lost — but "usually" is not "always", and drifting into a shared platform without examining the trade-off is how organizations end up resenting a template they never consciously chose. Concrete angles include asking which local processes the team would fight to keep and why, what happens when the consortium changes the template underneath them, and whether the exit and data-portability terms are understood before signing. A strong answer treats this as a strategic choice made with eyes open, weighing provider dependency and roadmap risk against scale and upgrade relief, rather than either defaulting to the shared option because it is fashionable or clinging to a bespoke platform out of habit. What is our honest plan to stop shadow spreadsheets and local workarounds re-emerging after go-live, so the ERP stays the single system of record rather than one source among many? The whole point of an integrated ERP is to remove the fragmentation that shadow systems create, yet local spreadsheets have a way of surviving a go-live and quietly re-fragmenting the data the programme was meant to unify. This question tests whether the team has thought past the cut-over to the durable operating discipline that keeps cost centres, budgets, procurement approvals, and workforce establishment living in the ERP rather than in someone's private workbook. It matters in health and care because a shadow establishment spreadsheet that disagrees with payroll, or an off-system procurement tracker, silently rots the data quality that board reporting and audit depend on, and does so precisely because it is convenient for the person maintaining it. The tension worth surfacing is that shadow systems usually exist for a reason — the ERP process felt slower, or a genuine gap was never closed — so simply banning them fails unless the underlying need is addressed. Useful angles include asking which current spreadsheets would have to die at go-live, why each exists, and what in-system capability or process change would remove the temptation to rebuild it. An honest answer pairs a clear expectation that the ERP is authoritative with a plan to fix the gaps that drive people off-system, and names who will notice and challenge a shadow system when it reappears. Are we being genuinely honest about ERP programme risk — the sector's track record of overrun and under-delivery — and have we built our timeline, contingency, and go-live approach around that reality rather than an optimistic plan? Large ERP implementations have a well-earned, cross-sector reputation for overrunning on time and cost and under-delivering on benefit, and this question asks whether the team has internalized that failure literature or is quietly assuming it will be the exception. The stakes in a public health body are unforgiving: a slipped date is recoverable, but a botched payroll or ledger cut-over is a newsworthy, trust-destroying event with parliamentary and press consequences, so optimism that overrides readiness is not courage but recklessness. The tension to debate is the constant pressure — from imposed dates, sunk cost, and the wish to show progress — to compress the timeline, thin contingency, and prefer a big-bang go-live over a phased one that would be safer but slower. Concrete angles include asking what the plan assumes will go right, where the contingency actually sits, whether a phased cut-over is feasible, and what the explicit criteria are for delaying go-live if readiness is not there. A good answer names the specific risks this programme carries rather than gesturing at ERP risk in general, builds in real contingency and a defensible phasing decision, and treats a data-driven "not yet" as a legitimate and expected outcome rather than a failure of nerve. In practice: a health & care example # An acute NHS trust is running a fifteen-year-old on-premise finance and procurement system that its vendor will soon stop supporting. Reporting takes days, purchase-to-pay is heavily manual, and the workforce establishment lives in a tangle of spreadsheets that never quite agrees with payroll. The trust decides to move to a cloud ERP delivered through a regional NHS consortium's templated Oracle Cloud instance, alongside neighbouring providers. The finance director resists the temptation to treat this as an IT swap. A programme is stood up with an executive sponsor, a full-time programme manager, and — crucially — a data-quality workstream that spends months cleansing the chart of accounts, de-duplicating twelve thousand supplier records, and reconciling the employee master against ESR (the NHS electronic staff record) before any migration. Process owners in finance, procurement, and HR are seconded to redesign their workflows to the consortium template rather than replicate the old system. The trust chooses a phased go-live: finance and procurement first, workforce and reporting in a later wave, with parallel running across two month-ends and a well-staffed hypercare team on standby. Integrations to e-rostering, the bank, and the analytics warehouse are mapped and tested end to end. The go-live is not painless — a supplier-payment backlog builds in week one and takes a fortnight to clear — but because reconciliation and hypercare were properly resourced, no staff are paid late and month-end closes on time. A year on, the trust closes its books in days rather than weeks, procurement approvals are enforced in-system, and the establishment finally reconciles with payroll. The shared consortium platform also means the next upgrade arrives as a routine cloud release rather than another multi-year project. Sector lenses # Startup # A digital-health startup rarely runs a full ERP; it stitches together cloud SaaS tools — a lightweight accounting package, an HR-and-payroll app, a couple of spreadsheets — because a heavyweight integrated suite is disproportionate to a team of thirty. The system-of-record discipline still matters, though: even at seed stage, one clean chart of accounts and a single authoritative payroll source prevent the reconciliation chaos that scares off investors during due diligence. The right move is to keep the stack simple, integrable, and well-governed, and to defer a "real" ERP until scale genuinely demands it. The startup's risk is the mirror image of the enterprise's — not over-customization, but sprawl: a dozen disconnected apps with no master-data owner and no one accountable for the numbers. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home, a domiciliary-care agency, or a single-site clinic — carries the full weight of financial, payroll, and procurement duties with almost no dedicated finance or IT capability, so a heavyweight ERP is out of reach but the system-of-record discipline is not optional. The practical answer is a small, well-integrated set of cloud packages — accounting, payroll, and stock — chosen so that one chart of accounts and one authoritative payroll source hold, because a care home that pays staff late or a pharmacy whose stock and ledger disagree faces the same regulatory and cash consequences as a large trust but with no back-office team to absorb them. The temptation to run the business on a founder's spreadsheet is strongest here and most dangerous, since there is rarely anyone to notice when the numbers drift. Where a professional body, franchise, or local network offers a shared or standardized finance platform, adopting it is usually the shrewd move: it buys the standardization and support the organization cannot resource itself. The discipline is to keep the stack simple and governed by whoever owns the money, and to resist bespoke workaround
