x: Topic 6.0 — Financial Management & Business Cases In health and care, a business case is not a funding formality but a clinical, ethical, and public-trust argument: it commits scarce public money to one patient benefit instead of another, and you are accountable for both the spending and the outcome. Why this matters in health and care # Every pound you spend on a digital service is a pound not spent on a hip replacement, a district nurse, or a mental-health crisis line. That is the uncomfortable truth beneath financial management in health and care. You are not deploying private capital in pursuit of a return to shareholders; you are stewarding public money raised through taxation, and the people who pay are also the people who depend on the services you fund. A weak business case does not merely waste money — it diverts care from people who needed it and erodes the public trust that lets the system function at all. The financial rules of UK health and care are also genuinely different from those of a commercial organization, and directors who ignore this get caught out. Money arrives in fixed annual envelopes, split into capital and revenue with a firm wall between them. Approvals run through layered spend controls that can add months. Benefits are frequently non-cash — hours of clinical time released, harm avoided, waits reduced — so they never show up cleanly in a profit-and-loss account and are easy to overstate on the way in and forget on the way out. And the standard appraisal method, the HM Treasury Green Book with its Five Case Model, is not optional guidance you can route around: for material investment it is the language in which your case will be judged. Getting this right is a safety and equity issue as much as a money issue. Underfunding the boring parts — service management, cyber resilience, accessibility, benefits tracking — is how digital services quietly decay until they fail patients. Overstating benefits is how organizations sink money into products that never deliver the clinical time they promised. Your job as a director is to get money approved, spend it well, and prove afterwards that it did what you said it would. Core concepts # A business case is the structured argument for why an investment should be made and how it will be delivered and controlled. In UK central government and the NHS, business cases follow the Five Case Model set out in HM Treasury's Green Book, which requires five linked arguments: the strategic case (why this is needed and how it fits strategy), the economic case (which option delivers best public value), the commercial case (whether it is deliverable through the market), the financial case (whether it is affordable), and the management case (whether you can actually deliver it). A case that is strong on strategy but silent on affordability or delivery is not a case at all. Business cases progress through three stages as certainty grows: the Strategic Outline Case (SOC) establishes the need and a preferred way forward; the Outline Business Case (OBC) identifies the preferred option after detailed appraisal; and the Full Business Case (FBC) confirms arrangements after procurement, immediately before contract signature and full spend. Each stage is a decision gate, and the effort you invest should match the money at stake. The economic case rests on comparing options by value. Cost–benefit analysis values costs and benefits in money and nets them off; cost-effectiveness analysis compares cost per unit of outcome when the outcome resists monetary valuation, which is common in health. The detailed valuation of health outcomes — quality-adjusted life years, willingness-to-pay thresholds — belongs to Topic 6.1 — Health Economics; here you need to know which method your case demands and why. Both methods discount future cash flows to present value, so understanding net present value matters when you compare options with different timing. Two cost concepts protect you from short-termism. Whole-life cost , and its close cousin total cost of ownership , count everything from build through years of operation, support, licensing, and eventual decommissioning — not just the shiny implementation cost. Ignoring these is the single most common way a "cheap" option turns out ruinously expensive. Meanwhile opportunity cost — the value of the best alternative you gave up — is the real price of any choice in a fixed budget, and it should be explicit in every prioritization conversation. Two further concepts shape credibility. Optimism bias is the well-documented human tendency to underestimate cost and time and overestimate benefit; the Green Book requires you to correct for it with explicit uplifts to your estimates. And benefits realisation management is the discipline of defining, tracking, and actually banking the benefits you promised, rather than declaring victory at go-live and moving on. Finally, the NHS distinction between capital expenditure and revenue spending — the Capital and Revenue Departmental Expenditure Limits, CDEL and RDEL — governs which money you can spend on what, and is explained in the best-practices section because it trips up almost everyone. Best practices # Write the Five Case Model as one argument, not five documents. The strategic, economic, commercial, financial, and management cases must reinforce each other. A common failure is a compelling strategic case bolted to a financial case that does not add up or a management case that names no accountable owner and no delivery plan. Draft the cases together, check they tell a consistent story, and make sure the benefits claimed in the economic case are the same benefits your management case commits to tracking. Reviewers approve coherence; they reject cases that contradict themselves. Match the business-case stage to the decision, and do not over-engineer early cases. A Strategic Outline Case should be light — enough to test the need and secure permission to invest in a proper Outline Business Case. Reserve deep appraisal for the OBC, when you are choosing between real options, and confirm arrangements at Full Business Case after procurement. Spending months on a granular FBC-quality analysis before you have even confirmed the need wastes effort and delays value; conversely, rushing an FBC on the back of a thin SOC invites nasty surprises after contracts are signed. See Topic 1.3 — Evidence-Driven Decisions for how to calibrate the evidence you gather to the weight of the decision. Cost the whole life, not the launch. Estimate the total cost of ownership across the realistic service life: build, licences, hosting, third-line support, clinical safety maintenance, security patching, accessibility upkeep, and decommissioning. Digital services are not one-off projects that end at go-live; they are living systems that cost money every year they run. A business case that shows a large capital build with no honest revenue tail for operations is not affordable — it is a future crisis. Topic 3.8 — Service Management & Live Operations describes what those running costs actually buy. Correct for optimism bias explicitly, then reduce it with evidence. Apply the Green Book's optimism-bias uplifts to cost and duration, and state your assumptions plainly. Better still, narrow the uplift with reference-class forecasting: look at what comparable projects actually cost and how late they ran, and anchor your estimates to that reality rather than to your team's best-case hopes. Reviewers trust a case that names its uncertainty and shows how it will be managed far more than one that presents suspiciously precise single-point numbers. Design benefits so they cannot quietly evaporate. For every benefit you claim, name the metric, the baseline, the owner, and the date by which it must be visible. If the benefit is released clinical time, say who will use that time for what, because "hours saved" that are never redeployed are not benefits — they are a spreadsheet fiction. Build benefits tracking into the operating model from day one and report against it after go-live, not just at approval. This is the difference between a case that promised value and a case that delivered it. Respect the capital–revenue wall and plan for it. In the NHS, capital (CDEL) and revenue (RDEL) budgets are separate and tightly controlled, and you generally cannot move freely between them. Cloud-hosted, subscription-based digital products are largely revenue spending, which can clash with an organization's capital-heavy funding and its annual capital cycle. Work out early which envelope funds which part of your case, secure a recurring revenue line for the years of operation, and never assume a one-off capital grant will keep the lights on. Getting this wrong is how funded builds die for want of running costs. Make opportunity cost visible in every prioritization. Because the budget is fixed, funding your case means not funding something else. State what you are displacing and why this investment delivers more public value. This honesty strengthens your case with boards who see too many proposals presented as free, and it aligns your financial argument with portfolio decisions made through Topic 5.3 — Enterprise Project Portfolio Management (EPPM). Plan the approval and spend-controls route before you need it. Material NHS and central-government digital spend passes through layered approvals — internal capital groups, regional or Integrated Care Board sign-off, and national spend controls above defined thresholds — and these add time. Map the route, thresholds, and evidence each gate expects at the start, and sequence your case so approvals do not block delivery. Coordinate with procurement early, because commercial and financial approvals interlock; Topic 6.3 — Procurement & Commercial covers that handshake. Questions to discuss with your team # Are the benefits in our business case real, owned, and trackable — or are they decoration to get money approved? Walk through each claimed benefit and ask whether it has a named owner who will be accountable after go-live, a baseline you can actually measure today, and a credible mechanism by which it converts into value. Released clinical time is the classic trap: hours "saved" that no one plans to redeploy deliver nothing. Interrogate whether cash-releasing benefits will genuinely leave the budget or merely shift work around. Discuss how you will report benefits realization quarterly after launch, not just claim it at approval. Consider what happens, and who is accountable, if a benefit does not materialize. Be honest about which benefits are firm and which are aspirational, and label them as such in the case. A team that cannot answer these questions has written a funding request, not a business case. Do we understand the whole-life cost, and have we secured recurring revenue to run this for years? Push past the implementation cost to the total cost of ownership across the service's realistic life, including support, licensing, security, accessibility, and eventual replacement. Ask specifically which parts are capital (CDEL) and which are revenue (RDEL), and whether you have a committed recurring revenue line or merely a one-off capital pot that ends at go-live. Discuss how the annual capital cycle interacts with a product that needs continuous, predictable funding to stay safe and useful. Consider what the service will cost in year three and year five, not just year one. Explore what you will decommission or stop funding to make room for these running costs. If the answer to "who pays to run this next year" is unclear, you have found the biggest risk in the case. Where is optimism bias hiding in our numbers, and what would an honest sceptic say? Examine your cost and timeline estimates and ask whether they reflect what comparable projects actually cost or what you hope this one will cost. Discuss whether you have applied Green Book optimism-bias uplifts and whether you can narrow them with reference-class evidence from similar deliveries. Consider inviting someone outside the team to challenge the estimates before the board does. Ask what assumptions, if wrong, would break the case, and how sensitive the conclusion is to each. Talk about how you present uncertainty honestly without undermining the case — a well-managed risk is more credible than a false precision. Think about the incentive to lowball costs to clear an affordability threshold, and how that always surfaces later as an overspend. A case that survives friendly scepticism will survive the real thing. What are we choosing not to fund by approving this, and can we defend that trade-off out loud? In a fixed budget every yes is also a no, so make the displaced alternative explicit rather than pretending the money is free. Discuss what else competes for the same envelope — a diagnostics upgrade, more district-nursing capacity, a cyber-resilience programme — and why this investment delivers more public value than the best thing you are giving up. Consider whether the opportunity cost falls on the same population your case claims to help, or shifts harm to a different group whose need is quieter. Talk about how this decision fits the portfolio view in Topic 5.3 , so the choice is made across proposals rather than in isolation. Be honest about whether the case is genuinely the best use of the marginal pound or simply the proposal with the most energetic sponsor. A team that can name what it is displacing, and defend that to a board, has a stronger case than one that presents its ask as cost-free. Does our Five Case argument actually cohere, and can we point to the person who will deliver it? Read the strategic, economic, commercial, financial, and management cases together and ask whether they tell one consistent story or five disconnected ones. Check that the benefits promised in the economic case are exactly the benefits the management case commits to tracking, and that the financial case reconciles to the numbers in the economic case rather than quietly diverging. Discuss whether the commercial case is deliverable through the market you actually face, or assumes a supplier and a route that may not exist. Interrogate the management case hardest: name the accountable owner, the delivery plan, and the governance that will hold the spend to account after approval. Consider what a reviewer sees when the cases contradict each other — a proposal written to clear a gate rather than to make a good decision. A case where every part reinforces the others, with a real person accountable for delivery, is the one that survives scrutiny and actually lands. Have we mapped the approval and spend-controls route, and sequenced it so it does not strangle delivery? Material NHS and central-government digital spend passes through layered gates — internal capital groups, Integrated Care Board or regional sign-off, and national spend controls above defined thresholds — each of which takes time and expects specific evidence. Discuss whether you know your thresholds, which gate each part of the case must clear, and what documentation each reviewer will demand, or whether you are discovering the route as you go. Consider how the commercial and financial approvals interlock with procurement, so a delay in one does not silently stall the others ( Topic 6.3 ). Talk about how to sequence approvals against the delivery timeline so that sign-off gates do not become the critical path, and about what you will do if a gate slips. Be honest about the temptation to rush a thin case to hit a funding window, and how that weakens it precisely when scrutiny is highest. A team that has mapped the route from the start controls its own timeline; one that has not will have the timeline dictated to it. In practice: a health & care example # An Integrated Care Board (ICB) wants to fund a shared digital platform that lets community nurses, GPs, and social-care teams see a single coordinated care record for people with complex long-term conditions. The director of digital, Priya, is asked to build the business case. She starts with a Strategic Outline Case, deliberately light: the strategic case links the platform to the ICB's aim of reducing avoidable admissions among frail patients, and to the operating model in Topic 1.1 . It secures permission to invest in a proper appraisal. At Outline Business Case stage she works through the Five Case Model in earnest. The economic case uses cost-effectiveness analysis rather than pure cost–benefit analysis, because the core benefit — avoided admissions and released community-nursing time — resists clean monetary valuation; she hands the health-outcome valuation to her health-economics colleague per Topic 6.1 . She appraises a shortlist against a "do minimum" baseline and calculates each option's whole-life cost over seven years, not just the build. The numbers force honesty. The implementation cost is capital, but the platform is a cloud subscription, so the bulk of the seven-year cost is recurring revenue — RDEL — that the ICB must commit annually. Priya applies Green Book optimism-bias uplifts to cost and timeline, then narrows them using data from two neighbouring ICBs that ran similar programmes; both overran their first estimates by roughly a third, which she now builds in. For benefits, she names an owner for each: the chief nurse owns "community-nursing hours released" and commits to redeploying them to proactive visits, so the benefit does not evaporate into an untracked spreadsheet line. At the board, a non-executive challenges affordability. Priya is ready: she states the opportunity cost plainly — this platform means deferring a separate diagnostics project — and shows the recurring revenue line secured for all seven years. The board approves the OBC. After procurement, the Full Business Case confirms the supplier and final costs, and it passes national spend-control review because the route was mapped from the start. Eighteen months after go-live, the quarterly benefits report shows admissions down and evidence that released nursing hours were actually redeployed — because someone was accountable for making that happen. Sector lenses # Startup # A digital-health startup selling into the NHS lives on the other side of these business cases, and understanding them is a commercial advantage. Your buyer needs a Five Case argument to justify purchasing your product, so package evidence that helps them: credible whole-life cost figures, realistic benefit estimates they can defend, and reference data from comparable deployments that narrows their optimism-bias adjustment. Be honest about running costs, because a case built on unrealistic savings collapses at the first benefits review and poisons the relationship. Startups that help customers build defensible cases — rather than pushing inflated return-on-investment claims — win renewals, because the same discipline of tracking whether promised value actually landed protects your credibility with every future buyer. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home, or a single-site clinic — faces the same duties as a large trust but without a finance team, a business-case template, or anyone whose job is appraisal. Here the discipline is not a full Five Case Model but the honest version of its questions asked at your own scale: what is the whole-life cost including the annual licence and support, not just the sticker price, and can the practice afford that recurring revenue every year? Opportunity cost is sharp and personal, because funding a new system directly means not funding a locum session or a piece of clinical kit, so make the trade-off explicit before you commit. Beware suppliers pitching one-off costs that hide a subscription tail, and beware optimistic time-savings that assume staff you do not have to spare. Where you buy into a shared or Integrate

x: Topic 6.1 — Health Economics Health economics is how you turn "we built a thing and people used it" into a defensible claim that your digital service made a population healthier for the money it consumed — and the discipline that stops you fooling yourself. Why this matters in health and care # Every pound spent on a digital service is a pound not spent on something else — a district nurse, a diagnostic scanner, a mental-health worker. In a tax-funded system with fixed budgets, that trade-off is not abstract; it is the daily reality of every integrated care board (ICB) finance meeting. If your service consumes resource without producing health, someone somewhere gets less care. That is the moral weight health economics places on your work. Digital delivery leaders routinely over-claim on the wrong evidence. They report that an app was downloaded two hundred thousand times, that a portal sent a million messages, that appointments were "saved" — and mistake this activity for benefit. Activity is not health. A message delivered to someone who ignores it changes nothing; an appointment "saved" that pushes a patient into an avoidable admission has made things worse. Without a disciplined way to distinguish what you did from what changed , you cannot tell a genuinely valuable service from an expensive placebo. Consistent, comparable measurement is also a matter of equity and public trust. If each service invents its own metric, no one can weigh a diabetes app against a falls-prevention service against a new triage tool. The whole point of a shared unit of value is that it lets you compare unlike things and allocate scarce resource honestly across a population — including to the people whose health is worst and whose voices are quietest. This topic gives you the vocabulary and the guardrails to do that. It builds on Topic 1.3 — Evidence-Driven Decisions and Topic 6.0 — Financial Management & Business Cases, and feeds Topic 10.0 — Objectives & Key Results (OKRs). Core concepts # Start with the distinction that trips up most digital programmes: outputs versus outcomes . Outputs are the activity you produce — appointments delivered, messages sent, users onboarded, referrals processed. Outcomes are the change in health or wellbeing that follows — symptoms reduced, admissions avoided, life extended, quality of life improved. Outputs are cheap to count and easy to game; outcomes are what the system exists to create. A logic model makes the link explicit by mapping inputs → activities → outputs → outcomes → impact , forcing you to state the causal chain by which your spend becomes health, and to expose the assumptions in it. Value in health and care is best framed in terms of population health : the health outcomes of a defined group and the distribution of those outcomes within it. Population health management is the operational practice of using linked data to segment a population, target interventions, and track whether the whole group — not just the enthusiastic early adopters — got healthier. This framing matters because a digital service can improve the average while widening the gap, and a system accountable for a population must watch both. To compare value across unlike interventions you need a common currency for health. The dominant one is the quality-adjusted life year (QALY), which combines length of life and quality of life into a single number: one year in full health equals one QALY, a year at half quality equals 0.5 QALY, and death equals zero. Quality of life is usually measured with a standardized instrument such as the EQ-5D , a short questionnaire covering five dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) that converts a patient's self-report into a single utility score. The disability-adjusted life year (DALY) is a complementary measure — years of healthy life lost to illness and premature death — used heavily in public-health and global burden-of-disease work; QALYs measure health gained, DALYs measure health lost. Economic evaluation then compares cost against effect. Cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) expresses value as cost per unit of a natural outcome (for example, cost per case detected). Cost–utility analysis (CUA) is the special case that uses QALYs as the outcome, so different interventions become directly comparable. The headline statistic is the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER): the extra cost of your intervention divided by the extra QALYs it produces, relative to whatever it replaces. In the United Kingdom, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) commonly judges interventions against a cost-effectiveness threshold in the region of £20,000–£30,000 per QALY, above which an intervention is generally considered poor value — though this is a decision aid, not a mechanical rule, and higher thresholds apply in specific circumstances such as end-of-life or highly specialized care. Two wider tools complete the family. Cost–benefit analysis (CBA) values benefits in money rather than QALYs, so health gains can be weighed against non-health returns; and budget impact analysis asks a different question — the total cash an intervention costs a system in a given year — because a service can be cost-effective per QALY yet unaffordable now. Both matter because health is not an ordinary market: information asymmetry between clinicians and patients, externalities such as the herd immunity one person's vaccination confers on others, and third-party payment all mean value cannot be left to market forces and must be actively evaluated. Underneath all this sit two efficiencies. Technical efficiency is doing a given thing at least cost (delivering the same outcomes with fewer inputs). Allocative efficiency is doing the right things — distributing resource across competing uses so total population health is maximized. The bridge between them is opportunity cost : the value of the best alternative you gave up. Every "yes" in a fixed budget is a silent "no" to something else, and the discipline of health economics is to make that silent no visible. Two further families of measure keep the patient in view. Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) capture health status as the patient reports it — did the pain, function, or quality of life actually change. Patient-reported experience measures (PREMs) capture what the encounter was like — was it accessible, respectful, coordinated. Outcomes tell you whether the service worked; experience tells you whether people can and will use it, which is itself a determinant of outcome. Finally, hold the honest critique. QALYs embed value judgements — they can systematically undervalue interventions for older, disabled, or already-unwell people, because such people have fewer or lower-quality life-years available to gain. This is the equity critique, and it connects directly to health equity and the reduction of health inequalities. Some frameworks respond with explicit equity weighting , giving greater value to health gains for the worst-off. You do not have to resolve this debate, but you must not pretend the QALY is value-neutral. Best practices # Define your primary outcome measure before you build anything. The single most common failure in digital health economics is retrofitting an outcome to a service that is already live, at which point no baseline exists and any claim is contestable. Decide up front what health change you expect, how you will measure it (a validated PROM, a routine clinical metric, a linked-data outcome such as admissions), and what "success" looks like numerically. Write it into the business case ( Topic 6.0 — Financial Management & Business Cases) so evaluation is a design constraint, not an afterthought. Build a logic model and put it on the wall. Map inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, and impact for your service, and name the assumption on every arrow. The value of the exercise is that it exposes the weak links — the step where "people receive a reminder" is assumed to become "people attend and get healthier" — so you can test exactly those. Revisit it each phase; a logic model that never changes is a logic model no one is using. Report outputs and outcomes separately, and never let outputs stand in for outcomes. It is legitimate to track activity as a leading indicator and an operational health check, but label it as such. In every board pack, pair the output with the outcome it is meant to drive and the assumption connecting them, so no one can quietly promote "messages sent" into "lives improved." If you only have outputs so far, say so plainly and state when outcome data will arrive. Choose a comparable unit of value and stick to it. Where you plausibly affect length and quality of life, use QALYs (via CUA) so your service can be weighed against others in the portfolio. Where a QALY is a poor fit — many digital services shift experience, access, or process rather than measurable health state — use a defensible intermediate outcome and be explicit that it is not directly comparable to a QALY. Consistency across your portfolio matters more than sophistication in any one case: comparable-but-simple beats brilliant-but-unique. Compute value at the margin, not the average. Decisions are incremental, so the number that matters is the ICER: the extra cost per extra QALY versus the realistic alternative (usual care, or the tool you would decommission). Averages flatter you; a service can look cheap per user yet deliver almost no additional health over what people already had. Always name your comparator explicitly, because the ICER is meaningless without it. Make opportunity cost explicit in every recommendation. State what you would stop or forgo to fund this, and what health the population loses by that choice. This turns a one-sided "invest in our thing" pitch into an allocative-efficiency argument a finance director can trust. It also disciplines your own thinking: if you cannot name a credible thing worth displacing, the case is probably weaker than it looks. Measure the distribution, not just the mean — and weight for equity where you can. Break outcomes down by deprivation, age, ethnicity, disability, and digital access, and check whether your service narrowed or widened gaps (see Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility). A service that improves the average by helping the already-advantaged is failing the population-health test. Where your organization has an equity-weighting or health-inequalities framework, apply it, and at minimum report equity impact alongside the headline ICER. Use NICE's Evidence Standards Framework to right-size your evidence. NICE's Evidence Standards Framework for Digital Health Technologies (ESF) tiers evidence expectations by the risk and function of the product, so a simple information tool is not held to the same bar as a treatment-guiding algorithm. Use it early to decide what evidence you genuinely need — and pair it with the Digital Technology Assessment Criteria (DTAC) for the safety, clinical-safety, and interoperability baseline ( Topics 1.6 and 4.3). Right-sizing prevents both under-evidenced hype and paralysing over-evidencing. Prefer routine, linked data and validated instruments over bespoke surveys. Wherever possible measure outcomes through data the system already collects — attendances, admissions, prescriptions, coded clinical results — linked at population level, so your evidence is comparable, cheap to sustain, and hard to game. Where you need patient report, use validated PROMs and PREMs rather than inventing questions, so your numbers mean the same thing as everyone else's. Handle all of this within your information-governance and data-protection duties ( Topic 1.7 ). Plan the evaluation and its funding at the same time as the build. Economic evaluation is not free; it needs a baseline, a comparator, analytic capability, and time before benefits mature. Budget for it explicitly, agree who is accountable for the evaluation, and set honest timeframes — many population-health outcomes take one to three years to move. An unfunded evaluation is a decision to never really know whether the money bought health. Match the type of economic evaluation to the question, and always test affordability. Cost-utility analysis and its ICER answer "is this good value per unit of health," but they are not the only tools. Use cost-benefit analysis, which values benefits in money, when you must weigh health returns against non-health ones; and run a budget impact analysis — the total cash cost of adopting the intervention across the system in a given year — alongside the ICER, because a service can be cost-effective per QALY yet unaffordable this year. Present value and affordability side by side, so a finance director sees both a defensible ICER and a number the budget can actually bear. Remember why the healthcare "market" fails, and evaluate as the substitute for it. Value here cannot be left to ordinary market forces: patients rarely have the information to judge clinical value (information asymmetry between clinician and patient), benefits often spill onto uninvolved third parties (externalities such as the herd immunity one person's vaccination gives others), and the person consuming care is usually not the person paying for it. These are textbook market failures, and they are precisely why disciplined economic evaluation exists rather than price signals doing the work. Treat evaluation as the mechanism that stands in for a functioning market, not as optional paperwork. Use ready-made tools and borrow expertise for anything high-stakes. For public-health and prevention decisions, start from the GOV.UK health-economics return-on-investment (ROI) tools and guidance for public health teams — which already cover areas such as falls prevention, mental health, and cardiovascular disease — rather than building a bespoke model from scratch. For contested or high-value cases, draw on health-economics expertise, whether an in-house analyst or an academic centre such as LSE Health or the Office of Health Economics. Reusing validated tools and specialist review makes your numbers faster to produce and far harder to dismiss. Questions to discuss with your team # What is the single health outcome this service must change, and how will we know we changed it rather than merely observed it changing? This forces the team past comfortable activity metrics to the causal claim underneath. Debate whether your chosen measure is truly an outcome (a change in health or wellbeing) or a dressed-up output, and whether you can attribute the change to your service rather than to secular trend, regression to the mean, or a parallel initiative. Consider whether a randomized or stepped-wedge design is feasible, or whether you will rely on a well-constructed before-and-after with a matched comparator. Talk honestly about the baseline: do you have one, and if not, is it already too late to get it. A good answer names one primary outcome, a measurement instrument, a comparator, a plausible attribution story, and the date by which you will have real data — and admits what you cannot yet prove. When our outputs look great but our outcomes are flat, what will we do? Every digital team eventually faces a service with soaring usage and no measurable health gain, and the honest response is uncomfortable. Discuss in advance what evidence would make you iterate, pause, or decommission, so the decision is not hostage to sunk cost and reputational face-saving. Surface the tension between operational leaders who are rewarded for activity and finance or public-health leaders accountable for population outcomes, because they will read the same dashboard differently. Consider whether flat outcomes mean the service does not work, or that you are measuring the wrong outcome, or that benefits lag — and how you would tell these apart. A good answer sets stopping and pivoting criteria now, in writing, and names who owns the call. Whose health are we improving, and whose are we leaving behind or actively disadvantaging? The QALY and the average both hide distribution, and a service can raise the mean while widening inequality — often by working best for the confident, connected, digitally included. Debate which groups are likely to gain least (people with low digital access, sensory or cognitive impairment, limited English, the most deprived) and whether the service risks diverting resource away from them. Discuss whether to apply equity weighting, or at least to report outcomes disaggregated by deprivation and protected characteristics, and what you would change if the gap widened. Weigh the tension between technical efficiency (cheapest average gain) and allocative fairness (gain for those in greatest need). A good answer commits to measuring distribution from the start and states a clear position on the equity trade-off rather than hiding behind a single headline number. What is our comparator, and are we honestly measuring the health this service adds rather than the health people already had? An ICER or an "admissions saved" figure is meaningless without a credible alternative to measure against, yet the comparator is the part teams most often fudge. Debate what the realistic counterfactual actually is — genuine usual care, the tool you would decommission to fund this, or a do-nothing baseline — and whether your comparator group is fairly matched or quietly healthier and more motivated than the people who opted in. Confront selection effects head-on: patients who enrol in a digital service are frequently those who would have done better anyway, which flatters every marginal claim. Discuss whether a matched cohort, a stepped-wedge rollout, or a regression-discontinuity design is within reach, and what confounders you cannot control for. A good answer names the comparator explicitly, states how it is constructed, and is candid about the residual attribution risk rather than presenting a marginal gain as if it were certain. Can we actually afford this at scale, and have we separated "good value per QALY" from "fits this year's budget"? Cost-effectiveness and affordability are different questions, and a service can pass the first while breaking the second — an intervention with a defensible ICER can still be unaffordable once rolled out across a whole population in a single financial year. Discuss the budget impact analysis alongside the ICER: the total cash the service consumes annually, who holds that budget, and whether the savings it promises are cashable or merely notional capacity that never converts into a released post or bed. Surface the tension between a business case that looks strong per patient and a finance director who cannot find the money now, and between benefits that mature over three years and budgets that reset every twelve months. Consider phasing, cohort prioritization, or a smaller initial population as ways to reconcile value with affordability. A good answer presents value and affordability side by side and is honest about which claimed savings are real cash and which are not. Who owns the evaluation, and what will we do when the first honest numbers are disappointing? Economic evaluation needs a named owner, a funded analytic capability, and a timeframe before benefits mature — and without those, "we will evaluate later" quietly becomes "we will never really know." Debate who is accountable for producing the numbers, whether they are independent enough to report bad news, and how you will guard against the pressure to quietly redefine success once a service is live and politically committed. Discuss the realistic lag: many population-health outcomes take one to three years to move, so agree now what interim signals would reassure or alarm you, and what threshold of underperformance would trigger a redesign or a stop. x: Topic 6.2 — Benefits Realization & Value Management A benefit that is promised in a business case but never named, owned, baselined, and tracked to the point of banking is a benefit that will quietly evaporate — and in health and care that lost value is measured in clinician hours, patient outcomes, and public money that could have gone elsewhere. Why this matters in health and care # Every digital investment in health and care is justified by a promise: fewer missed appointments, faster diagnosis, safer prescribing, less time on the phone, better population health. These promises are the currency of business cases, board approvals, and public trust. Yet the sobering pattern across the public sector is that benefits are enthusiastically forecast, delivery is celebrated at go-live, and then the team disperses before anyone confirms the promised value ever arrived. The gap between "the system is live" and "the value has landed" is where most digital investment silently leaks. In health and care this gap is not merely a financial embarrassment. When you tell an integrated care board (ICB) that an e-referral system will release 12,000 clinician hours a year, and those hours never materialize because clinicians now do double-keying instead, you have not just wasted money — you have consumed scarce workforce capacity, eroded frontline trust in "digital", and told a story to the public that turned out to be false. Benefits realization is therefore an accountability and public-trust discipline as much as a financial one. It is how you prove that the opportunity cost of choosing this investment over a hip operation, a nurse, or a care package was worth paying. This topic is deliberately distinct from its neighbours. Topic 6.0 — Financial Management & Business Cases is about appraising and funding an investment up front. Topic 6.1 — Health Economics is about valuing health outcomes and cost-effectiveness with methods like quality-adjusted life years. This topic is about the discipline that comes after the sign-off and often long after delivery: naming the benefits, tracking them over time, and actually banking the value that was promised. Core concepts # Benefits realisation management (BRM) is the discipline of identifying, planning, measuring, and tracking the benefits of an investment from initial idea through to their eventual capture — and then confirming they were achieved. It treats benefits as things to be actively managed, not automatic by-products of delivering a system. A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome that is perceived as positive by one or more stakeholders. Benefits are classified along several axes. Cashable benefits release money that can be removed from a budget and spent elsewhere; non-cashable benefits release capacity or improve quality without a line you can literally cut (for example, freeing 30 minutes of a nurse's shift that is immediately reabsorbed into more care). Financial benefits can be expressed in money; non-financial benefits — safety, patient experience, equity, staff wellbeing — matter enormously in health and care but resist a simple currency value. A disbenefit is a measurable decline attributable to the change: the alert fatigue, the new manual workaround, the digitally excluded cohort. Disbenefits are real benefits with a minus sign and must be tracked with equal honesty. A benefits map or benefits dependency network links the capabilities a project delivers to the enabling changes people must make, to the business outcomes, and finally to the strategic objectives. It is closely related to a logic model and a theory of change : each shows the causal chain from "what we build" to "why it matters". Reading the map backwards forces a hard question — which capability actually causes this outcome, and what else has to be true? Benefits are measured with indicators . Leading indicators are early, predictive signals you can act on (adoption rate, percentage of referrals sent digitally); lagging indicators confirm the outcome after the fact (reduction in did-not-attend rates, waiting-time change). You need both: leading indicators tell you whether value is on track while you can still intervene; lagging indicators tell you whether it actually landed. Value management — a cousin of value engineering — is the wider practice of maximizing the ratio of benefit to resource across the whole life of an investment, deliberately trading scope, cost, and benefit rather than treating any one as fixed. It links directly to the business case , whose benefits sit downstream of the up-front cost–benefit analysis , and to the wider project portfolio , where benefits from many investments are aggregated — carefully, to avoid double-counting the same saving twice. The UK reference frameworks are HM Treasury's Green Book (the appraisal and evaluation guidance behind every public business case) and Managing Successful Programmes (MSP), which places benefits management at the heart of programme delivery. Best practices # Make benefits realization a named discipline, not a business-case appendix. Too often benefits are written once to win approval and never revisited. Establish benefits management as an ongoing activity with its own cadence, artefacts, and reporting line into the portfolio and the board. The test is simple: if the only place your benefits live is a spreadsheet inside the approved business case, you do not yet have benefits realization — you have benefits forecasting. Assign a named benefit owner for every benefit, in the operational line — not the project. Each benefit needs a single accountable person who runs the part of the organization where the value will actually land: a clinical director, an operations manager, a service lead. Projects and their senior responsible owners (SROs) exist to hand over; the benefit owner remains after the team disperses. If you cannot name the person who will be measured on a benefit two years from now, that benefit is orphaned and will not be realized. Map benefits to capabilities before you build anything. Draw the benefits dependency network from strategic objective back to the specific capability the investment delivers, and expose the enabling changes — training, process redesign, decommissioning the old system — without which the benefit cannot flow. This map is your early-warning system: if a capability has no line to any outcome, question the scope; if an outcome depends on a change nobody owns, the benefit is at risk. Revisit the map at every stage gate, not just at the start. Profile each benefit: when, how much, and how measured. A benefit profile states the baseline, the target, the measurement method and data source, the owner, the dependencies, and — critically — the expected timing. Many health and care benefits land months or years after delivery ends: a shared care record's reduction in duplicate testing accrues as clinicians change habits, not on go-live day. Profiling the trajectory stops you from declaring failure too early or success too soon. Baseline before you change anything, and protect that baseline. You cannot claim a reduction in did-not-attend rates if you never measured them beforehand, and a baseline captured after go-live is worthless. Agree the baseline, its data source, and its definition with the benefit owner and finance before deployment, and freeze it. Where seasonality or a rising demand trend would distort a naïve before-and-after comparison, agree the counterfactual up front so your later claim survives scrutiny. Track leading and lagging indicators together, and report them honestly. Watch adoption and usage as leading indicators from day one, because a benefit that depends on a system nobody uses is already dead. Confirm outcomes with lagging indicators over the profiled timeline. Report actuals against forecast on a fixed cadence to the portfolio board, including benefits that are behind or lost — a benefits report that only ever shows green is a fiction that will eventually cost you your credibility. Track disbenefits and unintended consequences with the same rigour as benefits. Every worthwhile change produces some negative effects: new workarounds, alert fatigue, cohorts excluded by a digital-first channel, extra load shifted to another team. Name the anticipated disbenefits in the same register as the benefits, measure them, and act to reduce them. Hiding disbenefits does not make them disappear; it just means a clinician, a patient, or an auditor discovers them for you (see Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility). Guard relentlessly against double-counting. The same released nursing hour cannot be banked by three different projects, and two systems cannot each claim the whole reduction in duplicate tests. Aggregate benefits at portfolio level with a deduplication check, attribute shared benefits transparently, and be especially sceptical of large workforce-time savings that never show up in the actual staffing budget. Double-counted benefits are how a portfolio's paper value drifts far above anything the organization ever banks. Distinguish cashable from non-cashable and be honest about which you are promising. Boards and finance directors care intensely whether a benefit will actually reduce a budget line or merely release capacity that gets reabsorbed. Non-cashable time savings are genuinely valuable — they let you meet rising demand without more staff — but they are not the same as money you can redirect. Label each benefit clearly, and never let a non-cashable efficiency be counted as a cash saving in a savings programme. Hand over benefits ownership formally, and keep tracking after the programme closes. Programme and project closure is the single most dangerous moment for benefits, because the people who cared about them leave. Build an explicit benefits handover into closure: the benefit owner signs for each remaining benefit, the tracking mechanism is confirmed as operational, and the portfolio office assumes reporting responsibility. Schedule post-implementation reviews at the points where benefits are actually profiled to land — often 6, 12, and 24 months after go-live — and feed the results back into how you forecast the next investment. Questions to discuss with your team # Who will still be accountable for each of these benefits in two years, when the project team, the SRO, and half the leadership have moved on? This is the defining weakness of public-sector benefits management: the accountability chain is built around delivery, and delivery structures dissolve at go-live. Walk through your benefits register and try to name, for each line, the operational post-holder who will be measured on it long after the programme closes — not the person, who may leave, but the role. Debate whether those owners have accepted the benefit, have the levers to realize it, and have it written into their own objectives and their service's plan. Consider the awkward cases: benefits that span two organizations in an integrated care system, or that depend on a national system your ICB does not control. A good, honest answer names a real operational owner for every benefit, admits which benefits are currently orphaned, and produces a concrete plan to re-home them before delivery ends rather than after. How would we know if a benefit we declared as realized had quietly evaporated six months later? Many digital benefits are real at go-live and gone by the next winter: the workaround creeps back, a reorganization changes the process, staff turnover erases the training, demand rises and reabsorbs the released time. Discuss which of your claimed benefits are genuinely sticky and which depend on behaviours or conditions that could silently reverse. Examine whether you are still measuring anything after the celebratory go-live report, or whether tracking stopped the moment the money was released. Consider the difference between a one-off benefit (a decommissioned licence) and a recurring one that must be continuously earned (a sustained reduction in duplicate testing). A strong answer distinguishes durable from fragile benefits, keeps lagging indicators running past closure, and treats a benefit as provisional until it has survived a full operational cycle — not banked the day the system went live. Are we being honest about disbenefits, non-cashable savings, and double-counting — or are we telling the board the story it wants to hear? Benefits reporting is under constant pressure to look positive, because green boards approve funding and amber ones invite scrutiny. Challenge your own numbers: which "cash savings" are actually reabsorbed capacity that will never reduce a budget line? Where might the same released hour or avoided test be counted by more than one project across the portfolio? Which disbenefits — the excluded digital cohort, the alert fatigue, the extra load on a downstream team — have you left out of the register because they spoil the case? Discuss how your incentives push towards optimism and what independent check (finance, audit, a portfolio office) could hold the numbers honest. A good answer accepts that a smaller, credible, and independently verifiable benefit is worth more than a large one nobody believes, and it reports disbenefits and shortfalls as a matter of routine rather than confession. Did we baseline the right thing, and would our before-and-after claim survive an auditor who assumes the world would have changed anyway? A benefit is only as trustworthy as the counterfactual behind it, yet most benefits claims are naïve before-and-after comparisons that quietly attribute every improvement to the system. Interrogate each headline benefit: what else was changing at the same time — a service reconfiguration, a new national target, a seasonal swing in demand, a workforce initiative — that could explain part or all of the movement? Discuss whether your baseline was captured before any change touched the process, frozen with an agreed definition, and paired with an explicit counterfactual rather than an assumption that the past would have simply continued flat. Consider the awkward cases where demand is rising, so holding a metric steady is itself a benefit, or where a comparator site or a segmented cohort would strengthen the claim. An honest answer can point to the specific baseline data, name the confounders it considered, and state plainly how much of the change it can and cannot defensibly attribute to the investment. What is the total value picture across benefits, disbenefits, and the cost of realizing them — not just the headline savings we quote upstairs? It is easy to report a single large number and quietly ignore the resources and side-effects that number rests on. Value management asks you to weigh the whole ledger: the benefits, the disbenefits with a minus sign, and the often-unbudgeted cost of actually banking the value — the change management, the training, the decommissioning, the ongoing measurement effort itself. Discuss whether the effort of tracking a marginal benefit exceeds what the benefit is worth, and whether you are deliberately trading scope, cost, and benefit rather than treating the original business case as fixed. Consider benefits that are non-financial but real — safety, equity, staff wellbeing — and how you weigh them against cashable ones without pretending they share a currency. A strong answer treats value as a managed ratio across the whole investment life, is willing to descope a benefit that costs more to chase than it returns, and does not let an impressive gross figure hide a thin net one. When a benefit depends on people across several organizations working differently, who owns the enabling change — and what happens if it never lands? In an integrated care system most benefits do not flow from the technology alone; they flow from clinicians, administrators, and social-care staff in separate organizations changing long-standing habits. This is where benefits realization and change management become inseparable, and where accountability is easiest to lose across organizational boundaries. Walk each significant benefit back to the specific behavioural or process change it depends on, and ask who — in which organization — owns making that change happen, and whether they have agreed to it. Discuss the failure cases: the trust that keeps the old system running "just in case", the partner organization whose staff have no logins, the process redesign that no single leader can mandate across the system. A good answer exposes every benefit whose enabling change is unowned or spans a boundary nobody controls, and it treats those as the real delivery risk rather than assuming go-live will carry the change for you. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system approves a £4.2m investment in a shared care record spanning three acute trusts, community services, and adult social care. The outline business case promises three headline benefits: a reduction in duplicate diagnostic tests worth £1.1m a year, 40,000 clinician and administrator hours released annually from chasing records, and improved patient safety from clinicians seeing a complete medication history at the point of care. Rather than filing these in the business case and moving on, the programme builds a benefits dependency network. It shows that the £1.1m in avoided duplicate tests depends not on the record existing but on clinicians actually checking it before ordering a test — an enabling behavioural change owned by each trust's clinical director, not the programme. The 40,000 hours depend on decommissioning the old fax-and-phone process, which depends in turn on a records team being redeployed rather than quietly kept "just in case". Reading the map exposes that the safety benefit has no baseline: nobody currently measures medication-history-related incidents in a way that could later demonstrate improvement. The programme therefore does three things before go-live. It agrees a baseline for duplicate testing rates and medication incidents with each trust's finance and clinical-governance leads, freezing the definitions. It assigns named operational benefit owners — clinical directors for the testing and safety benefits, the ICS chief operating officer for the released-time benefit — each of whom signs a benefit profile with baseline, target, timing, and measurement method. And it agrees leading indicators (percentage of clinicians accessing the record, decommissioning of the fax line) to watch from week one. Twelve months after go-live, the picture is honest and mixed. Adoption is strong and the fax line is gone, so the released-time benefit is broadly on track — but the ICS reports it as non-cashable capacity, not cash, because the hours were reabsorbed into clearing the elective backlog. Duplicate testing has fallen, though by £0.7m rather than £1.1m, and the programme reports the shortfall alongside a plan to improve clinical prompting. A disbenefit has emerged: social care staff without trust logins are excluded, creating a new phone workaround, which is now on the register with an owner and a remediation date. The safety benefit is tracking but will not be confirmable until 24 months. The board trusts the report precisely because it is not all green. Sector lenses # Startup # A digital-health startup lives or dies on demonstrating value fast, usually to a single trust or ICS running a pilot. Benefits realization is your commercial evidence base: the case study that wins the next contract is built on baselined, tracked benefits from the last deployment, so instrument value capture into the product from day one. Your risk is overclaiming — a slick dashboard showing a benefit the customer's finance director cannot reconcile will end the relationship faster than a modest, verifiable one. x: Topic 6.3 — Procurement & Commercial In one sentence: How you buy and contract for digital determines who controls your data, whether your services stay safe and interoperable, and whether public money delivers value — so procurement is a strategic and clinical-safety discipline, not a back-office formality. Why this matters in health and care # Almost nothing large in digital health and care is built entirely in-house. Electronic patient records, shared care records, patient-facing apps, infrastructure, analytics platforms, and the specialists who deliver them are bought from suppliers under contracts that can run for five, seven, or ten years. The commercial choices you make at the point of purchase — what you specify, who can bid, who owns the data, how you exit — shape the service far longer than any single delivery sprint. A poor contract locks in a poor service, and in this sector a poor service is not just inconvenient; it can be unsafe, inequitable, and a breach of public trust. The stakes are concrete. Public bodies in the United Kingdom spend hundreds of billions of pounds a year through procurement, and health and care is one of the largest components. Every pound is public money, subject to statutory duties of transparency and value, and to scrutiny by auditors, regulators, and — when things go wrong — Parliament and the press. A botched procurement wastes that money twice: on the failed contract and again on the remediation. Worse, a contract that hands a supplier control of clinical data with no exit route can trap an organization for a decade, unable to switch even when the service degrades. Procurement is also where equity and safety are quietly decided. Buy a system that cannot exchange data with others (see Topic 4.3 — Interoperability & Data Standards) and you have bought a silo that fragments care; specify only the cheapest input rather than the safest outcome and you may get exactly what you paid for. Getting the commercial ways of working right is inseparable from getting the clinical and equity outcomes right. Core concepts # Public procurement and its principles. Government procurement in the United Kingdom is the regulated process by which public bodies buy goods, works, and services. Since the Procurement Act 2023 came into force (for contracts advertised from early 2025), the regime for most public bodies in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland rests on a small set of principles that every commercial decision must honour: transparency, fair and equal treatment of suppliers, the pursuit of value for money and the public good, and integrity (acting with honesty and avoiding conflicts of interest). Health-specific rules — notably the NHS Provider Selection Regime for the procurement of health care services — sit alongside the general regime, so you must know which applies to a given purchase. Build vs buy vs configure. Every requirement invites three broad options: build it yourself, buy an off-the-shelf product, or buy a platform and configure it. Building gives control but demands durable in-house capability; buying is faster but risks lock-in and misfit; configuring a commercial off-the-shelf product is the common middle path. The decision hinges on whether the capability is a genuine differentiator (rare — usually worth building or heavily shaping) or a commodity (usually worth buying), and on the honest total cost of ownership over the whole life, not just the licence price (see Topic 6.0 — Financial Management & Business Cases). Routes to market. Rather than run a full competition every time, public bodies often buy through pre-established routes. A framework agreement is an arrangement with one or more suppliers, established by a central purchasing body, from which buyers call off contracts under agreed terms. In the UK the Crown Commercial Service (CCS) operates cross-government frameworks including G-Cloud (cloud hosting, software, and support) and the Digital Marketplace; NHS bodies operate health frameworks; and dynamic markets (the Procurement Act successor to dynamic purchasing systems) let new suppliers join over the life of the arrangement. These routes trade some bespoke tailoring for speed, pre-assured terms, and lawful compliance. Outcome-based vs input-based specification. An input specification tells the supplier exactly what to build and how; an outcome or performance-based contract defines the result you want and the measures of success, and lets the supplier propose how. Outcome-based specification suits complex, evolving digital services, but demands mature measurement and a client who can judge outcomes rather than count deliverables. Vendor lock-in, portability, and open standards. Vendor lock-in is being unable to switch supplier without prohibitive cost, because your data, integrations, or skills are trapped in one vendor's proprietary world. The commercial antidotes are data portability (your data exportable in usable form), open standards (see open standard ) written into the contract, and explicit exit and transition arrangements agreed before you sign, not after the relationship sours. Social value. The Public Services (Social Value) Act 2012 requires public bodies to consider the wider economic, social, and environmental benefits of what they buy — local employment, skills, carbon reduction, health inequalities. Social value is now routinely weighted in evaluation, and under the Procurement Act the pursuit of public good is explicit. SME access, contract management, and intelligent-client capability. Policy actively encourages access for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and start-ups, because a market dominated by a few giants is fragile and expensive. Once a contract is signed, contract management and supplier relationship management determine whether the value on paper is realized in practice. Where contract management enforces the terms, supplier relationship management is the in-life discipline of governing performance, sustaining a working partnership, and managing supplier risk and concentration across the years the contract runs. Underpinning all of it is intelligent-client capability: enough in-house understanding to specify, evaluate, and hold suppliers to account. You can outsource delivery; you can never outsource accountability. Best practices # Decide build vs buy vs configure deliberately, on total cost of ownership. Ask whether the capability is a true differentiator or a commodity, and cost the whole life — licences, integration, exit, and the in-house skills you must keep — not the sticker price. The default in a resource-constrained public body is to buy or configure a commodity and reserve building for the rare genuine differentiator. Write the reasoning down so it can be revisited when circumstances change. Engage the market before you specify, transparently. Pre-market engagement — supplier days, requests for information, published pipelines — lets you learn what the market can offer and lets suppliers prepare, without giving anyone an unfair edge. Done openly and recorded, it produces better specifications and more, and more diverse, bidders. Done secretly with a favoured supplier, it corrupts the competition and breaches the integrity principle; keep it even-handed and documented. Specify outcomes, not just inputs, where the work is complex. For evolving digital services, define the outcomes, service levels, and measures you care about, and let suppliers propose the how, rather than freezing a detailed solution you will regret. This suits agile delivery and lets better ideas surface. It only works if you can genuinely measure the outcomes and resist the temptation to drift back into managing tasks; pair it with clear acceptance criteria (see Topic 3.5 — Delivery Lifecycles). Write portability, open standards, and exit into the contract before you sign. Require that data be held in, or exportable to, open and interoperable formats (see Topic 4.3 — Interoperability & Data Standards), that interfaces use published standards, and that a costed exit and transition plan exists from day one. The moment of maximum leverage is before signature; afterwards the supplier has every incentive to make leaving hard. Treat open standards as a commercial lever, not merely a technical preference. Choose the route to market on fit, not habit. A framework or dynamic market is faster and lawfully safer than a bespoke competition, but only if its terms fit your need and its call-off rules give real competition rather than a rubber stamp. Check that the route allows the outcome-based, agile contracting you want and does not quietly exclude the SMEs you are trying to reach. Do not default to last time's framework simply because it is familiar. Weight social value and SME access honestly. Give social value a meaningful, published weighting tied to outcomes you will measure — local skills, reduced inequalities, carbon — and design the process so smaller firms can compete: proportionate requirements, prompt payment, SME-sized lots, no needless turnover thresholds. Token weighting that no one checks after award is theatre; genuine SME participation makes your supply market more resilient and often more innovative. Resource contract and supplier relationship management from day one. The value promised in a bid evaporates without active management: track performance against service levels, hold regular reviews, manage change, and build a relationship robust enough to survive problems. Name an accountable contract owner with the time and authority to do the job, not a signature that files the contract and moves on. Most realizable value — and most risk — lives in the years after award (see Topic 9.0 — Collaborating with Partner Organizations). Keep intelligent-client capability in-house. Retain enough architecture, clinical-safety, data, and commercial expertise to specify well, evaluate credibly, and challenge suppliers as equals. Outsourcing delivery is legitimate; outsourcing the ability to understand what you have bought is how organizations become captured by their vendors. You remain accountable to patients, regulators, and the public no matter who does the work (see Topic 6.4 — Governance & Assurance). Make agile delivery work inside a compliant contract. Fixed-price, fixed-scope contracts fight iterative discovery, but you can reconcile them: contract for outcomes and capacity, use phased break-points and off-ramps, price by sprint or capped time-and-materials, and align payment to working software rather than documents. Build change mechanisms into the contract so learning during delivery can be absorbed lawfully, honouring procurement rules while still delivering the way modern digital services demand. Manage the relationship actively through the life of the contract, not just the transaction. Run a regular cadence of governance meetings that reviews performance against service levels and the outcomes that matter clinically and operationally, agrees a joint roadmap, and resolves issues before they escalate. Treat your strategic suppliers as partners with a shared stake in the service, not adversaries to be caught out; the relationship, not the paperwork, is what carries you through the inevitable problems. Keep decisions, actions, and performance data documented so reviews build on evidence rather than memory, and so accountability survives changes of personnel on either side. Monitor supplier risk and concentration in-life, and keep exit readiness live. Watch the financial health of your critical suppliers — accounts, credit signals, ownership changes — so a failure or acquisition does not surprise you, and track how dependent you have become on any single provider across your portfolio. Keep the exit and transition plan a living document, rehearsed and re-costed rather than filed and forgotten, so leaving remains a real option. Agree clear escalation routes for when a supplier underperforms — from operational review to commercial and board level — and use them early, before a degrading service becomes a safety or continuity risk. Questions to discuss with your team # For this requirement, are we buying a commodity or a differentiator — and what is the honest whole-life cost of each option, including exit? This question forces the build-vs-buy-vs-configure decision into the open before momentum carries you toward the familiar supplier or the lowest headline price. In health and care the trap is subtle: a capability that feels unique to your trust is usually a commodity dozens of others have already bought, while genuinely differentiating work is rarer than teams like to believe. The debate should surface the real total cost of ownership — integration, data migration, the in-house skills you must retain, and above all the cost of leaving — rather than the licence fee that dominates most business cases. Weigh the pull toward building (control, fit, pride) against the discipline of buying a commodity and directing scarce engineering effort at what only you can do. Consider concrete comparators: what did a neighbouring organization pay over five years, and what did they pay to exit? A good answer names the differentiator explicitly, costs the whole life including a credible exit scenario, and records the reasoning so it can be challenged later; a weak one compares sticker prices and calls the cheapest option value for money. How would we leave this supplier if we had to — and have we written that into the contract before we sign? Exit is where lock-in is either prevented or cemented, and it is almost always neglected because, at signing, everyone is optimistic and the relationship is new. The tension is that the moment you have maximum leverage to demand data portability, open standards, and a costed transition plan is exactly the moment no one wants to talk about divorce. In a clinical setting the consequences are severe: patient data trapped in a proprietary format, integrations only the incumbent understands, and a service you cannot improve because switching would cost more than tolerating the status quo. Debate whether the contract actually guarantees data export in open, usable formats, whether interfaces use published standards, and whether a transition plan and its costs are agreed now rather than negotiated from weakness later. Consider real scenarios: the supplier is acquired, doubles its price, or lets the service degrade — what are your options on each? A strong answer describes a credible exit route with named formats, standards, timescales, and costs already in the contract; a poor one assumes you will simply renew because leaving is unthinkable, which is the definition of lock-in. Do we have the in-house capability to be an intelligent client for this — and if not, how do we build it rather than hand accountability to the supplier? This question tests whether you can specify, evaluate, and hold a supplier to account, or whether you depend on the very people you are meant to be managing. It matters acutely in digital health because accountability for clinical safety, data protection, and equity cannot be outsourced no matter who writes the code (see Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management and Topic 1.7 — Information Governance, Data Protection & Cyber Security); a supplier's assurance is not a substitute for your own understanding. The tension is that intelligent-client capability costs scarce skills that boards are tempted to cut in favour of visible delivery, and suppliers may quietly prefer a client who cannot challenge them. Discuss where your real gaps are — architecture, commercial, clinical safety, data — and whether you are filling them with retained expertise or papering over them with consultancy that deepens the dependency. Consider what happens at contract review or dispute: can your people credibly interrogate the supplier's performance and technical claims? A good answer identifies specific capabilities to retain and a plan to build them; a weak one assumes the supplier will tell you what you need to know. Can we actually measure the outcomes we intend to specify — and if not, are we honest that we are still buying inputs? Outcome-based specification is the right instinct for complex digital services, but it only delivers if you can define, capture, and judge the outcomes that matter, and many organizations write outcome language over an input mindset. The tension is that clinical and operational outcomes — reduced waits, safer prescribing, closed equity gaps — are slow, multi-causal, and hard to attribute to one system, so teams quietly retreat to counting deliverables and calling it outcomes. In digital health the risk cuts both ways: specify outcomes you cannot measure and you cannot hold the supplier to account; specify inputs for evolving work and you freeze a solution you will outgrow (see Topic 3.5 — Delivery Lifecycles). Debate which outcomes you can genuinely instrument, what proxy measures and service levels you will accept in the meantime, and who on your side has the analytical capability to judge them. Consider whether your acceptance criteria tie payment to demonstrated working software and real service levels rather than documents. An honest answer names the measures, admits where you are really buying inputs, and commits to building the measurement maturity the contract assumes; a weak one sprinkles the word "outcomes" through a specification no one can score. Are our social value and SME commitments real levers we will enforce, or weighting we will forget after award? Social value and SME access are statutory and policy expectations, but they curdle into theatre when they are weighted on paper at evaluation and never checked again once the contract is running. The tension is genuine: a meaningful social-value weighting and SME-friendly design — proportionate requirements, right-sized lots, prompt payment, no needless turnover thresholds — can widen and strengthen your supply market, yet they add process and can favour bidders who write good social-value narratives over those who deliver them. In health and care the prize is concrete — local digital skills, reduced access inequalities, lower carbon — but only if someone measures delivery after award rather than filing the promises. Discuss what weighting is high enough to change bidder behaviour, which commitments you will write into the contract as enforceable obligations, and who owns checking them in-life. Consider whether your process quietly excludes the SMEs and start-ups you claim to want, through scale, turnover, or insurance requirements they cannot meet. A strong answer ties social value to measurable, contracted outcomes and names the owner who will hold suppliers to them; a weak one treats the weighting as a box ticked at evaluation and forgotten by go-live. How exposed are we to the failure or dominance of a single supplier across our portfolio — and are we managing that concentration deliberately? Individual procurements are usually judged in isolation, but risk accumulates across the portfolio: buy enough from one dominant provider and its financial distress, acquisition, or price rise becomes an organizational and clinical-continuity risk, not just a commercial inconvenience. The tension is that consolidating on a single strategic supplier brings real benefits — integration, simpler management, volume discounts — while quietly deepening the dependency that makes you unable to leave or negotiate. In digital health a critical supplier's failure can threaten live clinical services, so concentration is a safety question as much as a commercial one (see Topic 9.0 — Collaborating with Partner Organizations). Debate how dependent you have become on any one provider, whether you monitor the financial health and ownership of your critical suppliers, and what your continuity plan is if one fails or is acquired.
