x: Topic 6.4 — Governance & Assurance Governance exists to help you make good, fast, safe decisions and to prove — to yourself, your board, and the public — that a digital service is being run responsibly, so treat it as an enabler of delivery rather than a tax on it. Why this matters in health and care # In most sectors, weak governance costs money and reputation. In health and care it can cost lives, entrench inequity, and erode the public trust on which the whole system depends. A poorly governed change to a clinical system can propagate a dosing error to thousands of patients before anyone notices; an ungoverned data flow can breach the confidentiality of the most vulnerable people you serve; an unassured go-live can lock in a service that quietly excludes those who most need care. The stakes are why "how you work" is a clinical-safety, equity, and trust issue, not merely an efficiency one. At the same time, governance in health and care has a well-earned reputation for being slow, ritualistic, and disconnected from delivery. Teams sit through board meetings that rubber-stamp decisions already made, complete templates nobody reads, and watch amber risks turn green the week before a review only to fail spectacularly afterwards. This is the paradox you must resolve. The answer is not less governance or more; it is proportionate governance that scales with risk and value, gives clear people clear accountability, and produces honest information fast enough to act on. This topic shows you how to build that, and how to layer independent assurance on top so that the people accountable — and the public — can be confident the controls actually work. It connects tightly to Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management, Topic 1.7 — Information Governance, Data Protection & Cyber Security, Topic 5.3 — EPPM, and Topic 10.4 — Visibility for the CEO & Senior Leaders. Core concepts # Governance is the system of decision rights, accountability, and oversight through which an organization directs and controls what it does. In digital health and care you are really managing three overlapping governance domains at once. Corporate governance covers the board's stewardship of the organization as a whole — finance, strategy, risk, and legal duties. Clinical governance is the framework through which health organizations are accountable for continuously improving the quality and safety of care. Information governance covers how the organization handles data lawfully, securely, and ethically. A digital service touches all three; if you govern only one, you will be blindsided by the others. Single-point accountability is the spine of good governance. The Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) is the one named individual personally accountable for a programme or major project achieving its objectives and realizing its benefits — a role popularized by UK government but universally useful. Decision rights below the SRO are made explicit through a responsibility assignment matrix , commonly the RACI (responsible, accountable, consulted, informed) form, which prevents the two classic failures of "everyone thought someone else owned it" and "everyone tried to own it". Assurance is distinct from governance. Governance is the act of directing and deciding; assurance is independent, objective confirmation that the governance and controls are actually working as intended. The dominant mental model is the "three lines of defence": the first line is operational management who own and manage risk day-to-day; the second line is oversight functions (risk, compliance, clinical safety, information governance) that set policy and challenge; and the third line is internal audit , independent of both, reporting to the board. External regulators and auditors form a de facto fourth line. Two further concepts hold the system together. Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk the organization is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives; without it, escalation is arbitrary. And the risk log — often extended to a RAID log (risks, assumptions, issues, dependencies) built on the same discipline as a risk register — is the working record that keeps a delivery honest. Review points are provided by staged assurance such as a phase-gate process and, in UK government, gateway-style reviews run by the Infrastructure and Projects Authority (IPA). Above the level of any single project sits enterprise risk management , the organization-wide discipline of identifying and managing the risks that could stop the whole enterprise achieving its objectives, rather than treating digital, clinical, financial, cyber and operational risk as separate silos. Best practices # Name one accountable SRO and mean it. Appoint a single, sufficiently senior individual who is personally accountable for the outcome, has the authority to make decisions, and stays with the programme long enough to be held to account. Write their accountability into the terms of reference and their objectives. Resist the temptation to spread accountability across a committee — committees advise and decide collectively, but they cannot be accountable, because accountability that is shared is accountability that is absent. Design governance to fit the risk and value, not the calendar. A small, low-risk internal tool does not need the same board, gates, and paperwork as a region-wide electronic patient record. Set tiers so that low-risk, low-value work flows through lightweight team-level governance, while high-risk or high-value work attracts formal boards and independent review. Publish the thresholds so teams know which tier they are in and can self-serve. Proportionality is what keeps governance from becoming a bottleneck that teams route around. Write terms of reference that clarify decision rights. Every board should have a short terms-of-reference document stating its purpose, membership, quorum, what decisions it can make, what it can only recommend, and what must escalate above it. Pair this with a RACI so that recurring decision types — architecture choices, clinical sign-off, budget release, go-live approval — have a named accountable owner. Ambiguous decision rights are the single most common cause of governance drift, where meetings multiply because no one is sure who can actually say yes. Separate assurance from governance and use the three lines. Do not let the people delivering a programme be the only people who assure it is safe. Ensure the second line — clinical safety officers, information governance leads, cyber security — has an independent voice and can escalate over the SRO's head when needed, and that internal audit periodically tests the whole system. This separation is what turns optimistic self-reporting into credible assurance, and it is a regulatory expectation in most health systems, not a nicety. Use integrated assurance and staged review points. Rather than commissioning uncoordinated reviews, plan an integrated assurance and approval schedule that aligns clinical safety, information governance, technical, and commercial reviews to the same decision points. Adopt gateway-style reviews at the transitions that matter — before committing money, before build, before go-live — modelled on IPA gateway reviews and, for public-facing digital services, the service assessments pioneered by the Government Digital Service (GDS) and adapted by NHS. A good gate is a supportive challenge that de-risks the next phase, not an exam to be gamed. Make risk appetite explicit and let it drive escalation. Agree, at board level, how much risk you are willing to carry in each domain — patient safety, data, delivery, finance, reputation — and express it concretely enough that a team can tell whether a given risk sits inside or outside appetite. Then wire escalation to appetite: anything outside appetite goes up automatically, with a named owner and a decision deadline. This stops the two failure modes of trivia clogging the board and serious risks quietly sitting in a spreadsheet. Run a living RAID log and a Board Assurance Framework. Maintain a RAID log that is reviewed every delivery cycle, with each entry owned, dated, scored, and actively worked — not a graveyard of stale amber items. At organizational level, maintain a Board Assurance Framework (BAF) that maps your principal strategic risks to the controls in place and the assurance you have that those controls work, exposing gaps where you are relying on hope. The BAF is what lets a board see, on one page, whether its most important objectives are actually protected. Report honestly and kill governance theatre. Insist on candid status reporting that surfaces bad news early, and protect the people who raise it. Watch for "watermelon reporting" — green on the outside, red on the inside — where dashboards stay green until the moment of failure; counter it by having assurance functions and delivery leads report on the same facts. Cut any meeting, template, or report that does not change a decision. Governance that produces documents nobody acts on is not caution, it is waste dressed as diligence. Manage risk at enterprise level, not just project level. Hold a board-level enterprise risk register and a written risk appetite statement that connect digital, clinical, financial, cyber and operational risk instead of treating each in its own silo. Many of the risks that actually sink digital health services — an ageing estate of legacy systems, a cyber attack, over-reliance on a single supplier — cut across every project and are owned by none of them, so give each cross-cutting risk a named executive owner and a place on the register. This is the difference between knowing that your programmes are each roughly on track and knowing whether the organization as a whole is inside its appetite. Aggregate the same risks up to the board without sanitizing them. Wire your three lines of defence so that a risk seen by a delivery team travels up to the enterprise register recognizably, not repackaged into reassuring language at each layer. The BAF and enterprise register are only as honest as the reporting beneath them, so guard against the watermelon effect where amber becomes green on its way to the top, and make it routine to escalate cross-cutting risks — legacy, cyber, supplier concentration — that no single project owns. A board that sees only aggregated, softened numbers cannot govern the risks that matter most. Questions to discuss with your team # Where is single-point accountability genuinely clear on our most important digital work, and where is it a comfortable fiction? Walk through your top three initiatives and ask, for each, who would personally answer to the board if it failed. If the honest answer is "the board", "the programme", or a name that keeps changing, you have a gap. Test whether the named SRO actually has the authority and time the role demands, or whether they are a figurehead while real decisions happen elsewhere. Consider whether accountability is undermined by a matrix in which the SRO cannot direct the people delivering. Discuss how continuity is protected when SROs move on, since accountability that resets every reorganization is no accountability at all. The aim is not to blame individuals but to make sure that when something goes wrong, one empowered person owns putting it right. Is our governance proportionate, or are we applying heavyweight process to low-risk work and vice versa? Map your current boards, gates, and approval steps against the actual risk and value of what passes through them. Look for the low-risk change that waited six weeks for a board that meets monthly, and the high-risk clinical change that slipped through on a team's own say-so. Ask whether teams are routing around governance because it is too slow, which is itself a serious risk signal. Consider whether you have published clear tiers and thresholds, or whether everything defaults to maximum ceremony out of caution. Debate where you could delegate decisions safely to move faster, and where you have been dangerously light. The goal is a system where the weight of governance visibly tracks the weight of the risk. How would we know if our reporting is telling us the truth? Discuss concrete recent examples where a status went from green to red with little warning, and ask what the early signals were and why they did not surface. Explore whether delivery leads and assurance functions report from the same facts or from separate, conveniently divergent versions. Consider what happens, socially and professionally, to someone who reports a red status here — are they thanked or punished? Ask whether your board sees independent assurance alongside management's own account, or only the latter. Examine whether your dashboards measure things that predict problems or only things that are easy to make green. The purpose is to build a culture where honest bad news travels fast, because a governance system that cannot hear bad news cannot govern. Have we written down our risk appetite concretely enough that a team can act on it, or is it a slogan? Take a live risk on one of your programmes and ask whether the people closest to it could tell, from your stated appetite, whether it sits inside or outside the line. Most organizations have a risk appetite statement that reads well and decides nothing — "we take a balanced approach to risk" tells no clinician whether an undetected allergy-display defect is tolerable. Discuss whether appetite is expressed per domain — patient safety, data, delivery, finance, reputation — because a single global figure hides the fact that you may have zero appetite for clinical-safety defects and real appetite for schedule slippage. Examine whether escalation is actually wired to appetite, so anything outside it rises automatically with a named owner and a deadline, rather than depending on someone choosing to raise it. Consider who owns the appetite and how often it is revisited, since an appetite set once and never revisited drifts out of step with the real world. An honest answer names a recent decision that the appetite statement genuinely shaped, and admits where the statement is currently too vague to bite. Do our gates and assurance reviews actually have teeth, or do failing programmes sail through them? Look back at your last few gateway or service-assessment reviews and ask whether any of them stopped, paused, or materially reshaped the work — if every programme has passed every gate, your gates are almost certainly theatre. Discuss whether reviews are treated as a supportive challenge that de-risks the next phase or as an exam to be gamed, with the evidence pack curated to secure a pass. Consider whether clinical safety, information governance, technical and commercial assurance arrive at the same decision points or as a scatter of uncoordinated reviews that exhaust teams without adding confidence. Examine what authority a gate reviewer actually has: can they hold a go-live, and will they be backed if they do, or will commercial pressure override them? Explore whether the people delivering are also, in effect, the people assuring — because a gate run by the optimists is not assurance. The aim is a review that a serious problem could not survive, because a gate nothing ever fails is a cost with no control behind it. Which of the risks that could actually sink us are owned by no single project, and who owns them? List the failures most likely to stop your digital services — an ageing estate of legacy systems, a cyber attack, over-reliance on one supplier, a workforce that cannot operate the new tools — and ask, for each, whose register it sits on. These cross-cutting risks are dangerous precisely because they belong to everyone and therefore no one, falling between the cracks of project-level governance. Discuss whether you hold a board-level enterprise risk register that connects digital, clinical, financial, cyber and operational risk, or whether each is managed in its own silo blind to the others. Consider whether a risk seen by a delivery team travels up to the board recognizably, or gets softened from red to amber to green at each layer until the board sees only reassurance. Examine whether each cross-cutting risk has a named executive owner with the authority to act across programmes. An honest answer confronts the gap between knowing each programme is roughly on track and knowing whether the organization as a whole is inside its appetite. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system (ICS) is rolling out a shared care record that lets clinicians across hospitals, general practice, and social care see a unified view of each patient. It is high-value and high-risk: it touches clinical decisions, links sensitive data across organizations, and serves a population with wide variation in digital access. Early on, accountability is muddy. Three chief information officers each feel partly responsible, a supplier is driving the timeline, and the programme board of eighteen people spends its meetings receiving updates rather than deciding. Reporting is green. Then a near-miss surfaces: a medication allergy recorded in one system is not displaying in another, and a clinician nearly prescribes a drug the patient is allergic to. The chief executives use this as a turning point and rebuild the governance. They appoint one SRO — a chief medical officer with the seniority to direct the programme and the standing to challenge the supplier. They rewrite the board's terms of reference, cut it to the decision-makers, and attach a RACI so clinical safety sign-off, information governance approval, and go-live authorization each have a named accountable owner. Risk appetite is made explicit: zero appetite for undetected clinical-safety defects, limited appetite for schedule slippage. That single statement reorders everything. Assurance is separated from delivery. The clinical safety officer and the information governance lead report independently and can escalate over the SRO to the chief executives; the shared-record work is added to each partner's Board Assurance Framework. An integrated assurance schedule sets three gates — before further build, before pilot, before full roll-out — each combining clinical safety, information governance, technical, and accessibility reviews, in the spirit of IPA gateway reviews and NHS service assessments. The RAID log is reviewed fortnightly, with the allergy-display defect logged as a red issue owned by name with a fixed resolution date. The first gate is uncomfortable: the review team finds the clinical-safety case is thinner than the green reports implied, and the roll-out is paused four weeks. It is exactly the watermelon the old reporting had hidden. Because the pause happens before pilot rather than after go-live, no patient is harmed, the supplier fixes the data-mapping, and the eventual roll-out is slower to start but far safer and more trusted. Governance did not slow delivery; it prevented a failure that would have stopped it altogether. Sector lenses # Startup # A health-tech startup rarely needs boards and gateway reviews, but it does need the essentials early, because regulators, buyers, and investors will ask. Name one accountable founder or executive for clinical safety and one for data protection, keep a lightweight RAID log, and write down your risk appetite even if it is a single page. The trap is treating governance as something to bolt on later; retrofitting evidence of safe, lawful decisions across a fast-moving product is painful and sometimes impossible. Build the minimum viable governance that a serious NHS buyer would recognize, and let it grow with you rather than lurching from nothing to bureaucracy overnight. x: Topic 6.5 — Technology Cost Management & Cloud FinOps In health and care, the running cost of technology is public money spent every hour whether anyone is watching or not, so managing that cost — especially in the cloud — is an operational discipline of stewardship, not an annual finance exercise. Why this matters in health and care # For most of the history of NHS technology, the money was spent once. You bought a server, a storage array or a licence, capitalized it, and it sat in a rack depreciating quietly for five years. The cost was visible, bounded and largely fixed. Cloud computing broke that model. Now the meter runs continuously, the bill changes daily, thousands of small decisions by engineers move real money, and the invoice arrives a month after the spending is already done. A misconfigured job left running over a bank-holiday weekend, a test environment nobody switched off, a storage bucket that quietly grows — each is public money leaking in real time. This matters in health and care for three reasons beyond ordinary thrift. First, it is public money held in trust: every pound spent on idle compute or a duplicated software licence is a pound not spent on care, and you are accountable for it to auditors, to your board and ultimately to the public (see Topic 6.4 — Governance & Assurance). Second, the money follows peculiar rules. NHS budgets split hard between capital and revenue, and the shift from buying assets to renting services quietly converts one into the other — a technical decision with a budgetary consequence that can blindside a finance director. Third, unmanaged cost is a safety and continuity risk in disguise: teams that fear a surprise bill under-provision resilience, delay patches, or cannot afford to run the environments a safe service needs. The failure mode is distinctive and common. Organizations move to the cloud expecting savings, celebrate the migration, and then eighteen months later discover the bill is larger than the data centre it replaced — and no one can say why. The problem is rarely the technology. It is that no one owns the running cost as a live discipline: engineers optimize for delivery speed, finance sees a single opaque invoice, and the feedback loop between a design decision and its cost never closes. This topic is about closing that loop. Core concepts # Cloud computing delivers computing resources — servers, storage, databases, networking — as an on-demand, metered service rather than as owned equipment. Its defining commercial feature is elasticity: you can acquire and release capacity in minutes and pay only for what you consume. That same elasticity is why cost management is hard. The technical architecture of cloud and legacy is covered in Topic 4.0 (see Topic 4.0 — Technical Architecture, Cloud & Legacy); this topic owns what happens to the cost once that architecture is running. The central accounting shift is from capital expenditure (capex) — money spent to acquire a fixed asset that is then depreciated over years — to operating expense (opex), an ongoing cost of running a service. Buying a server is capex; renting the equivalent cloud capacity is opex. In the NHS this is not a neutral bookkeeping detail: capital and revenue are separately allocated, separately controlled, and rarely fungible, so moving spend from capex to opex can relieve one pressure while creating another. The up-front appraisal of these choices — the Five Case Model, capital versus revenue basics — belongs to financial management and business cases (see Topic 6.0 — Financial Management & Business Cases); this topic picks up where the business case ends and the meter starts. FinOps — a contraction of "cloud financial operations" — is the operating discipline that brings engineering, finance and business teams together to manage cloud cost as a shared, data-driven responsibility. Promoted by the FinOps Foundation (part of the Linux Foundation), it is usually described as a lifecycle with three iterative phases: Inform (give everyone visibility of what is being spent and why, through allocation and reporting), Optimize (act on that visibility to eliminate waste and buy more cheaply), and Operate (embed cost awareness into everyday ways of working and governance). FinOps is deliberately not just cost-cutting; its goal is to maximize the business value of every pound of cloud spend, which sometimes means spending more because the return justifies it. Two allocation mechanisms make cost visible. Showback reports to each team or service what its technology consumption costs, for transparency and behaviour change, without moving money. Chargeback goes further and actually recovers the cost from the consuming unit's budget — a form of internal cost allocation that assigns shared-service costs to the cost centre that consumes them. Both depend on tagging : labelling every cloud resource with metadata (service, team, environment, patient-facing or not) so that an undifferentiated invoice can be split into meaningful lines. Three more ideas run through the topic. Total cost of ownership (TCO) is the full direct and indirect cost of a technology over its whole life — not just the licence or the compute, but the people, integration, support, exit and decommissioning around it. Software asset management (SAM) is the discipline of tracking and optimizing the software an organization owns and rents, increasingly dominated by software-as-a-service (SaaS) subscriptions and per-user software licences that renew silently. And unit economics expresses cost as a rate against something the organization cares about — cost per patient, per appointment, per referral, per API call — so that a rising bill can be judged against rising value rather than in a vacuum. Autoscaling , the automatic adjustment of capacity to match load, and the broader financial-management practices of ITIL sit alongside these as the operational levers. Best practices # Make cost visible before you try to cut it — Inform first. You cannot manage what no one can see, and the default cloud invoice is a single opaque number arriving a month late. Establish near-real-time cost visibility broken down by service, team, environment and, where you can, by clinical service, so that the people making design decisions can see the cost of those decisions within days, not quarters. Visibility alone changes behaviour: teams that can see their own spend routinely find waste no central finance report would ever have caught. Tag everything, and treat untagged spend as a defect. Cost allocation is only as good as the metadata underneath it; an untagged resource is money you cannot attribute, question or reclaim. Agree a mandatory tagging standard — owner, service, environment, cost centre, data classification — enforce it through automated policy so non-compliant resources are flagged or blocked at creation, and report the proportion of spend that is properly allocated as a headline metric. In a health context, tagging whether a workload is patient-facing or clinical-critical also lets you protect the right things when you optimize the rest. Choose showback or chargeback deliberately, and match it to your accountability. Showback builds cost awareness gently and is the right starting point for most organizations; chargeback creates real budgetary consequence but needs mature allocation and the political will to defend the numbers. Decide which behaviour you are trying to create — awareness, or genuine financial ownership — and be honest that premature chargeback with shaky data will generate disputes that discredit the whole effort. Whichever you choose, the aim is a closed loop where a team's decisions visibly affect a budget it recognizes as its own. Eliminate waste relentlessly: rightsize, schedule and delete. A large share of cloud spend in most estates is pure waste — over-provisioned instances, oversized databases, orphaned storage, and non-production environments running twenty-four hours a day for a nine-to-five team. Rightsize resources to observed load rather than guessed peak, schedule development and test environments to switch off overnight and at weekends, and put a lifecycle on storage and snapshots so nothing accumulates forever. This is the fastest, lowest-risk saving available and it recurs every month once automated. Buy committed capacity for your predictable baseline. Cloud providers discount heavily — often substantially — in exchange for a one- or three-year commitment through reserved instances, savings plans or committed-use agreements, and the steady baseline of a health service (the core electronic patient record, the always-on integration engine) is exactly the predictable load these instruments reward. Analyse your stable usage, commit to it to capture the discount, and keep on-demand or autoscaled capacity for the variable peak on top. Review commitments regularly so you do not lock in capacity you have since re-architected away, and coordinate purchases with procurement and commercial colleagues (see Topic 6.3 — Procurement & Commercial). Manage SaaS and licence sprawl as deliberately as cloud compute. The cloud bill is visible; the twenty SaaS subscriptions bought on departmental cards, the per-seat licences assigned to leavers, and the overlapping tools that do the same job are not — yet together they often rival the infrastructure spend. Maintain a live register of software subscriptions and entitlements, reconcile licences against actual named users and usage, cancel or downgrade what is unused, and consolidate duplicated tools. Software asset management here is both a cost discipline and a security one, because unknown SaaS is also unmanaged data flow (see Topic 1.7 — Information Governance, Data Protection & Cyber Security). Judge cost by unit economics, not by the size of the bill. A rising bill is not automatically bad and a falling one is not automatically good; what matters is cost relative to value delivered. Define unit-cost metrics that make sense clinically and operationally — cost per patient monitored, per appointment booked, per referral processed, per thousand API calls — and track them over time so you can tell efficiency from mere growth and defend spend that is genuinely earning its keep (see Topic 6.2 — Benefits Realization & Value Management, and Topic 10.1 — KPIs). Unit economics is also how you connect running cost back to the health-economic case for the service (see Topic 6.1 — Health Economics). Think in total cost of ownership across the whole estate, including exit. The sticker price of a platform is a fraction of its lifetime cost; integration, data migration, support staff, training, egress charges and the eventual cost of leaving all belong in the picture. Assess options on total cost of ownership over a realistic life, be especially wary of data-egress fees and proprietary services that raise the cost of exit, and remember that lock-in is a future cost even when it looks free today (procurement owns the contractual side of lock-in — see Topic 6.3 — Procurement & Commercial). A TCO view also stops the organization congratulating itself on a cheap platform that is quietly expensive to run. Embed cost into engineering and governance so it operates continuously. FinOps fails when it is a quarterly clean-up campaign and succeeds when cost is a standing consideration in design reviews, architecture decisions and delivery pipelines (see Topic 3.6 — DevOps & Engineering Excellence). Give teams cost budgets and anomaly alerts, put estimated cost impact into significant architecture decisions, and set automated alerts and hard spending guardrails so a runaway job is caught in hours, not on next month's invoice. The goal of the Operate phase is that cost-consciousness becomes ordinary engineering hygiene rather than an external audit. Balance cost against clinical value and sustainability, not cost alone. The cheapest option is not always the right one: an aggressive saving that removes resilience, delays a patch, or degrades a patient-facing service trades money for risk in the wrong direction. Weigh cost decisions explicitly against clinical value and against carbon, since compute you eliminate as waste is also emissions you avoid — cost and sustainability optimization frequently point the same way (see Topic 8.5 — Sustainability & Net Zero). Make the trade-offs visible and owned rather than letting cost pressure silently erode safety. Questions to discuss with your team # Who actually owns the running cost of our technology — and does that owner have both the visibility and the authority to change it? This matters because unowned cost is the cost that grows unchecked: engineers optimize for delivery, finance sees one invoice, and no one is accountable for the gap between them. Debate whether cost ownership sits with a central finance team that cannot influence engineering decisions, or with engineers who cannot see the bill, or ideally with a joint capability that spans both. Probe whether the owner can actually act — can they switch off an idle environment, block an untagged resource, or refuse a design that is needlessly expensive — or whether they can only report after the money is spent. Consider the health-specific tension: cost owners must never be able to compromise clinical safety or continuity in the name of saving, so where are those guardrails. A good, honest answer names a specific accountable owner or forum, confirms it has near-real-time visibility and real decision rights, and admits candidly where today the answer is "the bill just arrives and we pay it". How much of our cloud and software spend is genuinely delivering value, and how would we know? Most organizations cannot answer this, because they track the total bill but not the value it buys, so every cost looks equally justified or equally suspect. Discuss whether you have unit-cost metrics that connect spend to something clinical or operational — cost per patient, per appointment, per API call — or whether you only have an undifferentiated number that goes up. Surface the trade-off between cost-cutting and value: the aim is not the smallest bill but the best return, which sometimes means spending more on a service that clearly earns it. Consider how much of your spend is measurable waste — idle environments, over-provisioned instances, licences for leavers — versus genuinely productive load, and be honest about how confident you are in that split. A good answer distinguishes waste from value with evidence, has at least a few real unit-economic metrics, and resists the reflex that a smaller bill is automatically a better one. When we moved (or move) spend from capital to operating expenditure, who understood the budgetary and long-term consequences? The capex-to-opex shift is often treated as a purely technical migration, but it changes which budget the money comes from, converts a one-off cost into a permanent recurring one, and can quietly commit the organization to a rising liability for years. Debate whether your finance and digital teams jointly modelled this before committing — did anyone map the multi-year opex trajectory, the exit costs, and the effect on the capital-versus-revenue balance the NHS controls so tightly. Consider the honesty trap: cloud migrations are frequently sold on savings that assume disciplined cost management which then never materializes, so was your business case predicated on a FinOps capability you actually built. Explore what happens when the recurring bill grows faster than the budget that funds it, and who is accountable when it does. A good answer shows finance and digital reasoning together about the whole lifecycle, not a technical team optimizing for migration speed while finance discovers the consequences later (see Topic 6.0 — Financial Management & Business Cases). How confident are we that a runaway cost would be caught in hours rather than on next month's invoice? The defining hazard of metered cloud is latency between a mistake and its discovery: a misconfigured job, an accidental over-provision, or a test environment left running can burn public money silently for weeks before a monthly bill reveals it. Discuss whether you have anomaly alerts and hard spending guardrails wired to the people who can act, or whether your only detection mechanism is the invoice arriving a month in arrears. Probe the balance between guardrails that genuinely stop waste and controls so aggressive they throttle a legitimate clinical workload at the wrong moment — the alert that cries wolf is soon ignored, and the guardrail that blocks a safe service is worse than the spend it prevents. Consider who receives an anomaly alert at 2am and whether they have both the authority and the confidence to act on it without fearing they will break something patient-facing. A good answer describes a tested detection-and-response loop measured in hours, names who owns it, and is honest about how many past surprises were only found when the bill landed. How much software are we paying for that we cannot see — and who would notice if a subscription renewed for a tool no one uses? The cloud compute bill is at least visible; the sprawl of SaaS subscriptions bought on departmental cards, per-seat licences still assigned to leavers, and overlapping tools doing the same job is not, yet together these often rival the infrastructure spend. Discuss whether you hold a live register of software entitlements reconciled against actual named users, or whether renewals pass through silently because no single person owns the whole picture. Surface the security dimension as well as the cost one: unknown SaaS is also unmanaged data flow, so shadow software is both money leaking and an information-governance gap (see Topic 1.7 — Information Governance, Data Protection & Cyber Security). Consider the organizational reason this happens — devolved budgets and easy card payments make it frictionless to acquire software and nearly impossible to retire it — and what would have to change for someone to be accountable for the total. A good answer admits how much of the estate's software spend is genuinely mapped, distinguishes deliberate tools from accreted sprawl, and can point to a reconciliation that actually cancelled something. When cost pressure and clinical safety pull in opposite directions, how do we make sure safety wins — and can we prove it did? Every optimization lever in this topic — rightsizing, switching things off, deferring spend, buying the cheapest option — can, applied carelessly, remove resilience, delay a patch, or degrade a patient-facing service, trading money for risk in exactly the wrong direction. Debate whether your cost decisions carry an explicit safety check, so that a workload tagged clinical-critical is reviewed separately before any change touches it, or whether cost targets are allowed to erode safety quietly and invisibly. Consider the sustainability angle that usually aligns rather than conflicts: compute eliminated as waste is also carbon avoided, so cost and net-zero optimization frequently point the same way (see Topic 8.5 — Sustainability & Net Zero) — but be honest about the cases where they diverge and something has to give. Explore who holds the line when a savings target and a resilience requirement collide, and whether that trade-off is made visibly and owned or made silently under budget pressure. A good answer shows safety and continuity treated as constraints that cost may not override, with a real mechanism to enforce it, not merely a stated value that bends when the invoice grows. x: Topic 6.6 — Vendor & Service Integration Management (SIAM) In a health and care estate stitched together from dozens of suppliers, the service your patients and clinicians actually experience is only as good as the seams between vendors — so someone must own the end-to-end whole that no single contract describes. Why this matters in health and care # No modern NHS trust or integrated care system (ICS) runs on one supplier. A single clinical workflow — a GP referral that becomes an outpatient appointment, a letter, a test result and a prescription — can traverse an electronic patient record from one vendor, an integration engine from another, a hosting platform from a third, a network provider, a national spine service, and a managed-service desk run by a fourth party you have never met. The contract for each part may be sound. The service the patient receives lives in the gaps between them. This is the run-and-operate side of the commercial relationship, and it is where value is either realized or quietly lost. Procurement and commercial teams (see Topic 6.3 — Procurement & Commercial) buy well, award the contract, and hand over a signed agreement; what happens across the years that follow — whether suppliers cooperate or blame each other, whether an outage is fixed in an hour or festers for a week, whether you can ever leave — is the work of vendor and service integration management. Get it wrong and the failure is not abstract. A pathology interface that silently drops results, a shared care record that shows a stale allergy, an authentication service that locks clinicians out at handover: these are patient-safety events that begin as integration problems (see Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management). The stakes are sharpened by three features of the sector. Public money demands that the outcomes bought are the outcomes delivered, and that service credits and value are actively pursued, not left on the table. Statutory duties for data protection, clinical safety and cyber security must flow down an entire supply chain, including sub-contractors you did not choose (see Topic 1.7 — Information Governance, Data Protection & Cyber Security). And the concentration of critical services into a handful of large suppliers means that one vendor's ransomware incident, insolvency or capacity failure can take a whole region offline. Managing suppliers as a portfolio — not one contract at a time — is now a resilience duty, not an administrative one. Core concepts # Service integration and management (SIAM) is a management approach for coordinating multiple service providers and integrating them to deliver a single, end-to-end service to the business. It emerged as a discipline precisely because organizations moved away from a single prime contractor towards a multi-sourced operating model , and then discovered that someone still had to make the parts behave as a whole. SIAM is not a product you buy; it is an operating model with defined roles, processes and governance. The authoritative reference is the Scopism SIAM Body of Knowledge , which sits alongside ITIL and the wider practice of IT service management (ITSM) rather than replacing them. A SIAM model has three layers. The customer, or retained organization , keeps the accountabilities that can never be outsourced: strategy, demand, architecture, commercial ownership, and the final duty of care to patients. The service integrator is the layer — an internal team, an external supplier, or a hybrid — that coordinates the providers, owns cross-cutting processes such as major-incident management, and holds the end-to-end view. The service providers , often organized into service towers (hosting, end-user computing, clinical applications, networks), each deliver a defined slice. These are SIAM terms of art rather than encyclopaedia entries, so they are named here in plain language and grounded in the SIAM body of knowledge. Underneath sit the commercial mechanics. Outsourcing and its data-and-process variant, business process outsourcing , describe delegating work to an external provider; managed services describe the ongoing, subscription-style operation of systems on your behalf. Performance is governed by a service-level agreement (SLA) — a measurable, usually contractual commitment — increasingly complemented by an experience-level agreement (XLA), which measures the outcome a user actually experiences rather than the component metric a supplier finds convenient to hit. XLA has no settled encyclopaedia entry; treat it as an emerging practice, not a standard. Two risk concepts frame the topic. Third-party management is the discipline of overseeing external providers and, crucially, their own sub-contractors — the fourth parties deep in the supply chain . Supply chain risk management addresses the failures that propagate through that chain, and concentration risk — a term borrowed from banking — captures the danger of depending too heavily on a single supplier, platform or region. Managing these is what keeps a convenient sourcing decision from becoming a systemic vulnerability. Finally, avoiding vendor lock-in and driving continual improvement are the two forward-looking duties that stop a live service from ossifying. Best practices # Name the accountable owner for the end-to-end service, not just for each contract. The defining failure of multi-sourcing is that everyone owns a box and no one owns the arrows between them. Establish a retained-organization role — often a service-integration lead or a supplier-management office — that is accountable for the whole clinical or business service as the user experiences it, with the authority to convene suppliers and arbitrate. This owner holds the end-to-end SLA even where no single vendor can, and is the person a board can ask "why was the referral system down for six hours?" and get an answer rather than a round of finger-pointing. Choose and design the SIAM model deliberately, then write it into the contracts. Decide early whether the service integrator is internal, external or a hybrid, and be honest about the trade-off: an internal integrator keeps control and knowledge but demands scarce capability; an external one buys maturity but adds a layer to govern and a potential conflict of interest if it also runs a tower. Define the towers, the cross-cutting processes the integrator owns, and the collaboration obligations of every provider. Crucially, these obligations must appear in each provider's contract — a duty to cooperate, to attend the integrator's major-incident bridge, to share data — because a supplier will do at run-time only what it was bought to do at award-time (see Topic 6.3 — Procurement & Commercial). Segment your suppliers and spend your attention where it counts. Not every vendor deserves the same governance; treating a commodity licence reseller like a strategic EPR partner wastes effort and starves the relationships that matter. Use a segmentation model such as the Kraljic matrix to sort suppliers by business criticality and market difficulty into strategic, leverage, bottleneck and commodity categories, and match the governance rhythm to the segment — quarterly executive business reviews for strategic partners, light-touch performance monitoring for commodities. This is also how you focus assurance, relationship investment and exit planning on the few suppliers whose failure would genuinely hurt. Manage outcomes and experience, not just component metrics. A supplier estate can hit every individual SLA — 99.9% server uptime, tickets closed within target — while the clinician's actual day is miserable and the pathway is broken end to end. Complement component SLAs with experience-level agreements and end-to-end measures that reflect what patients and staff experience, and beware "watermelon" reporting: green on the outside, red on the inside. Where a metric can be met by gaming (closing and reopening tickets, reclassifying severity), redesign it so the supplier's incentive aligns with the outcome you actually want. Run one integrated incident and problem process across all suppliers. When an incident spans several vendors, the "swivel-chair" problem — each supplier insisting the fault lies elsewhere while the service stays down — is the single most damaging pattern in multi-sourcing. Give the service integrator the authority to declare a major incident, pull every relevant provider onto one bridge, and drive resolution regardless of whose component is at fault, with a no-fault "fix first, apportion blame later" rule. This mirrors the internal ITIL disciplines your service-management function already runs (see Topic 3.8 — Service Management & Live Operations), extended across the contractual boundary so a supply chain behaves as one operations team during a crisis. Make contract and performance management an active, evidenced discipline. A contract left in a drawer after signature is money and leverage abandoned. Hold structured performance reviews against the SLAs, track and actually claim service credits where they are due, maintain a shared risk-and-issue register, and keep an auditable record of performance that will matter at renewal or dispute. Service credits are not the point — they are a signal and a lever; a mature relationship uses persistent underperformance to trigger improvement plans and, ultimately, exit, not merely to bank a small rebate (see Topic 6.4 — Governance & Assurance). Flow clinical-safety, data-protection and cyber obligations all the way down the chain. Your statutory duties do not stop at your prime supplier; they must reach the sub-contractor hosting the data and the open-source library inside the product. Require flow-down of clinical-safety obligations under the relevant standards, data-processing terms, and cyber controls aligned to NCSC supply-chain guidance, and demand visibility of fourth parties so you know who is really in the chain. Assess concentration risk explicitly — if three of your critical services sit on one hyperscaler region or one managed-service provider, a single failure is a regional outage, and the mitigation is a decision the board must take knowingly (see Topic 3.9 — Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery). Plan the exit before you are desperate to take it. The cheapest time to secure your ability to leave is before you sign; the moment you most need it, all your leverage is gone. Maintain a live exit plan for every critical supplier covering data extraction in open, documented formats, knowledge transfer, transition support obligations, and the assets and licences you would need to re-provision elsewhere. Real portability is proven, not promised — test that you can export your data and stand it up somewhere else, because a contractual right to your data in a proprietary dump is not the same as being able to use it (see Topic 4.0 — Technical Architecture, Cloud & Legacy, on avoiding vendor lock-in in practice). Questions to discuss with your team # When an incident crosses three suppliers at 2am, who has the authority to make them all act as one team — and does every contract oblige them to answer the call? This matters because the swivel-chair failure is not a technical gap but an authority gap: suppliers behave rationally when they defend their own SLA and deflect blame, and only a designated integrator with contractual backing can override that. Debate honestly whether such a role exists in your organization today, whether it has real authority or merely convenes and pleads, and whether your provider contracts actually require cooperation on a shared major-incident bridge or merely encourage it. Consider the hardest cases — a fault that spans a national service, a hosting provider and an application vendor, where the root cause is genuinely ambiguous for the first hour. Look at whether you operate a no-fault "restore first, apportion later" rule, or whether resolution stalls while commercial teams argue about liability. A good answer names the accountable integrator, points to the contract clauses that compel cooperation, and can describe a recent cross-supplier incident where the model held — or admits candidly that last time, it did not. Which suppliers could we genuinely not survive the sudden loss of — and what would we actually do the morning they failed? This forces the concentration-risk conversation that sourcing convenience tends to bury: the estate accretes dependencies on a few strategic partners and a handful of platforms, and the aggregate exposure is rarely mapped until an incident reveals it. Discuss which vendors are single points of failure for a clinical service, whether the dependency is contractual, technical or knowledge-based, and how deep into the fourth-party chain the real risk sits — the sub-processor, the offshore support team, the one hyperscaler region. Weigh the trade-off honestly: consolidation buys efficiency, integration and better pricing, while diversification buys resilience at a cost, and the right answer is a deliberate board choice, not an accident of past procurements. Consider whether your exit and continuity plans for these suppliers are tested or merely written, and whether you could extract and re-host your data if a supplier went insolvent next week. An honest answer distinguishes the suppliers you manage from the few whose failure is an existential event, and shows that the residual risk on the latter has been consciously accepted at the right level. Are we measuring what our clinicians and patients experience, or only what our suppliers find easy to report green? This question surfaces the gap between component SLAs and real outcomes, which is where multi-sourced services quietly disappoint even while every dashboard is green. Explore where "watermelon" reporting hides in your estate — the individually-met metrics that add up to a broken pathway, the tickets closed by asking the user to try again, the uptime measured on a server no clinician touches. Debate whether you have any true end-to-end or experience-level measures, who owns them, and whether suppliers are incentivized on the outcome you want or on a proxy they can game. Consider the tension that richer, experience-based measurement costs money and effort and can be contested by suppliers whose credits depend on the old metric. A strong answer can point to at least one end-to-end measure that reflects the user's reality, explains how it is governed across suppliers, and is candid about where current SLAs reward the wrong behaviour and need renegotiating at the next break point. Who should run our integration layer — an internal team, an external supplier, or a hybrid — and have we been honest about the conflict of interest that choice creates? The make-or-buy decision for the service integrator itself is often made by default rather than deliberately, and it shapes every relationship that follows. Debate the real trade-off: an internal integrator keeps knowledge and control inside the retained organization but demands scarce, expensive capability that a trust may not be able to hold; an external integrator buys maturity and tooling quickly but adds a layer to govern, and becomes acutely problematic if that same supplier also runs a service tower and is effectively marking its own homework. Consider the middle cases — a hybrid where the retained organization owns accountability and arbitration while a partner provides the operational machinery — and whether your organization has the commercial and technical seniority to direct an integrator rather than be led by it. Look honestly at where the integration knowledge actually lives today, and what happens to your end-to-end view if that integrator's contract ends. An honest answer names who integrates, explains why that model was chosen for your context rather than inherited, and can point to the safeguards that stop an integrator who also delivers services from grading its own performance. Do our statutory duties for clinical safety, data protection and cyber security actually reach the fourth parties deep in the chain — or do they stop at the prime we signed with? This matters because accountability for a patient-safety or data-breach event does not follow the contract; it stays with the retained organization even when the failure occurred three tiers down, in a sub-processor or an offshore support team you never chose. Explore whether your flow-down clauses are real and tested — whether clinical-safety obligations under the relevant standards, data-processing terms and cyber controls are genuinely contractually imposed on sub-contractors, and whether you have any visibility of who those sub-contractors are. Discuss the tension that primes resist exposing their supply chain as commercially sensitive, while you cannot assess a risk you cannot see, and that demanding fourth-party transparency can slow procurement and narrow the market. Consider the concrete failure — the open-source library inside a product, the hosting sub-contractor, the third-party analytics tool — and whether an incident there would find your obligations enforceable or merely aspirational. A strong answer shows that flow-down is written, evidenced and occasionally audited, not assumed, and can name where in the chain visibility currently runs out. Once the contract is signed, who actively manages it — claiming credits, driving improvement, and holding suppliers to the value we bought — rather than filing it in a drawer? The defining leakage in multi-sourcing happens after award, when procurement's attention moves on and no one owns the years of run-and-operate where value is realized or quietly lost. Debate whether you hold structured performance reviews against the SLAs, whether you actually track and claim the service credits you are owed, and whether persistent underperformance triggers an improvement plan or is simply absorbed. Consider the tension that chasing credits can sour a relationship you depend on, and that a mature approach treats credits as a signal and a lever for improvement rather than a rebate to bank — but that suppliers learn quickly which customers never check. Look at whether you maintain an auditable record of performance that will matter at renewal or dispute, and whether continual improvement is a contractual expectation or an occasional favour. An honest answer describes who owns each strategic relationship, points to a recent case where evidenced performance management changed a supplier's behaviour, and admits candidly where contracts are running unmanaged and value is leaking year on year. In practice: a health & care example # Northmoor Integrated Care System runs a digital estate typical of its scale: a hosted electronic patient record from one major vendor, a shared care record platform from another, an integration engine and interface layer from a specialist, national services from NHS England, connectivity from a network provider, and a managed service desk operated by a systems integrator whose first-line support is itself sub-contracted offshore. Each contract was procured separately over a decade, each has its own SLA, and — until recently — each was governed by a different manager in a different directorate. The problem announces itself on a Monday. Clinicians report that GP referrals are arriving in the acute trust with missing attachments, sometimes hours late. The EPR vendor reports 100% uptime and closes the ticket. The integration supplier says its engine is passing every message it receives. The shared care record vendor says the same. The network provider shows no faults. Every supplier is green; the referral pathway is amber-going-red; and no one owns the arrow between the boxes. For nine days, patients wait while the tickets bounce. Northmoor's response is to stand up a service-integration function inside the retained organization, led by a head of supplier and service managem

x: Topic 7.0 — Team Structures, Roles & Responsibilities In one sentence: Digital health delivery succeeds or fails on how you draw the boundaries between teams and how clearly you name who does what — so structure teams for fast, safe flow of value, staff them multidisciplinarily, and make responsibilities explicit. Why this matters in health and care # The way you organize your teams becomes the way your services behave. Conway's Law — that a system's design mirrors the communication structure of the organization that built it — is not a curiosity in health and care; it is a patient-safety risk. Fragmented teams produce fragmented care records, brittle integrations, and hand-offs where clinical risk hides. In the NHS and social care you are also spending public money and carrying statutory duties: clinical safety under DCB0129/DCB0160, information governance under UK GDPR and the common law duty of confidentiality, and accessibility obligations. These duties cannot be bolted on at the end. They must be represented inside the team, by named people with the authority and time to discharge them. Get the structure right and multidisciplinary teams ship working software that clinicians trust and patients can use. Get it wrong and you get busy specialists optimizing their own silo while the service as a whole stalls — the classic pattern behind late, over-budget, and quietly abandoned digital programmes. Core concepts # Multidisciplinary teams (MDTs). A digital delivery team should contain every discipline needed to design, build, and run a service without constant external dependency — product, delivery, design, research, engineering, data, and the clinical and governance perspectives. This mirrors the clinical MDT concept staff already know: mixed expertise, shared accountability for an outcome. Team Topologies. A model (Skelton & Pais) that reduces effective team design to four fundamental types and three interaction modes, all in service of fast flow of value : Stream-aligned team — organized around a single valuable stream of work (a service, a user journey, a product) and owning it end to end. This is the default team type; most people should be on one. Platform team — provides internal self-service capabilities (shared infrastructure, an integration engine, a login service, a shared care record API) so stream-aligned teams go faster without reinventing them. Enabling team — a time-boxed team of specialists (e.g. clinical safety, accessibility, test automation) that coaches others to raise a capability, then withdraws. Complicated-subsystem team — owns a part needing deep specialist knowledge (a risk-scoring algorithm, an NHS Spine interface) that would overload a generalist team. The three interaction modes govern how any two teams relate: collaboration (working closely for a defined period, high-bandwidth, tolerating some inefficiency to discover things), X-as-a-service (one team consumes another's capability with minimal fuss, the low-friction default at scale), and facilitating (one team helps another learn). Naming the mode prevents the ambiguity that breeds delays and blame. Cognitive load . A team can only hold so much in its head. Team Topologies argues you should limit the domain each team owns to what it can reason about safely — a decisive principle when the domain is clinical. Conway's Law and the Inverse Conway Manoeuvre. Since architecture follows org structure — a sociotechnical system view that treats teams and technology as one design — deliberately shape teams to produce the architecture you want. If you want a modular, interoperable care record, do not build it with one monolithic team. Best practices # Staff a full multidisciplinary team around each service. Include, at minimum, a product manager, a delivery manager, a user researcher, a service/interaction designer, engineers, and a data/analytics capability, plus named clinical safety and information governance input. A team missing a discipline will either wait on someone else or skip that work — and the skipped work in health is usually safety, accessibility, or governance. Make most teams stream-aligned and give them end-to-end ownership. Organize around a user's journey (e.g. "outpatient referral") rather than a technology layer (e.g. "the database team"). End-to-end ownership shortens feedback loops and stops the hand-off gaps where clinical risk accumulates. Build platforms as products, consumed as a service. Treat your integration engine, identity service, or shared care record API as an internal product with its own team, roadmap, and users. Publish it "as-a-service" so stream-aligned teams self-serve, rather than raising tickets and waiting. Use enabling teams to spread scarce expertise, not to hoard it. Clinical safety officers, accessibility specialists, and security engineers are rare. Deploy them to coach delivery teams to a higher standard and then move on, rather than becoming a permanent bottleneck every team queues behind. Name every role and its decision rights explicitly. Use a responsibility model — RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) or a simpler "decider/adviser" split — for the decisions that matter: clinical safety sign-off, go-live, information governance approval, spend. Ambiguity here is where accountability evaporates. Give the Clinical Safety Officer real authority and real time. DCB0129/0160 require a named, suitably trained Clinical Safety Officer who can stop a release. Make the role explicit in the team, protect its time, and ensure it can say no — a CSO in name only is a governance failure waiting to be found by an incident. Manage cognitive load by bounding the domain. If a team owns too many services or too complex a clinical domain, split it. Watch for the signal: a team that can no longer confidently explain the safety implications of its own change is overloaded. Apply the Inverse Conway Manoeuvre deliberately. Draw the team boundaries to match the architecture and interoperability you want — modular teams for modular, standards-based (e.g. HL7 FHIR ) systems. Do not let an accidental org chart design your care record for you. Questions to discuss with your team # Where is our current org chart already designing our architecture for us — and is that the architecture we actually want? Conway's Law is not optional: whatever the shape of our teams, the systems will come to mirror it, so the honest first move is to look at the care record, the integrations, and the hand-offs we already have and ask which team boundary produced each seam. In a health and care setting those seams are where clinical risk hides — a fragmented record, a brittle Spine interface, a safety case no single team owns — so this is a patient-safety conversation, not an aesthetic one. The tension to debate is that redrawing team boundaries to get the architecture we want (the Inverse Conway Manoeuvre) is disruptive, threatens established fiefdoms, and cuts across funding and line-management structures we may not fully control. Consider mapping two or three of your most painful integrations back to the teams that own each end, and ask whether a stream-aligned boundary would have removed the hand-off entirely. A good answer names at least one concrete boundary you would move, is honest about who would resist and why, and distinguishes changes worth the disruption from those where an as-a-service interface would fix the friction more cheaply. Do our scarce specialists — clinical safety, information governance, accessibility — sit inside teams with real authority, or are they external gates everyone queues behind? Every service in this family carries statutory duties (DCB0129/0160 clinical safety, UK GDPR and the common law duty of confidentiality, accessibility law) that cannot be bolted on at the end, yet these capabilities are rare and expensive, which pulls organizations toward hoarding them centrally. The trade-off is genuine: embed a Clinical Safety Officer in every team and you spread thin expertise until it is diluted; centralize it and you create the heroic bottleneck where one person is Consulted on everything and every release waits. The enabling-team pattern — time-boxed specialists who coach teams to run their own hazard workshops and then withdraw — is the proposed resolution, but it only works if leadership protects the specialists' time to teach rather than do. Look honestly at your own release history: how often did go-live slip waiting on a single named person, and did that person have the authority and protected time to say no safely? A strong answer faces the scarcity squarely, picks a deliberate position on embed-versus-enable for each duty, and names the specific authority (the power to stop a release) that must never be diluted however you spread the capacity. How would we know a team has taken on more cognitive load than it can safely carry — and what would we actually do about it? Cognitive load is the quiet governor of safe delivery: a team can only reason about so much clinical domain and so many services before its confidence in the safety implications of its own changes starts to erode, and in health that erosion is invisible until an incident exposes it. The difficulty is that overload rarely announces itself — it looks like slightly slower delivery, more defects, more "let me check with someone", and teams under pressure tend to absorb rather than flag it, especially when splitting a team is politically costly or headcount is frozen. Debate what your early-warning signals would be (a team that can no longer confidently explain the safety case for its own release is a strong one), and whether you have any mechanism today that would surface overload before delivery visibly stalls. Consider the counter-pressure too: splitting teams creates new boundaries and hand-offs, so the cure can reintroduce the fragmentation risk of question one. An honest answer agrees on concrete, observable signals rather than a vague "we'd sense it", names who has the authority to bound a team's domain or split it, and admits the trade-off between load relief and boundary proliferation. Which of our shared capabilities should be run as platforms consumed as-a-service, and are we actually resourcing them that way — or just relabelling a ticket queue? The promise of a platform team is that stream-aligned teams self-serve an integration engine, an identity service, or a shared care record API without raising a ticket and waiting, so the whole system goes faster; the failure is calling something a "platform" while it remains an under-staffed central function that everyone still queues behind. The trade-off is real: building a capability as a genuine internal product means giving it its own team, roadmap, documentation, and users, which is a serious investment that competes with shipping user-facing features, and in a cash-limited NHS setting that investment is easy to defer indefinitely. In health and care the stakes are sharper because the shared capabilities are often the safety-critical ones — the person-matching index, the FHIR interfaces, the audit trail — where a thin platform team becomes a single point of failure for every service on top of it. Look at the capabilities several teams already depend on and ask, for each, whether the interaction is truly low-friction X-as-a-service or a disguised collaboration with hidden waits. An honest answer names which capabilities genuinely warrant platform investment now versus later, is clear about who funds and staffs them, and resists the temptation to declare a platform that has no product owner, no roadmap, and no self-service path. Where are we relying on contracted suppliers or borrowed staff, and which roles must we keep in-house to stay an intelligent client rather than a hollowed-out one? Much digital delivery in health and care is contracted out, and a supplier can bring capacity and specialism fast — but if the product ownership, technical assurance, and clinical safety sign-off all leave the building with the contract, the organization loses the ability to judge what it is being sold, specify what it needs, or safely own the result. The tension is between speed and capability: staff-augmentation and turnkey builds get something live quickly, yet they can quietly erode the in-house muscle that lets you hold a supplier to account, and they often deliver component-shaped, hand-off-heavy structures rather than stream-aligned teams that own an outcome. In this domain the non-negotiable retained roles cluster around accountability that cannot be delegated — the Senior Responsible Owner, the Clinical Safety Officer who signs off go-live, the product owner who decides priorities, and enough technical assurance to inspect what suppliers build. Examine your current delivery and ask which capabilities you could not reconstitute if a supplier walked away tomorrow. A good answer distinguishes work that is genuinely fine to contract from the intelligent-client core that must stay in-house, insists that contracted teams are held to outcome ownership rather than body-shop staffing, and names the safety and governance decisions that must always rest with your own accountable people. How will we know our team structure is actually producing fast, safe flow of value — and what would trigger us to redraw it? Team design is a means, not an end: the point of stream-aligned teams, platforms, and named interaction modes is faster, safer delivery of value, yet organizations rarely instrument whether the structure is delivering that, so reorganizations happen on politics and intuition rather than evidence. The difficulty is choosing signals that reflect flow and safety without gaming them — raw velocity or story-point throughput invites the wrong behaviour, while flow metrics (lead time from idea to live, deployment frequency, hand-off count per change) and safety indicators (how quickly hazards are closed, whether teams own their own safety case) tell you more about whether boundaries are helping or hurting. There is a real tension with stability: constant reorganization destroys the team longevity and shared cognitive space that make delivery safe, so you need a high bar and clear triggers before you redraw boundaries. Discuss what evidence would tell you a boundary is wrong — persistent cross-team waits, a safety case no single team owns, a platform nobody self-serves — and who is empowered to act on it. An honest answer commits to a small set of flow-and-safety signals you will actually watch, sets a deliberate threshold that protects team stability, and names the trigger conditions and the decision-maker for any future reshaping. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system (ICS) is rolling out a shared care record across acute, community, mental health, primary care, and social care. The instinct is to create one large "shared care record team". Instead the ICS applies Team Topologies. A platform team owns the shared record's core: the person-matching index, the FHIR APIs, and the integration engine, published as self-service capabilities. Several stream-aligned teams each own a real user journey on top of it — "view a patient's record in A&E", "social worker safeguarding view", "GP medication reconciliation" — and consume the platform as-a-service. A complicated-subsystem team owns the probabilistic patient-matching algorithm, where a false match is a genuine safety incident. An enabling team of clinical safety and accessibility specialists rotates through the stream-aligned teams, coaching them to run their own DCB0160 hazard workshops rather than doing it for them. Each team has a named product manager, delivery manager, and Clinical Safety Officer, and a RACI makes clear that go-live is accountable to the Senior Responsible Owner but cannot proceed without CSO and IG sign-off. When the A&E team needs a new data field, the interaction mode is explicit: X-as-a-service from the platform team via a documented API request, not a six-week collaboration. Delivery is faster and, crucially, the safety case for each journey is owned by the team that ships it. Sector lenses # Startup # A ten-person digital-health startup cannot staff four distinct team types — it usually is a single stream-aligned team in which one person wears several hats (an engineer who also runs user research, a clinician-founder who is the de facto Clinical Safety Officer). The priority is keeping the whole team inside one shared cognitive space so decisions are fast; a formal RACI is overkill when everyone is in the same room. The real risk is the founder-bottleneck: clinical safety and information governance rest on one busy person, and DCB0129/0160 obligations are easy to defer. As the company wins its first NHS contract, the first specialist hires should be the ones that de-risk that gate — a named CSO and an IG lead — before scaling engineering headcount. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home, or a single-site clinic — has real patients and ongoing operations but rarely a dedicated digital or IT team, so there is no "team topology" to design; the practice manager or a clinical lead is effectively the whole delivery capability alongside their day job. The realistic move is not to build platform and enabling teams but to name responsibilities explicitly on the people you already have — who is the Clinical Safety Officer for the systems you deploy, who owns information governance, who signs off a change — even if those are part-time hats on a handful of staff. Because the same statutory duties (DCB0129/0160, UK GDPR, accessibility) apply as they do to a large trust, the practical pattern is to lean on your suppliers' and your ICS's shared platforms and enabling support rather than reinvent them, while retaining just enough intelligent-client capability to hold suppliers to account. The single biggest risk is the one-person bottleneck: if the only person who understands the clinical system leaves, both safety and continuity walk out with them, so writing down the RACI and cross-training a second person matters more here than any formal team model. Enterprise # A large NHS trust or health-tech firm has the opposite problem: too many teams, drawn along legacy component and departmental lines, with hand-offs everywhere. This is where a deliberate team-design model earns its keep — reshaping component teams into stream-aligned ones, standing up platform teams for shared care-record and integration capabilities, and using enabling teams to spread scarce clinical-safety and accessibility expertise. RACI and explicit decision rights become essential because the sheer number of stakeholders makes informal coordination impossible. The Inverse Conway Manoeuvre is a live lever here: a decades-old org chart is already shaping the architecture, so leaders must redraw team boundaries intentionally rather than let the structure design the care record for them. Government # A national body (NHS England, DHSC) or local authority sets the standards others staff against — the Government Digital and Data capability framework, the Service Standard, DCB0129/0160 — and is accountable to Parliament and the public for how money buys team capacity. Structures here are shaped by procurement and funding rules: much delivery is contracted to suppliers, so the crucial roles to retain in-house are the intelligent-client ones (product ownership, technical assurance, clinical safety sign-off) that prevent capability being hollowed out. Accountability is formal and auditable — a named Senior Responsible Owner, published spend controls, transparency duties — so responsibility models are a matter of public record, not optional hygiene.
