x: Topic 7.1 — Agile Delivery Practices & Team Health In one sentence: How a delivery team actually works week to week — its cadence, its ceremonies, its working agreements, and above all its health — is not soft-skills decoration but the operating system that determines whether safe, usable digital care gets shipped and sustained. Why this matters in health and care # Topic 7.0 — Team Structures, Roles & Responsibilities drew the boundaries around your teams and named who does what. This topic is about what happens inside those boundaries once the work starts: the rhythm of a fortnight, the meetings people actually attend, the agreements that govern behaviour, and the human sustainability that keeps a team functioning under load. Structure is the anatomy; ways of working are the physiology. In health and care this matters more than in most sectors because the teams building and running digital services frequently support clinical operations that never stop. A team that maintains an electronic patient record, an e-prescribing system, or a bed-management platform is on the critical path of care delivery. When that team is exhausted, silenced, or drowning in unplanned work, the failure mode is not a missed marketing deadline — it is a delayed diagnosis, a medication error, or a safety incident that a rested, psychologically safe team would have caught and flagged. There is strong evidence that team climate affects clinical outcomes. Research into patient safety consistently links the ability of staff to speak up about risk with the prevention of harm, and reviews of NHS failings — from Mid Staffordshire onward — repeatedly find cultures where concerns were not voiced or not heard. The way your delivery team runs its stand-ups and retrospectives is a small-scale version of the same question: can people say "this isn't safe" without fear? How you work is a clinical-safety and public-trust issue, not merely a productivity one. Core concepts # Agile software development . A family of approaches, codified in the 2001 Agile Manifesto, that favour working software, close collaboration with users, and responding to change over exhaustive up-front planning. In health and care, agile is not licence to skip governance — it is a way to surface clinical-safety and information-governance questions early and often, rather than at the end. Agility is a means to safe, valuable delivery, not an end in itself. Iterative and incremental development . Building a service in small increments, each usable and each generating feedback that shapes the next. This is the core mechanic beneath all agile methods: you learn by shipping thin slices and observing real use, rather than by predicting everything in advance. Scrum . The most widely adopted agile framework, organizing work into fixed-length iterations called sprints (typically one to two weeks), each bracketed by planning at the start and a review and retrospective at the end, with a daily stand-up meeting to coordinate. Scrum's value is its predictable cadence and its built-in inspect-and-adapt loop; its risk is being adopted as ritual without the underlying transparency. Kanban . A continuous-flow method that visualizes work on a board, limits the amount of work in progress (WIP) at each stage, and manages flow rather than time-boxed batches. Kanban suits teams doing operational and support work where demand is unpredictable — much of health and care live-service work — because it does not force irregular arrivals into artificial sprint boundaries. WIP limits are its signature discipline: a team that agrees to work on no more than, say, three items at once finishes things faster than one that starts everything and completes nothing. Definition of Ready and Definition of Done. Two shared agreements that bound quality. A Definition of Ready states the conditions a piece of work must meet before the team will start it (clear user need, acceptance criteria, any clinical-safety or accessibility considerations identified). A Definition of Done states what "finished" means (tested, accessible, documented, safety impact assessed, deployed). In health and care, the Definition of Done is where you hard-wire non-negotiables — DCB0129/DCB0160 clinical-risk activities, accessibility to WCAG 2.2, information-governance sign-off — so they cannot be quietly dropped under deadline pressure. Team working agreement (or charter). A short, team-owned document setting out how the team chooses to work: core hours, meeting norms, how decisions are made, how disagreement is handled, how on-call is shared. It converts implicit assumptions into explicit, revisable agreements, which is especially valuable in multidisciplinary teams where clinicians, engineers, and researchers arrive with very different professional norms. Psychological safety . The shared belief, studied extensively by Amy Edmondson, that a team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking — that you can ask a question, admit a mistake, or raise a concern without being punished or humiliated. It is the single strongest correlate of effective teams in Google's well-known Project Aristotle research, and in healthcare it is directly linked to error reporting and learning. A team without it will hide problems until they become incidents. Occupational burnout . A syndrome, recognized by the World Health Organization, resulting from chronic unmanaged workplace stress, characterized by exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced efficacy. Sustainable pace — the agile principle that a team should be able to maintain its rhythm indefinitely — is the countermeasure. For teams supporting safety-critical clinical systems, burnout is a safety risk, because tired people supporting 24/7 services make errors. Continual improvement . The disciplined habit of making small, regular changes to how you work, informed by evidence. Team-level retrospectives are one instance of it; Topic 10.2 — Quality Improvement & Improvement Science covers the broader science, including Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles, which apply as much to your ways of working as to clinical pathways. Best practices # Choose cadence to match the nature of the work, not fashion. Use time-boxed sprints (Scrum) where work is plannable and you benefit from a predictable heartbeat and stakeholder rhythm; use continuous flow with WIP limits (Kanban) where demand is unpredictable, as in live-service support and operational teams. Many health and care teams do both — a "Scrumban" hybrid — running discovery and build in sprints while handling live incidents on a flow board. Decide deliberately and revisit the decision, rather than inheriting whichever your last supplier used. Run ceremonies for their purpose, and kill them when they stop serving it. A stand-up exists to surface blockers and coordinate the day, not to report status to a manager; a review or show-and-tell exists to get feedback from real users and stakeholders on working software; a retrospective exists to change how the team works next week. If a meeting no longer achieves its purpose, shorten it, restructure it, or stop it. The test is simple: would attendees pay to be there? Make show-and-tells the moment clinicians and users see real progress. A fortnightly review that demonstrates working software to the clinicians, patients, and operational staff who will use it keeps the feedback loop tight and builds the trust that adoption depends on. Invite the people who will live with the service, demonstrate on realistic (not cherry-picked) scenarios, and capture what you learn as backlog changes. This is your cheapest insurance against building the wrong thing. Write a Definition of Ready and a Definition of Done, and put the non-negotiables in Done. Agree the conditions for starting and finishing work, and encode clinical-safety activity, accessibility, information-governance sign-off, and adequate testing into your Definition of Done so they are structural, not heroic. When a deadline squeezes, an explicit Done gives the team the language to refuse to ship unsafe work. See Topic 3.6 — DevOps & Engineering Excellence for how continuous delivery pipelines can automate parts of Done. Limit work in progress. Starting is easy and satisfying; finishing is what delivers value and reduces risk. Agreeing WIP limits forces the team to swarm on completing work before pulling in more, which shortens lead times, exposes bottlenecks, and — critically in health — reduces the number of half-finished, partially-tested changes in flight at once. A visible board with explicit limits is often the single highest-leverage change a struggling team can make. Co-author a working agreement and treat it as living. Have the team write its own charter — meeting norms, core collaboration hours, decision-making, on-call fairness, how to disagree well — and review it periodically. Because digital health teams are multidisciplinary, spanning clinical and technical cultures with different defaults, making norms explicit prevents the quiet friction that erodes trust. A charter imposed from above is theatre; one the team owns is a genuine instrument. Protect sustainable pace deliberately, and watch the leading indicators of burnout. Plan to a capacity the team can hold indefinitely, not a heroic peak; guard against the permanent crunch that treats overtime as normal. Monitor leading signals — rising unplanned work, shrinking retrospective candour, people skipping leave, on-call fatigue — and act before they become resignations or incidents. For teams underpinning 24/7 clinical services, share on-call fairly, honour time back, and staff for resilience, not just the happy path (see Topic 3.8 — Service Management & Live Operations). Build psychological safety on purpose. Leaders set the tone: frame work as a learning problem, admit your own mistakes, respond to bad news with curiosity rather than blame, and thank people for raising concerns. Run blameless post-incident reviews. In a clinical-adjacent setting, the willingness to say "I think this release is unsafe" or "I don't understand this requirement" is the mechanism by which harm is prevented — so it must be actively cultivated, not assumed. Use lightweight team-health checks to make the invisible visible. Periodically run a structured self-assessment — the "squad health check" model popularized by Spotify, where a team rates itself green/amber/red across dimensions such as delivering value, learning, fun, mission clarity, and support — to surface trends over time. The value is not the scores but the conversation they start and the way they let a team spot a slide before it becomes a crisis. Keep it fast, anonymous where helpful, and owned by the team. Run retrospectives that actually change behaviour. A retrospective that generates a list of grumbles and no action is worse than none, because it teaches the team that speaking up is pointless. End each one with a small number of concrete, owned, time-bound experiments; start the next by checking whether the last ones happened. Treat improving your ways of working as its own continual-improvement backlog, linking to the improvement science in Topic 10.2 . Design for remote, hybrid, and asynchronous collaboration as the default. Health and care delivery teams are frequently distributed across trusts, regions, and suppliers, so treat good written communication, well-run video ceremonies, and asynchronous decision records as core competencies, not fallbacks. Default to documenting decisions where absent colleagues can find them, minimize meetings that could be a written update, and be deliberate about the few high-bandwidth moments (planning, retro, incident response) that genuinely benefit from being synchronous. Questions to discuss with your team # Does our cadence and set of ceremonies actually help us deliver safely, or are we performing agile rituals because we always have? Many teams inherit a ceremony schedule — daily stand-up, two-week sprint, sprint review, retro — without asking whether it fits the work in front of them, and the result is meetings that consume real hours while delivering diminishing value. The honest debate is about purpose: what is each ceremony for , and would a neutral observer watching ours conclude it achieves that? A live-service team fielding unpredictable clinical incidents may be poorly served by rigid sprints and better served by Kanban flow, while a discovery team benefits from the sprint heartbeat and the stakeholder rhythm it creates. There is a real tension between the reassurance of a familiar routine and the discipline of running only the events that earn their place. Consider timing your ceremonies for a month and asking, per meeting, what decision or coordination it produced. A good answer is unsentimental about killing or reshaping ceremonies, distinguishes coordination needs from status-reporting habits, and ties the choice of cadence to the actual predictability of your work rather than to what the framework diagram shows. Is it genuinely safe on this team to say "I think this is unsafe" or "I made a mistake" — and how would we know? Psychological safety is easy to claim and hard to possess, and in a team supporting clinical systems the cost of getting it wrong is measured in patient harm, not just missed deadlines. The uncomfortable question is not whether you believe your team is safe but what evidence you have: when did someone last admit an error in a stand-up, challenge a senior person's design, or halt a release on a hunch, and what happened to them afterwards? Look at your incident reviews — are they genuinely blameless, or does everyone quietly know who is being held responsible? There is a trade-off leaders must face honestly: the behaviours that feel like decisive leadership (moving fast, projecting certainty, reacting sharply to bad news) are often precisely the ones that teach people to stay quiet. Consider whether your quietest team members ever disagree in a meeting, and why they might not. A strong answer resists the comfortable assumption that "of course people can speak up here," points to concrete recent instances or admits their absence, and identifies specific leader behaviours to change rather than treating safety as a fixed trait of the group. Are we working at a pace we could sustain for a year — and what are we doing about the signals that we are not? Sustainable pace is one of agile's founding principles and one of the first things abandoned under pressure, particularly for teams whose systems underpin services that cannot go down. The tension is that heroics are visible and rewarded in the moment — the person who worked the weekend to fix production is thanked — while the slow erosion of a team's health is invisible until people leave or make mistakes. Ask what your leading indicators are: unplanned work crowding out planned work, untaken annual leave, on-call disturbing sleep, retrospectives going quiet, cynicism creeping into language. In a safety-critical context, a tired team is not merely unhappy; it is more likely to miss the defect or misread the alert that prevents harm, so this is a clinical-risk conversation as much as a wellbeing one. Consider whether your capacity planning assumes the happy path or budgets for incidents, leave, and learning. A good answer treats burnout as a system property to be designed against rather than a personal weakness, names the specific signals the team will watch, and commits to a concrete change — resourcing, on-call fairness, WIP limits — rather than an exhortation to be more resilient. When a deadline is bearing down, what does our Definition of Done actually stop us from dropping — and have we ever proved it holds? Every team can recite that clinical safety, accessibility, and information governance matter; the real test is what survives contact with a hard delivery date and an anxious stakeholder. The tension is that a Definition of Done is only meaningful when it costs you something — when it forces the team to not ship on the promised day because a DCB0160 hazard review or a WCAG 2.2 accessibility check is not complete. If your Done has never once caused you to hold a release, it may be decoration rather than a control. Look for the pressure points: who has the authority to say "this is not done", and would they be backed by leadership or overruled? Consider whether the non-negotiables are structural — encoded in the pipeline, in acceptance criteria, in sign-off gates — or whether they rely on someone remembering them at the worst possible moment. An honest answer can point to a specific occasion where Done was invoked under pressure, or admits candidly that it has not yet been tested and treats that as a gap to close rather than a comfort. Do the different professional cultures on this team — clinical, engineering, research, delivery — actually share a way of working, or are we quietly running on incompatible defaults? Multidisciplinary teams are mandated in health and care for good reason, but bringing a clinician, an engineer, a user researcher, and a data analyst into one team means bringing four sets of professional instincts about evidence, risk, pace, and what "good" looks like. The friction is often invisible: an engineer's bias to ship and iterate can read as recklessness to a clinician trained to be certain before acting, while a clinician's caution can read as obstruction to someone used to reversible deploys. A working agreement that stays generic ("be respectful, attend stand-up") never surfaces these differences, whereas a good one names how this team makes decisions, handles disagreement between disciplines, and reconciles clinical caution with iterative delivery. Consider whether your norms were genuinely co-authored or imported from whichever discipline shouted loudest. A strong answer treats the diversity of professional cultures as a source of safety rather than an inconvenience, points to explicit agreements that translate between them, and can describe a recent disagreement that the team's norms helped resolve well rather than papered over. How do we know our retrospectives and health checks are changing anything — and what happens to candour when they don't? A team can run a flawless retrospective every fortnight and a quarterly squad health check and still improve nothing, because the mechanism that matters is not the meeting but the follow-through. The corrosive failure mode is subtle: when actions are generated and never done, people slowly learn that raising problems is pointless, so candour decays and the very instrument meant to surface risk goes quiet — a particular danger where the unspoken problem is a safety concern. The honest question is evidential: of the last handful of retro actions or health-check signals, how many led to a visible change, and who owned them? There is a trade-off between generating a long, satisfying list of grievances and committing to a small number of owned, time-bound experiments the team will actually complete. Consider whether your next retro opens by checking whether the last one's actions happened, and whether amber-to-red health-check trends ever reach the people with the authority to resource a fix. A good answer measures the improvement habit by completed changes rather than meetings held, treats declining candour as an early warning in its own right, and links ways-of-working improvement to the same discipline the team would apply to a clinical pathway. In practice: a health & care example # A community NHS trust runs a digital team supporting its electronic patient record (EPR) and a patient-facing appointments app . The team is multidisciplinary — product manager, delivery manager, engineers, a user researcher, a clinical safety officer, and a data analyst — as set up under Topic 7.0 's structures. For a year they ran textbook Scrum: two-week sprints, full ceremony set. But they were also the team paged whenever the E

x: Topic 7.2 — Workforce Planning In one sentence: Workforce planning is the disciplined practice of matching the supply of people and skills to the demand your services will place on them — the right people, with the right capabilities, in the right place, at the right time, for a price you can afford. Why this matters in health and care # The scarcest resource in digital health and care is not money or technology; it is people with the right skills. Digital, data, and technology specialists are in acute national shortage, and health and care compete for them against better-paying private employers. A programme business case that assumes you can simply hire ten engineers next quarter is a fiction that will unravel at delivery time. Workforce planning turns that risk into a managed variable. It is a statutory and strategic expectation in the NHS: the NHS Long Term Workforce Plan frames workforce as a first-order planning object, and integrated care systems are expected to plan their workforce across organizational boundaries, including social care. Poor planning shows up as safety gaps (rotas that cannot be filled), wasted public money (emergency agency and contractor spend), and stalled transformation (a shared care record with no one to run it). Done well, workforce planning connects your service strategy to real people decisions — recruitment, training, skill mix, and retention — far enough ahead that you can actually act. This topic covers the analytical discipline; it feeds the longer-horizon Workforce Strategy (see Topic 7.3 ) and is delivered through People & Organizational Development (see Topic 7.5 ). Core concepts # Strategic vs operational workforce planning. Operational planning fills next quarter's rota and next month's vacancies. Strategic planning looks three to ten years out and asks what workforce a changed service model will need — for example, the roles required when AI-assisted triage or virtual wards become business-as-usual. Both are needed; the failure is doing only the operational and calling it planning. Demand and supply. Demand is the workforce your future services will require, derived from service plans, activity forecasts, demographics, and new models of care. Supply is the workforce you will actually have — current headcount adjusted for turnover , retirement, absence, training pipelines, and the labour market . The gap between them is the object of planning. Skills and capability frameworks. You cannot plan what you cannot name. Capability frameworks give a shared vocabulary of roles and skills. The Government Digital and Data (formerly DDaT) Profession Capability Framework defines the digital roles (product manager, delivery manager, user researcher, service designer, software engineer, data professionals, and more) and the skills and levels within each — a ready-made taxonomy for describing digital demand and supply. Build, buy, borrow. Three ways to close a gap: build (grow your own through training and development), buy (recruit permanent staff), or borrow (contractors, secondments, partners, suppliers). Each has different cost, speed, and retention-of-knowledge profiles. Workforce intelligence. The data foundation — establishment vs actual headcount, vacancy and turnover rates, skills inventories, age profiles, and pipeline data — without which planning is guesswork dressed up as analysis. The six-step methodology # The health and care sector's established approach is Skills for Health's Six Steps Methodology to Integrated Workforce Planning® , cited in the NHS Long Term Workforce Plan and used across NHS England, Wales, and Scotland. It gives a repeatable structure: Defining the plan — set scope, timeframe, and the service strategy the workforce must deliver; engage stakeholders. Mapping service change — translate future service models into their workforce implications. Defining the required workforce — describe the future workforce in numbers, roles, and skills (the demand side). Understanding workforce availability — assess current supply, turnover, pipelines, and the labour market. Planning to close the gap (action planning) — decide build/buy/borrow interventions, skill-mix changes, and development. Implementing, monitoring, and refreshing — enact the plan and revisit it as reality diverges from forecast. The steps are not strictly linear; you iterate, especially between demand (step 3) and supply (step 4) as the gap becomes clear. Best practices # Start from service strategy, not from the current establishment. Base demand on where the service is going — new care models, digital channels, demographic pressure — not on last year's structure with a percentage added. Planning that extrapolates the status quo will faithfully reproduce today's gaps. Do strategic and operational planning as one connected system. Let the long-horizon strategic view set the direction (which capabilities to build) and the operational view manage the near term (which posts to fill now). Reconcile them so they do not contradict each other. Name skills, not just headcount. "We need five more people" is not a plan. Use a capability framework (Government Digital and Data / DDaT) to specify roles, skills, and levels, so recruitment, training, and job design have a precise target. Model supply honestly, including attrition. Factor in turnover, retirement age profiles, maternity/parental leave, training completion rates, and competition from higher-paying employers. Optimistic supply assumptions are the most common cause of plans that fail on contact with the labour market. Choose build/buy/borrow deliberately per gap. Borrowing (contractors) is fast but expensive and lets knowledge walk out of the door; buying takes time in a competitive market; building is slow but retains capability. Match the mechanism to the gap's urgency and how strategic the capability is — build the capabilities that are core to you, borrow the transient ones. Manage the contractor/permanent balance explicitly. Contractors bridge urgent gaps and inject scarce skills, but an over-reliance on them raises cost, weakens retention of institutional knowledge, and creates fragility when they leave. Set a target ratio and a plan to convert critical contracted knowledge into permanent capability. Use scenario planning under uncertainty. You cannot forecast a decade precisely, so plan for several plausible futures (e.g. rapid AI adoption vs slow; generous vs constrained funding) and identify the "no-regrets" moves — the investments, such as digital literacy, that pay off across all scenarios. Build a workforce intelligence base and refresh the plan. Invest in the data — establishment, vacancies, turnover, skills inventory, pipeline — and treat the plan as a living document reviewed on a regular cycle, not a document produced once for a business case and shelved. Plan across the system, not one organization. In an ICS, workforce moves between acute, community, primary, and social care. Plan for shared and rotational roles and a shared talent pool, or organizations will simply poach scarce staff from each other. Plan for retention, not just recruitment. A plan that assumes you can hire your way out of a gap will fail in a tight labour market where digital, data and clinical-informatics skills are scarce and mobile. Model attrition honestly, invest in the conditions that keep people — development, flexibility, good leadership — and treat every avoidable leaver as a planning failure, not just bad luck (see Topic 7.5 — People & Organizational Development). Build the plan on trustworthy workforce data. Supply-and-demand modelling is only as good as the establishment, vacancy, skills and attrition data beneath it, which in many organizations is fragmented and out of date. Invest in a single, current view of who you have and what they can do, and be explicit about the assumptions and uncertainty in any forecast rather than presenting a false precision. Questions to discuss with your team # Are our supply assumptions honest, or are we quietly betting on being able to hire scarce specialists quickly and cheaply? Optimistic supply modelling is the single most common reason workforce plans collapse on contact with the labour market, because digital, data, and technology specialists are in acute national shortage and health and care compete for them against far better-paying private employers. The temptation is understandable: a business case reads better if it assumes twelve engineers arrive next quarter, and the people writing the case are rarely the people who later have to fill the rota. The debate to have is whether your plan has genuinely factored in turnover, retirement age profiles, parental leave, training-completion rates, and — crucially — the reality that a neighbouring trust's recruitment drive can worsen your local supply overnight. Consider stress-testing your own numbers: what is your actual digital-staff turnover, how many key people are near retirement, and where does local salary benchmarking put you against the market? A good answer replaces wishful headcount arithmetic with modelled attrition and a named source for every assumption, and it is candid about which posts you probably cannot fill on the timeline the plan claims. For each capability gap, have we made a deliberate build/buy/borrow choice — and are we drifting into contractor dependency by default? Closing a gap by building (growing your own), buying (permanent recruitment), or borrowing (contractors and suppliers) carries very different profiles of cost, speed, and knowledge retention, yet organizations under delivery pressure tend to reach reflexively for contractors because they are the fastest lever. That reflex is where the trouble starts: repeated borrowing with no strategy to convert critical knowledge into permanent capability lets institutional knowledge walk out of the door, raises cost structurally, and creates fragility when contractors leave mid-programme. The principle worth debating is matching the mechanism to the gap — build the capabilities that are core and strategic to you, borrow only the genuinely transient ones — and whether you have an explicit target contractor-to-permanent ratio rather than a number that simply accreted. Look at a real example from your own portfolio, such as standing up a platform team, and ask whether the borrowed capacity has a concrete knowledge-transfer and conversion plan or is silently becoming permanent. An honest answer records a deliberate decision per gap, sets a target balance with a plan to move toward it, and names the specific critical knowledge you are at risk of losing. Are we planning our workforce for where the service is going, and across the whole system — or extrapolating today's establishment in our own organization? Two failure modes compound each other here: basing future demand on last year's structure with a percentage added (which faithfully reproduces today's gaps and under-resources any real transformation), and planning your organization's workforce in isolation within an ICS where staff actually move between acute, community, primary, and social care. The tension is that starting from service strategy demands you first agree what the service will become — AI-assisted triage, virtual wards, a shared care record as business-as-usual — which is uncertain and contested, and planning across organizational boundaries means ceding some control and confronting the fact that partners may simply poach one another's scarce staff. This is where scenario planning earns its keep: model several plausible futures and identify the no-regrets moves, such as whole-workforce digital literacy, that pay off whichever future arrives. Ask whether your current plan names the new roles a changed care model requires, and whether social care is in the plan at all or conveniently out of scope. A strong answer derives demand from future service models rather than the current establishment, plans for shared and rotational roles across the system, and is explicit about the scenarios it is hedging against. Are we planning as hard for retention as we are for recruitment — and do we treat every avoidable leaver as a planning failure? Most workforce plans are written as recruitment plans, yet in a tight market for digital, data, and clinical-informatics skills you cannot hire your way out of a gap that a revolving door keeps reopening; every experienced leaver takes institutional knowledge with them and resets a training investment to zero. The uncomfortable truth is that the conditions that keep people — development pathways, flexibility, good line management, a sense of purpose — sit largely outside the recruitment team's control and rarely appear as line items in a business case, which is precisely why they get neglected. The trade-off worth debating is how much of your scarce funding and leadership attention goes into attraction versus the far less glamorous work of making people want to stay. Look honestly at your own attrition: where are people going, at what tenure, and are your regretted leavers clustered in exactly the scarce roles your transformation depends on? A candid answer models attrition explicitly, invests in the drivers of retention rather than treating turnover as background noise, and connects the plan to People & Organizational Development ( Topic 7.5 ) instead of assuming the labour market will keep refilling the bucket. How good is the workforce data underneath this plan, and are we honest about its uncertainty rather than dressing up guesswork as precision? Supply-and-demand modelling is only ever as trustworthy as the establishment, vacancy, skills, and attrition data beneath it, and in many organizations that data is fragmented across systems, out of date, or simply absent for the digital workforce — so a plan can look rigorous while resting on numbers no one has validated. There is a real tension here between the decisiveness a business case demands and the intellectual honesty of admitting how wide the error bars are; a forecast quoted to a single decimal place can imply a confidence the underlying data cannot support. The discussion to have is whether you have a single, current view of who you have and what they can do, and whether your plan states its assumptions and their uncertainty openly rather than burying them. Consider where your figures actually come from — is your skills inventory real or aspirational, and when was headcount last reconciled against the establishment? An honest answer invests in a trustworthy workforce-intelligence base, is explicit about which numbers are measured versus estimated, and presents ranges and scenarios rather than a false precision that will not survive contact with reality. Are we planning the workforce for a digitally changed service, or bolting digital roles onto a workforce still shaped for the old model? New models of care — AI-assisted triage, virtual wards, a shared care record as business-as-usual — do not simply add a handful of technical posts; they change what existing clinical and operational staff do every day, and a plan that only recruits engineers while ignoring the digital literacy of the wider workforce will stall at adoption. The tension is that upskilling the whole workforce is slow, competes for the same time and money as frontline delivery, and produces benefits that are diffuse and hard to attribute, so it is easy to defer in favour of visible new hires. The angle worth debating is whether digital capability is treated as everyone's concern — a no-regrets investment that pays off across every future scenario — or quarantined inside a specialist team that the rest of the organization is not equipped to work with. Ask whether your plan names the reskilling and digital-literacy uplift existing roles will need, not just the new roles a changed model creates. A strong answer plans for the whole workforce's capability, sequences upskilling alongside the technology rollout rather than after it, and recognizes that the scarcest constraint may be adoption capacity, not just specialist supply. In practice: a health & care example # An ICS plans the workforce for a three-year digital and data transformation , including a shared care record and expanded virtual wards. Using the six steps, the programme team first defines scope and engages clinical and operational leaders (step 1), then maps how virtual wards and the care record change roles (step 2) — new remote-monitoring nurse roles, data analysts, and a platform engineering team. Using the Government Digital and Data framework they specify the required workforce precisely (step 3): 4 product managers, 6 user researchers, 12 software engineers at defined levels, 5 data engineers, and clinical safety capacity. Supply analysis (step 4) reveals hard truths — current turnover of digital staff is 18%, two key engineers are near retirement, and local salary benchmarking shows the ICS pays below market. The gap plan (step 5) blends build, buy, and borrow: a graduate and apprenticeship pipeline plus internal reskilling for the medium term (build), a targeted permanent recruitment campaign with a revised pay case (buy), and a time-limited contractor team to stand up the platform while permanent staff are recruited and trained alongside them for knowledge transfer (borrow). Two funding scenarios are modelled; digital-literacy uplift for existing clinical staff is identified as a no-regrets move in both. The plan is reviewed quarterly against actual vacancies and turnover (step 6), and revised when a neighbouring trust's recruitment drive worsens local supply. Sector lenses # Startup # A digital-health startup's workforce plan is a cash-runway calculation as much as a capability one: every hire is weighed against months of runway, so build/buy/borrow tilts hard toward buying a few versatile senior people and borrowing specialists on contract. The realistic planning horizon is 12–18 months — tied to the next funding round — not the three-to-ten-year strategic view an ICS must take. Scenario planning still matters, but the scenarios are commercial (will the pilot convert to a paid contract?) rather than demographic. The existential risk is key-person dependency: losing one of three engineers can halt delivery, so even a tiny startup should name its single points of failure and cross-train against them. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home or domiciliary-care agency, a single-site clinic, or a small health-tech supplier past the startup stage — must meet the same duties as a large trust but with no dedicated workforce-planning or IT function to do it. Planning here is pragmatic and personal: the practice manager or owner holds the whole establishment in their head, so build/buy/borrow usually means training an existing member of staff into a digital task or borrowing a shared resource from a federation, primary care network, or supplier. The binding constraints are tight cash and thin cover — a single leaver or long absence can remove a capability entirely — so key-person risk and cross-training matter as much as they do for a startup, but against a backdrop of ongoing patient-facing operations that cannot pause. Because dedicated digital capability is unaffordable, the realistic move is to buy it as a service or share it across the system, and to invest in the digital literacy of the generalist staff you already have rather than hoping to recruit scarce specialists you could not retain. Enterprise # A large NHS trust or ICS plans an establishment across thousands of posts, using the Six Steps methodology and a workforce-intelligence base of vacancy, turnover, and skills data. x: Topic 7.3 — Workforce Strategy In one sentence: A workforce strategy is the long-term, evidence-based, partnership-built plan that ensures your organization will have people with the right values, skills, capacity and wellbeing to deliver care over a ten-year horizon — and in digital health and care, it must treat digital capability and wellbeing as first-order design principles, not afterthoughts. Why this matters in health and care # Workforce planning ( Topic 7.2 ) answers "how many people, with which skills, do we need next year, and how do we source them?" A workforce strategy answers a bigger and longer question: "what kind of workforce do we want to be over the next decade, and what must change — in culture, roles, learning, leadership and technology — to get there?" It is the difference between filling next year's rota and reshaping the profession. In health and care this is existential. Services are entirely dependent on people: as the Welsh strategy that anchors this topic puts it, "the delivery of health and social care to the population of Wales is completely dependent on our workforce." The sector faces an ageing workforce, rising and more complex demand, growing health inequalities, higher public expectations, and a global shortfall the World Health Organization has projected at millions of health workers by 2030. Technology adds a second pressure: the pace of digital change outstrips most organizations' ability to absorb it, so a workforce strategy that ignores digital capability will design tomorrow's workforce for yesterday's ways of working. There is also a hard evidence link that makes workforce strategy a quality and safety instrument, not an HR nicety: staff experience, engagement and wellbeing correlate with the quality and safety of care people receive. Compassionate cultures produce compassionate care. Under-valued, over-loaded staff produce worse outcomes and leave. A workforce strategy is therefore one of the highest-leverage documents a health or care leader will ever own — and, because so much of the workforce sits in social care, private and voluntary providers, and the volunteer and carer community, it is inescapably a partnership document (see Topic 9.0 — Collaborating with Partner Organizations). Core concepts # Strategy versus plan. The strategy sets vision, ambition and themes over ~10 years; the implementation plans (co-produced, refreshed on a cycle) turn themes into dated, owned actions. Keep the two artefacts distinct: the strategy is stable and directional; the plans are living and specific. The whole workforce. In health and care, "workforce" is not just directly-employed staff. It includes statutory, private and voluntary providers, agency staff, volunteers, and unpaid carers. A credible strategy explicitly encompasses all of them, because the person receiving care experiences one system, not an org chart. Fundamental principles as a golden thread. A good strategy names a small set of principles that must be woven through every theme and plan. In A Healthier Wales , these are wellbeing , Welsh language , and inclusion . Yours will differ (language may not apply; equity, safety and digital inclusion almost always will), but the pattern — a few non-negotiable threads running through everything — is the transferable idea. Values before roles. Modern workforce strategy is values-based: recruit, induct and lead for shared values, then build competence on top. "Values based recruitment" and a "common induction" recur throughout the Welsh actions for exactly this reason. Intelligence-led. You cannot reshape what you cannot see. Strategy depends on standardized workforce data, shared definitions across health and care, and modelling capability — a "centre of excellence for workforce intelligence" is the ambition, because today's data is fragmented and non-comparable across sectors. Best practices # Anchor the strategy in a compelling, evidence-based case for change. Set out the demographic, demand, inequality, financial and technological pressures explicitly, and cite the reviews and evidence behind them (in Wales: the Parliamentary Review, A Healthier Wales , the King's Fund, the WHO workforce projections, the Topol Review). Leaders and staff commit to change they can see is necessary; a strategy that opens with ambition but no diagnosis will not move anyone. Build it in genuine partnership, and say who you heard from. The Welsh strategy was shaped by engaging over 1,000 people and organizations and 200 formal consultation responses, through "social partnership" between employers, trades unions and government. Co-production is not a courtesy — it is what makes the actions deliverable, because the people who must change the work help design the change. Record the engagement so the strategy visibly belongs to the workforce, not to the centre. Express ambition as a clear "strategy on a page" with a dated horizon. Distil the whole thing into one page: the ambition, what will be different, what success looks like, and an implementation timeline. A Healthier Wales sets a 2030 ambition — "a motivated, engaged and valued health and social care workforce, with the capacity, competence and confidence to meet the needs of the people of Wales" — and 32 actions for the first three years, reviewed every three. A memorable, dated ambition aligns thousands of dispersed decisions. Organize around a small number of themes, each with an outcome statement. Themes give the strategy structure and let dispersed teams find their contribution. The Welsh seven — summarized in the table below — are a strong, transferable template because each is stated as a 2030 outcome ("by 2030, X will be the norm"), not an activity. Aim for five to eight; more fragments effort, fewer over-generalizes. Make "digitally ready workforce" an explicit theme, not a footnote. This is the point most relevant to a digital health organization. The Welsh Theme 4 — "Building a Digitally Ready Workforce" — commits to a digital capabilities framework, embedding digital in undergraduate curricula, and requiring every digital transformation programme to carry an organizational-development plan. That last action is the sharpest: no digital rollout without a workforce/OD plan attached (see Topic 7.5 — People & Organizational Development, and Topic 8.1 — Change Management). It operationalizes the Topol Review's finding that technology adoption is bottlenecked by workforce capability, not by the technology. Treat wellbeing as strategy, backed by frameworks and measures. Wellbeing recurs as a principle and a theme because the evidence linking it to care quality is strong. Concrete mechanisms matter more than sentiment: a Health and Wellbeing Framework with measurable standards; a Staff Governance Framework (the Welsh strategy borrows Scotland's, which enshrines social partnership in a system of corporate accountability for fair treatment of staff); a consistent staff-experience survey and engagement index; and wellbeing/engagement measures built into the organizational performance framework so boards are held to account for them. Design for seamless, multi-professional, multi-agency roles. Future care models are built around "what matters to me" to the person, which cuts across professional boundaries. Strategy should deliberately dissolve the boundaries that cause "gaps and duplication of care" — through competence frameworks for extended skills and advanced practice, common induction, and harmonized regulation and registration across health and social care. For a digital team this is the workforce mirror of interoperability: people, like systems, must work across organizational seams. Invest in education, learning and a "grow your own" pipeline. Shift from uni-professional training to inter-professional, flexible, accessible routes: apprenticeships, work-based learning, recognition of prior learning, and widening access to under-represented groups and rural/remote "grow your own" communities. Embed the new essentials — prevention, quality improvement, research, leadership, digital — into core curricula rather than bolting them on. A strategy that only recruits, without building the training pipeline, mortgages the next decade. Make leadership development collective, compassionate and distributed. Leadership is "needed at all levels," not equated with a few senior posts. Build a talent and succession pipeline, accessible leadership resources (often via a digital portal), and leaders who can work across organizational boundaries — because system transformation and partnership working demand shared, distributed leadership. Compassionate leadership is the causal lever on culture, and culture is the lever on care quality. Close the loop with workforce intelligence and measurable success. Commit to standardized data sets, shared definitions across health and care, modelling capability, and a defined workforce-planning methodology (in Wales, a "six-step" approach — see Topic 7.2 ). Define what success looks like up front (engagement, retention, skills, diversity, intelligence-led planning) and review the actions on a fixed cycle so the strategy stays "live and valid" rather than becoming a shelf document. Questions to discuss with your team # Does our workforce strategy treat digital capability as a first-order theme, or is it still buried inside "IT training"? This is the question that most often separates a strategy that will survive contact with transformation from one that won't. The Welsh strategy makes "Building a Digitally Ready Workforce" one of seven themes and — crucially — requires every digital transformation programme to carry an organizational-development plan, operationalizing the Topol Review's finding that technology adoption is bottlenecked by people, not products. Debate honestly whether your current plans would let a shared-care-record rollout stall because care-home staff have no devices, no protected learning time, and no digital confidence. A good answer names a digital capabilities framework, a mechanism that ties funding release to a workforce/OD plan, and someone accountable for it — not a vague aspiration to "upskill." Watch for the comfortable illusion that buying training licences equals capability. Are we genuinely co-producing this with the whole workforce — including social care, the independent sector, agency staff, volunteers and carers — or writing it centrally and consulting cosmetically? In health and care the person experiences one system, but the workforce spans many employers with very different terms, conditions and power. The Welsh strategy was shaped by engaging over 1,000 people and 200 formal responses through statutory social partnership, and it explicitly encompasses statutory, private, voluntary, volunteer and carer workforces — because a strategy the frontline did not help write is one the frontline will quietly ignore. Discuss who is actually in the room when you set direction, whose terms and conditions you are willing to put on the table, and whether your social-care and domiciliary partners see the strategy as theirs. A good answer can point to concrete co-production and to actions that address the pay, workload and recognition issues staff actually raised, not just the ones convenient to fund. Are we weighting retention as heavily as recruitment, and can we prove wellbeing is improving? "Many of our future workforce are with us today": a strategy that chases new hires while current staff leave through the back door never closes the gap, and in a sector with an ageing workforce and rising agency spend the maths is unforgiving. The evidence linking staff wellbeing and engagement to care quality and safety means retention and wellbeing are clinical issues, not HR ones — yet they are the easiest to reduce to warm words. Discuss whether you have a wellbeing framework with measurable standards, a consistent staff-experience survey that spans the NHS and the care market, and wellbeing/engagement measures built into the board's performance framework so leaders are actually held to account. A good answer shows you can see engagement where turnover is worst, and that a named leader owns moving it. Have we designed for roles that cross professional and organizational boundaries, or are we still planning profession by profession and employer by employer? Future care is organized around "what matters to me" to the person, which rarely respects the lines between professions, trusts, councils and providers — yet most workforce planning still happens in uni-professional, single-employer silos that reproduce the very "gaps and duplication of care" the strategy is meant to dissolve. This is the workforce mirror of interoperability: people, like systems, have to work across the seams, which means competence frameworks for extended skills and advanced practice, common induction, and harmonizing regulation and registration across health and social care. The tension is that boundary-crossing roles threaten established professional identities, pay structures and regulatory turf, so the honest debate is about who gives ground and how you manage the safety and accountability questions that follow. A good answer points to specific redesigned roles or advanced-practice pathways, names the regulatory and terms-and-conditions obstacles you are actually tackling, and shows how a digital programme (a shared record, remote monitoring) is being used to enable the new roles rather than merely digitizing the old ones. Is this a living strategy with owned, dated plans and a real review cycle, or a document that will age out on a shelf? The strategy is meant to be stable and directional over ten years while the implementation plans stay living, specific and refreshed on a cycle — but the failure mode is a handsome vision published once, with no owned actions, no dates, and no mechanism to keep it "live and valid" as demand, technology and finances move underneath it. Discuss whether every theme translates into dated actions with a named owner, whether you have committed to a fixed review rhythm (the Welsh model refreshes its actions every three years), and who has the authority and the standing forum to renew them. The trade-off is honesty about capacity: a strategy that promises constant refresh but has no resourced team behind it is as hollow as one that never revisits itself. A good answer can show the separation between the durable strategy and the living plans, point to the last review that actually changed something, and name the board or partnership that holds the cycle. Can we actually see our whole workforce — across health and social care — well enough to steer this strategy? You cannot reshape what you cannot see, and in this sector the data is fragmented and non-comparable across NHS, local-authority and independent providers, so a strategy built on partial or incompatible workforce intelligence is steering half-blind. Debate whether you have standardized data sets, shared definitions that mean the same thing to a trust and a care home, and the modelling capability to test scenarios rather than just count last year's headcount — the ambition of a "centre of excellence for workforce intelligence" exists precisely because today's picture is so poor. The tension is that better intelligence costs money and cooperation that independent providers have little slack to give, and that data-sharing across employers raises real information-governance questions. A good answer shows where you can already compare workforce data across sectors, is candid about the biggest blind spots (usually the domiciliary and care-home workforce), and names who is investing in closing them. In practice: a health & care example # An Integrated Care System (ICS) covering three NHS trusts, five local authorities, and a large independent-sector care market is rolling out a shared care record and a suite of patient-facing digital services over five years. Early pilots stall: clinicians distrust the new record, care-home staff have no devices or digital confidence, and turnover in the domiciliary workforce erases every training cohort within months. The ICS responds by writing a ten-year workforce strategy rather than another training plan. It opens with a shared case for change (demand, ageing workforce, digital opportunity) built from a joint engagement exercise across all partners — including care providers, unions and carers — so the strategy is co-owned. It sets a dated 2035 ambition and six themes, one of which is explicitly "a digitally-ready workforce." Under that theme it mandates that every digital programme business case must include an OD and workforce plan (devices, protected learning time, digital champions, capability uplift) before funding is released; without it, the spend control board declines the case. A wellbeing theme introduces a common staff-experience survey across NHS and social care so, for the first time, the ICS can see engagement in the care market — which turns out to be the real driver of the turnover that was defeating training. Within three years, adoption of the shared record rises not because the technology changed, but because the workforce was designed to receive it. Sector lenses # Startup # A 30-person digital-health startup rarely writes a ten-year workforce strategy — but it should write a one-page version, because its whole valuation rests on scarce talent (clinical-safety engineers, ML specialists, a part-time Caldicott Guardian) it cannot easily replace. The transferable moves are: name two or three workforce principles (e.g. clinical credibility, learning culture, wellbeing so people don't burn out in a high-growth sprint); decide build/buy/borrow deliberately (a fractional Clinical Safety Officer rather than an unfilled full-time post); and treat retention as survival, because losing the one person who understands your DCB0129 safety case is an existential risk, not an HR metric. Strategy here is lightweight and founder-owned, but the values-before-roles and retention-over-recruitment lessons apply at any size. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home or a domiciliary-care agency — is the workforce this strategy most often assumes but least resources: real patients and clients, a handful of staff, no dedicated HR or IT function, tight cash, and the same statutory and clinical-safety duties as a large trust. Its "strategy" is realistically a page in the practice or business plan that names a couple of workforce priorities (values-based recruitment, retention of hard-to-replace staff, basic digital confidence) and a "grow your own" instinct — training an existing healthcare assistant or care worker rather than competing for scarce hires it cannot outbid. The sharp risk is being on the receiving end of someone else's digital rollout — a shared care record or an electronic prescribing system — with no protected learning time and no OD plan, which is exactly where system pilots stall; so the transferable move is to insist that any programme it is asked to adopt comes with devices, training time and support attached, and to lean on partnership and shared resources (the ICS, the primary care network, the local authority) it is too small to provide alone. Enterprise # A large NHS trust or integrated care system is the natural home of a full workforce strategy: tens of thousands of staff across statutory, private, voluntary, agency, volunteer and carer workforces, a decade-long transformation, and a board accountable for safe staffing. Here the Welsh model transfers almost wholesale — a dated ambition, five to eight outcome-based themes, an explicit "digitally-ready workforce" theme that gates every transformation programme on an OD plan, a common staff-experience survey spanning the NHS and the care market, and a workforce-intelligence function with standard

x: Topic 7.4 — Digital Skills & Capability Building Digital skills are not an IT concern for a specialist few but a whole-workforce capability that determines whether new systems make care safer or more dangerous — so building them is a clinical-safety, equity and public-trust obligation, not an optional training line item. Why this matters in health and care # Most digital projects in health and care do not fail because the technology is broken. They fail because the workforce was never properly prepared to use it. A well-built electronic patient record, deployed into wards where nurses have had ninety minutes of e-learning and no floor-walking support, produces slower care, workarounds, frustration and — the part that should concentrate every leader's mind — new categories of clinical error. The technology works; the capability to use it safely does not exist yet. In this sector, an under-invested training plan is a patient-safety risk (see Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management). The scope of the challenge is larger than the digital and IT team, whose own development is covered in Topics 7.0 –43. The people who most need digital capability are the clinical and care staff, operational managers and senior leaders who use digital systems every hour of every shift but do not think of themselves as "digital" at all. A radiographer, a community district nurse, a care-home manager, a receptionist booking appointments, a GP prescribing electronically: their fluency, or lack of it, is where digital transformation succeeds or stalls. Capability is only as strong as the least-supported user in the workflow. There is an equity dimension too. Some staff are themselves digitally excluded — through age, disability, language, precarious employment, or simply never having had a device or protected time to learn. Social care is especially exposed: a fragmented, high-turnover, low-margin workforce, often without organizational email addresses, let alone laptops. If you design capability programmes only for confident, salaried NHS staff on hospital sites, you widen the very divide that shared care records were meant to close (see Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility, and Topic 7.6 — Workforce Equality, Diversity & Inclusion). And because capability shapes how safely and confidently staff handle patient data, it feeds directly into public trust: patients notice when the person in front of them is fighting the computer rather than caring for them. Core concepts # Digital literacy is the baseline: the capabilities that fit someone to live, learn and work in a digital society. In a health and care setting it means more than sending email — it spans information handling, communication, transactions, problem-solving, staying safe online, and the confidence to learn a new system without fear. It is not a fixed trait but a spectrum that everyone can move along with support. The Topol Review — Preparing the Healthcare Workforce to Deliver the Digital Future (2019), led by Eric Topol for what was then Health Education England — is the sector's anchor document. Its central finding is the thesis of this topic: the rate at which health systems adopt technology is limited not by the technology but by the workforce's readiness to use it, so employers must invest in education, training and lifelong learning, and give staff time to adapt. It calls for the whole workforce to gain digital literacy, and for a cadre of specialists to go much deeper. Health informatics — and its clinical, nursing and pharmacy sub-disciplines — is the professional field that bridges clinical practice and digital systems. The bridging leadership roles matter enormously: the Chief Clinical Information Officer (CCIO) , Chief Nursing Information Officer (CNIO) and their allied-health and pharmacy equivalents translate between clinical need and technical delivery, and lend clinical credibility to change that a Chief Information Officer alone cannot. Digital transformation fails or succeeds on capability, so treat capability as a design input, not a downstream afterthought. A capability (or digital-readiness) framework describes, in plain and assessable terms, what "good" looks like at each level and role — from basic digital literacy to advanced clinical informatics — so you can measure where people are and target investment at the gaps. A skills gap is the mismatch between the capabilities the workforce has and the capabilities the work now demands. Closing it durably requires lifelong learning and a learning organisation culture — one that continuously develops its people rather than training them once at go-live and moving on. Professional development , apprenticeships and defined career pathways professionalize the digital, data and technology (DDaT) workforce and give clinical staff a recognized route into informatics. The digital divide applies to staff as well as patients. Digital exclusion among the workforce — no device, no connectivity, no confidence, no protected time — is a capability problem you must design against explicitly, because the people it affects are often those caring for the most vulnerable citizens. Best practices # Treat capability as part of the system, and never deploy without a training and support plan. The single most reliable predictor of a failed rollout is a business case that funds the software but not the workforce change around it. Make it a rule — enforced at the spend-control or investment board — that no digital programme is approved without a costed capability and organizational-development plan attached (see Topic 7.5 — People & Organizational Development). This operationalizes the Topol Review's core finding and converts "we'll do some training" into an owned, funded commitment. Assess the baseline before you design the programme. You cannot close a gap you have not measured. Use a recognized capability or digital-readiness framework to survey current capability by role, team and site, distinguishing confidence from competence, and surfacing the pockets of digital exclusion you would otherwise miss. Repeat the assessment after deployment so you can show capability actually rose, not just that attendance was recorded. Embed training in the deployment itself, with floor-walking and super-users. Classroom e-learning weeks before go-live is largely forgotten by the time it matters. The evidence favours training close to go-live, in the real environment, with visible on-the-floor support — "floor-walkers" and local super-users (also called digital champions) who are peers, not IT strangers, and who stay embedded for weeks after launch. Budget for backfill so staff can actually leave the workflow to learn, and for the super-users' time, because unpaid goodwill is not a support model. Grow the bridging roles: CCIOs, CNIOs and clinical informaticians. Appoint, fund and give real authority to Chief Clinical and Chief Nursing Information Officers and their allied-health equivalents, and build a pipeline of clinical staff into informatics through fellowships and formal training. These roles give change clinical credibility, catch safety issues that technologists miss, and ensure systems are configured around real clinical workflow. A digital programme led only by technologists, however skilled, will design for the system it wishes clinicians used rather than the one they actually work in. Build career pathways and professionalize the DDaT workforce. Use apprenticeships (from digital-support technician to degree-level data and cyber routes), the recognized DDaT capability framework, and professional registration to turn ad-hoc digital roles into a profession with progression. This widens access — apprenticeships reach people who would never take a traditional degree route — and improves retention, because staff who can see a future stay. It also strengthens the talent pipeline your workforce strategy depends on (see Topic 7.3 — Workforce Strategy). Make it lifelong, and build a learning culture. Capability decays and technology moves, so one-off training at go-live guarantees a capability gap within months, worsened by turnover. Protect regular learning time, normalize continuing professional development in digital skills, and reward the curiosity and psychological safety that let people admit what they do not know. A genuine learning organization treats every incident, workaround and near-miss as data about capability, not a reason to blame an individual. Design explicitly for digitally excluded staff. Assume that some of your workforce — disproportionately in social care, domiciliary and bank/agency roles — lack devices, connectivity, organizational logins or confidence, and design programmes that reach them rather than the confident majority who least need help. Offer multiple formats, plain-language materials, one-to-one coaching, and basic-skills routes such as the Essential Digital Skills framework. Inclusion here is not charity; it is the precondition for the shared records and integrated pathways that only work if every part of the workforce can use them. Develop leaders' and managers' digital capability, not just frontline users'. Boards and senior managers sponsor, fund and govern digital change, yet are often the least digitally fluent people in the building, which produces unrealistic timelines, thin support budgets and a rush to go-live. Invest deliberately in leadership digital literacy — enough to challenge a supplier, read a capability plan critically, and understand why floor-walking matters — through board development, digital-leadership programmes and reverse mentoring. Capable sponsors make the difference between a programme that protects learning time and one that sacrifices it to the deadline. Measure capability and close the gaps you find. Define what capability means, baseline it, set targets, and track movement — completion rates, confidence surveys, competency assessments, adoption and proficient-use metrics, and reductions in error and workaround rates. Report capability alongside delivery milestones so the board sees it as a first-order outcome, and feed the gaps back into the next round of investment. What gets measured and reported to the board is what gets funded. Tie capability building to change management and communications. Skills without motivation and clear communication produce trained-but-resistant staff, so run capability building as one strand of a coherent change approach (see Topic 8.1 — Change Management, and Topic 8.2 — Communications & Engagement). Use a recognized model — ADKAR's sequence of Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement is a useful reminder that Knowledge and Ability sit inside a wider arc. Capability is necessary but not sufficient; people also need to understand why the change matters and to see it reinforced. Questions to discuss with your team # Would our next major system go-live fail on capability rather than technology — and how would we know before it did? This question forces an honest look at the gap between your delivery plan and your capability plan. Trace a specific forthcoming rollout — a shared care record, an e-prescribing module, a new referral system — and ask whether the training, floor-walking, super-user and backfill provision is actually funded and staffed, or whether it is a paragraph of good intentions in the business case. Debate where your digitally excluded and hardest-to-reach staff are (often social care, community, night shifts, bank and agency workers) and whether the plan reaches them or only the confident hospital-based majority. Consider your leading indicators: baseline capability assessments, confidence surveys, super-user readiness, and protected-time commitments that you can check weeks before go-live rather than discovering the gap in a post-incident review. A good, honest answer names the specific groups at risk, points to funded and owned mitigations, and admits where the current plan is thin — rather than asserting that "training is covered." Are we building capability that lasts, or training people once and moving on? Capability decays, technology changes and staff turn over, so a programme that peaks at go-live and then stops will have a fresh gap within a year — worse in high-turnover parts of the workforce. Discuss whether you have protected, recurring learning time or whether "digital skills" is squeezed out by operational pressure the moment a ward is short-staffed. Examine your induction: does every new starter, including bank and agency, get the digital capability they need, or do gaps compound with each hire? Weigh the tension between the immediate operational cost of releasing staff to learn and the slower, larger cost of workarounds, errors and disengagement when they cannot. A good answer describes concrete mechanisms — protected CPD time, refreshed super-user networks, digital capability built into every induction and appraisal — and evidence that capability is being sustained, not just an aspiration to a "learning culture." Do we treat our own workforce's digital exclusion as seriously as we treat patients'? Digital inclusion effort in health and care overwhelmingly targets patients and citizens, yet a meaningful share of staff are themselves excluded — without devices, connectivity, organizational logins, confidence or protected time — and this is most acute among the social care and community colleagues who care for the most vulnerable people. Discuss who in your workforce is being quietly left behind, and whether your capability programmes assume a level of baseline access and confidence that many staff do not have. Consider the equity consequence: if only confident, salaried, hospital-based staff can use the shared record, integrated care fails precisely at the seams it was meant to join. Weigh practical responses — device provision, basic-skills routes such as Essential Digital Skills, one-to-one coaching, plain-language materials, reaching staff who have no work email. A good answer can point to who owns staff digital inclusion, how excluded staff are identified, and what is actually being done — not a general belief that "our people are fine with computers." Do we have the clinical-informatics bridging roles — CCIOs, CNIOs and clinical informaticians — with real authority, or is our change led only by technologists? Digital change designed without clinical credibility tends to fit the workflow its designers imagine rather than the one staff actually work in, and it misses the safety issues that only clinical eyes catch. Discuss whether your Chief Clinical and Chief Nursing Information Officers (and allied-health and pharmacy equivalents) are genuinely appointed, funded and empowered — with time protected from their clinical duties — or whether the title exists on paper while decisions are made elsewhere. Consider the pipeline behind them: are you growing clinical staff into informatics through fellowships and formal training, or relying on a single overstretched champion whose departure would leave a vacuum? Weigh the tension between the cost of releasing scarce clinicians into informatics roles and the far larger cost of systems configured around technical convenience rather than clinical reality. A good answer can name the post-holders, describe the authority and time they actually have, and point to a route by which the next generation of clinical informaticians is being developed — not a job title with no mandate. Is our board and senior-management layer digitally capable enough to sponsor this well — and would they know if they were not? Boards and senior managers set the timelines, approve the budgets and govern digital change, yet are frequently the least digitally fluent people involved, which quietly produces unrealistic go-live dates and thin support budgets. Discuss honestly whether your leaders could challenge a supplier's claims, read a capability plan critically, or explain why floor-walking and backfill matter — and whether anyone has ever assessed their digital capability rather than assuming seniority implies fluency. Consider practical development routes: board-level digital-leadership programmes, reverse mentoring with younger or more digitally confident staff, and exposure to the frontline reality of using the systems they sponsor. Weigh the awkward tension that the people who most need this development are often the least likely to ask for it, and that raising it requires psychological safety at the top. A good answer describes concrete steps being taken to build leadership digital capability and evidence that capable sponsorship is protecting learning time and support budgets — not a comfortable assumption that "the board is on board." Are we professionalizing digital roles into real careers, or leaving them as ad-hoc jobs that people pass through and leave? Capability is not only built through training courses; it is sustained by a workforce that can see a future in digital, data and technology roles and therefore stays. Discuss whether you use apprenticeships, the recognized DDaT capability framework, professional registration and defined career pathways to turn scattered digital roles into a profession with progression — or whether digital posts are filled reactively, without a route from, say, a digital-support technician to a degree-level data or cyber specialist. Consider who this widens access to: apprenticeships and internal pathways reach people who would never take a traditional degree route, including existing clinical and care staff. Weigh the tension between the short-term ease of buying in contractors and the long-term fragility of a workforce with no home-grown pipeline and high churn. A good answer points to actual pathways, apprenticeship numbers and registration uptake, and to retention evidence — not an aspiration to "invest in our people" with no structure behind it. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system (ICS) spanning two acute trusts, a community and mental-health trust, five local authorities and roughly two hundred independent care providers is deploying a shared care record over three years. The first phase, into the acute trusts, goes reasonably well: hospital staff are salaried, on-site, and used to clinical systems. The second phase — extending access to community teams and care homes — stalls badly. District nurses on aged tablets with poor connectivity abandon the record mid-visit; care-home staff, many without individual logins or any prior clinical-system experience, either share a single account (an information-governance breach) or ignore the record entirely. Adoption in the settings that most needed integration is near zero. The ICS pauses and rebuilds around capability rather than technology. It runs a baseline digital-readiness assessment across community and social-care partners and discovers the real problem: not resistance, but exclusion — no devices, no confidence, no protected learning time. It funds a package that pairs each cluster of care homes with an embedded digital champion drawn from the care workforce itself, provides devices and individual logins, and delivers short, hands-on, in-the-workplace training with weeks of floor-walking rather than a one-off webinar. A newly appointed CNIO ensures the record is configured around community and care-home workflow, not just acute needs. Crucially, the ICS makes a standing rule: no further rollout phase is funded without a costed capability and OD plan, and capability metrics are reported to the board alongside delivery milestones. Within two phases, adoption in care homes rises from near zero to routine use — because the workforce was, at last, designed to receive the system.
