x: Topic 7.5 — People & Organizational Development In one sentence: People and organizational development is the deliberate work of growing your people's capability and confidence and reshaping the organization's culture, leadership, and ways of working so that digital change becomes something the organization is able to sustain rather than merely survive. Why this matters in health and care # You can buy technology and you can hire staff, but you cannot buy a learning culture, psychological safety, or digital confidence — you have to develop them. Most digital transformations fail not on the technology but on the human system around it: staff who fear the change, leaders who cannot model new behaviours, and an organization with no muscle for continuous learning. In health and care this is acute. The Topol Review concluded that preparing the workforce for a digital future would require sustained effort at every level, and that the binding constraint is a digitally ready workforce — engaged, skilled, and confident — not the availability of technology itself. Meanwhile the evidence is strong that team climate directly affects patient safety: psychological safety and compassionate leadership are associated with staff speaking up about risk, learning from error, and better outcomes. People and OD is also where equity is won or lost. Digital transformation can widen or narrow inequalities among staff and, through them, among patients. Investing in inclusive development, digital literacy, and fair access to opportunity is both a statutory expectation (the NHS People Promise, the Public Sector Equality Duty) and a practical condition for change to stick. This topic is the human counterpart to Workforce Planning (see Topic 7.2 ) and the enabler of Change Management (see Topic 8.1 ). Core concepts # Learning organisation and learning culture. An organization that continuously improves by enabling its people to learn — where reflection, experimentation, and knowledge-sharing are normal, expected, and rewarded, rather than squeezed out by operational pressure. Continuing professional development (CPD). The structured, ongoing development of skills and knowledge across a career. In digital health this must cover both the deepening of professional expertise and the broadening of digital and data literacy across all staff. Communities of practice . Groups who share a craft or domain — user researchers, clinical safety officers, information governance leads — and meet across team and organizational boundaries to develop standards, share learning, and reduce isolation. They are how expertise spreads in a federated system. Psychological safety . A shared belief, defined by Amy Edmondson , that a team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking — that you can ask a question, admit a mistake, or raise a concern without fear of humiliation or punishment. It is the precondition for both safety-critical candour and the experimentation digital work depends on. Compassionate and inclusive leadership. The leadership model at the heart of the NHS People Promise and Our Leadership Way : leaders who attend, understand, empathize, and act, and who create cultures where all staff feel they belong. Its explicit purpose is to build effective teams and psychologically safe cultures. Talent management and succession . The systematic identification and development of people for future critical roles, so the organization is not left exposed when a key individual leaves — especially important where digital expertise is scarce. Organisational development (OD) interventions. Planned, evidence-based efforts to improve an organization's health and effectiveness — culture change, team development, leadership development, and structural or process redesign. Best practices # Build learning into the working week, not the annual appraisal. Protect time for development, reflection, and experimentation as a normal part of delivery. A learning culture that exists only in a once-a-year form is not a learning culture; capacity to learn must be designed into how teams work. Make digital literacy a whole-workforce programme, not an IT topic. Following the Topol Review, treat digital and data capability as something every role needs at an appropriate level — clinical, operational, managerial — using the NHS Digital Readiness resources and structured self-assessment. The goal is confidence and engagement, not just tool training. Develop compassionate and inclusive leaders deliberately. Leadership behaviour sets the team climate that determines whether people speak up. Invest in leadership development aligned to the NHS People Promise and Our Leadership Way , and hold leaders accountable for the culture they create, not only the targets they hit. Cultivate psychological safety as a safety-critical asset. Actively build teams where questions, dissent, and error-reporting are welcomed — through how leaders respond to bad news, how mistakes are handled, and how concerns are followed up. In a clinical-digital context, silence about risk is the failure mode you most need to prevent. Stand up communities of practice across boundaries. Give each discipline (research, design, clinical safety, data, engineering) a cross-team community with time, sponsorship, and a remit to set standards and share learning. This spreads scarce expertise (complementing the enabling-team pattern in Topic 7.0 ) and reduces the isolation of lone specialists. Use coaching and mentoring to grow people, not just direct them. Embed coaching as a leadership habit and offer mentoring for those moving into digital and leadership roles. Coaching builds the autonomy and problem-solving capacity that self-organizing delivery teams need. Manage talent and succession for scarce digital roles. Identify critical roles and the people who could grow into them, and develop them ahead of need. Given the digital labour shortage ( Topic 7.2 ), losing a key architect or Clinical Safety Officer with no successor is an avoidable, self-inflicted risk. Treat equality, diversity, and inclusion as integral, not adjacent. Make development opportunities, recruitment, and progression demonstrably fair, and pay attention to who is and is not getting digital opportunities. Inclusion is both a duty and a driver of the diverse thinking that safe, usable services require. Run OD interventions with evidence and evaluation. Approach culture and behaviour change as you would any intervention: diagnose the current state, choose an evidence-based approach, and evaluate whether it worked. Culture-change initiatives that are asserted rather than measured tend to fade with the away-day that launched them. Questions to discuss with your team # Is it genuinely safe on our teams to admit a mistake or raise a concern about a new system — and how would we actually know? Psychological safety is not a soft nicety in a clinical-digital context; the evidence links team climate directly to patient safety, because staff who fear humiliation or blame stay silent about the near-misses and usability problems that are the earliest signals of risk. The hard part of this conversation is that almost everyone believes their own team is safe, so the useful question is evidential rather than aspirational: what would you expect to see if it were true, and do you see it? A telling and counter-intuitive signal is reported near-misses rising rather than falling when a new record goes live — because reporting finally feels safe — so a suspiciously quiet incident log may be a warning, not reassurance. Debate how your leaders actually respond when they hear bad news about a system they championed: do they act on it visibly, or defend the system and subtly punish the messenger? Consider too that safety varies team by team and manager by manager, so a single organizational average can hide real cold spots. An honest answer moves past "of course we're safe" to concrete evidence — how mistakes were handled last month, whether concerns were followed up, what happened to the last person who raised an awkward problem. Is our digital-literacy investment reaching the anxious and the late adopters, or flowing to the already-confident and quietly widening the gap? The Topol Review's core conclusion is that the binding constraint on digital transformation is a digitally ready workforce, not the technology, and readiness means confidence and engagement across every role — yet development effort has a natural tendency to reach the people who seek it out, who are usually the ones who need it least. This matters beyond fairness: People and OD is where equity is won or lost, and inequitable uplift among staff translates, through them, into inequitable services for patients, which also engages the Public Sector Equality Duty. The trade-off to debate is that supporting the anxious and the resistant is slower, more resource-intensive, and less visibly rewarding than showcasing your champions, so it is exactly the work that gets squeezed under operational pressure. Look honestly at who has actually taken up your digital-readiness support and who has not, and whether you have protected time for the people who learn slowly rather than only for the enthusiasts. A good answer can point to how it reaches late adopters specifically, treats digital literacy as a whole-workforce programme rather than an IT topic, and monitors uptake by staff group so widening gaps are caught rather than assumed away. When we say we are changing the culture, are we doing evidence-based OD — or launching an away-day and hoping? Culture-change-by-away-day is a recognized failure mode precisely because it feels like action: a launch event, a poster campaign, a leadership framework published, and then nothing sustained or measured, so the initiative fades within months of the event that launched it. The deeper tension is that culture follows what leaders do, not what strategies assert, which makes the uncomfortable question whether your leaders' own behaviour and the climate they create are part of the intervention or conveniently exempt from it. Treating OD as you would any clinical intervention — diagnose the current state, choose an evidence-based approach, and evaluate whether it actually worked — is the discipline that separates real change from theatre, but it requires agreeing measures of behaviour change rather than measures of activity. Debate what you would count as evidence that a culture initiative succeeded: attendance at training and a signed-off strategy are outputs, whereas staff confidence, reported near-misses, adoption, and observed leadership behaviour are impact. Consider a past initiative honestly and ask whether it was ever evaluated at all, or simply assumed to have worked because it was launched. A strong answer commits to diagnosing before intervening, names impact measures rather than output measures, and refuses to exempt leadership behaviour from the change it asks of everyone else. When operational pressure spikes, is protected learning time the first thing we sacrifice — and what does that tell us about whether we truly value development? A learning culture is built into how teams work or it does not exist, yet development, reflection, and experimentation are precisely the activities that feel optional when the rota is short and the waiting list is growing. The revealing question is not whether you have a training budget but what actually happens to protected time on a bad week: if it is quietly cancelled first and every time, then in practice you have decided that learning is a luxury, whatever the strategy says. The genuine tension here is real and not to be waved away — patient-facing operational demand is a legitimate and often safety-critical claim on the same hours, so this is a hard prioritization, not a straw man. The trap is that treating development as the permanent shock-absorber for operational pressure guarantees that skills and confidence decay, staff revert to workarounds, and the organization loses its capacity to absorb the next change. Discuss who actually loses their learning time when things get tight — is it shared, or does it always fall on the same frontline groups who most need to build digital confidence? An honest answer looks at the last few months of cancelled sessions rather than the policy, acknowledges the real trade-off with operational demand, and names what the organization is willing to protect even under pressure. If one of our two hardest-to-replace digital specialists left next month, would their knowledge walk out with them — and what have we done to spread it while we still can? Digital expertise is scarce, and a lone specialist — a key architect, a Clinical Safety Officer, an information-governance lead — is often genuinely alone, so their departure is an avoidable, self-inflicted risk rather than bad luck. The uncomfortable part of this conversation is that the people most critical to keep are usually the busiest, which makes investing their time in succession, documentation, and communities of practice feel like a cost you cannot afford right up until the moment you cannot afford not to have. There is a real trade-off to name: time a specialist spends mentoring a successor or writing down tacit knowledge is time not spent shipping, and under delivery pressure that trade is easy to defer indefinitely. Communities of practice are part of the answer because they spread scarce expertise across boundaries and reduce the isolation that drives burnout and single-person knowledge loss. Consider concretely who could step into each critical role today, who is being actively developed to do so tomorrow, and whether any of your specialists are one resignation away from leaving a hole no one can fill. A strong answer identifies the specific roles where you are exposed, shows real successors in active development rather than named on a chart, and treats knowledge-spreading as ongoing work rather than an exit-interview scramble. Are we coaching people to grow their own judgement, or just training them to follow the new system's steps? Self-organizing delivery teams and confident frontline staff need autonomy and problem-solving capacity, not just the ability to click through a workflow, and the difference between coaching and instruction is the difference between people who can adapt when the system behaves unexpectedly and people who freeze or work around it. This matters in a digital-health setting because a member of staff who understands why a safety check exists will protect the patient when the software does something odd, whereas one who has only memorized the steps may not. The tension is that directing and tool-training are faster and feel more controllable, while coaching is slower, harder to measure, and asks leaders to tolerate people reaching their own answers — which is uncomfortable under time and safety pressure. There is also a genuine question of where autonomy is appropriate: some clinical-digital tasks demand strict adherence to protocol, so this is about growing judgement within safe boundaries, not licence to improvise everywhere. Debate whether your managers actually coach or simply instruct, and whether people moving into digital and leadership roles get mentoring that builds their independence or supervision that keeps them dependent. An honest answer distinguishes where standardization is essential from where judgement should grow, and points to coaching and mentoring as deliberate habits rather than occasional favours. In practice: a health & care example # A community health and social care provider is deploying a new electronic patient record and expanding remote monitoring — a change that lands hardest on people, not servers. Rather than run tool-training alone, the OD and digital teams design a people programme. Every staff group completes a digital-readiness self-assessment based on the Topol/NHS Digital Readiness materials, and tailored digital-literacy support is offered from confident champions down to anxious late adopters — with protected time to learn. Communities of practice are established for digital champions and for clinical safety leads across sites, meeting monthly to share what works and to set shared standards. Frontline and middle managers go through a compassionate leadership development strand, because the programme team recognizes that whether staff raise problems with the new system depends on how their manager responds when they do. Psychological safety is made explicit: teams are encouraged to report near-misses and usability problems with the new record, and leaders visibly act on what they hear rather than defending the system. Coaching supports several nurses moving into new remote-monitoring roles, and a succession plan is drawn up for the two hardest-to-replace digital roles. Progress is evaluated not by attendance at training but by staff confidence surveys, reported near-misses (rising, as intended, because reporting feels safe), and adoption. When a ward struggles, the response is coaching and community support, not blame — and adoption there recovers. Sector lenses # Startup # In a startup, "organizational development" is culture-setting by the founders, not a formal OD function — the habits established in the first dozen hires become the culture, for good or ill. Psychological safety is easy to achieve when everyone shares a room but fragile under funding pressure, and there is rarely protected learning time or a CPD budget, so development happens on the job. There is no succession plan and no community of practice; a lone specialist is genuinely alone, which makes burnout and single-person knowledge loss the acute risks. The winning move is to bake learning and candour into rituals early — blameless retrospectives, an explicit "it is safe to raise problems" — while it is cheap, because retrofitting culture into a scaled company is far harder. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home or domiciliary-care agency, a single-site clinic, or a small health-tech supplier past the pre-revenue stage — has real patients and staff but rarely any dedicated OD, learning, or digital-training function, so development lands on an already-stretched manager or owner alongside everything else. It must meet the same duties as a large trust — the Public Sector Equality Duty, fair development opportunities, safe reporting cultures — without the budgets, protected learning time, or leadership-development programmes an enterprise takes for granted. Psychological safety is shaped almost entirely by one or two visible leaders, which is a strength when they model candour and a serious risk when they do not, because there is no wider system to dilute a blame culture. Digital-literacy uplift has to be pragmatic and low-cost: making use of free NHS Digital Readiness materials, learning during quiet clinic hours, and leaning on external communities of practice and peer networks (a Primary Care Network, a pharmacy association) rather than building internal ones. Succession is acute, since a single departing person may hold all the digital knowledge and cover is thin, so cross-training even one colleague and writing down the essentials matters more here than any formal talent pipeline. The realistic move is to protect small, regular pockets of learning and to be deliberate about candour and knowledge-sharing, because the organization has no slack to absorb either skills decay or a sudden loss of expertise. Enterprise # A large trust or health-tech firm has dedicated OD, learning, and leadership-development functions but fights scale and inertia: a learning culture must be sustained across thousands of staff and many sites, against relentless operational pressure. Communities of practice, talent-management pipelines, and structured succession for scarce digital roles become formal, s

x: Topic 7.6 — Workforce Equality, Diversity & Inclusion In one sentence: Building a digital, data and technology workforce that fairly reflects the people it serves — and where everyone can belong, contribute and progress — is not an optional value statement but a statutory duty, a clinical-safety concern, and a precondition for building services that work equitably for the whole population. Why this matters in health and care # Health and care is delivered by people, for people. Who builds your digital services shapes what those services assume, who they work for, and who they quietly exclude. A team that is homogeneous in background, disability status, gender, ethnicity or lived experience will tend to build products that work well for people like them and badly for everyone else — and it will do so without noticing, because the gaps are invisible from the inside. In a sector where a poorly designed service can mean a missed diagnosis, an inaccessible appointment, or a family unable to reach care, this is a safety and equity issue, not merely a matter of fairness to staff. The stakes are also legal and public. NHS and social-care organizations are public authorities bound by the Equality Act 2010 and the Public Sector Equality Duty, and are held to account through the NHS Workforce Race Equality Standard (WRES) and Workforce Disability Equality Standard (WDES). The evidence gathered under these standards is stark and persistent: staff from ethnic minority backgrounds and disabled staff report worse experiences of recruitment, progression, bullying and disciplinary processes than their white and non-disabled colleagues. A workforce that does not feel it belongs cannot give its best, and the well-documented link between staff experience and patient experience means that inequity among staff becomes inequity for patients. This topic is about the workforce — your colleagues, recruits and leaders — and is deliberately distinct from the user-facing concerns of Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility. The two are joined: an inclusive workforce is one of your strongest defences against inequitable services. Treat this alongside Topic 7.0 — Team Structures, Roles & Responsibilities, Topic 7.3 — Workforce Strategy, and Topic 7.5 — People & Organizational Development. Core concepts # Equality, diversity, inclusion and belonging. These four words are often bundled but differ. Equality is fair treatment and the absence of unlawful discrimination. Diversity is the range of difference present in a workforce — visible and invisible. Inclusion is whether that difference is actually welcomed, heard and able to shape decisions. Belonging is the felt experience of being accepted as yourself. You can be diverse without being inclusive (people present but ignored), and inclusive-sounding without belonging (people masking who they are to fit in). Aim for all four. The Equality Act 2010, protected characteristics and the Public Sector Equality Duty. The Equality Act 2010 is the UK's consolidated anti-discrimination law. It protects nine protected characteristics : age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation. The Public Sector Equality Duty (PSED, section 149) requires public bodies to have due regard to eliminating discrimination, advancing equality of opportunity, and fostering good relations — in employment as well as in services. WRES, WDES and the pay gaps. The Workforce Race Equality Standard (WRES) and Workforce Disability Equality Standard (WDES) are mandated NHS mechanisms that require organizations to report on a fixed set of indicators — such as likelihood of being appointed from shortlisting, entry into formal disciplinary processes, and experience of harassment — broken down by ethnicity and disability. Gender and ethnicity pay-gap reporting (see gender pay gap ) exposes the average earnings difference between groups, which is largely a story about who holds the senior, better-paid roles rather than unequal pay for the same job. Intersectionality. Intersectionality is the recognition that characteristics combine: a disabled woman of colour does not experience "race issues" and "gender issues" and "disability issues" as separable streams, but as a single, compounded experience. Single-axis monitoring (race or gender or disability) can hide the very groups facing the sharpest disadvantage. Unconscious bias and its limits. Implicit stereotypes are the automatic, unexamined associations that shape decisions such as who gets shortlisted or stretched. Awareness matters, but the evidence that one-off "unconscious bias training" changes behaviour is weak — awareness without structural change tends to fade. Bias is better designed out of processes than trained out of individuals. Bias in HR and AI hiring tools. Algorithmic bias is the tendency of automated systems to reproduce and amplify the inequities in their training data. CV-screening, video-interview scoring and "culture fit" algorithms have repeatedly been shown to disadvantage women, disabled applicants and minority candidates, while wearing a veneer of objectivity. Automating a biased process makes it faster and harder to challenge, not fairer. Reasonable adjustments and the social model of disability. A reasonable adjustment (reasonable accommodation) is a change to a job, workplace or process that removes a disadvantage a disabled person would otherwise face — often free or low-cost. It flows from the social model of disability : people are disabled by barriers in the environment, not solely by their condition, so the fix is usually to remove the barrier. Psychological safety and allyship. Psychological safety — the shared belief that you can speak up without humiliation or punishment — is the mechanism through which inclusion becomes real: without it, difference stays silent. Allyship is the active use of one's own advantage to support colleagues from marginalized groups; done well it shifts effort off those already carrying it, done badly it is performative. Best practices # Treat EDI as a delivery and safety issue, not an HR side-quest. Frame inclusion in the language your teams already use: better products, fewer blind spots, safer services. Homogeneous teams ship the biases they cannot see, from pulse oximeters calibrated on light skin to forms that assume a stable address; diverse, included teams catch these earlier. Owning EDI as an engineering and product concern — not delegating it to a standalone committee — is what turns intent into changed practice. Redesign recruitment to remove bias, don't just train recruiters. Anonymize applications, use structured interviews with pre-agreed questions and scoring, and always have a diverse, trained panel. Write job descriptions that describe the outcome rather than a narrow pedigree, and cut "nice to have" requirements that screen out capable non-traditional candidates. These structural changes reduce the influence of implicit stereotypes far more reliably than asking people to be less biased. Scrutinize any AI or automated hiring tool before and during use. If a supplier offers CV-screening, gamified assessment or video-interview scoring, demand evidence of validation against adverse impact across protected characteristics, and keep a human accountable for every decision. Under the Public Sector Equality Duty you cannot outsource your duty to an algorithm. Treat these tools as you would any clinical algorithm — subject to bias testing, transparency and the governance in Topic 8.4 — AI & Emerging Technology Governance. Fix progression and retention, not just the front door. Diverse hiring is undone if people cannot progress or choose to leave. Analyse your own WRES and WDES data: where in the pipeline do ethnic minority and disabled staff fall away, and why? Invest in sponsorship, stretch opportunities, transparent promotion criteria, and reverse mentoring — and act on exit-interview themes rather than filing them. Make reasonable adjustments fast, funded and normal. Establish a clear, low-friction route to workplace adjustments — ideally a passport that travels with the person between roles — so no one has to re-justify their needs each time they move. Most adjustments are cheap or free; the real barrier is usually delay, stigma or a manager who does not know the process. Applying the social model of disability , assume the barrier is fixable and start from "how", not "whether". Build psychological safety and real allyship, not just networks. Staff networks for disabled, LGBTQ+, and ethnic minority colleagues are valuable but should not carry the whole burden of change. Give them sponsorship, time and a route to influence decisions, and expect the majority — especially leaders — to practise allyship by using their position to remove barriers. The test of psychological safety is whether a junior colleague would challenge a senior one's assumption in a design review; build the conditions where they would. Set EDI objectives into leadership accountability. What leaders are measured on is what changes. Put specific, evidenced EDI objectives into senior appraisals and board reporting, tied to your WRES/WDES action plans and pay-gap trends. Boards should see the same disaggregated data quarterly that they see for finance and performance, and be expected to explain movement. Measure honestly and resist tokenism. Collect and use disaggregated data — including intersectional cuts where numbers allow — but pair the numbers with lived experience gathered safely. A single senior appointment from an under-represented group is not a strategy, and celebrating it as one can demoralize the people still facing the barriers. Measure the system (shortlisting rates, disciplinary rates, adjustment turnaround, staff-survey belonging scores), not the anecdote. Close the loop from workforce inclusion to equitable services. Explicitly connect your inclusive-workforce work to equitable outcomes for patients and citizens ( Topic 1.9 ). Involve staff with relevant lived experience in research, design and testing — with proper support and recognition, not as unpaid representatives. The purpose is not only fairness to staff but services that do not fail the people least like the average developer. Questions to discuss with your team # Where in our recruitment, progression and retention pipeline are people from under-represented groups actually falling away — and what in our process, not in them, is causing it? This question forces a move from good intentions to evidence, which is where most EDI conversations quietly stall. In a digital, data and technology function the under-representation is often severe — these roles skew heavily male and, at senior levels, white — so the temptation is to blame a "pipeline problem" in wider society and stop there. The honest work is to look at your own data: relative likelihood of appointment from shortlisting, who enters formal capability or disciplinary processes, who is promoted, and who resigns and why. WRES and WDES give you a national frame for this, but the value is in interrogating your local numbers and asking which specific steps — the wording of adverts, the composition of panels, the informal "tap on the shoulder" that decides who gets stretch work — produce the drop-off. A good answer names concrete stages and process changes with owners, resists the comfort of externalizing the cause, and commits to re-measuring rather than assuming the fix worked. When we adopt tools and processes that promise to make hiring or performance "objective" — including AI — how do we know they are not just automating our existing bias? Digital teams are drawn to automation and data, which makes them unusually exposed to the seductive idea that an algorithm removes human bias from hiring. In reality, systems trained on historic decisions learn historic inequities, and a video-interview scorer or CV-ranker can disadvantage disabled applicants, women or minority candidates while appearing neutral and being harder to challenge than a human panel. The tension to debate is speed and consistency versus fairness and accountability: automation can standardize, but standardizing a biased baseline entrenches it. Consider whether your suppliers can evidence adverse-impact testing, whether a named human remains accountable for each decision, and whether a rejected candidate could meaningfully contest the outcome. Under the Public Sector Equality Duty the duty cannot be delegated to a vendor, so a good answer treats these tools with the same scrutiny as a clinical algorithm — bias-tested, transparent, and always with a human in the loop. Is it genuinely safe for the least powerful person in the room to say "this design assumes something that will fail people like me" — and how would we know? Inclusion only changes products when difference can be voiced, and voice depends on psychological safety, which is unevenly distributed and easy to overestimate from a position of comfort. In practice the person best placed to spot that a service will exclude carers, disabled users or a particular community is often the most junior or the only person from that background in the team — precisely the person who pays the highest price for speaking up and being wrong. The debate should surface how your team actually responds when someone raises an equity concern that slows delivery down: is it welcomed as a caught defect, or treated as a distraction from the sprint? Look for evidence rather than reassurance — when did a challenge like this last happen, who raised it, and what changed as a result? A strong, honest answer distinguishes the team's stated openness from its observed behaviour, acknowledges that belonging is not felt equally by everyone present, and identifies what would have to be true for the quietest voice to be heard. When a colleague needs a workplace adjustment, does our process make it fast, funded and dignified — or does the burden of proof and delay fall on them? Reasonable adjustments are where a stated commitment to disability inclusion meets daily reality, and digital teams have both an advantage and a blind spot here. The advantage is that many adjustments in a technology role — assistive software, flexible hours, remote or asynchronous working, changes to meeting formats — are cheap, quick and already within the team's gift; the blind spot is assuming that because the tooling exists, the barrier is solved. The tension to examine is speed and dignity versus process and scrutiny: an adjustment delayed for weeks of assessment, or one that must be re-justified every time someone changes team, is a barrier in its own right, however well-intentioned the paperwork. Consider whether a manager actually knows how to action a request without escalation, whether an adjustments passport travels with the person, and who pays — the individual's energy and disclosure, or a properly funded central budget. Applying the social model of disability, an honest answer starts from "how do we remove this barrier" rather than "should we", names a turnaround time it is prepared to be held to, and treats stigma and delay, not cost, as the real obstacles. Whose disadvantage does our data hide because we only ever look at one characteristic at a time? Most monitoring counts race, sex and disability on separate axes, which is exactly how the groups facing the sharpest, compounded disadvantage stay invisible — a disabled woman of colour is not the average of three separate gaps, and single-axis dashboards will never show her. In a digital, data and technology function the numbers in any one intersectional cell are often small, which is both a genuine statistical difficulty and a convenient reason never to look. The trade-off to debate is rigour and anonymity versus visibility: cutting data too finely risks identifying individuals and breaching confidence, yet refusing to cut it at all guarantees you miss the people the standards exist to protect. Pair the quantitative limits with lived experience gathered safely, so that where the cell is too small to report, the story is not simply lost. A strong answer commits to examining intersectional patterns wherever numbers responsibly allow, is candid about where they cannot, and resists treating a headline WRES or WDES figure as the whole picture when it may be averaging away the worst-affected. Are we asking under-represented colleagues and their networks to fix inclusion in their spare time, while the people with the most power stay comfortable spectators? Staff networks and individual advocates do vital work, but there is a recurring injustice in expecting those who carry the disadvantage to also carry the unpaid labour of remedying it, often on top of a full delivery role. The question surfaces who actually does the work of change: who runs the network, who sits on the inclusion panels, who is asked to speak on the panel or review the design for accessibility — and whether that effort is recognized, resourced and reflected in workload, or simply assumed. The tension is between valuable grassroots energy and a leadership that quietly outsources its own accountability to it; a network with sponsorship, time and real influence is empowerment, the same network with none of those is exploitation. Genuine allyship means the majority — especially senior leaders — using their position to remove barriers rather than delegating the effort downward. An honest answer looks at where the burden currently sits, whether lived-experience contribution to research and design is paid and credited or extracted for free, and what leaders are personally doing rather than sponsoring others to do. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system (ICS) is scaling up a central digital, data and technology directorate of around two hundred people, pulling together staff from several trusts and new external hires. Early data is uncomfortable: the directorate is 80% male, its senior band is almost entirely white, and its inherited WRES and WDES figures show ethnic minority and disabled staff far more likely to enter formal processes and far less likely to be promoted. A "culture fit" screening tool, brought over from a partner trust, is quietly ranking out candidates with career breaks and non-linear paths. The chief digital information officer refuses to treat this as an HR problem. The directorate rewrites its job descriptions around outcomes, drops inflated degree and "10 years' experience" filters, anonymizes first-sift applications, and requires diverse, trained interview panels using structured scoring. The culture-fit algorithm is suspended pending adverse-impact evidence the supplier cannot produce, and is replaced with a structured work-sample task. A reasonable-adjustments passport is introduced so disabled staff moving between the constituent trusts never have to re-justify their needs. Progress is measured honestly. The board sees disaggregated shortlisting, progression, disciplinary and adjustment-turnaround data every quarter, alongside belonging scores from the staff survey, and each senior leader carries a specific EDI objective. The disability and ethnic-minority staff networks get sponsorship, time and a standing slot in design reviews, so lived experience shapes services rather than decorating a report. Within a year the shortlisting gap narrows and adjustment turnaround falls from weeks to days; the progression gap barely moves, and the directorate says so plainly rather than claiming a win. Sector lenses # Startup # A small digital-health startup has no EDI function, and the founders' first dozen hires set a culture that is extremely hard to change later — homogeneity compounds through referral hiring from similar networks. The upside is agility: it is far cheaper to build inclusive recruitment habit

x: Topic 8.0 — Phasing in Innovation In one sentence: Introduce innovation as a deliberate, staged journey — small, evidenced, and safe first, then spread with confidence — rather than as a single leap or a graveyard of pilots that never scale. Why this matters in health and care # Health and care sit on a knife-edge between two failures. Move too slowly, and patients are denied treatments and tools that demonstrably work, while staff burn out on processes that better technology could ease. Move too fast, and you risk patient safety, waste public money, entrench inequity, and breach statutory duties around clinical safety and data protection. The NHS has a well-documented weakness at the second stage of innovation: not invention, but adoption and spread . The King's Fund and others describe a system rich in pilots and poor at scaling them — a pattern nicknamed "pilotitis", where innovations are trialled endlessly in one site and never rolled out. Every stalled pilot represents money spent, staff goodwill consumed, and a benefit never realized at population scale. For a senior leader, phasing innovation well is therefore both a safety discipline and a value discipline. You are accountable for introducing change in a way that generates evidence, protects patients, satisfies regulators, and reaches enough people to justify the investment. This topic is about doing that on purpose rather than by accident. It connects tightly to change management (see Topic 8.1 — Change Management), which handles the human side of the same journey. Core concepts # Diffusion of innovations . Everett Rogers' classic model describes how a new idea spreads through a population over time, following an S-shaped adoption curve across five groups: innovators, early adopters, the early majority, the late majority, and laggards. Rogers identified five attributes that predict how fast something spreads: relative advantage, compatibility with existing practice, simplicity, trialability, and observability of results. If your innovation scores poorly on these, expect slow adoption regardless of how good the underlying idea is. Pilots, proofs-of-concept , and "pilotitis". A pilot is a time-boxed, small-scale test designed to learn , not to deploy . The pathology of pilotitis arises when piloting becomes an end in itself — when there is no pre-agreed route from a successful pilot to routine adoption, and no owner accountable for scaling. A good pilot is designed from the outset with its exit in mind: what decision it will inform, what evidence it must produce, and who acts on that evidence. Spread and scale. These are different problems. Spread is horizontal — the same innovation adopted by more sites. Scale is vertical — the depth of adoption and the infrastructure, funding, and workforce change needed to sustain it. NHS improvement bodies distinguish the two deliberately, because an innovation can spread thinly to many sites without ever scaling into embedded, funded, business-as-usual practice. Evidence generation alongside adoption. In digital health you rarely have complete evidence before you start; you build it as you go. Real-world evaluation — studying an innovation in routine conditions rather than a controlled trial — lets you adopt and learn simultaneously, provided you design the evaluation up front rather than bolting it on afterwards. The regulatory and assurance stack. In the UK, three overlapping regimes govern digital health innovation. The MHRA (Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency) regulates software that meets the legal definition of a medical device , including Software as a Medical Device (SaMD). NICE publishes the Evidence Standards Framework (ESF) for digital health technologies, setting out the level of evidence expected for a technology's function and financial risk. DTAC (the Digital Technology Assessment Criteria) is the NHS's baseline for suppliers, covering clinical safety (DCB0129/DCB0160), data protection, technical security, interoperability, and usability. These are not optional extras; they are the entry conditions for safe adoption. Best practices # Start from the problem, not the product. Anchor every innovation to a clearly stated clinical, operational, or population-health problem, with a baseline measure of how bad it is today. Technologies chosen because they are exciting, or because a supplier is persuasive, tend to fail Rogers' "relative advantage" test in practice. Make the problem statement the thing you protect when the solution changes. Design the pilot with its exit already decided. Before a pilot starts, write down the decision it will inform, the success criteria, the evidence it must produce, the funding route if it succeeds, and the named owner who will act. If you cannot answer "what happens the day this pilot succeeds?", you are building pilotitis. A pilot without a scaling plan is a hobby. Phase by cohort and by geography. Roll out in deliberate waves — an alpha cohort of willing early adopters, then a private beta of a few representative sites, then progressively wider geography — with a go/no-go gate between each wave. Early cohorts should be chosen for their appetite and their ability to give honest feedback, not for being easy. Each wave de-risks the next. Generate evidence as you adopt. Build a real-world evaluation into the rollout from day one: agreed metrics, a baseline, a comparison where feasible, and a cadence for reviewing results. Align the evidence you gather to the NICE Evidence Standards Framework tier appropriate to your technology, so the evidence is credible to future adopters and commissioners, not just to you. Clear the regulatory pathway early and in parallel. Establish at the outset whether the technology is a medical device (MHRA), what NICE ESF tier applies, and whether it meets DTAC. Doing this late is the single most common cause of a promising innovation stalling at the point of scale. Treat clinical safety cases (DCB0129 for manufacturers, DCB0160 for deploying organizations) as first-class deliverables, not paperwork. Balance innovation with equity . Ask, for every phase, who is being left out by the digital divide — patients without smartphones, digital connectivity, English fluency, or the confidence to use a new tool. An innovation that improves average outcomes while widening inequality fails a core NHS duty. Build inclusion into cohort selection and evaluation metrics, not as an afterthought. Use the national infrastructure that exists. England's fifteen Health Innovation Networks (formerly Academic Health Science Networks, AHSNs) exist specifically to support adoption and spread; the Accelerated Access Collaborative curates nationally-backed innovations. Do not rebuild adoption capability from scratch — plug into these networks for real-world evidence, peer sites, and route-to-scale support. Scan the horizon deliberately. Maintain a lightweight horizon-scanning function so that innovation is a managed portfolio, not a series of reactions to whichever supplier got a meeting. Knowing what is coming — in regulation, in technology, in adjacent systems — lets you sequence adoption rather than being surprised by it. Questions to discuss with your team # What is our honest, named plan for what happens the day this pilot succeeds — and if we cannot answer that, why are we starting it? This is the single question that separates disciplined phasing from pilotitis, and it is worth putting on the table before any money is committed. In a digital health or care organization the temptation to launch a promising trial is strong — a supplier is keen, a clinician is enthusiastic, a grant is available — but enthusiasm at the start says nothing about the route to scale at the end. The debate should surface the tensions between clinical curiosity and organizational commitment: who owns scaling, where the recurrent funding comes from, and what specific go/no-go decision the evidence will inform. A good, honest answer names a scaling owner, a funding route, and a pre-agreed exit decision, and it is candid where those do not yet exist. Concrete angles include reviewing your current portfolio for pilots with no scaling owner, and testing whether a "successful" pilot last year actually changed practice anywhere. The uncomfortable but valuable version of this conversation is admitting that some of your live pilots are really hobbies, and deciding to stop them. Who is being left behind by each phase of this rollout, and are we willing to slow the innovation to avoid widening inequity? Health and care carry a statutory and moral duty around equity, and digital innovation can quietly improve average outcomes while excluding the people who most need care — those without smartphones, connectivity, English fluency, or digital confidence. The tension to debate is real: inclusion measures, non-digital fallbacks, and diverse cohort selection cost time and money and can slow adoption, so a team under pressure to show results will be tempted to pilot in the easiest, most digitally-engaged sites first. A serious discussion looks at who is in and out of your alpha and beta cohorts, whether deprivation and low digital access are deliberately represented, and what the fallback pathway is for excluded patients. It should also confront the measurement question — are inclusion metrics built into the evaluation from day one, or bolted on afterwards to reassure a board? An honest answer accepts that an innovation which widens inequality is a failure even if its headline numbers improve, and it commits to designing inclusion into cohort selection rather than retrofitting it. The best version names the specific excluded groups in your population and the concrete provision made for them in each wave. Have we cleared the regulatory and clinical-safety pathway in parallel from the start, or are we quietly hoping to sort it out before scale? Discovering late that a tool is an unassessed medical device, fails DTAC, or lacks a clinical safety case is the most common way a genuinely promising innovation stalls at exactly the point it should spread. In a digital health organization this question forces an early, sometimes deflating conversation about MHRA medical-device status, the applicable NICE Evidence Standards Framework tier, and the DCB0129 and DCB0160 safety cases — work that is heavy, unglamorous, and easy to defer behind the excitement of the product. The trade-off to debate is speed versus assurance: front-loading regulation slows the first pilot but is the only way to avoid a wall at scale, and treating safety cases as paperwork rather than first-class deliverables stores up risk. Useful angles include mapping each live innovation against the three regimes today, and asking whether your clinical safety officer has been engaged as a designer or merely as a signatory at the end. A good answer treats the regulatory pathway as core delivery managed in parallel, names who owns each safety case, and is honest about which current initiatives are proceeding on hope rather than assessment. When we say we want to "scale" this, do we mean genuine scale — funded, staffed, embedded as business-as-usual — or are we quietly settling for thin spread across many sites? Spread and scale are different problems, and conflating them is how organizations congratulate themselves on adoption that never actually beds in. Spread is horizontal — more sites using the innovation — while scale is vertical, the depth of adoption plus the recurrent funding, infrastructure, and workforce change needed to sustain it, and an innovation can spread thinly to dozens of sites without ever scaling into embedded practice anywhere. The tension to debate is that spread is visible and reportable — a map with more pins on it looks like success to a board — whereas scale is expensive, slow, and demands hard decisions about permanent budget and staffing that no one wants to own. A serious discussion distinguishes the two explicitly for the innovation in front of you: what depth of adoption counts as "done", what workforce redesign it implies, and whether the recurrent money to sustain it actually exists. Concrete angles include auditing where a widely-spread innovation is genuinely load-bearing versus merely installed, and asking whether last year's "rollout" changed any job description or funding line. An honest answer admits when the plan is really spread dressed up as scale, and either commits the resources to embed it properly or is candid that it will remain shallow. How are we choosing our early cohorts — for honest feedback and representativeness, or for an easy win that flatters the evidence? The sites you pilot in shape everything you learn, and there is a strong pull towards the most enthusiastic, best-resourced, most digitally-engaged teams because they make the innovation look good. That pull is dangerous: early cohorts chosen for ease produce evidence that does not transfer, so the innovation sails through alpha and beta and then fails when it meets ordinary sites with real constraints, tired staff, and patients on the wrong side of the digital divide. The trade-off to debate is that appetite and honesty matter — you do want willing early adopters who will give candid feedback rather than polite silence — but appetite must be balanced against representativeness so that deprivation, low digital access, and awkward workflows are deliberately in the sample, not designed out of it. Useful angles include naming who is in your alpha and beta and why, checking Rogers' attributes (relative advantage, compatibility, simplicity, trialability, observability) against a typical rather than a flagship site, and asking whether any of your cohorts would embarrass the evidence if they spoke freely. A good answer picks cohorts for their ability to tell you the truth and to stand in for the real system, and it treats a pilot that only works in ideal sites as a warning, not a success. Is our innovation a deliberately managed portfolio, or a series of reactions to whichever supplier or clinician got a meeting? Phasing innovation well is a portfolio discipline, not a sequence of one-off enthusiasms, and the difference shows in whether you can say what you are deliberately not doing. Without a lightweight horizon-scanning function and an owned portfolio view, innovation becomes reactive — driven by persuasive suppliers, grant deadlines, and individual champions — and the organization ends up with many overlapping, half-owned initiatives competing for the same scarce assurance, evaluation, and scaling capacity. The tension to debate is between openness to genuinely good ideas that arrive unbidden and the discipline to sequence adoption against strategy, capacity, and what is coming in regulation and technology. Concrete angles include listing every live innovation and who sponsored it, asking how many were chosen versus merely accepted, and testing whether your go/no-go gates function as real investment decisions or as rubber stamps. An honest answer acknowledges where the current portfolio is really a pile of reactions, and commits to horizon scanning and prioritization so that limited capacity backs the innovations that matter most rather than the ones that shouted loudest. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system (ICS) wants to reduce avoidable admissions among people with heart failure. Rather than buying a remote-monitoring platform for its whole population on day one, the programme lead frames the problem with a baseline: current admission rates, the cohort size, and the target reduction. They confirm the regulatory picture first — the platform is a Class I medical device, the supplier holds a DCB0129 safety case, and the ICS completes its own DCB0160 deployment safety case and a DTAC assessment. They map the product to the relevant NICE ESF evidence tier and design a real-world evaluation with the local Health Innovation Network as evaluation partner. The rollout is phased. An alpha runs in one community heart-failure team of enthusiastic clinicians for eight weeks, purely to learn about workflow, alerts, and false positives. A beta then extends to three geographically and demographically varied localities — deliberately including an area with high deprivation and low digital access, with telephone-based fallback so the innovation does not widen inequity. A go/no-go gate reviews admission data, clinician workload, patient-reported experience, and inclusion metrics before wider spread. Only after the beta shows a credible admissions reduction and a workable staffing model does the ICS commit recurrent funding and spread to remaining localities — with the scaling owner, funding, and evaluation already agreed. The pilot never became a dead end because its exit was designed before it began. Sector lenses # Startup # For a small, venture- or grant-funded digital-health company, phasing is existential rather than merely prudent: runway is finite, so a pilot that stalls without a route to a paid contract can be fatal. Startups compete on Rogers' trialability and observability — a lightweight, low-commitment pilot that quickly shows results is how they win the reference sites that unlock the next funding round. They usually carry the manufacturer's clinical-safety burden themselves (DCB0129) and self-fund DTAC and their NICE ESF evidence, which is heavy for a small team, so they should pick one narrow beachhead cohort rather than spreading thin. Crucially, they must design the pilot's exit as a commercial decision (who signs a recurring contract on success), not only a clinical one, because a clinically successful pilot that no budget adopts still kills the company. Their advantage is speed and focus; their risk is running out of cash before evidence and adoption catch up. Small business # For an established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home, a domiciliary-care agency, a single-site clinic, or a small health-tech supplier past the startup stage — phasing is constrained less by runway than by having real patients to protect and almost no spare capacity to run a proper pilot. Such organizations carry the same statutory duties as a large trust — DTAC-level expectations, DCB0160 clinical safety when deploying, data protection — but without a clinical safety officer, an information-governance team, or an evaluation partner on staff, so the honest move is to adopt innovations that others have already evidenced rather than to pioneer unproven ones alone. Their sensible phasing is a small, cheap, reversible trial in their own single setting, with a manual fallback kept running so a failed tool never leaves patients stranded. Because they cannot spread across sites, "scale" for them means deepening one workflow reliably, and their best route to assurance and route-to-scale support is to lean on the local Health Innovation Network and on suppliers who bring a ready-made DCB0129 safety case. Their advantage is that a single owner can decide and act quickly; their risk is that thin digital capability tempts them either to avoid useful innovation altogether or to adopt it without the safety and equity checks the duties still require. Enterprise # A large NHS trust, ICS, or established health-tech supplier has the convening power to run genuine multi-site betas and the standing infrastructure — clinical safety officers, information governance, evaluation partners, Health Innovation Network links — that a startup lacks. Its characteristic failure is the opposite: death by pilot, dozens of simultaneous small trials none of which is owned through to spread, because accountability is diffuse and priorities compete. Phasing here is a portfolio-governance problem: each go/no-go gate should be a formal investment decision tied to recurrent funding and a named senior responsible owner, in the spirit of Management of

x: Topic 8.1 — Change Management In one sentence: Technology and process changes only deliver benefit when the people affected understand, want, are able to make, and sustain the change — so lead the human transition as deliberately as you lead the technical delivery. Why this matters in health and care # Most digital health and care programmes that fail do not fail on the technology. They fail because clinicians work around the new system, care workers quietly revert to paper, or the promised benefits never materialize because behaviour never actually changed. The system was delivered; the change was not. In health and care the stakes are unusually high. Frontline staff are stretched, safety-conscious, and rightly sceptical of change imposed from above — they have seen systems come and go. A poorly led change can compromise patient safety directly (through workarounds and errors), demoralize a fragile workforce, and destroy the trust needed for the next change. Public money spent on a system nobody adopts is money wasted twice. Change management is the discipline that closes the gap between a solution being available and it being adopted, embedded, and sustained . It is the essential partner to phasing in innovation (see Topic 8.0 — Phasing in Innovation) and to organizational development (see Topic 7.5 — People & Organizational Development). This topic gives you the frameworks and the practices to lead people through change without breaking them. Core concepts # Kotter's 8 steps. John Kotter's model, from Leading Change , is a top-down, leadership-driven sequence for large organizational change: (1) create a sense of urgency, (2) build a guiding coalition, (3) form a strategic vision, (4) enlist a volunteer army, (5) enable action by removing barriers, (6) generate short-term wins, (7) sustain acceleration, and (8) institute change in the culture. Kotter's strength is programme-level structure and momentum. Prosci ADKAR. ADKAR is a people-centred model describing the five things an individual must experience for change to stick: A wareness of the need, D esire to participate, K nowledge of how, A bility to do it, and R einforcement to sustain it. Its power is diagnostic — if adoption is stalling, you can identify which element is missing for a given group and target the fix. Kotter structures the programme; ADKAR guides the person-level communications, training, and coaching. The two are complementary, not competing. Bridges' Transition Model. William Bridges distinguishes change (the external event) from transition (the internal, psychological process people go through). His three phases — the Ending (letting go of the old way, with its associated loss), the Neutral Zone (a disorienting in-between where the old is gone but the new is not yet fluent), and the New Beginning — remind leaders that resistance is often grief, and that the Neutral Zone is where performance dips and needs the most support. Stakeholder analysis . A structured map of who is affected, their influence, their interest, and their current stance, used to target engagement effort. Not everyone needs the same treatment: high-influence, currently-sceptical clinicians need very different handling from low-influence, already-enthusiastic staff. Benefits realisation . Change is not done when the system goes live; it is done when the intended benefits are measurably achieved. Benefits realization links each change to a named benefit, an owner, a baseline, and a tracking cadence — closing the loop that phasing in innovation opened. Best practices # Establish a genuine, honest case for change. Kotter's urgency must be real, not manufactured. Articulate the problem in terms frontline staff recognize — patient safety, their own workload, waiting times — with evidence, and be candid about what is not working today. Fabricated urgency is quickly detected and breeds cynicism. Build a guiding coalition that includes clinical and frontline credibility. A change sponsored only by executives and IT will be seen as done to staff. Recruit respected clinicians, nurses, care workers, and administrators as visible advocates — Kotter's "guiding coalition" and "volunteer army" — because peers persuade peers far more effectively than hierarchy does. Engage frontline staff early, as co-designers not recipients. The people who will use a system daily know where it will break. Involve them in design and testing before go-live, and act visibly on what they tell you. Early, authentic engagement converts potential resisters into owners and surfaces safety issues while they are still cheap to fix. Diagnose resistance with ADKAR before you respond to it. Resistance is information, not defiance. Use ADKAR to locate the true blocker: is it awareness (people don't understand why), desire (they understand but won't), knowledge (they want to but don't know how), or ability (they know but can't in their real workflow)? Each demands a different intervention; blanket "more communication" wastes effort on the wrong gap. Manage the transition, not just the change. Use Bridges' model to name the loss honestly, support people through the Neutral Zone with extra help, floorwalkers, and tolerance of a temporary productivity dip, and mark the New Beginning. Expect performance to fall before it rises, and resource for it rather than panicking. Communicate relentlessly, in both directions. Repetition and multiple channels beat a single grand announcement; people need to hear a message several times, from several sources, before it lands. Equally, build listening channels — staff surveys, drop-ins, feedback loops — so communication is dialogue, not broadcast. Generate and celebrate short-term wins. Long change programmes lose energy. Deliberately engineer early, visible, credible wins — a ward that saves time, a clinician who champions a real improvement — to prove the change works and sustain momentum, exactly as Kotter prescribes. In unionized and partnership environments, change with staff, not around them. In the NHS, work through the social partnership model: engage trade unions and staff-side representatives early via the Social Partnership Forum approach, so that service change is co-created rather than imposed. Partnership working is not a constraint to route around — it is a route to more durable change and it is a statutory and cultural expectation. Embed and sustain — plan reinforcement from the start. The ADKAR "R" and Kotter's step 8 are about permanence: update policies, job descriptions, training induction, and audit so the new way becomes "how we do things here". Withdraw the old system decisively; a live fallback guarantees reversion. Assign a named owner for sustainability past go-live. Close the loop with benefits realization and adoption metrics. Measure adoption directly — logins, feature use, workaround rates, staff and patient experience — against the baseline, and track the benefits the change promised. Report them honestly, including where benefits are behind plan, so the organization learns and the next change is better led. Questions to discuss with your team # When adoption of our last big system stalled, which ADKAR element was actually missing — and did we diagnose it, or just send more communications? This question turns an abstract framework into an honest post-mortem of your own track record, which is where the real learning sits. In health and care, resistance from stretched, safety-conscious frontline staff is easy to mislabel as defiance and answer with yet more awareness messaging — posters, town halls, a fresh email — when the true blocker is often ability, because the new system slows clinicians during a ward round or does not fit the real workflow. The discussion should force the team to distinguish awareness (people do not understand why), desire (they understand but will not), knowledge (they want to but do not know how), and ability (they know but cannot in practice), and to be specific about which one bit last time. A good answer draws on actual evidence — staff surveys, workaround observations, super-user feedback — rather than leadership assumption, and it accepts that blanket "more communication" is usually effort spent on the wrong gap. The most valuable version of this conversation identifies a current change where the team is about to make exactly that mistake again, and redirects the intervention to the element that is genuinely missing. Are we honestly planning and resourcing for the productivity dip, or are we quietly assuming go-live is the finish line? Bridges' Neutral Zone — the disorienting period after the old way is gone but the new is not yet fluent — is where performance predictably falls, and in a safety-critical care setting the temptation to panic, blame staff, or reach for the old system is dangerous. The tension to debate is uncomfortable because it means budgeting explicitly for a temporary drop in output: floorwalkers, extra staffing, lighter caseloads in the first days, and tolerance from leaders who are themselves under pressure to show immediate benefit. A serious discussion confronts whether the organization treats go-live as victory — declaring success at deployment while behaviour has not yet changed — and whether there is a named owner for adoption and benefits past the launch date. It should also examine the decommissioning question: is the old system being decisively retired on an agreed date, or left running as a fallback that guarantees reversion? An honest answer names the expected dip, resources it, resists blaming the frontline for early slowness, and commits to tracking real adoption metrics rather than assuming the system delivers benefit merely because it is live. Are we changing with our staff and their representatives, or around them — and would they agree with our answer? In the NHS and wider care system, partnership working with trade unions and staff-side representatives is a statutory and cultural expectation, not a courtesy, and a change imposed from above by executives and IT will be seen as done to the frontline. The debate should test the honesty of the coalition: does it include respected, practising clinicians and care workers as visible advocates, or is it sponsored only by the board and the CIO? It should confront whether staff are engaged early as co-designers who can surface where a system will break and where safety risks hide, or consulted late once decisions are effectively made. There is a genuine trade-off to discuss — early, authentic engagement and partnership are slower and can feel like ceding control, but they convert resisters into owners and produce far more durable change than hierarchy can impose. A good answer is candid about which groups feel change is happening around them, engages staff-side through the social partnership model before rather than after key decisions, and is willing to be judged by whether frontline staff themselves would call the process genuine. How many simultaneous changes are we asking the same frontline team to absorb right now, and who is looking at the total load rather than each programme in isolation? Every programme tends to believe its own change is the priority, but the clinician or care worker on the ward experiences the cumulative weight of all of them at once — a new ePMA system, a restructured rota, a fresh safety mandate and an estates move can land in the same quarter, and change fatigue is a genuine cause of adoption failure that no single Kotter sequence will fix. The tension worth surfacing is organizational: change is usually governed programme-by-programme, so nobody owns the aggregate demand on a given team, and the honest question is whether anyone in the room can even name the full portfolio hitting the frontline this year. A serious discussion weighs sequencing and pacing against the pressure to deliver everything now, and asks whether some changes should be deliberately slowed, bundled, or stopped to protect the capacity of the people expected to adopt them. It should also examine who holds the authority to say "not yet" across programmes, because without that role the default is overload. An honest answer maps the real change load on key groups, accepts that prioritizing means some worthwhile initiatives wait, and names an owner for the cumulative pace rather than assuming each programme's local plan adds up to something humane. When frontline staff build workarounds to our new system, do we treat them as a compliance problem to stamp out or as a safety signal to learn from? Workarounds are one of the most reliable pieces of intelligence a change programme receives, because they show precisely where the designed workflow collides with the reality of care — yet the instinctive response is often to police them as non-compliance rather than to ask what unmet need they solve. In a safety-critical setting this instinct is dangerous: a nurse who keeps a paper list beside the electronic system may be compensating for a genuine gap that, left unexamined, becomes the root cause of a medication error. The discussion should confront the uncomfortable trade-off between standardization and local adaptation — some workarounds are drift that erodes safety and must be closed, while others are frontline wisdom that should be designed back into the system — and the team needs an honest way to tell the two apart rather than defaulting to either blanket enforcement or blanket tolerance. It should ask whether there is a real, blame-free channel for staff to report why they are deviating, and whether anyone acts on what comes back. A good answer treats workaround rates as a leading adoption metric, investigates the reasons before judging them, and can point to at least one case where a workaround changed the design rather than triggering a reprimand. What happens to this change when the programme funding ends and the dedicated team disbands — who owns it as business as usual? Change programmes are resourced as temporary endeavours, but adoption has to be sustained indefinitely, and the moment of greatest risk is often not go-live but the quieter point when the project team moves on, the backfill money stops and the change has to survive on the ordinary operational line. The ADKAR "R" and Kotter's eighth step both point here, yet reinforcement is the element most easily cut when budgets tighten, so the honest question is whether the new way is genuinely embedded in policy, job descriptions, induction, audit and appraisal, or whether it is still being propped up by champions whose protected time is about to vanish. The tension to debate is that sustainability work is unglamorous and competes with the next exciting programme for attention and money, so it is chronically under-resourced despite being where benefits are actually retained or lost. The team should identify who the named operational owner is once the programme closes, and whether that person has the authority and capacity to hold the line. A good answer can point to concrete mechanisms that outlast the funding — the old process decommissioned, the new one written into how people are trained and assessed — rather than relying on goodwill and heroics that fade within a year. In practice: a health & care example # An acute trust is replacing paper drug charts with electronic prescribing and medicines administration (ePMA). The programme director knows the technology is the easy part. She builds a guiding coalition co-chaired by a respected consultant and the chief nurse, not the CIO alone, and creates a network of ward-based "digital champions" — practising nurses and pharmacists given time to support peers. A stakeholder analysis identifies night-shift staff and locum doctors as high-risk, low-engagement groups, so extra effort is targeted there. Using ADKAR , early staff surveys reveal the blocker is not awareness (everyone knows paper charts cause errors) but ability — clinicians fear the new system will slow them during ward rounds. The response is workflow-specific training and floorwalkers at go-live, not more posters. Bridges' Neutral Zone is planned for explicitly: the trust accepts and staffs for a two-week productivity dip, keeps prescribing volumes light in the first days, and resists the temptation to blame staff for early slowness. Change runs in partnership : staff-side representatives are engaged from the outset on shift and workload impacts through the trust's partnership forum, avoiding a dispute that could have derailed go-live. Early wins — a ward reporting fewer transcription errors within a fortnight — are publicized. Paper charts are formally retired on an agreed date so there is no fallback to revert to. Afterwards, benefits realization tracks medication error rates and administration timeliness against baseline, and the results feed the trust's wider digital roadmap. Sector lenses # Startup # In a small digital-health company the "change" being managed is usually your customer's, not your own: your product lands on a ward or in a GP practice, and its adoption depends on how well the buying organization leads its people through Kotter's steps and the ADKAR journey. The startup's leverage is design and enablement — build the change into the product (in-app guidance, low-friction onboarding, floorwalker-ready training materials) so that Awareness, Knowledge, and Ability are cheap for the adopter to reach. With no in-house change team and thin margins, founders often have to coach the customer's champions directly and treat implementation support as part of the offer, not an add-on. Internally, the startup's own change is fast and informal, but it should still name the loss when it pivots, because even a ten-person team hits Bridges' Neutral Zone. The trap is shipping software and assuming behaviour follows; a stalled adoption at a reference site is both a lost renewal and lost evidence. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home, a domiciliary-care agency or a single-site clinic — has to lead the same human transition as a large trust but with none of the apparatus: no change manager, no training team, often no dedicated IT at all, and a partner or registered manager running the change on top of a clinical or operational day job. The frameworks still apply, but they must be radically compressed: the "guiding coalition" may be the practice manager and one enthusiastic nurse, and the ADKAR journey has to be led in staff-meeting slots and over shoulders rather than through a communications plan. Cash is tight and every hour a receptionist or carer spends learning a new system is an hour taken from patients, so the Neutral Zone dip is felt immediately on the bottom line and there is little slack to absorb it — sequencing the change to a quieter period and leaning hard on the supplier's onboarding support matters more here than anywhere. The same regulatory and safety duties (CQC expectations, information governance) apply as to big organizations, without the resources to meet them, so a small provider should be ruthless about adopting supplier defaults and proven templates rather than designing its own. The advantage is intimacy: with a handful of staff who all know each other, resistance is visible early and a credible owner can carry the whole team through the change personally. Enterprise # A large trust or ICS is where the full apparatus earns its keep: a guiding coalition with clinical credibility, a formal stakeholder analysis, structured ADKAR diagnosis, planned Neutral-Zone support, and measured employee engagement all matter because the change touches thousands of staff across professions and sites. Scale brings resources (dedicated change managers, training teams, communications functions) but also inertia, competing programmes, and change fatigue from too many simultaneous go-lives.
