x: Topic 8.2 — Communications & Engagement Communication and engagement are the craft that turns a well-planned digital change into something patients and staff understand, trust, and actually use — and in health and care, poor communication is a safety, equity, and public-trust failure, not merely a missed message. Why this matters in health and care # A digital change that is technically sound can still fail because nobody explained why it mattered, nobody listened to the people it affected, or a rumour outran the facts. In health and care the stakes are unusually high: a nurse who misunderstands a new e-observations workflow can miss a deteriorating patient; a community that distrusts how its data will be used can opt out of a shared care record en masse; a poorly worded outage notice can send anxious patients to an already-overwhelmed emergency department. Communication is therefore woven into clinical safety (see Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management) and public trust (see Topic 1.8 — Data Ethics, Consent & Public Trust), not bolted on at launch. Public-sector communication also carries a distinct duty of honesty. You are spending public money, you are accountable to patients who cannot easily take their custom elsewhere, and you operate in a media and political environment where any misstep — a delayed rollout, a data incident, a controversial supplier — can dominate local headlines. Health and care audiences are diverse in language, digital confidence, and trust in institutions, so a single broadcast message rarely reaches everyone equitably (see Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility). Getting this right is a leadership responsibility, not something to delegate wholesale to a communications team at the last minute. This topic is deliberately distinct from Topic 8.1 — Change Management. Change management is the model for how an organization moves from a current state to a future state; communications and engagement are the practised craft of messages, channels, narrative, and listening that make that movement land with real people. You need both, and they must be planned together. Core concepts # Strategic communication is the purposeful use of communication by an organization to reach a defined goal — here, to help a digital change succeed. It starts from objectives and audiences, not from a list of messages you want to send. Stakeholder engagement is the process of involving the people affected by a decision so they can genuinely influence it. Engagement sits on a spectrum, often summarized as inform, consult, involve, collaborate, and empower; only the informing end is one-way. Real engagement means stakeholders shape the outcome, not just hear about it. Stakeholder mapping identifies who is affected and how, typically along axes of interest and influence, so you can tailor effort. Related to it is audience segmentation, drawn from market segmentation : dividing a broad population — staff, patients, carers, the public — into meaningful groups with shared needs, so the same change can be explained differently to a ward sister, a GP practice manager, and an 80-year-old with limited internet access. Storytelling and narrative give a change meaning. People remember and act on a clear story about why this matters for patients and staff far more than on a feature list or a benefits-realization table. A good narrative names the problem, the change, and the better future in language the audience already uses. Internal communications is the discipline of communicating with staff, and it is tightly bound to employee engagement — an engaged workforce adopts change; a disengaged one endures or resists it. This is distinct from external and public communications aimed at patients, carers, and citizens, which carries different regulatory, accessibility, and trust considerations. Participatory design , often called co-design, involves the people affected in shaping the change itself, blurring the line between engagement and design (see Topic 3.0 — User Research & Service Design). It is the strongest antidote to the broadcast-only mindset. Crisis communication is the sub-discipline for communicating during incidents and outages — protecting safety and trust when something goes wrong (see Topic 3.8 — Service Management & Live Operations and Topic 3.9 — Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery). It intersects with the wider craft of public relations and with countering misinformation and rumour, which spread fastest when official information is absent. Finally, sentiment analysis and other listening methods let you measure not just reach but understanding and feeling — did the message land, and how do people feel about it? And nudge theory reminds you that how you frame and time a message shapes behaviour, which brings both power and an ethical obligation to use it honestly. Best practices # Start from objectives and audiences, not messages. Before drafting anything, be explicit about what behaviour or understanding you need to change, and in whom. Write a short communications and engagement plan that names each audience segment, what they currently think and feel, what you want them to think, feel, and do, and how you will know it worked. A plan built from "what do we want to announce" produces noise; a plan built from "who needs to do what differently" produces adoption. Map stakeholders and segment audiences deliberately. A ward clerk, a consultant, a caseworker, a patient with a learning disability, and a local councillor are not one audience. Map who is affected by interest and influence, then segment by need, channel, digital confidence, and language. Tailor the message and the medium to each segment — the same change becomes a two-minute team-brief for staff, a plain-language leaflet co-produced with a patient group, and a factual briefing for the local authority. Lead with a clear narrative about why it matters for patients and staff. People act on meaning, not mandates. Craft a simple story: the problem today, the change you are making, and the better outcome for patients and for the staff doing the work. Anchor it in something concrete — fewer missed results, less duplicate data entry, faster referrals — and use the words your audience uses, not internal programme jargon or acronyms. Test the narrative on a few real staff and patients before you scale it. Shift from broadcast to genuine two-way engagement. A cascade of emails and posters is informing, not engaging. Build in structured listening — drop-in sessions, floor-walking, staff and patient panels, co-design workshops — and show visibly that you changed something because of what you heard. When people see their feedback alter the design or the rollout plan, trust and adoption rise; when engagement is theatre, cynicism sets in and spreads. Choose channels and cadence for the audience, not for your convenience. Match the channel to the segment: intranet and team huddles for staff, but also print, text, community groups, and trusted intermediaries for patients who are digitally excluded. Set a predictable cadence so people know when to expect updates, and repeat key messages across channels — most people need to hear something several times, in several forms, before it registers. Silence is itself a message, and usually the wrong one. Work with professional communications and engagement teams early. Your organization's communications, patient-experience, and engagement colleagues bring brand, accessibility, media-handling, and audience expertise you do not have. Bring them in at planning, not at launch, and give them the clinical and technical substance they need. Equally, do not outsource ownership: leaders and delivery teams must supply the honest content and stand behind it. Plan incident and outage communications before you need them. When a system fails, the communications vacuum fills with rumour and anxiety within minutes. Pre-agree who speaks, through which channels, how fast, and with what holding message; pre-draft templates for common scenarios; and rehearse them alongside your business-continuity plans (see Topic 3.9 — Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery). During an incident, tell people what you know, what you don't yet know, what you are doing, and when you will next update them — even if the answer is still "we don't know yet." Confront resistance, rumour, and misinformation directly and honestly. Resistance often carries real signal — a workflow that genuinely doesn't fit the ward, or a legitimate fear about workload or safety. Listen for the truth in it, address it, and correct false information quickly with facts, named sources, and a calm tone rather than defensiveness. The fastest way to let misinformation win is to say nothing; the fastest way to lose trust for good is to be caught spinning. Measure understanding and sentiment, not just volume. Opens, clicks, and attendance tell you reach, not effect. Add measures of comprehension (can people explain the change back?), sentiment (how do they feel?), and behaviour (are they actually using the new service?). Use surveys, pulse checks, listening in forums, and sentiment analysis of free-text feedback, and feed what you learn back into the plan so communication becomes a loop, not a broadcast. Hold honesty and transparency as non-negotiable. In public services, trust is your scarcest and most valuable asset, and it is destroyed far faster than it is built. Do not overclaim benefits, hide delays, or bury bad news; acknowledge trade-offs, admit when a rollout has gone wrong, and be clear about how patient data is used. Honest communication may be uncomfortable in the moment, but it is the only foundation that survives contact with scrutiny, and it makes every future message more credible. Questions to discuss with your team # Who are our real audiences for this change, and how does what we say and how we say it differ for each? It is tempting to treat "staff" and "the public" as two blocks, but a digital change lands on a caseworker, a night-shift nurse, a carer, and a patient with limited English very differently. Debate whether you have genuinely segmented your audiences or are relying on a single all-staff email and a press release. Consider who is easy to reach and therefore over-communicated to, and who is hard to reach and therefore ignored — often the same people who are already digitally excluded. A good answer names specific segments, the channels and intermediaries that actually reach each, and the different framing each needs, and it is honest about where you currently have blind spots. Watch for the failure of designing all your communication for the audiences most like yourselves. Where on the spectrum from informing to empowering is our engagement really sitting — and where should it be? Many programmes claim to engage while in practice only informing, running consultations after the key decisions are already made. Discuss, for each major decision in this change, how much influence patients and staff genuinely have, and whether that matches what you are implying to them. Surface the tension between the time real co-design takes and the delivery pressure to move fast, and be honest that pretend-engagement is worse than none because it breeds cynicism. Consider concrete mechanisms — co-design workshops, patient panels, staff reference groups — and what you will visibly change as a result. A strong answer distinguishes where you will genuinely share power from where you are only informing, and commits to being truthful about the difference rather than dressing one up as the other. If a serious incident or outage hit this system tomorrow, are we ready to communicate within the hour — honestly and to everyone affected? Incident communication is where trust is won or lost fastest, yet it is the part teams rehearse least. Walk through a realistic scenario — the system is down across every ward at 2pm — and ask who has authority to speak, what the holding message is, which channels reach staff and patients (including those offline), and how you will keep updating. Debate the tension between the instinct to say nothing until you know everything and the reality that silence breeds rumour and unsafe workarounds. Consider how you would correct misinformation on social media, and how honest you are willing to be about what went wrong. A good answer points to pre-agreed roles, rehearsed templates tied to your business-continuity plans, and a shared commitment to say what you know, what you don't, and when you will next speak. What is our single, honest story about why this change matters — and would a nurse or a patient recognize themselves in it? Programmes accumulate messages, benefits tables, and slide decks, but people act on a clear narrative, not a feature list. Discuss whether you can state, in two plain sentences, the problem today, the change you are making, and the better outcome for patients and for the staff doing the work — and whether that story uses the words your audiences actually use rather than programme jargon. Surface the tension between a narrative that is compelling and one that is truthful: it is easy to craft an inspiring story that quietly overpromises, and in health and care an overclaimed benefit erodes the trust you need for the next change. Test whether the story survives contact with a sceptical ward sister or a wary patient group, and whether front-line staff would tell it to a colleague unprompted. A good answer produces a narrative that is concrete, tested on real people, and honest about trade-offs, and it names who owns and stewards that story so it stays consistent across every channel. How will we know our communication actually worked — beyond opens, clicks, and attendance? It is comfortable to report that an email reached ten thousand inboxes and reassuring to count workshop attendees, but reach is not understanding, and neither is behaviour change. Debate what evidence would genuinely tell you the message landed: can staff explain the change back in their own words, how do people feel about it, and are they actually using the new service as intended? Consider the practical methods — comprehension checks, pulse surveys, listening in team forums, sentiment analysis of free-text feedback — and be honest about the effort and the risk that you measure what is easy rather than what matters. There is a real tension between wanting flattering numbers to show a board and wanting uncomfortable signals early enough to act on them. A good answer commits to a small set of measures spanning understanding, sentiment, and behaviour, names who reviews them, and closes the loop by feeding what you learn back into the next round of communication. Where are we tempted to overclaim, soften, or delay bad news — and what will keep us honest when the pressure is on? Trust is the scarcest asset in public services and it is spent far faster than it is earned, yet the daily pressures of funding bids, board confidence, and political scrutiny all pull towards optimistic messages and buried delays. Discuss specifically where this change is vulnerable: a benefit that may not fully materialize, a slipping timeline, a contentious supplier, or a sensitive question about how patient data is used. Surface the tension between managing legitimate reputational risk and the temptation to spin, and be clear that being caught overclaiming or concealing does more lasting damage than the bad news itself would have. Consider what structures keep you honest — a named senior owner for difficult messages, a habit of acknowledging trade-offs openly, transparency about data use, and permission for staff to raise concerns without blame. A good answer identifies the specific honesty risks in this programme and the concrete commitments and guardrails that will hold when it becomes uncomfortable to tell the truth. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system (ICS) is rolling out a shared care record that lets clinicians across acute, community, mental health, GP, and social care see a single view of a person. The technology is ready; the risk is trust and adoption. A previous national data-sharing initiative in the region had collapsed under public suspicion, and local staff remember it. The programme director does not start with a launch date. She commissions a communications and engagement plan built around audiences: front-line clinicians in each setting, practice managers, social workers, the local Healthwatch, community and faith groups in the most under-served neighbourhoods, and the general public. Each segment gets its own narrative. For staff, the story is "stop asking patients to repeat themselves and stop chasing results across five systems." For the public, co-produced with a patient panel and translated into the area's main community languages, the story is "your care team can see the information they need to keep you safe — and here is exactly who can see what, and how to opt out." She works hand-in-glove with the ICS communications team and the patient-experience lead from week one. Engagement is two-way and visible. Co-design workshops with community groups surface a specific fear — that immigration status or mental-health history could leak to non-clinical bodies — and the programme changes its access model and its public materials in response, then says so publicly. Staff floor-walking reveals that the log-in flow adds clicks on busy wards; that feedback reshapes the rollout sequencing and a fix is prioritized. Cadence is predictable: a fortnightly staff bulletin, monthly public updates, and standing panels. When, three weeks after go-live, the record is unavailable for four hours during a supplier incident, the pre-agreed crisis plan activates. Within forty minutes a holding message goes to every clinical team through the intranet, team huddles, and a text cascade, explaining the outage, the paper-based fallback, and the next update time; a plain-language notice reassures patients that their data is safe and no appointments are affected. A false claim on local social media that "the whole NHS system has been hacked" is corrected within the hour with a calm, factual statement from a named director. Trust holds, because the groundwork of honesty had already been laid, and opt-out rates stay low. The programme measures not just how many staff logged in, but whether they can explain what the record does and how they feel about it — and feeds that back into the next round of messages. Sector lenses # Startup # A small digital-health company has a founder-led, fast, informal communications style and little budget for a dedicated engagement function. Its strength is speed and authenticity — the clinical lead can speak directly and credibly to early-adopter clinicians. Its risk is over-claiming to win contracts and then failing to communicate honestly when the product breaks, which in a small market destroys reputation quickly. The founders should invest early in a simple, honest narrative, a basic incident-communications template, and disciplined listening to their first customers, because word of mouth among a handful of NHS trusts can make or break them. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home, or a single-site clinic introducing a new digital system — has real patients and staff but no communications team, and the practice manager or registered manager typically absorbs engagement alongside everything else. The audiences are small and personally known, which is an advantage: a team huddle, a noticeboard, a letter to patients, and a conversation with the patient participation group can reach most people directly and authentically. x: Topic 8.3 — Behavioural Science & Adoption Deploying a system changes what is possible; only behaviour change makes it real, so treat adoption as a designed, measured outcome — not a hopeful by-product of go-live. Why this matters in health and care # A system that is installed but unused is not a neutral outcome. In health and care it is a live risk: half-adopted tools breed workarounds, dual recording, and gaps where information should flow, and each of those is a route to a clinical incident. When a hospital buys electronic prescribing but a proportion of prescribers keep scribbling on paper, the record is now split across two media and the safety case built on the digital system quietly fails. Deployment and adoption are different achievements, and the distance between them is measured in behaviour. On the patient and citizen side the stakes are about equity and outcomes. An app that manages a long-term condition only helps the people who download it, activate it, and keep using it week after week — and those people are disproportionately younger, wealthier, more digitally confident, and healthier to begin with. If you measure success by "the service is available", you can report a triumph while widening the very inequalities the NHS exists to narrow. The people who most need a diabetes or hypertension pathway are often the least likely to adopt it unaided. Behavioural science is the discipline that takes adoption seriously as an object of design and evidence. It sits alongside — not inside — change management (see Topic 8.1 — Change Management), which leads the organizational transition, and communications and engagement (see Topic 8.2 — Communications & Engagement), which builds understanding and trust. Behavioural science is narrower and more specific: it asks what makes a single target behaviour more or less likely for a real person in a real context, and it uses that understanding to make the desired action the easy, obvious one. Because you are influencing people's health decisions with public money, doing this well — and doing it ethically — is part of your duty of care, not an optional refinement. Core concepts # Behaviour change and behavioural science. Behavioral economics and the wider behaviour change field start from a realistic model of people: attention is scarce, effort is costly, defaults are sticky, and decisions are shaped by context far more than by information alone. Giving clinicians a memo, or citizens a leaflet, rarely changes what they do; changing the surrounding environment usually does. The practical question is never "do people know they should?" but "what makes the right action easy, and the wrong action harder, here?" The COM-B model and the Behaviour Change Wheel. COM-B, developed by Susan Michie and colleagues at University College London, states that any behaviour (B) requires three conditions: Capability (the physical and psychological ability to do it), Opportunity (the social and physical context that permits and prompts it), and Motivation (the reflective and automatic drives toward it). The Behaviour Change Wheel wraps COM-B in a systematic method: diagnose which of Capability, Opportunity, or Motivation is the binding constraint, then select intervention functions (education, training, enablement, environmental restructuring, incentivization, and others) that address that specific gap. Its discipline is that it forces you to diagnose before you intervene, rather than defaulting to yet more training or yet more communications. Nudge theory and choice architecture. Nudge theory , from Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein, holds that small changes to the way choices are presented — the choice architecture — can steer behaviour without removing options or changing economic incentives. Defaults, framing, ordering, and salience are the levers. The UK's Behavioural Insights Team (the "Nudge Unit"), founded inside the Cabinet Office in 2010, made this operational in public services, testing interventions such as social-norm messages and SMS reminders through controlled trials. Adoption, activation, and sustained use. These are three distinct behaviours, not one. Adoption is starting — logging in, downloading, enrolling. Activation is reaching the point where the user experiences the core value (the "aha" moment: sending a first secure message, completing a first remote reading). Sustained use is continued, embedded use weeks and months later. Many services are strong on adoption, collapse at activation, and are graveyards by month three — so measuring only the first tells you almost nothing. Friction, defaults, reminders, and feedback. Friction is anything that makes a behaviour harder — a login, a form field, a step, a wait. Reducing friction on the path you want, and adding it to paths you don't, is the most reliable behavioural lever you have. Defaults set the outcome for people who do nothing and are powerful precisely because so many people do nothing. Reminders solve forgetting; feedback (progress, comparison, confirmation) sustains motivation once the behaviour has begun. Habit formation. A habit is a behaviour that becomes automatic through a cue–routine–reward loop repeated in a stable context. Sustained use of a clinical system is really a habit-formation problem: you want opening the system to become the unthinking first step of a ward round, not a conscious decision each time. Habits form through repetition tied to existing cues, which is why embedding a new tool into an established workflow beats bolting it on beside one. Incentives and their limits. Incentives — financial, professional, or reputational — can shift behaviour, but crudely applied they backfire. They can crowd out intrinsic motivation, produce gaming to the metric, and stop working the moment they are withdrawn. Self-determination theory explains why autonomy, competence, and relatedness usually sustain behaviour more durably than external reward alone. Diffusion and adoption curves. How an innovation spreads through a population is described by diffusion of innovations and the technology adoption life cycle — innovators and early adopters first, then the majorities, then laggards. This connects behavioural science to the wider question of phasing in innovation (see Topic 8.0 — Phasing in Innovation): behavioural levers must be tuned to where a group sits on that curve. Best practices # Define the target behaviour precisely, for a named group, in a named context. "Improve engagement" is not a behaviour; "district nurses record a wound assessment on the mobile app during the home visit, not afterwards on paper" is. Behavioural science only works on specifics: who, does what, when, where, instead of what. Write the behaviour down at that resolution before you design anything, because a vague target guarantees a vague intervention. Diagnose the barrier with COM-B before choosing a fix. Ask whether the binding constraint is Capability (they can't — skills, understanding, or the device fails), Opportunity (the context blocks it — no time, no signal, no prompt), or Motivation (they won't — no perceived benefit, competing habits, or distrust). The intervention follows from the diagnosis: a Capability gap needs training or simplification, an Opportunity gap needs environmental change, a Motivation gap needs a different lever entirely. Skipping diagnosis is why organizations answer an Opportunity problem with more emails and wonder why nothing moves (see Topic 8.1 — Change Management on diagnosing resistance). Reduce friction on the desired path relentlessly. Every extra click, login, free-text field, and context-switch loses a fraction of your users, and the fractions compound. Count the steps in the current journey, then delete, pre-fill, and default your way to fewer. Single sign-on, sensible defaults, and forms that arrive pre-populated from the record often move adoption more than any amount of persuasion, because they change Opportunity rather than merely appealing to Motivation. Set defaults deliberately and ethically. Because most people accept the default, the default is a design decision with real consequences — make it the safe, recommended option, and make opting out easy and transparent. Opt-out structures (for example, a default appointment slot the patient can change) raise uptake far more than opt-in equivalents. The ethical line is that the default must serve the person, the alternative must remain genuinely available, and you must be open about what you have done. Use reminders and feedback to convert intention into action and sustain it. Well-timed prompts close the gap between wanting to act and acting — the classic behavioural finding behind SMS appointment reminders that cut did-not-attend rates. Feedback (a progress bar, a streak, a "your reading is in range" confirmation, a peer comparison) sustains a behaviour once begun. Keep prompts specific, timely, and sparing; a channel that over-notifies is soon muted or uninstalled. Design for habit by embedding into existing workflow and cues. Do not ask people to remember to use a new tool; attach it to something they already do at a fixed point — the login that starts the shift, the moment before discharge, the existing daily huddle. Stable cues plus repetition build automaticity. A tool that lives inside the workflow becomes a habit; one that sits beside it stays a chore and is abandoned under pressure. Use incentives cautiously, and watch for gaming and crowding-out. If you attach a payment or a performance target to a behaviour, expect people to optimize for exactly what you measure — sometimes at the expense of what you meant. Prefer intrinsic and professional motivators (autonomy, mastery, peer norms, visible patient benefit) where you can, and treat financial incentives as a short-term catalyst rather than a permanent prop. Always ask what breaks when the incentive is removed, because a behaviour that only exists while you pay for it was never adopted. Test interventions rather than assuming them. Behavioural effects are context-dependent and frequently surprise even experts, so pilot, A/B test, or run a small randomized controlled trial where you can — the working method of the Behavioural Insights Team. A two-arm comparison of two reminder wordings costs little and can double effectiveness. Testing also protects you from confidently rolling out a nudge that does nothing, or worse, backfires for a subgroup. Check the equity effect of every nudge, and design for the disadvantaged first. Nudges and digital defaults tend to work best for people who are already advantaged — literate, connected, confident, well — which means an intervention can lift the average while widening the gap. Segment your adoption data by age, deprivation, language, and disability, and design assisted routes, human fallbacks, and proxy access for those the digital path leaves behind (see Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility and Topic 3.3 — Patient & Citizen-Facing Digital Services). An adoption strategy that only reaches the easy-to-reach is a failure dressed as a success. Measure behaviour and adoption, not deployment. Instrument the actual behaviours — logins, activation events, feature use, sustained-use cohorts, workaround and reversion rates, did-not-attend and adherence rates — and report them against a baseline, segmented by group. Deployment metrics ("system is live in 40 sites") flatter you; behavioural metrics tell you the truth. Make sustained use at ninety days, not go-live, the definition of done (see Topic 10.1 — Key Performance Indicators). Questions to discuss with your team # For the change we are about to make, what is the single precise behaviour we need, from whom, and which of Capability, Opportunity, or Motivation is actually blocking it today? This question forces the team past the comfortable abstraction of "driving adoption" into the specific behaviour that has to happen — and by whom, when, and where. In a health and care setting the honest answer is often uncomfortable: the barrier is not that clinicians lack awareness or motivation, but Opportunity, because the system adds ninety seconds to a consultation they do not have, or Capability, because it fails on the ward's ageing hardware. Debate should surface the difference between what leadership assumes the barrier is and what frontline observation and data actually show, because the two frequently diverge. Consider whether you have watched real users attempt the behaviour, or are inferring from complaints and hope. A good answer names one behaviour at high resolution, cites evidence for which COM-B component is binding, and commits to an intervention that matches that diagnosis rather than defaulting to more training or more communications. The best version identifies a case where the team was about to fix the wrong component and redirects the effort. Where are we relying on nudges and defaults that may work better for our already-advantaged users than for those who need the service most — and how would we even know? This is the equity question that behavioural science makes unavoidable, because the same techniques that lift overall uptake can quietly widen inequalities. The tension to debate is real: an opt-out default or a slick digital-first journey can raise your headline numbers while leaving older, poorer, less digitally confident, or non-English-speaking patients further behind, and an average that improves can hide a gap that grows. The discussion should confront whether your adoption data is segmented at all — by deprivation, age, language, disability — or whether you are reporting a single flattering figure. It should also examine what assisted and non-digital routes exist for people the nudge does not reach, and whether those routes are resourced or merely notional. A serious answer accepts that "available to all" is not the same as "adopted by all", commits to measuring the distribution and not just the mean, and treats a widening gap as a failure condition that would stop or change the rollout. The weakest answer is the one that has never looked. Where is the ethical line between helping people make good health decisions and manipulating them — and are we on the right side of it, transparently? Influencing behaviour in health carries a duty that ordinary marketing does not, because the power asymmetry is greater and the subject is people's bodies and lives. The debate should distinguish legitimate choice architecture — making the healthy or recommended option easy, while keeping alternatives genuinely available and being open about what you have done — from covert manipulation, dark patterns, exploiting fear, or hiding the opt-out. Consider concrete cases: a default screening appointment the patient can freely change is defensible; a design that makes declining deliberately difficult, or that uses shame, is not. The team should ask whether they would be comfortable explaining each nudge to the person it targets, and to a regulator or the public, because transparency is the practical test of ethical influence. Autonomy, informed consent, and trust are not obstacles to adoption but its foundation (see Topic 1.8 — Data Ethics, Consent & Public Trust), and a manipulative win today spends the trust you need for every future change. A good answer sets a clear standard, applies it to your actual designs, and is willing to remove a nudge that works but cannot be defended openly. Have we distinguished adoption from activation from sustained use — and does anyone here actually own the number that says people are still using this at ninety days? Teams routinely collapse three different behaviours into one word, "uptake", and then celebrate the wrong one. Adoption (signing up) is the easiest to achieve and the most flattering to report; activation (reaching the first moment of real value) is where most services quietly haemorrhage users; sustained use months later is what actually delivers the clinical benefit in the business case. The discussion should confront where your own data stops — many programmes can quote sign-ups but have never instrumented the activation moment or plotted a retention curve, so they cannot even see the week-two cliff, let alone explain it. It should also name an accountable owner: if "adoption" belongs to everyone in general it belongs to no one in particular, and the ninety-day figure becomes an orphan that no dashboard carries. Debate what your definition of "done" really is, because if go-live counts as success the whole system is optimized to stop caring exactly when the hard part begins. An honest answer separates the three behaviours, shows the funnel with real numbers, and points to a named person answerable for sustained use — not a benefits case that assumed it. Are we embedding this behaviour into an existing workflow and cue, or bolting a new tool on beside one and hoping people will remember it? Habits form when a behaviour is tied to a stable, pre-existing cue and repeated, which is why the integration question is a behavioural question and not merely a technical one. The tension to surface is that the easiest thing to deliver — a standalone app or a separate portal with its own login — is often the thing most certain to be abandoned under pressure, because it competes for attention and memory rather than riding on something the user already does. The team should examine, concretely, what existing moment the desired behaviour will attach to: the login that starts the shift, the step before discharge, the morning medication round. It should also be honest about the cost of the alternative, because embedding into the electronic record or the daily workflow is harder, slower, and more political than shipping a separate tool, and that difficulty is exactly why organizations skip it. A good answer identifies the real cue and commits to in-context integration even when a standalone build would be quicker; the weak answer ships beside the workflow and blames the users when the tool is quietly dropped the first busy week. What have we actually tested here rather than assumed — and are our incentives quietly training people to game the metric? Behavioural effects are notoriously context-dependent and frequently wrong-foot even experts, so a plan built on confident assumption rather than a small comparison is a plan carrying hidden risk. The discussion should ask what could be piloted or A/B tested cheaply before scaling — two reminder wordings, two default settings, an assisted route against none — because a two-arm test costs little and routinely changes the answer, and because scaling an untested nudge can entrench something that does nothing or backfires for a subgroup. The conversation must also turn to incentives, financial or performance-target, and ask what behaviour they are really rewarding: attach a payment or a target to a number and people will optimize for that number, sometimes at the expense of the outcome you meant, and the behaviour may collapse the moment the incentive is withdrawn. Consider whether any current target could be met while the underlying clinical intent is missed, which is the signature of gaming. A strong answer names what will be tested and how, treats financial incentives as a short-term catalyst to be monitored for side-effects rather than a permanent prop, and asks of every incentive what breaks when it stops. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system is rolling out a remote monitoring service for people with heart failure: patients take daily weight and symptom readings on a supplied device, and a virtual ward team reviews them. The technology works in the pilot. Six months in, the programme lead notices the pattern that behavioural science predicts — strong sign-up, a sharp drop after week two, and a small, demographically skewed group still using it by month three. x: Topic 8.4 — AI & Emerging Technology Governance In one sentence: Artificial intelligence in health and care is a learning, data-dependent, and often opaque technology that can scale both benefit and harm faster than any system you have governed before, so you must govern it as a clinical-safety, equity, and public-trust matter throughout its whole lifecycle — not treat it as ordinary software you buy once and forget. Why this matters in health and care # Most of the software you have deployed behaves the same way tomorrow as it does today: its logic is written down, its behaviour is testable, and when it is wrong it tends to be wrong in a visible, repeatable way. Artificial intelligence breaks all three of those comforts. It learns statistical patterns from data rather than following rules a person wrote; its behaviour depends entirely on the data it was trained on and the data it now meets; and its reasoning is frequently opaque even to the people who built it. That combination is why AI needs its own governance discipline rather than being folded into a generic software checklist. In health and care the consequences are not abstract. A model that under-detects disease in a group who were under-represented in its training data does not make an isolated error — it makes the same error, silently, thousands of times, entrenching and scaling health inequalities. A generative model that fabricates a plausible-sounding clinical detail can mislead a stretched clinician at exactly the wrong moment. A tool that works beautifully in the population it was validated on can quietly decay when the population, the care pathway, or the upstream data changes. AI can scale good decisions and it can scale bias, error, and harm with equal efficiency. This topic is about governing that risk without either breathing the hype or banning the technology. It deliberately does not repeat the foundations laid elsewhere: clinical safety (see Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management), information governance, data protection and cyber security (see Topic 1.7 — Information Governance, Data Protection & Cyber Security), and evidence-driven decision-making (see Topic 1.3 — Evidence-Driven Decisions). It anchors to them, and adds what is specific to learning systems. Treat it as the AI-shaped extension of your existing assurance, and as the governed sibling of phasing in innovation (see Topic 8.0 — Phasing in Innovation). Core concepts # Artificial intelligence and machine learning. For a leader, the practical distinction is this: most AI in health and care today is machine learning — systems that infer patterns from examples rather than executing hand-written rules. This is why the data is the product as much as the code: change the training data and you change the behaviour. It also means a model does not "know" anything; it estimates, and it can be confidently wrong. Understanding this at a conceptual level is enough to ask the right governance questions; you do not need to read the mathematics. Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) and the MHRA. When software has a medical purpose — diagnosing, screening, triaging, calculating a dose, predicting deterioration — it is very often a medical device in law, regardless of whether it runs on a phone or a server. Medical software of this kind, known as Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), is regulated in the United Kingdom by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) . If you are commissioning or building an AI tool with a clinical purpose, the first governance question is whether it is a regulated device and, if so, whether it holds valid conformity marking. Getting this wrong is not a technicality; deploying an unregistered medical device is unlawful and unsafe. The AI Airlock. The MHRA has established a regulatory sandbox called the AI Airlock to work through how AI as a medical device should be regulated in a controlled, monitored setting. A regulatory sandbox lets a regulator and a small number of developers examine hard, novel questions — for example how to validate a model that updates over time — under supervision, before general rules are set. Be sober about what this is: the Airlock is a learning environment for the regulator and a handful of participants, not a fast-track approval route, and being associated with it does not mean a product is approved for general clinical use. Algorithmic bias and fairness. Algorithmic bias is the tendency of a system to produce systematically unfair outcomes for particular groups. In health and care its most common source is the training data: if a group is under-represented, mislabelled, or measured with a biased instrument, the model learns to serve that group worse. Because the model then applies this at scale and with an air of objectivity, biased AI can widen the very inequalities your organization is statutorily obliged to reduce. Explainability and the black box. Explainable artificial intelligence concerns whether a human can understand why a model produced a given output. Many high-performing models are effectively "black boxes": accurate in aggregate but unable to give a clinician a trustworthy reason for an individual decision. In a clinical setting this matters for accountability, informed consent, and the clinician's duty to exercise judgement — a doctor cannot meaningfully take responsibility for advice they cannot interrogate. Model drift and post-market surveillance. A model's accuracy is not fixed. Concept drift — a change over time in the relationship between inputs and the thing being predicted — means a model validated last year can silently degrade this year as populations, pathways, or upstream data change. This is why AI requires ongoing post-market surveillance and monitoring, not just a one-off validation at go-live. MLOps and the model lifecycle. MLOps is the operational discipline of deploying, monitoring, versioning, and retraining models reliably in production. It is the machinery that makes lifecycle governance real: knowing which model version is live, on which data, with what performance, and being able to roll back. Human-in-the-loop. A human-in-the-loop design keeps a person — usually a clinician — meaningfully in the decision, with the authority and the information to override the model. Done well it preserves accountability; done as a rubber stamp it provides only the illusion of oversight. Generative AI and large language models. Generative artificial intelligence , including large language models (LLMs) , produces fluent text and other content. Its realistic near-term value in health and care is largely administrative — drafting documentation, summarizing, easing paperwork. Its defining risk is hallucination : the confident generation of false but plausible content, compounded by confidentiality risks when patient data is entered into third-party services. Digital therapeutics and health apps. Digital therapeutics (DTx) are software-driven, evidence-based interventions that prevent, manage, or treat a condition — distinct from general wellness apps precisely because they make a clinical claim, which means many are Software as a Medical Device and demand the same evidence and assurance as any other intervention you prescribe or recommend. Best practices # Classify the tool before you do anything else. Establish, in writing and with clinical and regulatory input, whether the AI has a medical purpose and is therefore a regulated medical device, and whether it holds valid MHRA conformity marking. This single determination governs everything downstream — the assurance route, the liabilities, the lawfulness of deployment. When in doubt, seek regulatory advice rather than assuming an administrative tool is out of scope. Run AI through your existing clinical-safety and IG machinery, extended not bypassed. Every clinical AI deployment needs the clinical risk management of DCB0129/DCB0160 (see Topic 1.6 ) and a Data Protection Impact Assessment under your information governance framework (see Topic 1.7 ). Do not let novelty or supplier enthusiasm create a parallel, lighter process. AI-specific hazards — bias, drift, opacity, automation bias — should be added to the hazard log, not substituted for it. Interrogate the training data for representativeness and bias. Ask who is in the data and who is missing, how outcomes were labelled, and whether the measuring instruments were themselves biased across groups. Require the supplier to report performance broken down by relevant subgroups — age, sex, ethnicity, deprivation — not just headline accuracy. A tool that cannot demonstrate equitable performance is a health-inequality risk however impressive its average. Demand clinical validation appropriate to the risk, and prefer prospective evidence. Retrospective accuracy on curated data is the weakest form of evidence. For anything influencing clinical decisions, seek validation in a population and workflow like yours, ideally prospective, and route the claim through the appropriate assurance framework — the NICE Evidence Standards Framework for digital health technologies and the Digital Technology Assessment Criteria (DTAC) as baseline assurance. Match the strength of evidence to the magnitude of potential harm. Insist on meaningful human-in-the-loop and clear accountability. Define who is accountable for a decision the AI informed, and ensure the human has both the authority to override and the information to do so. Guard actively against automation bias — the tendency to defer to the machine — through training, interface design, and audit of override rates. If overrides never happen, your "human in the loop" is decorative. Treat go-live as the start of monitoring, not the end of assurance. Stand up post-market surveillance from day one: monitor real-world performance, watch for concept drift, and define the thresholds and process for retraining, pausing, or withdrawing the model. Establish model versioning and rollback through sound MLOps so you always know what is live and can revert safely. A model that is never re-checked is a slowly failing safety control. Govern generative AI to its realistic uses and against its real risks. Permit LLMs where the value is genuine and the risk is contained — administrative drafting, summarization, documentation support with human review — and prohibit unmanaged entry of patient-identifiable data into third-party services. Assume any generative output may be fabricated until a human verifies it, and never let unverified generated content enter the clinical record. Clear, enforced policy beats both a blanket ban that drives shadow use and a free-for-all that leaks data. Apply information governance to the whole data lifecycle, including training. The data used to train, fine-tune, and evaluate a model is subject to the same lawful-basis, minimization, and transparency obligations as any other use (see Topic 1.7 ). Be explicit about the basis for training on patient data, whether it is de-identified adequately, and what the supplier may do with it. Contracts should forbid re-use of your data to train products for others without a lawful basis and your agreement. Keep a human-readable model register and demand transparency from suppliers. Maintain an inventory of AI in use: purpose, regulatory status, training data provenance, validation evidence, monitoring plan, and accountable owner. Require suppliers to be transparent about how a model works, its limitations, and its failure modes; opacity from a vendor is itself a risk signal. You cannot govern what you have not written down. Horizon-scan deliberately and phase in through controlled evaluation. Beyond today's AI, watch emerging technologies — ambient documentation, foundation models, and further out, quantum and novel sensing — with structured horizon-scanning rather than reactive procurement. Introduce anything genuinely novel through the controlled, reversible, evaluated approach of phasing in innovation (see Topic 8.0 ), starting small, measuring honestly, and retaining the ability to stop. Treat digital therapeutics and health apps as interventions, not consumer downloads. When an app makes a clinical claim — to treat, manage, or prevent a condition — it is an intervention that patients will act on, and it deserves the same scrutiny as a drug or a device before you prescribe or recommend it. Establish whether it is Software as a Medical Device with valid conformity marking, demand evidence proportionate to its claim, and complete a clinical safety assessment (see Topic 1.6 ) rather than trusting an app-store rating or a supplier's enthusiasm. An unassured app that a clinician endorses carries your organization's name and your accountability if it harms. Route health apps through existing assurance and keep a curated, safe library. Assess digital therapeutics through the same machinery you already run — DTAC as baseline, the NICE Evidence Standards Framework matched to the clinical claim, and clinical safety and IG review — and build the real-world evaluation evidence over time (see Topic 8.6 ). Maintain a curated library of apps you have assured and stand behind, with each app's regulatory status, evidence, and owner recorded, so clinicians recommend from a safe, governed shortlist. The alternative — an uncontrolled sprawl of unassessed apps recommended informally across teams — is unmanageable and unsafe. Questions to discuss with your team # For each AI tool we are considering or already using, do we actually know whether it is a regulated medical device — and can we produce the evidence? This sounds like a compliance formality but it is the load-bearing question, because the answer determines what is lawful, who is liable, and what assurance you owe the public. It is easy to assume a tool that "just helps with triage" or "just summarizes notes" is harmless administrative software when its medical purpose in fact makes it a regulated device requiring MHRA conformity marking. The discussion should force you to name each AI tool in use or in the pipeline, state its intended purpose in plain clinical terms, and identify who made the device-classification call and on what basis. It should surface the uncomfortable cases where a tool was procured through an ordinary IT route with no regulatory check at all. Be honest about whether you could, today, produce the conformity documentation and validation evidence if a regulator or a coroner asked. The value of the conversation is that it converts a vague sense that "someone must have checked" into a documented, owned position — and reveals the tools where nobody has. Have we demanded to see how this model performs for the groups most likely to be harmed, or have we accepted a headline accuracy figure? Average accuracy is the number suppliers lead with and the number that hides algorithmic bias, because a model can be highly accurate overall while performing markedly worse for an under-represented group. In health and care that is not a statistical curiosity; it is a mechanism for widening the inequalities you are legally and morally bound to reduce, applied silently and at scale. The team should discuss what subgroup evidence you have actually seen — performance broken down by age, sex, ethnicity, and deprivation — and whether you know who was in the training data and who was missing. It is worth naming the discomfort here: pressing a supplier on fairness can feel like obstructing an exciting innovation, and the honest question is whether you are willing to say no to a tool that cannot demonstrate equitable performance. Consider also how you would even detect inequitable outcomes after deployment, since bias that was invisible at procurement will be invisible in production unless you monitor for it. A good discussion ends with a concrete evidentiary bar for fairness that applies before any clinical AI goes live, and a plan to keep watching afterwards. When this model is wrong — and it will be — who is accountable, will a human really catch it, and how will we even know? Every model fails sometimes, and learning systems can drift into failing more often over time, so the mature question is not whether errors occur but whether your safeguards are real. The team should test whether the human-in-the-loop is meaningful or decorative: does the clinician have the authority and the information to override, and if you looked at override rates, would you find they ever actually override, or has automation bias set in? Discuss who is named as accountable for a decision the AI informed — the clinician, the organization, the supplier — because "the algorithm did it" is not a defensible position to a patient or a coroner. Confront your monitoring honestly: do you have post-market surveillance that would detect concept drift, defined thresholds for pausing or withdrawing the model, and the MLOps machinery to know which version is live and to roll it back? For generative tools, add the hallucination question — what stops fabricated content entering the clinical record, and who verifies output before it is trusted? The most useful version of this conversation exposes the gap between the reassuring diagram of "human oversight" and what would genuinely happen at 3am on a busy ward. What is happening to our patients' data when we train, fine-tune, and run these models — and what has the supplier reserved the right to do with it? AI concentrates data-governance risk precisely because the data is the product: a model is only as trustworthy as the lawful basis, minimization, and transparency behind every dataset it touched, including the training and evaluation data that predates go-live. The team should be able to state, for each tool, the lawful basis for any use of patient data, whether de-identification is adequate rather than merely asserted, and where the data physically flows once it leaves your control. A recurring trap is the contract that quietly permits the supplier to re-use your data to improve products it will sell to others; discuss whether your agreements forbid that without a lawful basis and your explicit consent, and whether anyone has actually read those clauses. This connects directly to your information governance framework (see Topic 1.7 ), and it is where enthusiasm for a capable tool most often outruns due diligence. An honest answer names who owns the DPIA, what the supplier may and may not do, and where you are currently exposed — rather than assuming that because the demo was impressive the paperwork must be sound. How do we decide what NOT to adopt, and can we resist the pressure to buy the thing everyone is excited about? The hardest governance discipline with a fast-moving technology is saying "not yet" or "not this", and a team that cannot articulate its criteria for declining will end up adopting by drift and hype rather than by evidence. Discuss what would make you walk away from an otherwise attractive tool — weak subgroup evidence, an unclear regulatory status, a use case where the realistic benefit is thin relative to the risk — and whether those red lines are written down or merely felt. There is a real tension here between the cost of missing a genuine improvement and the cost of a scaled failure that damages public trust, and reasonable people will weigh them differently. It is worth naming the political reality that pressure to adopt often comes from a board, a supplier relationship, or a national mandate, not from the clinical need itself. The topic's stance is to horizon-scan deliberately and phase in through controlled, reversible evaluation (see Topic 8.0 ), so an honest answer describes how a promising-but-unproven tool enters as a small, measured, stoppable pilot rather than a wholesale rollout — and who holds the authority to stop it. x: Topic 8.5 — Sustainability & Net Zero In health and care, cutting carbon is not a corporate-responsibility side-project bolted onto delivery — it is a clinical, ethical, and financial dimension of every digital service you build, buy, and run. Why this matters in health and care # Climate change is a health emergency, not an abstract environmental concern. Heatwaves, floods, air pollution, shifting patterns of infectious disease, and disrupted food and water systems all land, eventually, in your clinics, ambulances, and waiting lists. The effects of climate change on human health fall hardest on the same populations who already carry the heaviest burden of illness and the least access to services — so sustainability sits alongside the equity and inclusion concerns you met in Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility. The National Health Service (NHS) is a large emitter in its own right. It accounts for a substantial share of England's carbon footprint and a large slice of public-sector emissions, which means the way it delivers care is materially part of the problem or part of the solution. In October 2020 the NHS became the first national health service in the world to commit formally to reaching net zero , through the Greener NHS programme and its report Delivering a Net Zero National Health Service . Digital leaders sit at a pivotal point. Technology can strip enormous carbon out of the wider system — through virtual care, reduced travel, and paperlight working — while quietly generating its own footprint through data centres, cloud services, devices, and electronic waste. If you do not measure and manage both sides of that ledger, you risk congratulating yourself on savings you have merely moved somewhere less visible. Treating sustainability as a first-class delivery concern, with the same rigour you apply to clinical safety ( Topic 1.6 ) and information governance ( Topic 1.7 ), is how you keep that honest. Core concepts # Net zero and the two NHS targets. Net-zero emissions means balancing the greenhouse gases you emit with an equivalent amount removed, so your net contribution to warming is nil. The NHS sets two distinct goals. The NHS Carbon Footprint covers emissions the NHS controls directly — its own estate, fleet, and energy — with an ambition to reach net zero by 2040, and an interim milestone of an roughly 80% reduction in the late 2020s to early 2030s. The NHS Carbon Footprint Plus is wider, adding emissions the NHS can influence but not directly control, most importantly its supply chain and procured goods; the ambition there is net zero by 2045, with an 80% reduction milestone later in the 2030s. Treat the dates as directional ambitions rather than precise contractual deadlines, and check current Greener NHS guidance for the exact figures. Emission scopes. Standardized carbon accounting, most commonly the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard , divides emissions into three scopes. Scope 1 is direct emissions from sources you own or control. Scope 2 is indirect emissions from the electricity, heat, and cooling you buy. Scope 3 is everything else in your value chain — suppliers, cloud providers, staff travel, procured devices, and the disposal of what you throw away. For digital services, Scope 3 usually dominates, which is why procurement and supplier behaviour matter so much. Carbon footprint. A carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gas load attributable to an activity, product, or organization, usually expressed in tonnes of carbon-dioxide equivalent. For a digital service, the footprint spans the manufacture and disposal of hardware, the energy consumed running it, and the network and data centre capacity behind it. Cloud does not make emissions disappear; it relocates them to a provider whose energy mix and efficiency you should still ask about. Green computing and sustainable ICT. Green computing — sometimes called green software or sustainable information and communications technology (ICT) — is the practice of designing, running, and disposing of digital systems to minimize their environmental impact. It ranges from efficient code and right-sized infrastructure to renewable-powered hosting and hardware longevity. Electronic waste and circularity. Electronic waste , or e-waste, is discarded electrical and electronic equipment — laptops, tablets, phones, medical devices, servers. It is one of the fastest-growing waste streams globally and much of it is never properly recycled. A circular economy approach — repairing, refurbishing, reusing, and recovering materials rather than defaulting to replacement — reduces both waste and the large embodied carbon locked up in manufacturing new devices. Sustainable and social-value procurement. Sustainable procurement buys goods and services in a way that weighs environmental and social impact alongside price and quality across the whole life-cycle. In England, the Public Services (Social Value) Act 2012 requires public bodies to consider economic, social, and environmental well-being when commissioning services, and NHS procurement policy now expects suppliers to publish carbon-reduction plans (see Topic 6.3 — Procurement & Commercial). Greenwashing. Greenwashing is presenting something as more environmentally sound than it really is. In digital health it shows up as vague "carbon-neutral cloud" claims, unaudited offsets, or counting a saving twice. Naming and avoiding it is a matter of professional integrity. Best practices # Measure before you claim, using recognized scopes. You cannot manage what you have not counted. Establish a baseline for your digital estate across Scopes 1, 2, and 3 — energy for on-premises kit, cloud and hosting, staff devices, and the embodied carbon of hardware — using the GHG Protocol structure. Even a rough, well-documented estimate beats an eloquent claim with no numbers behind it, and it gives you something to improve against year on year. Make sustainability a stated criterion in every business case. Fold carbon into the options appraisal alongside cost, benefit, and risk (see Topic 6.0 — Financial Management & Business Cases). Ask each option "what is the carbon cost, and what is the carbon saving?" so the greener choice is visible rather than accidental. Where a lower-carbon option costs more up front, say so honestly and let decision-makers weigh it; do not bury the trade-off. Right-size and decarbonize your infrastructure. Over-provisioned servers, idle test environments, and always-on workloads waste energy and money together. Turn off what you are not using, consolidate where you can, and prefer hosting regions and providers powered by renewable energy. Ask cloud suppliers for their power-usage effectiveness, their energy mix, and their own net-zero commitments — and treat evasive answers as a signal. Design services to cut system-wide carbon, not just IT carbon. The biggest wins usually sit outside the data centre. Virtual appointments, remote monitoring, e-prescribing, and shared care records can remove millions of patient and staff miles and reams of paper. Design for these outcomes deliberately, and measure the travel and materials you displace so the saving is evidenced rather than assumed. Be honest about rebound effects. Efficiency gains are often partly eaten by increased use — cheaper, easier virtual appointments can generate more appointments overall, and faster infrastructure invites heavier workloads. This rebound (or "Jevons") effect does not mean the intervention was wrong, but it does mean net savings are smaller than gross savings. Claim the net figure, and design demand-management and clinical-appropriateness rules so convenience does not quietly inflate consumption. Extend device life and design for a circular economy. The embodied carbon in manufacturing a laptop or tablet typically dwarfs the energy it uses in service, so keeping devices in use longer is one of the highest-leverage things you can do. Set longer refresh cycles, repair rather than replace, buy refurbished where clinically safe, and route end-of-life kit to certified reuse and recycling — never landfill or informal export. Build these expectations into contracts with your hardware and managed-service suppliers. Weight procurement for social value and demand carbon-reduction plans. Use the Social Value Act and NHS procurement policy to score suppliers on their environmental commitments, not just their price. Require credible, published carbon-reduction plans from significant suppliers, and check that a plan is a real trajectory with milestones rather than a glossy pledge. Since Scope 3 dominates the digital footprint, supplier behaviour is where most of your influence actually lies (see Topic 6.3 — Procurement & Commercial and Topic 9.0 — Collaborating with Partner Organizations). Report transparently and resist greenwashing. Publish your emissions and your progress, including where you are behind. Be precise about offsets — say what is actually reduced versus what is compensated elsewhere, and prefer removing emissions to buying credits. Avoid double-counting savings that another organization is also claiming, and never present an unaudited vendor slogan as your own achievement. Embed carbon into your metrics and governance. Put a small number of sustainability measures into your organizational objectives and key results and your key performance indicators (see Topic 10.0 — Objectives & Key Results (OKRs)), and review them in the same forums that review delivery and finance. Assign a named owner. Sustainability that lives only in an annual glossy report and never in an operational dashboard will not move. Questions to discuss with your team # Where does the carbon in our digital services actually sit — and are we measuring it, or guessing? This question forces you past comfortable assumptions. Most teams instinctively look at the data centre or the office lights, but for digital services the largest share is usually Scope 3: the embodied carbon of thousands of devices, the cloud capacity you rent, and the supply chain behind your software. The tension to debate is effort versus precision — a perfect carbon account is expensive and slow, while a rough one may mislead. A good, honest answer names your biggest emission sources with rough magnitudes, admits where the numbers are weak, and commits to improving the measurement over time rather than waiting for perfect data before acting. It also distinguishes what you control (your estate) from what you merely influence (your suppliers), because the tactics differ sharply between the two. When we claim a digital intervention saves carbon, are we counting the whole picture — including rebound and the footprint of the tech itself? Virtual appointments are the classic example. It is easy to multiply avoided car journeys by an emission factor and declare victory, but the honest calculation subtracts the footprint of the devices, networks, and data centres that make the appointment possible, and adjusts for rebound — the extra appointments that happen precisely because the service is now easier to access. The trade-off to surface is optimism versus credibility: overstated savings feel good and win funding, but collapse under scrutiny and corrode trust. A good answer shows a net figure, states its assumptions plainly, and is comfortable saying the saving is real but smaller than the headline. It should also ask whether the intervention improves care and equity, not only carbon, because a greener service that widens the digital divide is not a win. How will we hold suppliers to account for their emissions without either greenwashing or excluding good small suppliers? Because Scope 3 dominates, your leverage is largely through procurement — but this cuts two ways. Demand too little and you enable vague, unaudited claims; demand too much and you may lock out exactly the small, innovative digital-health suppliers the system needs, who lack the resources to produce elaborate carbon reports. The debate is about proportionality: what should you require of a two-person startup versus a hyperscale cloud provider? A good answer sets tiered, credible expectations — published carbon-reduction plans and evidence from large or high-impact suppliers, lighter proportionate commitments from small ones — and describes how you will verify claims rather than take them on faith. It should connect to your social-value scoring and to the collaboration practices in Topic 9.0 , treating suppliers as partners in reducing shared emissions rather than boxes to tick. How long should we keep devices in service, and what stops us from extending their life? The embodied carbon locked up in manufacturing a laptop, tablet, or monitoring device usually dwarfs the energy it burns in use, so a longer refresh cycle is one of the highest-leverage moves available — yet the pressures pushing the other way are real. Security teams worry about unsupported operating systems, clinicians need devices that perform, and managed-service contracts are often written around a default three- or four-year swap-out. The tension to work through is embodied carbon versus supportability and risk: keeping kit too long can create clinical-safety and cyber exposure, while binning it too soon wastes carbon and money. A good answer sets refresh cycles by evidence rather than habit, distinguishes devices that genuinely must be retired from those merely assumed to be obsolete, and builds repair, refurbishment, and certified reuse into hardware and managed-service contracts. It should also confront where end-of-life kit actually goes, because informal export or landfill quietly undoes the circular story you tell yourself. Who owns our carbon numbers, and do they live on an operating dashboard or only in an annual report? Sustainability that surfaces once a year in a glossy publication changes almost nothing; carbon only moves when it sits in the same forums, dashboards, and objectives that govern delivery and finance. The hard question is accountability: is there a named owner with the authority to change decisions, or is sustainability everyone's aspiration and no one's job? The trade-off to surface is attention and competition for it — a live carbon metric competes with cost, waiting times, and safety for scarce management focus, and will lose unless it is deliberately given standing. A good answer names an owner, puts a small, honest set of measures into the OKRs and KPIs reviewed alongside operational performance (see Topic 10.0 ), and describes the forum where a bad trend actually triggers action. It should be candid about how carbon will be weighed when it conflicts with other priorities, rather than pretending such conflicts never arise. When the lower-carbon option costs more or is harder to deliver, how will we make that trade-off — and who decides? Sustainability is easy to endorse in the abstract and awkward in the specific, because the greener choice sometimes carries a higher price, a longer timeline, or a delivery risk. If you never name those moments, the default — cheaper, faster, higher-carbon — wins silently every time, and your net-zero commitment becomes rhetoric. The tension is transparency versus convenience: burying the carbon cost of an option keeps the business case tidy but removes the decision from the people accountable for it. A good answer folds carbon explicitly into options appraisals alongside cost, benefit, and risk (see Topic 6.0 ), states honestly where the low-carbon route costs more up front, and puts the choice in front of decision-makers rather than pre-empting it in a spreadsheet. It should also say who holds the pen — whether a delivery lead can quietly trade carbon away, or whether that decision is escalated and recorded. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system (ICS) is rolling out a remote monitoring service for patients with heart failure across a largely rural region. The clinical case is strong: earlier detection of deterioration, fewer emergency admissions, and patients kept safely at home. The programme director, aware of the ICS Green Plan, insists sustainability is assessed from the start rather than retrofitted. The team builds a simple carbon model. On the savings side, they estimate the patient and community-nurse miles displaced by monitoring at home instead of in clinic — significant in a rural area with long travel distances. On the cost side, they count the tablets and monitoring devices issued to patients, the cloud hosting for the platform, and the eventual disposal of the kit. Crucially, they apply a rebound adjustment: because the service surfaces problems earlier, some patients will now have appointments they would previously have gone without, so gross travel savings overstate the net figure. The honest net saving is still clearly positive, and now defensible. Two design decisions follow directly. First, rather than issuing every patient a new tablet, the team sources refurbished devices and sets up a return-and-refurbish loop so kit is reissued rather than binned when a patient no longer needs it — cutting embodied carbon and cost together. Second, in the procurement for the monitoring platform, they score suppliers on published carbon-reduction plans and renewable hosting, applying the Social Value Act, while keeping the requirements proportionate so a promising small supplier is not excluded. At the go-live review, the ICS reports the net carbon saving alongside the clinical and financial results, states its assumptions openly, and flags the device supply chain as its largest remaining Scope 3 exposure. No heroic claims, no buried trade-offs — a credible story that survives challenge from the finance committee and the local sustainability lead alike. Sector lenses # Startup # A small digital-health startup has little estate and few staff, so its own Scope 1 and 2 emissions are tiny — but its customers increasingly ask about sustainability, and NHS procurement will require a carbon-reduction plan. The pragmatic move is to get the basics credibly in place early: choose a renewable-powered cloud region, avoid over-provisioning, write architecturally efficient software, and produce an honest, proportionate carbon-reduction plan you can actually stand behind. Resist the temptation to buy cheap offsets and call yourself "carbon neutral" — buyers and regulators increasingly see through it, and a modest, truthful position ages far better than an inflated one. Sustainability done plainly can be a genuine differentiator when you sell into the NHS. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home, a single-site clinic, or a small health-tech supplier past the startup stage — carries the same duties as a large trust but with none of the spare capacity, no dedicated sustainability or IT function, and cash that is already committed to running the service. The realistic approach is to concentrate on a few high-leverage, low-effort moves rather than a full carbon-accounting programme: extend device refresh cycles and buy refurbished where safe, switch to a renewable energy tariff and a greener hosting or cloud region, turn off idle kit, and route old equipment to certified reuse instead of the skip. When a bigger NHS partner or commissioner asks for a carbon-reduction plan, produce a short, honest one sized to the organization rather than copying an enterprise template you cannot sustain. Lean on shared resources — federation, primary care network, integrated care board, or trade-body guidance and emission factors — so you are not inventing the method alone. Done this way, sustainability lowers running costs as often as it raises them, which matters most when margins are thin.
