x: Topic 8.6 — Research & Real-World Evaluation In health and care, a digital innovation is only as trustworthy as the evidence that it actually works in practice — so you must design that evidence in from the start, at a rigour proportionate to the risk and the claims you make. Why this matters in health and care # Every digital product you deploy makes an implicit promise: this will help patients, staff, or the system without causing harm. In most sectors an unproven promise costs a customer or a quarter of revenue. In health and care it can cost lives, widen inequity, or erode the public trust on which the whole system depends. Enthusiasm and a good demo are not evidence, and a plausible mechanism is not proof of benefit. The history of digital health is full of tools that looked convincing and were adopted at scale before anyone had shown they worked — and some that quietly caused harm, missed diagnoses, or drove clinicians to workarounds. Regulators, commissioners, and clinicians have responded by raising the bar: they now expect credible, proportionate evidence before, during, and after deployment. If you cannot demonstrate that your service delivers the outcomes you claim, you should expect it to be challenged, defunded, or withdrawn — and rightly so. Evidence is also an equity and safety issue, not a bureaucratic hurdle. A tool that improves average outcomes can still harm a subgroup — the digitally excluded, people with limited English, or a population under-represented in your training data. Only deliberate evaluation reveals this. Generating good evidence is therefore part of your duty of care, your stewardship of public money, and your credibility with the people you serve (see Topic 1.3 — Evidence-Driven Decisions, and Topic 1.6 — Clinical Safety & Risk Management). Core concepts # Start with a distinction that governs everything else: the difference between research , service evaluation , and clinical audit . Research aims to generate new, generalizable knowledge — findings intended to be true beyond your local setting. Service evaluation asks how well this service is working here , using the standards the service itself has adopted. Clinical audit compares current practice against an existing, agreed standard and closes the loop with change. The distinction is not academic pedantry: it determines your governance path. Research involving National Health Service (NHS) patients, staff, or data almost always needs formal ethics approval; most service evaluation and audit do not. Misclassifying research as evaluation to dodge approvals is a serious governance failure. In England, research governance runs through the Health Research Authority (HRA), an arm's-length body of the Department of Health and Social Care. The HRA protects and promotes the interests of participants and coordinates approvals so a study is reviewed once for the whole country. Ethical review is carried out by a Research Ethics Committee (REC) — the UK equivalent of an institutional review board — which judges whether a study is ethical, proportionate, and safe for participants. Applications are submitted through the Integrated Research Application System (IRAS), a single online portal that routes your project to the RECs, HRA Approval, and other permissions it needs. The HRA's online decision tools help you determine whether your project counts as research at all. Much digital-health evidence is now built from real-world data (RWD) — information gathered outside controlled trials, such as electronic health records, device logs, registries, and claims data — analysed to produce real-world evidence (RWE) about how an intervention performs in ordinary conditions. RWE is powerful because digital tools generate rich usage data as a by-product, and because it reflects the messy reality that trials often exclude. It is also fragile: observational data are riddled with confounding and bias, so a naïve before-and-after comparison can mistake a seasonal trend or a co-occurring change for your effect. That is why evaluation design matters. The strongest design for causal claims remains the randomised controlled trial (RCT), which reduces bias by allocating participants at random. Digital contexts often favour pragmatic variants — cluster-randomized trials, and the stepped-wedge trial , in which sites cross over from control to intervention in randomized waves, fitting a phased roll-out you were going to do anyway. Where randomization is impractical, quasi-experimental designs help: interrupted time series (ITS) analysis tracks an outcome across many points before and after go-live to detect changes in level and trend, and is often the best feasible design for a system-wide digital change. Simple before-and-after comparison is the weakest and most misleading, because it cannot separate your effect from everything else that changed. Two further anchors shape the work. The evidence bar for digital health in England is set by the Evidence Standards Framework for Digital Health Technologies, published by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE): it grades tools by potential risk and specifies the strength of evidence expected for each tier. And a persistent distortion to guard against is publication bias — the tendency to share positive results and bury negative ones, which flatters the whole field and lets ineffective tools spread. Best practices # Classify your project before you design it. Use the HRA's decision tools to determine whether your work is research, service evaluation, or audit, and record the reasoning. This single step sets your governance path, your timeline, and your permissions. Get it wrong in the optimistic direction and you risk running unapproved research on patients; get it wrong in the cautious direction and you burden a simple evaluation with months of unnecessary process. Build evaluation in from the start, not as a bolt-on. Decide what "working" means, and how you will measure it, during discovery — before a line of production code (see Topic 3.4 — Discovery Phases). Capture a baseline before go-live, because you can never reconstruct it afterwards, and instrument the product to emit the outcome and usage data your design needs. Retrofitting evaluation onto a live service almost always yields weaker evidence at higher cost, and often no usable baseline at all. Match the rigour to the risk and the claim. A booking tool that reorders a waiting list needs less evidential weight than an algorithm that triages chest pain. Use the NICE Evidence Standards Framework to locate your tool's risk tier, and make claims your evidence can bear: if you have an interrupted time series showing reduced did-not-attend rates, say that — do not imply a mortality benefit. Proportionality protects patients from under-evidenced risk and protects you from wasting effort over-proving low-stakes tools. Choose the strongest design that is feasible, and name its limits. Reach for randomization when you can, and consider a stepped-wedge design when a phased roll-out makes a simultaneous control group impossible. When randomization is genuinely infeasible, prefer interrupted time series over naïve before-and-after, and pre-specify your analysis to resist the temptation to fish for a favourable result. Every design has weaknesses; state yours plainly so readers can weigh the evidence honestly. Use real-world data deliberately, and treat confounding as the enemy. Digital services generate abundant RWD, but abundance is not validity. Plan which data you will use, its quality and completeness, and the biases it carries, and involve an analyst or methodologist early rather than mining logs after the fact. Pre-register your outcomes and analysis where possible so the data cannot be tortured into telling you what you hoped to hear. Partner with people who generate evidence for a living. Universities, the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), and your regional Health Innovation Network — the bodies formerly known as Academic Health Science Networks (AHSNs) — bring methodological rigour, independence, funding routes, and credibility you cannot manufacture in-house. Independent evaluation carries far more weight with commissioners and clinicians than a supplier's own analysis. Engage them early, because the best designs are set before deployment, not after (see Topic 9.0 — Collaborating with Partner Organizations). Measure outcomes and economics, not just activity. Logins, click-throughs, and satisfaction scores are necessary but not sufficient; commissioners fund outcomes and value. Wherever you can, tie your evaluation to clinical outcomes, safety signals, equity across subgroups, and cost consequences, working with health economists to frame benefit in terms decision-makers use (see Topic 6.1 — Health Economics). Always disaggregate results by population so a tool that helps on average but harms a subgroup cannot hide behind the mean. Publish your results — including the disappointing ones. Commit up front to sharing findings, positive or negative, through a report, a preprint, or a peer-reviewed paper. Publishing negative results is a professional obligation: it spares other organizations from repeating your mistakes and counters the publication bias that lets ineffective tools proliferate. A culture that can say "we evaluated this and it did not work, so we stopped" is more trustworthy, not less. Close the loop and act on what you learn. Evidence that changes no decision is waste. Feed findings back into your roadmap, your business case, and your phasing decisions — scaling what works, fixing what half-works, and decommissioning what does not (see Topic 8.0 — Phasing in Innovation). Then re-evaluate, because a digital tool that worked at pilot scale in one setting can behave differently at national scale or in a different population. Questions to discuss with your team # Is what we are about to do research, service evaluation, or audit — and how confident are we in that answer? This is the first question because the answer sets your entire governance path, and getting it wrong has serious consequences. Talk through who your data subjects are, whether you are randomizing anything, whether you intend to produce generalizable knowledge, and whether you plan to publish — all signals that push a project towards "research". Resist any pressure to label something as evaluation simply because the approval route is faster; that pressure is exactly where governance failures begin. Use the HRA decision tool together, in the room, and write down your reasoning and who agreed it. A good answer is not just a label but a documented, defensible judgement that your information governance and clinical-safety colleagues have seen. If you are genuinely unsure, the honest move is to ask the HRA or your R&D office rather than guess in the direction that suits your timeline. What would count as convincing evidence that this works — and to whom? Different audiences demand different evidence: a clinician wants safety and outcome data, a commissioner wants cost and value, a regulator wants to see the appropriate NICE tier met, and a patient wants to know it is safe and fair for people like them. Debate what "works" actually means for your tool, and what result would make you stop — because a team that cannot articulate a stopping condition is not really evaluating. Consider which design is feasible given your roll-out plan, your data, and your budget, and be honest about the trade-off between rigour and speed. Discuss whether you need independent evaluation to be believed, and if so, who should do it. A good answer names the decision-makers, the outcomes that would move them, the design that can credibly produce those outcomes, and the threshold at which you would conclude the tool has failed. How will we handle a negative or disappointing result? Ask this before you have the result, because the answer is far more honest in advance. Explore what you would do if the evaluation showed no benefit, or benefit for the majority but harm for an excluded subgroup, and who would need to hear it. Surface the real pressures: sunk cost, supplier relationships, reputational worry, and the career incentives that make people want good news. Discuss your prior commitment to publish regardless of outcome, and what governance would hold you to that promise when the result is embarrassing. A good answer treats a well-run evaluation that produces a negative result as a success of process, not a failure of the team — and has a concrete plan for decommissioning gracefully, communicating candidly, and protecting the people who delivered the honest finding. What must we capture and instrument before go-live — and have we actually built it in? An evaluation is only as good as the baseline and the data it can draw on, and both are far cheaper to secure before launch than after. Work through what "before" state you need — admission rates, waiting times, error rates, current pathway costs — and confirm it is being recorded now, disaggregated by the subgroups you care about, because you can never reconstruct a baseline you failed to capture. Check whether the product itself will emit the outcome and usage data your chosen design needs, or whether that instrumentation is still a backlog wish. Debate the timing tension: pressure to ship often strips out measurement to hit a date, and every such cut quietly weakens the evidence you will later be asked to produce. Involve an analyst or methodologist while the design is still soft, not once the logs are already flowing. A good answer is a concrete list of what is captured, from when, at what granularity, and who has confirmed it is live — not an intention to sort it out after roll-out. How good is the data we intend to rely on, and what could confound our conclusion? Real-world data is abundant but rarely clean, and a plausible chart can hide seasonality, a concurrent service change, regression to the mean, or a coding shift that has nothing to do with your tool. Interrogate the provenance, completeness, and quality of every source you plan to use, and name the biases each one carries — who is missing from electronic records, which fields are unreliable, how consistently a code is applied. Ask what else changed in the same window as your go-live, because an interrupted time series or before-and-after that ignores those events will credit your tool with other people's effects. Decide in advance which comparison or design gives you the fairest counterfactual, and pre-specify the analysis so the data cannot be quietly reshaped to flatter the result. A good answer shows you have mapped the data's weaknesses honestly and chosen a design that can survive a sceptic pulling on each of them. Who should run this evaluation, and how independent does it need to be to be believed? Marking your own homework is the fastest way to have credible findings dismissed, so decide early whether a supplier's or in-house analysis will convince the audience you actually need to move. Weigh the cost and time of engaging an NIHR-supported academic team, a university, or a Health Innovation Network against the reputational and commercial value of independent, publishable evidence. Discuss where the conflicts of interest sit — the people who built or bought the tool are rarely the right people to judge whether it works — and how you will insulate the evaluation from pressure to produce good news. Consider what partners bring beyond independence: methodological rigour, funding routes, and standing with commissioners and clinicians you cannot manufacture in-house. A good answer matches the degree of independence to the stakes and the scepticism of the decision-makers, and secures that partnership before the design is fixed rather than after the results disappoint. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system (ICS) commissions a remote-monitoring app for patients with chronic heart failure, hoping to cut unplanned admissions. The supplier's slides show a 30% reduction elsewhere, and there is pressure to roll out fast across all twelve boroughs before the winter. The digital delivery lead pauses to classify the work. Because the ICS wants generalizable findings and intends to publish, and because it will analyse identifiable patient data for a new purpose, this is research, not service evaluation — so an IRAS application and REC review are needed. Rather than treat that as a blocker, the lead approaches the regional Health Innovation Network and a local university's NIHR-supported research team, who help design the study and co-write the application. Instead of switching everything on at once, they adopt a stepped-wedge design: the twelve boroughs go live in randomized waves over nine months, so every borough eventually gets the app while the staggered start provides a fair comparison. A baseline of admission rates, disaggregated by deprivation and ethnicity, is captured before the first wave. Using the NICE Evidence Standards Framework, the team places the tool in a tier that carries clinical risk and sets the evidence expectation accordingly, pre-registering admission rates, mortality as a safety signal, and cost per admission avoided as outcomes. Nine months on, the interim analysis is sobering: overall admissions fall modestly, but among the most deprived cohort — who use the app least — there is no benefit and a worrying rise in late presentations. The team does not bury this. They report it to the ICS board, pause the roll-out to those cohorts, redesign onboarding and add telephone support for digitally excluded patients, and publish both the shortfall and the redesign. The result is a service that genuinely helps and a decision-making board that trusts the evidence because it has seen the team tell the truth when it hurt. Sector lenses # Startup # A small digital-health company lives or dies by evidence, but rarely has the money or in-house methodology to generate it alone. Your fastest credible route is partnership: an NIHR-funded academic collaborator or a Health Innovation Network real-world evaluation gives you independent findings that investors and NHS buyers actually believe, far more than a self-published white paper. Be disciplined about proportionate claims — over-claiming to win a pilot is the quickest way to fail a later evaluation and lose your reputation. Build data capture into your product architecture from day one, because retrofitting it after your seed round is expensive and yields a poorer evidence base. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home, or a single-site clinic adopting a digital tool — is expected to evaluate what it deploys, yet has no R&D office, no methodologist, and barely any spare hands. Your realistic move is not to run a trial but to run a disciplined service evaluation: capture a simple baseline before you switch on, agree a handful of honest outcome measures, and record what actually changes for your patients. Lean hard on shared infrastructure you do not have to build — your Health Innovation Network, a local university, or a federation or primary care network that can pool data and expertise across several small sites. Be especially wary of accepting a supplier's headline claim at face value when you cannot independently check it, and be clear that classification duties still apply to you even at small scale. Proportionate, well-documented local evidence is both achievable and enough to justify continuing, adapting, or dropping the tool. Enterprise # A large NHS trust or ICS has an R&D office, information-governance machinery, and existing academic ties — assets a startup would envy — but also the inertia to deploy tools trust-wide before evaluating them. x: Topic 9.0 — Collaborating with Partner Organizations In one sentence: Digital health and care outcomes now depend less on what any single organization builds and more on how honestly, safely, and durably it collaborates across the boundaries between NHS trusts, councils, social care, the voluntary sector, universities, and suppliers. Why this matters in health and care # No single organization holds the whole of a person's care. A frail older adult moves between a GP practice, an acute trust, a community team, a council reablement service, a care home, and perhaps a hospice — each a separate legal entity, with its own systems, governance, and incentives. The value your programme delivers is realized at these seams, and it is at these seams that harm accumulates: the missed allergy, the duplicated assessment, the discharge that collapses because the package of care was never arranged. Collaboration is therefore not a soft skill layered on top of delivery; it is the delivery. Integrated Care Systems (ICS) in England, and Regional Partnership Boards in Wales, exist precisely because Parliament judged that competition between organizations had gone too far and that population health requires organizations to plan and act together. The legal architecture — the Health and Care Act 2022 , Integrated Care Boards (ICBs), and Integrated Care Partnerships (ICPs) — is a statutory instruction to collaborate. The stakes are concrete. Collaboration touches public money (shared platforms funded from multiple budgets), safety (data flowing between clinicians who have never met), equity (whether the third sector reaches communities the NHS cannot), and statutory duty (each partner remains individually accountable to its own regulator and to the Information Commissioner ). Get the collaboration right and you compound everyone's effort; get it wrong and you multiply everyone's risk. Core concepts # The partner landscape. Your collaborators are not interchangeable. NHS trusts and foundation trusts operate under NHS England oversight and national contracts. Local authorities are democratically accountable, cash-constrained, and own adult social care and public health. Social care providers are largely private or voluntary, fragmented, and thinly resourced for digital. The voluntary, community and social enterprise (VCSE) sector brings reach and trust but little infrastructure; within it, a social enterprise trades to fund a social mission rather than to distribute profit, which makes it a willing delivery partner but one whose surpluses are already committed. Universities bring evidence and evaluation. Industry suppliers bring capability and a commercial motive. Each has a different clock, a different funding cycle, and a different definition of success. Integrated Care Systems. An ICS is a partnership of the organizations in a geography that plan and deliver joined-up health and care. It has two statutory bodies: the ICB (an NHS body that plans and funds most NHS services) and the ICP (a broader committee, jointly convened with local government, that sets the integrated care strategy). Crucially, an ICS is not a single organization and not a single data controller — it is a set of controllers who must agree how to act together. Governance of collaboration. Because no partner can direct another, collaboration runs on agreements rather than authority . The instruments are a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to set intent, a joint committee or programme board to make decisions, terms of reference that name who decides what, a shared roadmap so partners invest in step, and — where personal data moves — a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA) or Information Sharing Agreement (ISA) underpinned by Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). Information governance and the Caldicott Principles. Information governance sets the framework; the eight Caldicott Principles govern the use of confidential patient information: justify the purpose, use it only when necessary, use the minimum necessary, access on a strict need-to-know basis, ensure everyone is aware of their responsibilities, comply with the law, and — the newer principles — the duty to share information can be as important as the duty to protect it, and inform patients about how their data is used. Every partnership needs a named Caldicott Guardian and a Senior Information Risk Owner (SIRO) at each controller, working under UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 . Interoperability and open standards. Shared care records only work if systems can exchange meaning, not just files. That means interoperability built on recognized standards — HL7 FHIR for exchange, SNOMED CT for clinical terms, and NHS England's data and interoperability standards — and rejecting bespoke point-to-point integrations that lock value inside one vendor relationship. Best practices # Start from a shared population outcome, not a shared system. Anchor the collaboration in an outcome every partner already cares about — reducing emergency admissions from care homes, say — and let the technology follow. Partners will compromise on architecture far more readily than on purpose, so make the purpose the thing you agree first and revisit often. Make governance proportionate and visible. Stand up a joint board with clear terms of reference, a single shared roadmap, and named decision rights before you write a line of code. Keep it light enough to move but formal enough to survive a change of personnel; document who can commit each organization, because verbal agreements evaporate when the sponsoring director leaves. Treat information governance as an enabler, not a gate. Engage Caldicott Guardians, SIROs, and Data Protection Officers at the start, complete a joint DPIA, and put a signed Data Sharing Agreement in place that names purposes, lawful bases, controllers, and retention. Invoke the seventh Caldicott Principle explicitly: for direct care, the duty to share can be as important as the duty to protect, and framing IG this way turns it from a blocker into a partner. Mandate open standards and interoperability in every agreement. Require FHIR-based exchange and recognized terminologies (SNOMED CT, dm+d) as a condition of participation, and align to NHS England's shared care record and interoperability requirements. Open standards are how you keep future options open; they are the single most effective defence against vendor lock-in (see Topic 9.1 — Working with Local & National Governments on national mandates). Manage suppliers as a portfolio, and design against lock-in from day one. Insist on data portability, exit clauses, documented APIs, and ownership of your own configuration and data. Follow the Provider Selection Regime for in-scope health care services and public procurement rules elsewhere; a supplier who resists open standards or an exit plan is telling you their commercial strategy is your dependency. Invest in the shared care record as shared infrastructure. A shared care record — the read-only view across a system, distinct from any one electronic patient record — is a collaboration asset owned by the ICS, not by a vendor. Govern it jointly, fund it jointly, and hold its data quality to a common standard, because a record that partners do not trust is a record they will not use. Align incentives before you rely on goodwill. Collaboration fails when the organization asked to invest is not the one that reaps the benefit — a hospital funds a scheme that saves a council money. Surface these asymmetries early and use pooled budgets, gain-share arrangements, or Better Care Fund mechanisms so that effort and reward sit together. Build trust deliberately and protect it. Trust is the operating currency of partnership and it is built by keeping small promises, sharing bad news early, and never surprising a partner in public. Create the routines — regular joint stand-ups, a shared risk log, a single version of the truth — that let trust accumulate rather than reset with every reorganization. Treat VCSE and community organizations as genuine delivery partners. Voluntary and community organizations reach the digitally-excluded and seldom-heard groups the statutory system struggles to reach — carers, homeless people, migrants, older adults offline — because they hold trust the NHS and councils cannot buy. Bring them in to co-design and to deliver support, not merely to be consulted late, and connect their work to your digital inclusion offer so that assisted-digital and face-to-face routes are staffed by the people communities already turn to (see Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility). Partner fairly and sustainably with small, under-resourced organizations. Make governance and data-sharing proportionate to a partner that may have no IG team and a handful of laptops, rather than imposing statutory-sector process on volunteers. Fund the work properly — cover staff time, kit, and overheads instead of treating VCSE effort as free capacity to be drawn down — because a partner asked to deliver on goodwill will quietly withdraw when the grant runs out, taking the community reach with them. Questions to discuss with your team # When a partner's interests diverge from ours mid-programme, how do we decide whether to compromise, escalate, or walk away? Every partnership starts with a shared purpose, but purposes drift: a council faces an in-year budget cut, a trust reorganizes, a supplier is acquired, an election changes a leader's mandate. Because no partner can direct another, the collaboration runs on agreement rather than authority, so the team needs a settled view of how it will behave when goodwill is tested rather than improvising under pressure. The tension is between protecting the relationship — the operating currency of partnership — and protecting the outcome, the patients, and your own statutory accountability, which cannot be delegated to a joint board. Consider concrete triggers: what would make you invoke the exit clause in a supplier contract, escalate to the ICP, or accept a smaller shared scope rather than lose the partner entirely? An honest answer names the few red lines that are non-negotiable (patient safety, lawful basis for data sharing, your own regulatory duties), distinguishes them from the many things that are genuinely tradeable, and agrees who holds the authority to make the call so it does not fall to whoever happens to be in the room. It also acknowledges that walking away is sometimes the responsible choice, and that a partnership kept alive only to avoid an awkward conversation quietly multiplies everyone's risk. Are we treating social care providers and the voluntary sector as genuine partners, or as afterthoughts we expect to keep pace with the NHS? Partnerships default to NHS-to-NHS deals because those partners share systems, funding language, and a national regulator, while care homes, domiciliary providers, and VCSE organizations are fragmented, thinly resourced for digital, and operating on margins that leave no room to absorb integration costs. Yet these are precisely the partners who reach the people the NHS struggles to reach and who often carry the workload when a scheme succeeds. The trade-off is uncomfortable: designing for the thinnest-resourced partner slows the programme and raises its cost, but excluding them hollows out the very integration the ICS exists to deliver. Concrete angles worth debating include whether your governance has committing officers from social care at the table or only NHS directors, whether your data-sharing agreements assume infrastructure a small care home simply does not have, and whether incentive asymmetry — a hospital funding a scheme that saves a council money, or a care home bearing monitoring workload for someone else's benefit — is being addressed through pooled budgets or gain-share, or quietly ignored. A good answer is specific about which under-resourced partners matter most for your population outcome, what practical support (funding, kit, training, simplified onboarding) they need to participate as equals, and how you will know whether they are genuinely engaged or merely nominally signed up. How do we make information governance an enabler that partners trust, rather than a gate that stalls every data flow? Confidential patient information moving between organizations that have never met is where collaboration creates its most acute risk and its most valuable benefit, and IG is the mechanism that decides which. Teams routinely treat IG as a late sign-off, which guarantees that Caldicott Guardians, SIROs, and DPOs raise objections at go-live that could have been designed out months earlier — but the opposite failure is just as real, where an over-cautious reading of the rules blocks sharing that is lawful and in the patient's direct-care interest. The seventh Caldicott Principle is the crux of the debate: the duty to share information can be as important as the duty to protect it, yet organizations instinctively over-weight protection because the penalties for a breach are visible and the harms of not sharing — the missed allergy, the duplicated assessment — are diffuse and unattributed. The team should examine whether it engages IG at inception with a joint DPIA and a signed Data Sharing Agreement naming purposes and lawful basis, or whether it treats IG as a hurdle to clear at the end; and whether each controller's Caldicott Guardian and SIRO understand the shared purpose well enough to say yes quickly. A strong answer frames IG as a partner in the design, is precise about the lawful basis and the minimum necessary dataset, and can point to the routines — a shared risk log, named accountable people at each controller — that let partners trust each other with data rather than defaulting to defensive refusal. When a supplier offers a faster proprietary route, how do we hold the line on open standards and portability? Every collaboration eventually faces a supplier or a partner offering a quicker, cheaper path that quietly depends on a bespoke integration, a proprietary data model, or a format only they can read. The pressure to accept it is real: budgets are annual, patients are waiting, and open standards can feel like an abstract principle set against a working demo. But point-to-point connectors calcify into dependencies no one can afford to replace, and the value locks inside one vendor relationship precisely where the collaboration meant to keep it shared. The tension is between short-term delivery velocity and long-term optionality — the ability to swap a component, add a partner, or exit a contract without renegotiating the whole record. Concrete angles to debate: does every partner and supplier agreement actually mandate FHIR-based exchange, recognized terminologies (SNOMED CT, dm+d), documented APIs, and ownership of your own configuration and data, or are these aspirations that erode under delivery pressure? An honest answer is specific about which standards are non-negotiable conditions of participation, names who has the authority to refuse a non-compliant offer, and is candid that the cheapest option today is often the one that hands a supplier your dependency for a decade. How do we make this partnership durable enough to survive a reorganization or the departure of its sponsor? Health and care is reorganized often, and collaboration built on the goodwill of two named directors dissolves the moment either of them moves. Because verbal agreements evaporate when the sponsoring director leaves, a partnership that has not written down who can commit each organization is one bad week away from stalling. The trade-off is between the speed of personality-led momentum, which gets an early pilot moving, and the resilience of documented governance, which feels bureaucratic until you need it. The team should ask whether decision rights and each partner's committing officer are actually named in the terms of reference, whether the shared roadmap and risk log would still make sense to someone who inherits them cold, and whether the collaboration's purpose is anchored in a population outcome the partners' successors will still care about. Consider what happens at the next ICS boundary change or council election: does the partnership carry its institutional memory, or does it reset? A strong answer describes the routines — a single version of the truth, a standing joint board, written decision rights — that let the collaboration renew itself rather than depend on the individuals who happened to start it. Who owns, funds, and assures the quality of the shared infrastructure we all depend on? A shared care record, a joint platform, or a common data pipeline is a collaboration asset that belongs to the system rather than to any one partner or vendor — but "owned by everyone" too easily becomes owned by no one. The hard questions are who pays to run it once the launch funding ends, who is accountable when its data quality slips, and who arbitrates when partners disagree about what it should do next. The tension is that every partner benefits from the shared record yet each has its own budget cycle and its own priorities, so the infrastructure is chronically under-funded relative to how much everyone relies on it. A record that partners do not trust is a record they will not use, so data quality is not a technical afterthought but the thing that determines whether the collaboration delivers at all. Concrete angles: is the shared care record jointly governed and jointly funded by the ICS, or dependent on a single organization's grant and a vendor's roadmap; is there a common data-quality standard that every contributing partner is held to; and who has the mandate to invest in it as shared infrastructure rather than treating it as someone else's cost? An honest answer names the accountable owner, the sustainable funding mechanism, and the quality standard, and is frank about whether the current arrangement would survive the first partner deciding it can no longer afford its share. In practice: a health & care example # A fictional ICS, "Rivermouth", wants to cut avoidable A&E attendances from its 60 care homes. The partners are two acute trusts, a community trust, the county council (which commissions the homes), the homes themselves (mostly small private providers), a local hospice, a university evaluation team, and a telehealth supplier. Rivermouth resists the temptation to procure a platform first. Instead the ICP agrees a single outcome — a 20% reduction in avoidable conveyances over two years — and stands up a joint delivery board with terms of reference naming decision rights and each partner's committing officer. A shared roadmap sequences the work: first a shared care record view for care home staff, then remote vital-signs monitoring. Information governance runs in parallel, not after. The ICB's Caldicott Guardian convenes the controllers, a joint DPIA is completed, and a Data Sharing Agreement names the lawful basis for direct care and the minimum dataset the homes may see. The telehealth contract is let under the Provider Selection Regime with mandated FHIR interfaces, an exit plan, and council ownership of the configuration. The asymmetry is addressed head-on: the acute trusts benefit from fewer admissions, but the homes bear the workload. A gain-share from the Better Care Fund reimburses homes for staff time on monitoring. Eighteen months in, conveyances are down 14%, the university's independent evaluation confirms the trend, and — because the standards were open — the ICS can swap one homes-facing app without renegotiating the whole record. Sector lenses # Startup # A small digital-health company collaborates from a position of weakness: it needs the partnership more than the partnership needs it, and a single stalled Data Sharing Agreement can burn the runway. Keep the ask narrow — one dataset, one lawful basis, one named outcome —

x: Topic 9.1 — Working with Local & National Governments In one sentence: Digital health and care leaders succeed inside the public system not by resisting its rules on funding, assurance, and accountability but by learning them well enough to move fast within them and shape them over time. Why this matters in health and care # Almost every pound you spend and every service you run is bounded by the machinery of government. National bodies set the mandate, the standards, and the money; local government owns social care and public health; and Parliament, ministers, and the public hold all of it to account. A digital leader who treats this machinery as an obstacle to be circumvented will burn credibility and get blocked; one who treats it as the terrain will get funded, assured, and adopted. The stakes are distinctive in health and care. You are spending public money on services that must be safe, equitable, and defensible in front of a select committee, an auditor, or a coroner. Funding arrives on political cycles that rarely match delivery cycles. Standards are not optional preferences but conditions of approval. And the same transparency that makes government trustworthy — Freedom of Information, published spend, public board papers — means your decisions will be read by people who were not in the room. Getting this right protects patients and public money at once. A well-made business case wins investment that survives scrutiny; a service that passes assessment is one the public can trust; alignment to national strategy means your work is amplified rather than overridden at the next reorganization. The discipline of working with government is what turns a good idea into a funded, assured, sustained service. Core concepts # The national bodies and what they control. Learn who holds which lever. NHS England sets the operational mandate, funding flows, and many digital standards. The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) sets policy and sponsors legislation. The devolved governments — in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland — run their own health systems with their own bodies (NHS Scotland, NHS Wales, HSC in Northern Ireland). The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) owns health protection. NICE appraises clinical and cost-effectiveness and sets the Evidence Standards Framework for digital health technologies. The MHRA regulates medical devices , including software as a medical device. The Care Quality Commission (CQC) inspects and registers providers. Each is a gate or an enabler depending on how early you engage it. Policy, legislation, and mandates. Government works through hierarchy: legislation (e.g. the Health and Care Act 2022 ) enables, national strategy directs, and annual planning guidance and the NHS mandate turn direction into obligations with deadlines. Knowing where your work sits in this chain tells you whether you are complying, contributing, or freelancing. Funding cycles and the business case. Public spending is appraised through HM Treasury 's Green Book using the Five Case Model — strategic, economic, commercial, financial, and management cases — progressing through a Strategic Outline Case, Outline Business Case, and Full Business Case. Money is split between capital (assets) and revenue (running costs), governed by different rules and rarely interchangeable, and is released in cycles set by Spending Reviews and annual budgets rather than by project readiness. Assurance and standards. Digital spending passes through controls. The Government Digital Service (GDS) spend controls and the Service Standard require services above thresholds to pass service assessments at alpha, beta, and live. In health specifically, the NHS Service Standard, the Digital Technology Assessment Criteria (DTAC), the Clinical Risk Management standards (DCB0129/DCB0160), and NICE's evidence standards form the assurance stack. These are not bureaucracy for its own sake; they are how the system decides your service is safe and worth the money. Transparency and accountability. Public bodies operate in the open: Freedom of Information requests, published spend over £25,000, public board papers, National Audit Office and Public Accounts Committee scrutiny, and the Nolan Principles of public life. Assume anything you write may be read publicly, and let that raise your standard rather than your defensiveness. Best practices # Map the accountability chain before you plan the work. Identify which national body owns the mandate, the standard, and the money for your area, and where your work sits in the chain from legislation to planning guidance. Knowing whether you are complying with a mandate or proposing something novel changes who you must convince and how. Write the business case in the government's own language. Use HM Treasury's Green Book Five Case Model and progress through Strategic Outline, Outline, and Full Business Cases; be explicit about capital versus revenue and about benefits that are measurable and monetized where possible. A case that assessors recognize structurally is a case they can approve; a brilliant idea in the wrong format stalls. Engage assurance early and treat it as design input. Book pre-assessment conversations with GDS/service assessors, DTAC, and clinical safety (DCB0129/DCB0160) before you build, not after. Assessment findings are cheap when they arrive in discovery and ruinous when they arrive at go-live (see Topic 9.0 — Collaborating with Partner Organizations on IG engaged early). Align explicitly to national strategy and standards. Show how your work delivers the NHS mandate, planning guidance, and open-standards requirements, and cite them by name. Alignment is protection: work that visibly advances the national direction survives leadership changes and budget rounds; work that ignores it is the first thing cut. Plan delivery around funding cycles, not against them. Sequence work so that value lands within the financial year money is released, and never assume multi-year revenue that has not been secured through a Spending Review or budget. Design increments that each stand alone, so a funding pause degrades scope gracefully rather than stranding a half-built platform. Do policy engagement properly and transparently. Engage with officials and ministers through the proper channels, register interests, and follow the rules on lobbying and transparency; bring evidence, not just advocacy. Done openly, policy engagement is a legitimate and valuable way to shape the system; done in the shadows it destroys the trust your work depends on. Design for transparency from the start. Assume board papers, spend, and decision records will be public, and write them to a standard you would defend in front of the Public Accounts Committee. Publishing your reasoning, your data-quality limits, and your risks openly builds the credibility that closed decision-making erodes. Respect the political cycle without being captured by it. Elections, ministerial changes, and reorganizations reset priorities on a rhythm that ignores delivery timelines. Keep the mission steady, translate it into whatever the current priority language is, and protect the delivery team from every change of political weather. Questions to discuss with your team # Where does our work actually sit in the chain from legislation to planning guidance, and are we complying, contributing, or freelancing? Government works through a hierarchy — legislation enables, national strategy directs, and the NHS mandate and annual planning guidance turn direction into dated obligations — and knowing your position in that chain tells you who you must convince and how much latitude you have. Teams often cannot answer this cleanly, which is dangerous because work that visibly advances the national direction survives leadership changes and budget rounds, while work that cuts across the mandate is the first thing overridden at the next reorganization. The tension worth debating is between alignment as genuine protection and alignment as box-ticking theatre: it is entirely possible to cite the planning guidance on paper while freelancing in practice, and a large organization can get away with that until an audit says otherwise. Concrete angles include naming which national body owns the mandate, the standard, and the money for your specific area (and the correct devolved system if you are outside England), identifying whether you are delivering an existing obligation or proposing something genuinely novel, and being honest about the parts of your programme that no mandate actually requires. A good answer maps the accountability chain for this initiative specifically rather than gesturing at national strategy in the abstract, distinguishes the work that is mandated from the work that is discretionary, and shows the alignment concretely enough that an assessor or auditor would recognize it — not merely asserts it in a slide. How do we design delivery so that a funding pause, a Spending Review, or an election does not strand a half-built platform? Public money arrives on political cycles set by Spending Reviews and annual budgets, split between capital and revenue that are governed by different rules and rarely interchangeable, and released on a rhythm that almost never matches delivery cycles. The recurring failure is to assume multi-year revenue that was never actually secured and to build something whose value only materializes after the money it depends on has evaporated. The trade-off to debate is between the efficiency and coherence of one big build and the resilience of standalone increments that each land within a funded period — the former is cheaper if nothing goes wrong and ruinous if the funding weather changes, which in government it reliably does. Worth examining concretely: have you separated the one-off capital build from the recurring revenue for support, and secured the revenue line explicitly rather than hoping for it; can your programme degrade scope gracefully if a general election pauses new spending, so the first increment still demonstrates value; and are you depending on a single enthusiastic official whose priorities reset at the next reshuffle? A strong answer sequences the work so each release stands alone and delivers something real within the money already committed, treats unsecured future revenue as a risk rather than a plan, and anchors the mission to the published national mandate so it outlives any individual sponsor. Are we treating assurance and transparency as things to fear and defer, or as design inputs and sources of credibility? The assurance stack — service assessment, DTAC, clinical safety under DCB0129/DCB0160, and the relevant NICE evidence tier — is how the system decides your service is safe and worth the money, and it is radically cheaper when engaged in discovery than when it surfaces findings at go-live and forces expensive rework. In parallel, public bodies operate in the open: Freedom of Information requests, published spend, public board papers, and National Audit Office and Public Accounts Committee scrutiny mean your decisions will be read by people who were not in the room. The instinct on both fronts is defensive — to treat assurance as a hurdle to clear late and transparency as a threat to manage — and the discussion should confront how much that instinct is quietly shaping the team's behaviour. Concrete angles include whether you have booked pre-assessment conversations with service assessors and clinical-safety leads before building rather than after, whether the NICE evidence tier is agreed up front so the evaluation is designed to meet it, and whether your board papers and spend records are written to a standard you would willingly defend in front of the Public Accounts Committee. An honest answer recognizes that assessment findings are cheap in discovery and ruinous at launch, that publishing your reasoning, data-quality limits, and risks openly builds credibility that closed decision-making erodes, and that both assurance and transparency should raise the team's standard rather than its defensiveness. Are we engaging the correct national system for our geography, or quietly defaulting to England's bodies and rules? Health and care is devolved, and Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland run their own systems with their own bodies, standards, and funding routes rather than NHS England, so a plan that names the wrong machinery is not merely imprecise but unworkable. The failure is easy to make and easy to miss: teams steeped in NHS England guidance, the English Service Standard, and DTAC assume those apply everywhere, and the assumption survives until a Scottish board or a Welsh commissioner asks which of their standards you have met. The tension is that much good practice genuinely does transfer — the Green Book, clinical-safety discipline, the habit of engaging assurance early — while the institutions, evidence expectations, and approval gates do not, so the discussion has to separate the portable method from the geography-specific apparatus. Concrete angles include naming the correct national body that owns the mandate, the standard, and the money for each jurisdiction you serve, checking whether a service designed for one nation can even be deployed in another without re-assurance, and being explicit about cross-border data flows and information-governance differences. A good answer identifies the right national system for every geography in scope, distinguishes the transferable discipline from the jurisdiction-specific gates, and refuses to treat "the NHS" as a single undifferentiated buyer. Are we engaging with policy and ministers through the proper channels, with evidence rather than advocacy, and to a standard we would be content to see published? Shaping the system is legitimate and often necessary — the rules, standards, and priorities are made by people you can reach — but the line between influencing policy openly and lobbying in the shadows is exactly the line that governs whether that engagement builds trust or destroys it. Public life runs on the Nolan Principles and on transparency rules, registers of interest, and lobbying disclosure, and a digital leader who forgets that a meeting note or a Freedom of Information request can surface the whole exchange is one bad email from a credibility crisis. The tension worth debating is between the genuine value of getting into the room early to shape a standard before it hardens and the risk of being seen — rightly or wrongly — to have secured advantage through access rather than merit. Concrete angles include whether you engage officials and ministers through the proper channels rather than back doors, whether you bring evidence and honest limitations rather than one-sided advocacy, whether interests are registered and the rules on lobbying followed, and whether every exchange would read well if published. An honest answer treats openness as the source of the influence rather than a constraint on it, brings evidence that acknowledges what you do not yet know, and holds every contact to a standard the team would defend in front of the Committee on Standards in Public Life. How do we hold the mission steady across elections, reshuffles, and reorganizations without either ignoring the political weather or being captured by it? Government resets priorities and vocabulary on a political rhythm — elections, ministerial changes, and structural reorganizations — that pays no attention to delivery timelines, and a team can be whipsawed into rewriting its strategy with every reshuffle or, at the opposite extreme, into ignoring the shift until its funding and cover quietly evaporate. The skill is neither rigidity nor weathervaning but translation: keeping the underlying clinical or public-value mission constant while re-expressing it in whatever the current priority language happens to be, so the work is recognized as delivering today's agenda without actually changing what it does. The trade-off to debate is how much to bend the framing and the roadmap toward a new minister's emphasis before you are no longer delivering your original mission at all, and who on the team is responsible for absorbing that political turbulence so delivery engineers do not feel it. Concrete angles include whether the mission is anchored to a published, durable national mandate rather than to a single sponsor's preference, whether you have a deliberate way to re-translate the same work into new priority language, and whether the delivery team is shielded from every change of political weather. A strong answer keeps the mission and the increments steady, retranslates the narrative deliberately rather than reflexively, protects the team from churn, and can tell the difference between adapting the framing and abandoning the purpose. In practice: a health & care example # A fictional ICB wants to fund a regional digital service that lets people manage long-term conditions from home. The temptation is to procure a product and announce it. Instead the team maps the terrain first: NHS England owns the digital standards and much of the money, NICE's Evidence Standards Framework will judge the clinical claim, DTAC and DCB0129 clinical safety are conditions of deployment, and the county council co-funds because social care benefits. The business case is written to the Green Book Five Case Model, moving from a Strategic Outline Case to a Full Business Case, and it separates the one-off capital build from the recurring revenue for support — securing the revenue line explicitly rather than assuming it. Benefits are monetized where possible and stated qualitatively where not, so assessors trust the numbers. Assurance is engaged in discovery. An early conversation with service assessors reshapes the onboarding journey; the DTAC and clinical-safety work runs alongside the build; the NICE evidence tier is agreed up front so the evaluation is designed to meet it. The team aligns the pitch to the current planning guidance and cites it by name, which protects the programme when a ministerial reshuffle changes the departmental emphasis. When a general election pauses new spending, the increment-by-increment design means the first release — remote monitoring for one condition — still lands within the funded year and demonstrates value. The public board papers, published in full, and an early National Audit Office-style self-review turn the transparency that leaders often fear into a source of credibility that helps unlock the next tranche. Sector lenses # Startup # A digital-health startup meets government as a supplier and a hopeful, not a rule-setter, and its survival depends on decoding assurance before the runway runs out. Treat DTAC, clinical safety (DCB0129/DCB0160), and the relevant NICE evidence tier as product requirements from day one, because a failed assessment late in a pilot can be fatal where an enterprise would merely reschedule. Learn to read the Green Book Five Case Model so a bid speaks the buyer's language, and target funding routes built for small firms — NHS innovation accelerators, SBRI competitions, framework agreements — rather than waiting on a Spending Review the company cannot influence. Guard against building for one enthusiastic official whose priorities reset at the next reshuffle; anchor to the published national mandate so the product outlives its first sponsor. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home, a domiciliary-care agency, or a single-site clinic — meets government not as a hopeful supplier but as a regulated operator that must satisfy CQC registration, DTAC-aligned procurement, and clinical-safety expectations with no dedicated digital or compliance team to lean on. The same duties that a large trust discharges through a governance department land on a practice manager or an owner already running the service

x: Topic 9.2 — Global & International Digital Health In one sentence: The principles in this book travel across borders, but the systems, laws, and social contracts they land in do not — so your job is to learn deliberately from other health systems, adopt the shared global standards, and adapt everything else to context rather than copying it. Why this matters in health and care # Digital health is not a British invention, and the United Kingdom is not its centre of gravity. The hardest, most instructive work in the field is happening in Estonia, India, Rwanda, Brazil, and Kenya as much as in London or Leeds. If you lead digital delivery in the NHS, an Integrated Care System, or an arms-length body and you look only inward, you will re-solve problems that others solved a decade ago, and you will miss the standards, tools, and cautionary tales that would have saved you years. This matters for reasons that go beyond efficiency. Health is a global commons: pathogens, evidence, clinical guidelines, and — increasingly — the software that runs care systems all move across borders. The same clinical-safety, equity, and public-trust concerns that define how you work at home reappear, amplified, when data and technology cross jurisdictions. A remote-monitoring tool that is safe in a well-connected English city may be unsafe when deployed where connectivity fails; a consent model that is lawful under one country's regime may be unlawful under another's; an algorithm trained on one population may quietly harm a different one. There is also a duty of humility. The UK both learns from and contributes to global health, and the flow runs in both directions. Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) have pioneered mobile-first care, community health worker platforms, and open-source national infrastructure that richer systems now study. Treating international digital health as charity, or as a menu of models to lift and drop into England, is the fastest route to failure. Treating it as a discipline of careful, reciprocal learning is how you make this book's claim of "internationally transferable principles" honest rather than hollow. Core concepts # Global health and digital health. Global health is the study and practice of improving health and achieving health equity for all people worldwide. Digital health is the use of information and communication technologies — records, apps, devices, analytics, and artificial intelligence — to deliver and improve care. The intersection is the subject of this topic: how digital tools and ways of working move, or fail to move, between health systems that differ in wealth, law, infrastructure, and culture. The WHO global strategy and digital public goods. The World Health Organization (WHO) published a Global Strategy on Digital Health that frames digital health as an enabler of universal health care — often called universal health coverage (UHC), the goal that everyone can use the services they need without financial hardship. A central idea is the digital public good : open-source software, open data, open standards, and open content — sometimes called "global goods" — that any country can adopt and adapt rather than buying proprietary systems it cannot own or afford. WHO-endorsed tools such as DHIS2 (a health information platform used in more than seventy countries) and OpenMRS (an open-source medical record) are canonical examples. International interoperability and terminology standards. Borders are crossed not by moving whole systems but by sharing a common language. Three standards do most of the work: HL7 Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) for exchanging structured clinical data; SNOMED CT , the international clinical terminology governed by SNOMED International; and WHO's ICD-11 , the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases, used for mortality, morbidity, and reimbursement coding worldwide. These are the shared vocabulary that lets an English record, an Estonian record, and a WHO statistical return mean the same thing. (See Topic 4.3 — Interoperability & Data Standards.) mHealth and leapfrogging. mHealth — mobile health — is the delivery of health services and information through mobile phones. In many LMICs, mobile-first care is not a downgrade but the primary channel, and it illustrates leapfrogging : skipping a generation of infrastructure (here, fixed-line connectivity and paper-heavy hospital IT) to move straight to newer technology. The lesson for richer systems is not that phones are cheap, but that constraint breeds designs — offline-first, low-bandwidth, SMS-fallback — that are more resilient than many "advanced" alternatives. Data sovereignty and cross-border data flows. Data sovereignty is the principle that data is governed by the laws of the jurisdiction in which it is collected or stored. Health data is among the most tightly controlled categories, and legal regimes diverge sharply: the UK and EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) rests on lawful bases and data-subject rights; the US Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) protects a narrower set of "covered entities"; the EU's Artificial Intelligence Act and the EU Medical Device Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2017/745) impose risk-tiered controls on software as a medical device. A tool that is compliant in one regime can be unlawful in another, and cross-border data flows require an explicit legal transfer mechanism, not an assumption. Learning across health systems. Countries run natural experiments you cannot run at home. Estonia built a whole-of-government data exchange layer and near-universal digital records; India built a set of open digital "stack" components for identity, payments, and health that private and public actors build on top of; Rwanda scaled drone-delivered blood and community health platforms. Each is a source of transferable lessons and non-transferable specifics — and telling the two apart is the core skill this topic teaches. Best practices # Adopt the global standards before you invent local ones. Default to HL7 FHIR, SNOMED CT, and ICD-11 for exchange, terminology, and classification, because these are the shared language that makes any future international comparison, collaboration, or supplier switch possible. Every bespoke local code system you create is a wall you will later have to demolish. Where a national profile exists — the UK Core FHIR profiles, for instance — use it, and contribute back rather than forking quietly. Prefer digital public goods and open standards over proprietary lock-in. When you procure or build, weight open-source, openly-specified, and independently-governed options heavily, because they preserve your ability to own, audit, and exit. Digital public goods such as DHIS2 and OpenMRS are proven at national scale and free of licence rent; even where you choose a commercial product, insist on open standards and data portability so you are never a hostage. (See Topic 9.0 — Collaborating with Partner Organizations on designing against vendor lock-in.) Learn from other systems as a discipline, with named owners and honest translation. Treat international learning as real work: assign someone to study a comparator system, understand why it works there — its laws, funding, digital identity, and social trust — and separate the transferable principle from the local specific. A study visit that returns with "we should copy Estonia" has failed; one that returns with "here is the identity and consent problem Estonia solved, and here is how our constraints differ" has succeeded. Never lift and shift a national model. Estonia's success rests on a small population, a mandatory national digital identity, and a high-trust settlement built over two decades; India's health stack rests on a particular public-private architecture and a billion-person identity system. Extracting one component and dropping it into England ignores the scaffolding that makes it safe. Adopt the pattern and rebuild the implementation for your legal, demographic, and trust context. Map the legal regime before any data crosses a border. Establish, in writing, the lawful basis, the transfer mechanism, and the controller relationships before health data leaves a jurisdiction — do not assume a UK-lawful flow is lawful onward. Where you operate across GDPR, HIPAA, the EU AI Act, and the EU Medical Device Regulation, treat the strictest applicable regime as your floor, and record how data sovereignty is respected for every population whose data you hold. Design for the harshest realistic conditions, not the demo. Borrow the LMIC discipline of offline-first, low-bandwidth, and graceful degradation, because it produces services that survive the connectivity failure, the old device, and the rural notspot at home too. A tool that only works on fast fibre in a clinic is not resilient; equity and clinical safety both improve when you assume the network will fail. Anchor everything in equity and universal coverage, and check who is excluded. Ask, for every deployment, whether it narrows or widens the gap — across countries and within your own population — because a digital service that serves the connected and confident while leaving others behind is a step away from universal coverage, not towards it. Measure uptake by group, not just in aggregate. (This connects to Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility.) Govern AI and emerging technology to the highest applicable international bar. Algorithms trained in one population can harm another, and the regulatory ground is shifting fast under the EU AI Act and comparable frameworks. Document training data provenance, validate on your own population, and align governance to the strictest regime you touch rather than the most permissive. (See Topic 8.4 — AI & Emerging Technology Governance.) Questions to discuss with your team # When we admire another country's digital health system, can we articulate exactly which parts are transferable to our context and which depend on conditions we do not share? This question guards against the most common and most expensive error in international learning: mistaking a specific implementation for a general principle. Estonia's near-frictionless data exchange depends on a mandatory national digital identity and a high-trust social settlement; India's health stack depends on a particular public-private architecture and a population-scale identity system; both took many years and specific political conditions. Your team should be able to name the underlying problem each system solved — secure identity, consented data exchange, reaching remote populations — and then describe honestly how your legal regime, funding, demographics, and public trust differ. The discussion should surface what scaffolding a borrowed model would need to be safe here, and whether that scaffolding is realistic. A mature answer separates the pattern worth adopting from the implementation that cannot travel, and it treats "we should just copy them" as a red flag rather than a plan. It also asks the reciprocal question: what does our system do that others could learn from, which sharpens the humility the whole exercise requires. Before any health data crosses a border — including to a cloud region, a supplier, or a research partner in another country — do we know the lawful basis, the transfer mechanism, and which regime governs it? Cross-border data flows are where good intentions meet hard law, and the failure is usually silent: data moves through a cloud region or a supplier's overseas support desk without anyone establishing a legal transfer mechanism. Your team should distinguish clearly between the UK and EU GDPR world of lawful bases and data-subject rights, the US HIPAA model that protects a narrower set of covered entities, and the emerging controls of the EU AI Act and Medical Device Regulation for clinical software. The discussion must cover data sovereignty concretely: for each population whose data you hold, which nation's law governs it, and are you honouring that? It should also confront the practical traps — a "global" SaaS product with support staff on another continent, an AI vendor whose model is retrained on your data, a research collaboration that assumes reciprocity the law does not grant. A strong answer treats the strictest applicable regime as the floor, records the transfer mechanism in writing before data moves, and can name who is accountable when a regulator asks. Are we designing for the connectivity, devices, and literacy of everyone we serve, or only for the confident, connected user in the demo? Much of the world's most resilient health technology was built under constraint — intermittent power, low bandwidth, shared or basic phones, multiple languages — and that discipline produces services that also serve the excluded within a wealthy system. Your team should examine whether its designs assume fast connectivity, modern devices, and high digital literacy, and what happens to a patient when those assumptions fail. The equity stakes are direct: a service that works only for the well-connected widens the gap it was meant to close, both between countries and within your own population, moving away from universal coverage rather than towards it. The conversation should look at offline-first behaviour, graceful degradation, SMS or voice fallback, language and reading-level accessibility, and whether uptake is measured by group rather than only in aggregate. It should also ask whether you are borrowing proven LMIC design patterns or ignoring them out of a sense that they are "not for us". A good answer can point to specific design choices that protect the hardest-to-reach user and to metrics that would reveal exclusion early. When we build or buy, are we choosing digital public goods and open standards that we can own, audit, and exit — or quietly accepting proprietary lock-in because it is convenient today? The choice between an open, independently-governed platform and a polished proprietary one is where a system's long-term sovereignty is won or lost, and the pressure almost always runs towards the closed option because it demos better and asks less of you now. Your team should be able to say why it weighted open-source, openly-specified, and portable options in a specific recent decision — or admit honestly that it did not. Digital public goods such as DHIS2 and OpenMRS are proven at national scale and free of licence rent, but they demand in-house capability and a maintenance commitment that a commercial contract appears to remove; that trade-off is real and should be argued, not assumed away. The discussion must also cover exit concretely: if this supplier doubled its price or left the market in three years, could you move your data and your service, and have you tested that claim rather than trusted a contract clause? A mature answer treats data portability and a documented exit as non-negotiable even when the chosen product is commercial, and it can name what the organization would have to build or fund to make the open option viable. Are we treating lower-income partners as sources of proven design and genuine collaborators, or as recipients of our charity — and can we say clearly what we contribute back? International digital health carries a persistent power asymmetry, and the charity framing — where a wealthy system "helps" an LMIC by donating technology — is both patronizing and a reliable route to failure, because it ignores that mobile-first care, community health worker platforms, and open national infrastructure were often pioneered in exactly those systems. Your team should examine a real or proposed partnership and ask who owns the result, who maintains it, and whether the flow of learning genuinely runs both ways. The tensions are concrete: a donated platform that becomes an unfunded dependency, a "collaboration" that extracts data or validation from a partner population without reciprocal benefit, a study visit that takes lessons but offers nothing in return. It should also confront the reciprocal humility the topic demands — what does your own system do that others could learn from, and are you sharing it as openly as you expect them to share with you? An honest answer can point to co-ownership arrangements, contributions back to shared open cores, and a partnership that would still make sense if the funding direction were reversed. For any algorithm or AI model we deploy, can we show it was validated on the population it will actually serve, and governed to the strictest regime we touch rather than the most permissive? A model trained and validated on one population can quietly harm a different one, and international digital health multiplies this risk because tools, training data, and vendors cross borders faster than the evidence of their safety does. Your team should be able to distinguish a model's provenance — where its training data came from, which population it was validated against — from the population it is now being asked to serve, and treat any gap as a live clinical-safety concern rather than a paperwork detail. The regulatory ground is shifting fast and unevenly: the EU AI Act imposes risk-tiered controls on high-risk clinical software, the EU Medical Device Regulation treats many algorithms as software as a medical device, and UK law is lighter in places, which creates a temptation to govern to the most permissive regime you can defend. The discussion should surface who is accountable for revalidation, how model updates and vendor retraining are controlled, and whether the organization documents training-data provenance at all. A strong answer revalidates on the local population before deployment, aligns governance to the highest applicable international bar to keep options open, and can explain that choice to a regulator without embarrassment. In practice: a health & care example # A fictional English arms-length body, the "National Remote Monitoring Service", is asked to procure a platform for home monitoring of long-term conditions, with an option to collaborate on a shared open-source core with health ministries in two partner countries — one a high-income EU neighbour, one an LMIC scaling community health workers. The temptation is to buy a polished commercial platform and treat the international angle as a diplomatic courtesy. The team resists. It starts from standards: any platform must exchange data as HL7 FHIR, code observations in SNOMED CT, and classify conditions to ICD-11, so that data means the same thing across all three countries and the service is not locked to one vendor. It shortlists a digital-public-good core (an OpenMRS-derived stack) alongside two commercial options, scoring each on data portability and exit as heavily as on features. On the law, the team maps the regimes before a byte moves. Data for English patients stays under UK GDPR in a UK cloud region; the EU partner's collaboration runs under EU GDPR with a documented transfer mechanism; no personal data flows to or from the LMIC partner at all — only de-identified aggregate indicators and the open-source code itself, which is a digital public good and carries no sovereignty risk. The monitoring algorithm is treated as software as a medical device and validated against the English population separately, because a model tuned elsewhere cannot be assumed safe here; its governance is aligned to the EU AI Act's high-risk expectations even where UK law is lighter, to keep options open. The design borrows from the LMIC partner rather than lecturing it. The community-health-worker platform there is offline-first with SMS fallback, and the English service adopts the same pattern — which turns out to matter for rural notspots and older patients at home. Eighteen months on, the shared open-source core is maintained jointly, each country runs its own lawful deployment, and
