x: Topic 9.3 — Digital in Adult Social Care Adult social care is not "NHS-lite": it is a fragmented, means-tested, provider-led market with its own workforce, funding, and information realities, and delivering digital well there means designing for those realities rather than importing acute-hospital assumptions. Why this matters in health and care # Adult social care in England supports around a million people at any one time — older people, disabled adults, people with learning disabilities, people with mental ill health — to live with dignity, safety, and as much independence as possible. It is delivered not by a single national organization but by roughly 18,000 independent, voluntary, and public providers running care homes and domiciliary ("home care") services, commissioned by 150-odd local authorities and paid for by a mix of means-tested public funding and self-funders. This is a different shape of system from the NHS, and digital ways of working that ignore the difference tend to fail. The stakes are high and specific. Social care records describe the most intimate details of a person's life — continence, capacity, finances, relationships, risk of abuse — held often by small organizations with thin governance and, historically, low digital maturity. Care is delivered by a workforce of around 1.5 million people, much of it low-paid, high-turnover, and digitally under-supported, using their own phones or none at all. When you get digital right here, you reduce medication errors, speed hospital discharge, spot deterioration earlier, and give overstretched carers time back. When you get it wrong, you create data breaches, safeguarding failures, and exclusion of the very people least able to advocate for themselves. How you work is a safety, equity, and public-trust issue, not merely an efficiency one. Core concepts # Adult social care in England is governed principally by the Care Act 2014 , which places statutory duties on local authorities to assess needs, promote wellbeing, and safeguard adults at risk. Quality is regulated by the Care Quality Commission (CQC) , which inspects and rates providers. Unlike NHS care, most publicly funded social care is subject to a financial means test : people above a capital threshold pay for their own care ("self-funders"), which shapes who commissions what and where the money flows. The provider market is dominated by thousands of small independent businesses and voluntary sector organizations, alongside some large national chains. This fragmentation is the single most important fact for anyone planning digital delivery: there is no single system to log into, no national roll-out lever, and no shared IT department. A digital social care record (DSCR) is the sector's equivalent of an electronic health record , replacing the paper care plans and handover notes that still dominate many services. Assuring these records against a national standard, and connecting them to health, requires interoperability — the ability of systems to exchange and use each other's data. Technology-enabled care (TEC) covers telecare (alarms and sensors that summon help), telehealth (remote monitoring of health conditions), and broader assistive technology . Much legacy telecare depends on the analogue public switched telephone network (PSTN) , which is being retired in favour of digital telephony — a change with direct safety implications for alarm users. Two further concepts run through the whole topic. Co-production (approach) means designing services with people who draw on care and unpaid carers, not merely for them. And safeguarding — protecting adults at risk of abuse or neglect — is a statutory duty that digital systems must actively support, never undermine. Best practices # Start from the provider's reality, not the NHS template. A domiciliary care worker moving between homes on foot with a five-year-old phone, a care-home nurse on a night shift, and a self-funding family choosing a service all operate very differently from a hospital ward. Do your discovery in real settings, watch a shift, and design for intermittent connectivity, shared devices, and low prior digital confidence. Solutions ported directly from acute NHS contexts — heavy clinical systems, single-sign-on estates, dedicated IT support — routinely collapse in the social care market because none of those preconditions hold. Treat the fragmented market as the delivery problem, not a footnote. You cannot mandate change across 18,000 independent businesses; you have to make adoption attractive, affordable, and low-risk for each one. Use the national assured-solutions route so providers choose from suppliers that already meet a defined standard, and lean on local authorities, integrated care systems, and Care Provider Associations to broker, fund, and support at the local level (see Topic 9.0 — Collaborating with Partner Organizations). Plan for a long tail of small providers who will move last and need the most hand-holding. Adopt digital social care records to a national standard, and fund the change, not just the software. DSCRs cut duplicate recording, make information legible at handover, and support safer medication administration. But a licence is the cheap part: the cost and risk sit in data migration from paper, device provision, connectivity, and the weeks of frontline support needed before staff trust the system. Budget for change management and floor-walking (see Topic 8.1 — Change Management), and measure adoption by real use at the point of care, not by contracts signed. Use the assured-supplier / assured-solutions approach to de-risk procurement. Small providers cannot each run a rigorous supplier evaluation covering clinical safety, cyber security, and data protection. National assurance — where solutions are checked against standards before they reach the market — lets a care home make a safe choice from a shortlist rather than a cold procurement. Point providers to the assured list, and where you commission at scale, make assurance a contractual expectation rather than an afterthought (see Topic 6.3 — Procurement & Commercial). Plan the PSTN-to-digital telecare switchover as a safety programme. Millions of telecare alarms rely on the analogue phone network that is being switched off; a device that silently stops working is a life-safety risk for a person who has fallen. Maintain a register of telecare users, coordinate with telecoms providers and the local authority, prioritize vulnerable users for supported migration, and test end-to-end that an alarm still reaches a monitoring centre after the line changes. Never assume the switch is "just a telecoms upgrade" that will look after itself. Design information sharing around the person, and make it two-way with health. The value of a shared care record is realized at the interfaces: a care home that can see a resident's medications, or a hospital discharge team that can see a person's home-care package. Connect DSCRs to shared care records and use recognized standards so data flows both ways (see Topic 4.3 — Interoperability & Data Standards). Sharing must be lawful, proportionate, and explainable to the person, with a clear basis under data protection law and honest conversations about consent. Co-produce with people who draw on care and unpaid carers. The people who use telecare, care planning, and family portals know where they fail in ways no procurement scorecard captures. Involve them and their unpaid carers from discovery through to live running, pay for their time, and reflect diverse needs — cognitive impairment, sensory loss, digital exclusion, English as an additional language. Co-production is both an ethical duty under the Care Act's wellbeing principle and the most reliable way to avoid building the wrong thing (see Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility). Raise the cyber-security and data-protection floor in small providers. A single care home may hold thousands of highly sensitive records with no dedicated IT and a manager who has never heard of multi-factor authentication. Offer practical, proportionate support — the national Data Security and Protection Toolkit, Cyber Essentials, template policies, and named help — rather than compliance paperwork that gets copied without understanding. Assume that ransomware and phishing will target the weakest link, and make good hygiene the path of least resistance. Build workforce digital capability as core, not optional. A large part of the social care workforce has had little employer investment in digital skills, and turnover means training is never "done." Bake basic digital confidence into induction, provide role-relevant support in the flow of work, and identify digital champions on the floor (see Topic 7.4 — Digital Skills & Capability Building). Capability is what turns a purchased system into daily practice; without it, adoption stalls and the investment is wasted. Make safeguarding an explicit design requirement. Digital systems can strengthen safeguarding — flagging risks, evidencing concerns, speeding referrals — or weaken it, if surveillance-style monitoring erodes dignity or if access controls leak sensitive information. Design so that recording a safeguarding concern is easy, access is appropriately restricted, and the person's rights and voice are respected. Test explicitly for coercion, controlling family access, and the risk that "monitoring" tips into intrusion. Questions to discuss with your team # Where are we unconsciously treating social care as "NHS-lite," and what would we do differently if we designed for the care market on its own terms? This question forces the team to surface imported assumptions — that there is central IT, salaried digitally-confident staff, a single accountable body, or a mandate to roll out. In social care almost none of that holds, so a plan built on NHS reflexes will quietly fail. Debate concrete examples: are you assuming providers can absorb a procurement, spare staff for training, or run their own information governance? A good, honest answer names the specific NHS-shaped assumptions in your current plan, distinguishes what genuinely transfers from what does not, and reshapes ownership, funding, and support around a fragmented provider market rather than a single organization. How will we support the long tail of small and voluntary providers who move last and need the most help, without either abandoning them or forcing a pace they cannot manage? Averages hide the problem: national adoption figures can look healthy while the smallest, least-resourced providers — often serving the most marginalized people — remain on paper. The tension is between momentum and inclusion, and between standardizing (efficient, but blunt) and tailoring support locally (effective, but costly). Consider who funds and delivers the hand-holding — local authority teams, Care Provider Associations, peer champions — and what "good enough" looks like for a six-bed home versus a national chain. A strong answer sets a realistic trajectory, names who owns support for the hardest-to-reach, and defines success as real use at the front line rather than licences sold or a headline percentage. How do we share information between health and social care in a way that is genuinely safe, lawful, and trusted by the people it describes? Interoperability is usually framed as a technical challenge, but in social care the harder questions are ethical and relational: this is data about capacity, finances, abuse, and intimate care, held by many small organizations. Debate the lawful basis for sharing, when consent is meaningful versus when it is a tick-box, and how you explain sharing to someone with fluctuating capacity or an unpaid carer acting on their behalf. Weigh the safety benefit of a hospital seeing a care plan against the harm of over-broad access or a breach at a poorly defended provider. A good answer pairs the technical standards with a clear, person-centred information-governance story, proportionate access controls, and a plain-English account you would be comfortable giving to the person themselves. Are we running the PSTN telecare switchover as a life-safety programme, and who is accountable if an alarm fails silently? It is tempting to file the analogue switch-off under "telecoms" and assume the network operators will handle it, but a telecare alarm that appears connected yet cannot raise a call is a direct risk to a person who has fallen and lives alone. The tension is that responsibility is genuinely shared — telecoms providers, device suppliers, monitoring centres, local authorities, and the person's own household all touch the chain — and shared responsibility easily becomes nobody's responsibility. Debate whether you hold a current register of telecare users, whether you have prioritized the most vulnerable for supported migration, and whether you test end-to-end that a migrated alarm still reaches a monitoring centre rather than trusting that the line "looks fine." Consider what happens to people who self-fund their own alarm and sit outside any local authority list. An honest answer names a single accountable owner for the switchover, treats silent failure as the primary hazard, and can point to real end-to-end tests rather than assurances on paper. How will we build and sustain digital capability in a workforce that is low-paid, high-turnover, and rarely given time to learn? A purchased system only becomes safer care when frontline staff use it confidently, yet much of the social care workforce has had little employer investment in digital skills and churns faster than any one-off training programme can keep up with. The trade-off is between the cost of continual, role-relevant support and the hidden cost of stalled adoption, workarounds, and reversion to paper when confidence runs out. Consider who owns training when staff are employed by thousands of separate providers, how you reach night shifts and domiciliary workers who are never in an office, and whether digital confidence is built into induction rather than bolted on. Look at practical levers — floor-walking at go-live, digital champions on the rota, support in the flow of work — and be honest about which providers can spare the time at all. A strong answer treats capability as a permanent running cost tied to turnover, not a project milestone, and measures it by real use at the point of care. How do we make sure digital strengthens safeguarding and dignity rather than sliding into surveillance? Digital tools can flag risks, evidence concerns, and speed referrals, but the same monitoring capabilities can erode the autonomy and privacy the Care Act exists to protect, especially for people with cognitive impairment who cannot easily object. The tension is real: a sensor that detects a fall also watches a person in their own home, and a family portal that reassures relatives can also enable a controlling one. Debate where "monitoring for safety" tips into intrusion, who decides, and how the person's own voice and consent are weighted when capacity fluctuates. Consider whether recording a safeguarding concern is genuinely easy for staff, whether access controls keep sensitive information appropriately restricted, and whether you have tested for coercion and controlling access rather than assuming good intent. An honest answer can show that dignity and safeguarding were designed in as explicit requirements — with the person's rights foregrounded — not treated as acceptable casualties of a monitoring feature. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system in the East Midlands sets out to lift digital maturity across adult social care. Baseline data shows that of 320 CQC-registered providers in its footprint, fewer than half use any digital care record; the rest run on paper, and a cluster of small domiciliary agencies have no shared devices at all. The system's digital team resists the temptation to run a single procurement and mandate one product. Instead, working with the two upper-tier local authorities and the local Care Association, they stand up a small support team and point providers to the nationally assured DSCR suppliers, so each provider chooses a solution that already meets clinical-safety, cyber, and data-protection standards. Funding is routed to providers as grants that cover not just licences but devices, connectivity, and, critically, the staff time to migrate paper records and train teams. The support team offers floor-walking during go-live, template information-sharing agreements, and help completing the Data Security and Protection Toolkit. A local care-home manager, initially sceptical, adopts a DSCR after a peer champion from a neighbouring home shows how it cut two hours of nightly paperwork and made the morning handover legible. Within a year, medication administration errors flagged in the home fall, and the ambulance service reports faster, better-informed responses because paramedics can see current care plans. In parallel, the system runs the PSTN switchover as a distinct safety programme. It builds a register of roughly 9,000 telecare users across the two authorities, coordinates with telecoms providers, prioritizes people living alone with a history of falls, and tests that each migrated alarm still reaches the monitoring centre. Two "silent failure" cases — alarms that appeared connected but could not raise a call — are caught in testing rather than in an emergency. Throughout, an involvement group of people who draw on care and unpaid carers reviews the family portal and the telecare messaging; their feedback reshapes the consent wording and adds a large-text mode. The programme is judged a success not because every provider is digital, but because adoption is real at the front line, the most vulnerable were prioritized, and no one was left behind by the telephone switch-off. Sector lenses # Startup # A small health-tech company selling into social care faces a market of thousands of tiny buyers with little cash, low digital confidence, and no procurement capacity — the opposite of a single enterprise sale. Getting onto the national assured-solutions list is often the difference between a viable business and a stalled one, because assurance is what lets a wary care-home manager trust you. Design for shared, cheap devices and patchy connectivity, price for organizations running on thin margins, and invest in onboarding and support, because your churn will track your customers' staff turnover. Resist the urge to bolt on features for large chains at the expense of the small providers who are most of the market. Small business # An established small provider — a single care home, a domiciliary agency, a community pharmacy, or a family-run residential service — has real residents and staff but rarely a dedicated IT person, so digital change lands on a registered manager already stretched thin. Adopting a digital social care record is worth it for the nightly paperwork and safer medication administration it saves, but only if you can fund the devices, connectivity, and staff time to migrate from paper alongside running the service every day. Lean hard on the nationally assured-supplier list so you can make a safe choice without running your own procurement, and take up the free support on offer — the Data Security and Protection Toolkit, template information-sharing agreements, and local Care Association help — rather than trying to become an IT department. You carry the same duties on safeguarding, data protection, and the PSTN telecare switchover as a national chain, so know which of your alarm users and records depend on the analogue line and get supported migration underway early. A peer champion from a neighbouring provider who has already been through it is often worth more than any vendor pitch. Enterprise # A large care provider or an NHS trust integrating with socia

x: Topic 10.0 — Objectives & Key Results (OKRs) Objectives and Key Results give your organization a disciplined way to turn strategy into a small number of ambitious, outcome-focused goals — but in health and care their real value is forcing you to ask what better looks like for patients, not just what your teams are busy doing. Why this matters in health and care # Digital delivery in health and care rarely fails for lack of activity. Teams are busy: shipping features, closing tickets, running programmes, attending boards. The harder question — the one that separates organizations that improve care from those that merely spend money on technology — is whether all that motion is pointed at outcomes that matter to patients, clinicians, and the public purse. Objectives and Key Results (OKRs) exist to make that alignment explicit, and to make it honest. In a commercial company, a misaligned goal wastes money. In health and care, it can waste the one thing the system has least of — clinical time and patient trust. A digital team that hits every delivery milestone but never moves a single measure of access, safety, or equity has succeeded at the wrong thing. Because you steward public money and, indirectly, clinical outcomes, the discipline of naming what you are actually trying to achieve — and being willing to be graded honestly against it — is not a management fashion. It is part of how you justify your existence to boards, regulators, and the people you serve. OKRs also carry a specific risk in this sector that deserves naming up front. Health and care is heavily target-driven, and staff are rightly wary of any new goal-setting language that smells like a performance-management stick. Used well, OKRs create focus, transparency, and permission to attempt ambitious change. Used badly, they become another top-down cascade of quotas that punish honesty and reward gaming. This topic is about getting the first version and avoiding the second. Core concepts # Objectives and Key Results is a goal-setting framework that pairs a single qualitative Objective — an ambitious, memorable statement of what you want to achieve — with two to five quantitative Key Results that measure whether you got there. The Objective answers "where do we want to go?"; the Key Results answer "how will we know we have arrived?" A well-formed set reads as a sentence: we will achieve this Objective, as measured by these Key Results. The method has a clear lineage. It grew from management by objectives , the approach Peter Drucker popularized in the 1950s, and was sharpened into its modern form by Andrew Grove at Intel, who described it in his 1983 book High Output Management . It reached wide adoption when John Doerr , who had learned the method from Grove, introduced it to Google in 1999; Doerr later codified the approach for a general audience in his book Measure What Matters . The single most important concept is the distinction between an OKR and a key performance indicator (KPI). OKRs drive focus and change — they name the handful of things you want to be different by the end of the quarter or year. KPIs monitor the ongoing health of business-as-usual — the vital signs you watch continuously to make sure nothing breaks. Topic 10.1 — Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) covers measurement in depth; this topic is about goal-setting. Confusing the two is the most common OKR mistake, and we return to it throughout. Two further distinctions shape practice. First, committed versus aspirational (stretch) OKRs : committed OKRs are commitments you fully expect to deliver, while aspirational OKRs are deliberate stretches where landing at 60–70 per cent is a success. Second, outcomes versus tasks : a Key Result should measure a change in the world ("reduce the median wait for first digital triage from nine days to three"), not the completion of an activity ("launch the new triage form"). This connects directly to the SMART criteria for well-formed goals and, in health and care, to clinical and population-health outcomes. The framework depends on alignment and transparency without a rigid top-down cascade . Everyone can see everyone else's OKRs, and team goals connect visibly to organizational strategy — but teams set their own OKRs rather than receiving them as quotas. Finally, stretch goals only work under psychological safety : if missing an aspirational target is punished, people set timid goals and the whole method collapses into theatre. The failure of gamed targets is well described by Goodhart's law — when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Best practices # Write the Objective to inspire and the Key Results to measure. The Objective should be a short, qualitative, motivating sentence a tired clinician could remember — "Make it genuinely easy to get community physiotherapy" — not a metric. The Key Results then make it unambiguous by attaching numbers: the change in wait time, the change in did-not-attend rate, the change in access for people who cannot use online tools. Keep to one Objective per team per quarter where you can, and never more than a few, so focus is real rather than nominal. Express Key Results as outcomes, not tasks. "Ship the new referral template" is a task — you can complete it and change nothing. "Cut the proportion of referrals returned for missing information from 30 per cent to under 10 per cent" is an outcome. Outcome Key Results force you to have a theory about why your work matters and expose it to reality. When a Key Result can only be written as a deliverable, it usually belongs on a roadmap or delivery plan, not in your OKRs. Limit the number ruthlessly. The power of OKRs comes from what they exclude. A team with one Objective and three Key Results has decided what matters most this quarter; a team with five Objectives and twenty Key Results has decided nothing and merely inventoried its backlog. Resist the organizational instinct to make every worthy activity an OKR. Most of what a good team does is business-as-usual, measured by KPIs, and should stay off the OKR list. Distinguish committed from aspirational OKRs, and say which is which. Some goals you must hit — a regulatory deadline, a clinical-safety commitment — and these are committed OKRs where anything below 100 per cent is a problem. Others are deliberate stretches where 100 per cent would prove you set the bar too low. Label each type explicitly so teams and boards read the scores correctly, and so a 0.6 on a stretch goal is celebrated as ambition rather than mistaken for failure. Align through transparency, not a rigid cascade. Publish every team's OKRs where colleagues can see them, and make sure each set connects visibly to the organization's strategy (see Topic 1.2 — Digital Strategy & Roadmapping). But let teams draft their own OKRs and negotiate them upward, rather than receiving decomposed quotas from above. A mix of top-down direction and bottom-up ownership produces goals people believe in; a pure cascade produces goals people comply with and quietly resent. Run a deliberate cadence of setting, check-in, and grading. Set OKRs at the start of a cycle — quarterly for teams is common, annually for the organization. Check in frequently (weekly or fortnightly) on confidence and blockers, not just at the end. Grade honestly at the close, usually on a 0.0–1.0 scale, and treat the grade as a prompt for a learning conversation, not a verdict. The reflection at grading — what we learned, what we would change — is where most of the value lives. Connect OKRs to strategy and to benefits. OKRs should be the near-term, measurable expression of your longer-term strategy and roadmap ( Topic 1.2 ), and they should feed the benefits you have committed to in your business cases (see Topic 6.2 — Benefits Realization & Value Management). When an Objective cannot be traced to a strategic aim or a promised benefit, question why it exists. This traceability is also what makes your OKRs credible to a board and useful for Topic 10.4 — Visibility for the CEO & Senior Leaders. Anchor Key Results in clinical, operational, and population-health outcomes where you can. A digital team's OKRs are stronger when at least some Key Results reach through to outcomes clinicians and patients recognize — waiting times, safety events avoided, uptake among under-served groups — rather than stopping at system metrics like uptime or logins. Use the analytics capability described in Topic 4.5 — Data, Analytics & Population Health Management to source these honestly. Where a true outcome is too slow or noisy to measure in a quarter, choose a well-evidenced leading indicator and be explicit that it is a proxy. Protect psychological safety so stretch goals stay safe. Aspirational OKRs only work if people can miss them, say so plainly, and learn without penalty. Separate OKR grading from individual performance appraisal, pay, and ranking — the moment a Key Result determines someone's bonus, it stops measuring reality and starts measuring self-protection. Say this explicitly and repeatedly, because sceptical staff will assume the worst until the organization proves otherwise over several cycles. Questions to discuss with your team # Which of our current goals are genuinely OKRs, and which are actually KPIs or task lists in disguise? This is the foundational sorting exercise, and most teams get it wrong the first time. Walk through everything you are currently calling a goal and ask, for each, whether it names something you want to change (a candidate OKR) or something you want to keep healthy (a KPI, belonging in Topic 10.1 — Key Performance Indicators). Then check whether each supposed OKR is written as an outcome or merely as a task you could tick off without improving anything. The honest result is usually uncomfortable: a long list of activities, a few real KPIs, and only two or three genuine change-focused Objectives. That narrowing is the point. A good answer leaves you with a short, defensible set of OKRs, a separate dashboard of business-as-usual KPIs, and a delivery plan for the tasks — three different things that were previously tangled together. Are our stretch goals safe to miss, and does everyone actually believe that? Aspirational OKRs are supposed to encourage ambition, but they only do so if the organization has genuinely decoupled missing a stretch from being punished. Discuss candidly whether your staff — especially clinicians and delivery leads scarred by target regimes — believe that landing at 0.6 on an aspirational Key Result will be read as healthy ambition or as failure to be explained to a committee. Look at where OKR grades actually flow: do they touch appraisals, pay, contract reporting, or public league tables? If they do, people will rationally set timid goals and game the numbers, exactly as Goodhart's law predicts. A good answer names concrete protections — grades kept out of individual performance management, stretch OKRs explicitly labelled, leaders modelling honest misses — and acknowledges that trust here is earned slowly, over several cycles, not declared in a policy. Do our OKRs reach through to outcomes that patients and clinicians would recognize, or do they stop at things only our team cares about? It is easy to write Key Results about logins, releases, and uptime because they are inside your control and quick to measure. It is harder, and far more valuable, to connect at least some Key Results to waiting times, safety, health outcomes, or equity of access. Discuss which of your Objectives could be expressed in terms a ward sister or a patient would find meaningful, and where you are hiding behind system metrics because the real outcome is slow, noisy, or politically awkward to own. Consider the equity dimension explicitly: an OKR that improves an average while widening the gap for digitally excluded people has arguably made care worse, not better (see Topic 1.9 — Digital Inclusion & Accessibility). A good answer includes at least one outcome-level Key Result per Objective, is honest about which measures are proxies, and has a clear line back to strategy ( Topic 1.2 ) and to promised benefits ( Topic 6.2 ). How few OKRs are we actually willing to commit to, and what are we consciously choosing not to pursue this cycle? The discipline of OKRs lives in subtraction, yet almost every team drifts towards more Objectives rather than fewer, because saying no to a worthy idea feels like neglect. Discuss what would happen if you allowed yourselves only one Objective and three Key Results for the quarter: which of your candidate goals survive, and who would be disappointed by the ones that fall away. In health and care this conversation is politically charged, because competing services, clinical directorates, and commissioners all press for their priority to be named, and a digital team can end up with an OKR list that is really a peace treaty between stakeholders rather than a statement of focus. Be honest about the cost of spreading thin: a team nominally pursuing eight Objectives is usually making real progress on none, while patients wait for the one improvement that mattered most. A good answer names the two or three things that genuinely matter this cycle, records the worthy ideas you are explicitly parking, and can defend the exclusions to the people who lobbied for them. When an OKR score comes back low, what do we actually do with it — and what does that reveal about the culture we have built? The grade itself matters far less than the conversation it triggers, and the nature of that conversation is the truest test of whether OKRs are working. Talk through a concrete recent miss, or imagine one: does the discussion turn to what you learned and what you would change, or to who is accountable and how the number will be explained upward? In a sector shaped by decades of performance management, the reflex to treat a low score as a failure to be defended is strong, and it quietly teaches people to set safer goals next time. Consider who is in the room when grades are reviewed, whether the tone differs for committed versus aspirational OKRs, and whether anyone has ever been visibly rewarded for an honest, instructive miss. A good answer describes grading as a structured learning ritual, points to real examples where a low score changed the next cycle's plan, and can show that reporting a miss plainly has never cost anyone their standing. How do our OKRs behave when the world changes mid-cycle — a winter crisis, a safety incident, a funding shift — and can we re-point them without abandoning the discipline? OKRs are usually set for a quarter or a year, but health and care rarely respects a planning calendar, and a rigid set of goals can become either an irrelevance teams ignore or a straitjacket that keeps them working on yesterday's priority while a crisis unfolds. Discuss what your team would do if, six weeks into a cycle, an urgent operational pressure made your headline Objective suddenly less important than keeping a service safe. The tension is real: change OKRs too readily and they lose all meaning as commitments; hold them too rigidly and you privilege a plan over patients. Explore who has the authority to re-open a set mid-cycle, how you would record the change and its rationale, and how you avoid using "circumstances changed" as a cover for quietly dropping goals you were going to miss anyway. A good answer establishes a clear, sparing mechanism for mid-cycle change, distinguishes genuine re-prioritization from face-saving, and keeps a visible trail so the shift is transparent to the board and to other teams that were aligned to the original goal. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care board (ICB) has a digital team supporting community services across several boroughs. For years the team reported activity: features delivered, tickets closed, systems patched. The board could see it was busy but could not see whether it was helping. A new director introduces OKRs, starting with a single Objective for the community physiotherapy service, chosen because waits are long and complaints are rising. The Objective is deliberately human: Make it genuinely easy and fair to get community physiotherapy. The team drafts three Key Results as outcomes, not tasks. First, reduce the median time from referral to first meaningful contact from twenty-one days to seven. Second, hold the did-not-attend rate at or below its current level, so speed is not bought with chaos. Third — the equity Key Result — ensure that first-contact waits for patients in the two most deprived neighbourhoods are no worse than the service average, disaggregated and published. They mark the first two as committed and the wait-time target as aspirational, since seven days is a genuine stretch. Crucially, the director separates these OKRs from the team's KPIs. System uptime, form-completion rates, and support-ticket volumes stay on a business-as-usual dashboard, watched continuously but never confused with the quarter's goals. The OKRs are published on the intranet alongside every other team's, so the physiotherapy service leads, the analytics team, and the board can all see them and see how they connect to the ICB's access strategy. The cadence does the work. At fortnightly check-ins the team reports confidence, not just progress, and surfaces blockers early — the biggest turns out to be triage sitting in a shared inbox, not the online form everyone assumed was the problem. By quarter-end the median wait has fallen to nine days: a 0.7 on the aspirational Key Result. Rather than treat that as failure, the grading conversation examines what the remaining bottleneck is and rolls a refined Objective into the next quarter. Because no one's appraisal hangs on the score, the team reports the miss plainly, and the honesty makes the next set of OKRs more ambitious, not less. Sector lenses # Startup # A health-tech startup lives and dies by focus, which makes OKRs a natural fit — but the classic trap is turning them into a feature backlog. With a small team and investor pressure, every Key Result is tempted to become "ship X," measuring output rather than whether customers or patients are better off. Resist this: pick one or two Objectives per quarter and write at least one Key Result as an outcome your NHS buyers would recognize, such as adoption by real clinicians or a measurable change in a care pathway. Lightweight cadence — a shared doc, a weekly confidence check — is enough; heavy tooling is not the point. Above all, keep OKR grades away from a tiny team's sense of personal worth, so honest misses stay possible when you most need the truth. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home, or a small supplier with real customers but no dedicated digital function — needs OKRs that fit around a working day, not a planning department. The discipline here is to pick a single Objective the whole team can hold in their heads, such as making it easier for patients to get repeat medication, and to express it with one or two outcome Key Results drawn from data you already collect, rather than building new dashboards you have no time to maintain. Cadence should be minimal but real: a ten-minute check at an existing team meeting beats a formal quarterly ceremony no one has capacity to run. The trap to avoid is letting the OKR become another compliance task layered on top of ongoing operations, because a small business carries the same regulatory and safety duties as a large trust with a fraction of the staff to meet them. Keep grading light and blameless, because in a team of a handful of people a punitive score poisons everything, and one honest, well-chosen Objective delivered is worth more than a suite of goals that quietly lapse. Enterprise # A large NHS trust, ICS, or established supplier has the opposite problem: OKRs proliferate

x: Topic 10.1 — Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) A key performance indicator (KPI) is a small, carefully chosen number that tells you whether a service is safe, fair, effective, and trusted — and in health and care, choosing and reading those numbers well is itself a matter of clinical safety and public accountability, not administrative housekeeping. Why this matters in health and care # In health and care, the numbers you watch shape the care people receive. A waiting-list KPI that counts "patients booked" but not "patients seen" can hide a cohort quietly deteriorating at home. A digital service dashboard that is green on uptime but silent on whether disabled users can complete a booking will let an access problem grow into a health inequality. What you measure signals what you value, and staff, suppliers, and algorithms all optimize towards the measured target — sometimes at the expense of the unmeasured thing that actually mattered. The stakes are higher here than in most sectors because the failure modes are human. The Mid Staffordshire and other inquiries repeatedly found organizations that hit their headline financial and activity targets while care quality collapsed underneath. Metrics were reported upwards as green while patients came to harm — the pattern now widely called "watermelon reporting" (green on the outside, red on the inside), which Topic 10.4 — Visibility for the CEO & Senior Leaders examines in depth. Good KPIs are one of your defences against that gap between the reported picture and the real one. KPIs also spend public money and public trust. Every indicator you publish becomes part of how citizens, regulators, and commissioners judge the system. Over-claiming, cherry-picking, or gaming a target is not just poor management; it erodes the trust that digital health depends on to get people to share data and adopt new services. This topic is the measurement partner to Topic 10.0 — Objectives & Key Results (OKRs): where OKRs drive focused change, KPIs monitor the ongoing health of the services and systems you run. Core concepts # A performance indicator , or KPI, is a metric selected because it reflects progress against an objective that matters. A performance metric is any measurement of activity or state; a KPI is the subset you have deliberately elevated to "watch this one". The word key is load-bearing — if everything is a KPI, nothing is. A useful discipline is to hold a handful of KPIs per service, each with a named owner, a definition, a data source, and a reason it earns a place on the board. A good KPI has four properties. It is aligned to an outcome that genuinely matters to patients, citizens, or clinicians, not merely to internal activity. It is actionable — when it moves, someone can do something about it. It is timely — it arrives soon enough to act on, not six weeks after the quarter closed. And it is hard to game — it cannot be improved on paper without improving the real thing. Metrics that fail the last test invite Goodhart's law : "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." Indicators are commonly split into leading and lagging. A lagging indicator confirms an outcome after the fact (30-day mortality, annual patient satisfaction). A leading indicator moves earlier and predicts the lagging one (medication-reconciliation completeness, deployment frequency, the proportion of referrals triaged within 24 hours). You need both: lagging indicators tell you whether you are winning, leading indicators tell you in time to change the result. Many economic and operational frameworks describe this leading/lagging distinction. A parallel and equally important split is process, output, and outcome measures . A process measure counts whether you did the thing (appointments offered, records migrated). An output measure counts what was produced (letters sent, tests resulted). An outcome measure captures what actually changed for the person — an outcome measure such as symptom improvement, avoided admission, or a patient-reported quality-of-life score. Health and care systems have a chronic bias towards activity because activity is easy to count and often how money flows. Resist it: privilege outcomes and experience, and use process measures as the leading indicators that explain them. Because no single number is safe on its own, use balanced measurement . The balanced scorecard discipline of Kaplan and Norton pairs each performance measure with others so that improving one at the expense of another becomes visible. The Institute for Healthcare Improvement formalizes this as outcome, process, and balancing measures — the balancing measure watches for the harm your improvement might cause elsewhere (faster discharge balanced against readmission, for instance). Not every number that goes up is progress. A vanity metric looks impressive and rises reliably but does not inform a decision — total registered users, cumulative logins, page views. The lean startup movement popularized the contrast between vanity and actionable metrics: an actionable metric ties a change you made to a change in behaviour or outcome you can act on. Cumulative counts are the classic tell — they only ever rise, so they can never signal that something is wrong. Finally, distinguish measurement for improvement from measurement for judgement . Judgement asks "did you hit the target this month?" and reduces a living process to a two-point, red-or-green comparison against last period — a comparison that is almost always statistically meaningless because it cannot tell signal from noise. Improvement asks "is this process changing, and can we trust the change?" and answers it with statistical process control (SPC): plotting a metric over time on a run chart or control chart with control limits, so you can see whether variation is ordinary (common-cause) noise or a genuine signal (special-cause) worth acting on. NHS England's Making Data Count programme has made this the recommended way to present operational data across the NHS, precisely to kill the "up on last month, down on target" reflex that drives bad decisions. Best practices # Start from the outcome, then work back to the indicator. Name the thing that must be true for a patient, citizen, or clinician — fewer avoidable admissions, faster access, safe medication — and only then ask what would tell you it is happening. This keeps you from the default trap of measuring what your systems happen to log. If you cannot connect a candidate KPI to an outcome anyone cares about, it is probably a vanity metric. Keep the set small and give every KPI an owner and a definition. A board or service should watch a handful of KPIs, not fifty. Each needs a precise definition (what counts, what is excluded, over what period), a named owner accountable for it, and a documented data source. Ambiguous definitions are how two teams argue for a month about a number they were measuring differently. Balance every KPI so it cannot be gamed in isolation. For each measure, ask "how would a rational person improve this number without improving the real thing, and what balancing measure would catch them?" Pair access with safety, throughput with readmission, cost with experience, delivery speed with change-failure rate. Balanced sets make gaming visible and honour the reality that health and care outcomes are multidimensional. Privilege outcome and experience measures over activity. Activity counts are seductive because they are abundant and often tied to funding, but they answer "how busy were we?" not "did it help?". Wherever you can, elevate outcome measures and patient-reported experience and outcome measures (PREMs and PROMs) into the KPI set, and demote raw activity to the supporting layer. Where an outcome is slow or hard to measure, choose a validated leading process measure that reliably predicts it. Present KPIs as time series with SPC, not two-point comparisons. Adopt the Making Data Count approach: plot the metric run-chart or control-chart style so common-cause variation and special-cause signals are distinguishable at a glance. This stops teams reacting to noise, celebrating a lucky month, or being punished for an unlucky one. It also changes the boardroom conversation from "why did we miss?" to "has the process actually changed?" — which is the improvement question (see Topic 10.2 — Quality Improvement & Improvement Science). Segment KPIs by population to reveal inequality. An aggregate number hides distribution. A "good" average waiting time can conceal that patients from the most deprived neighbourhoods, or those needing an interpreter, wait far longer. Break every equity-relevant KPI down by deprivation, ethnicity, age, disability, and digital access, in line with health equity duties and frameworks such as NHS Core20PLUS5. In digital services, segment adoption and completion rates too — a headline uptake figure can mask that your service excludes exactly the people who need it most (see Topic 4.5 — Data, Analytics & Population Health Management). Treat data quality as a prerequisite, and measure it. A KPI is only as trustworthy as the data beneath it. Track the data quality of the fields your KPIs depend on — completeness, validity, timeliness, coverage — using instruments like the NHS Data Quality Maturity Index, and show data-quality caveats alongside the number. If 30% of records are missing the field, say so on the dashboard; a confident-looking KPI built on poor data is worse than no KPI. Use delivery metrics for the digital service itself, chosen with the same rigour. For the software you build and run, the DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) four keys — deployment frequency, lead time for change, change-failure rate, and time to restore service — give a balanced view of speed and stability. They resist gaming as a set: you cannot ship faster by breaking things, because change-failure rate and restore time will catch it. Complement them with reliability and safety KPIs that matter clinically, such as incident rates and availability of safety-critical functions (see Topic 3.6 and Topic 3.8 ). Layer your reporting so each audience gets the right altitude. A frontline team needs granular, real-time process measures; a service board needs a balanced handful with SPC; a system leadership needs a curated few outcome and equity measures. Design the layers deliberately so the top view is an honest aggregation of the ones below, not a hand-picked flattering subset. This is your structural defence against watermelon reporting ( Topic 10.4 ). Review and retire KPIs on a schedule. Indicators decay: a measure that drove real improvement can become a gamed ritual once the behaviour it targeted is embedded, and new risks emerge that nothing is watching. Put KPIs on a regular review where you ask of each one "is this still telling us something we act on?" and retire the dead wood. A stale KPI set is not neutral — it actively misdirects attention. Questions to discuss with your team # For each of our headline KPIs, how would someone improve the number without improving the reality — and would we notice? This is the Goodhart's law stress test, and it is best done as a deliberately adversarial exercise. Take each KPI and have the team play the role of a stretched service trying to hit it: discharge before midnight to reset the clock, re-band a waiting patient, close and reopen a ticket to reset resolution time, batch-register users who never return. The point is not cynicism about colleagues but recognition that pressure plus a single-number target produces predictable distortions, especially when pay, reputation, or contract penalties ride on the figure. A good answer names the specific gaming route for each KPI and identifies the balancing measure or data check that would expose it — and honestly flags any KPI where you currently have no such safeguard. If a metric cannot be defended this way, the discussion should end with a decision to pair it, redefine it, or drop it. Which of our numbers are we reporting for improvement, and which for judgement — and are we presenting each in a way that matches? Teams routinely take a metric built to help a service learn and hand it, unchanged, to a committee that uses it to hold someone to account, or vice versa. The tension is real: leaders need assurance, and improvement needs safety to see problems honestly, and the same chart cannot always serve both without distortion. Walk through your actual board and operational packs and label each metric's true purpose, then ask whether the presentation fits — are you showing a two-point red/green comparison where an SPC chart would prevent knee-jerk reactions to noise? A good, honest answer will admit where judgement-culture has crept into improvement forums (making staff hide problems) and where vague improvement narratives are being used to dodge legitimate accountability. The aim is a conscious choice per metric, with SPC as the default presentation, rather than an accidental muddle. Do our KPIs reveal or conceal inequality, and whose experience is missing from them entirely? Aggregate KPIs are comfortable precisely because they average away the people at the margins, and in health and care those margins are where avoidable harm concentrates. Discuss which of your indicators are segmented by deprivation, ethnicity, disability, age, and digital access — and which are still reported only as a single system-wide figure that could look healthy while a subgroup is failed. Push further to the people who never enter your data at all: patients who could not get past the login, who abandoned the digital form, who were never referred, who declined to share the demographic field you segment by. A strong answer identifies at least one KPI where segmentation changed or would change the story, acknowledges the data-quality and consent limits on segmentation honestly, and commits to a specific step — even a proxy or a small qualitative study — to see the currently invisible. Anything less risks a dashboard that is technically accurate and morally blind. How many KPIs are we actually watching, and which ones would we lose nothing by retiring? The word key only means something if the set is small, yet indicators accumulate faster than anyone removes them — a national return here, a contractual metric there, a number a former director once asked for and no one has dared drop since. The tension is that every KPI feels defensible in isolation, so the set grows until the board packs are a hundred pages that no one reads and the genuinely important signals are buried among zombie metrics produced out of habit. Walk your actual reporting and count the indicators honestly, then ask of each one whether anyone acted on it in the last year and what decision it informs; the metrics that survive neither test are dead wood that still consumes analyst time and dilutes attention. A good answer names a specific number you will hold per service, identifies at least one KPI to retire outright, and puts in place a scheduled review so the set stays curated rather than quietly re-inflating. Be wary of the reflex that retiring a metric is an admission of failure — a disciplined subtraction is a sign of maturity, not neglect. How much do we actually trust the data beneath each headline KPI, and does the dashboard say so? A confident-looking number built on a field that is 30% incomplete is more dangerous than no number at all, because it invites decisions that the data cannot support while wearing the authority of a clean figure. In health and care this is acute: demographic fields needed for equity segmentation are often sparse, coding practice varies between sites, and the very act of digitizing a paper process can shift what gets recorded and when. Discuss, for each KPI, whether you know its completeness, validity, timeliness and coverage, and whether those caveats travel with the number onto the board pack or get quietly stripped away as it moves upward. A strong answer points to a concrete instrument — a data-quality check, the DQMI, a completeness threshold below which a metric is flagged — and shows at least one place where a data-quality caveat is displayed alongside the KPI rather than hidden. The honest version admits where you are currently reporting a number you cannot fully stand behind, and treats fixing the data as part of the KPI, not a separate backlog item. Do the layers of our reporting honestly roll up, and where could red turn green on the way to the board? Different audiences legitimately need different altitudes — a frontline team wants granular real-time process measures, a board wants a balanced handful with SPC, a system wants a curated few outcomes — but each aggregation is an opportunity for the underlying picture to be smoothed, averaged or hand-picked into something more comfortable than the truth. This is the structural root of watermelon reporting: the more layers between the ward and the board, the more places a distribution can be flattened into a reassuring mean, or a struggling site can be netted off against a strong one. Trace one KPI from its frontline source all the way to the top view and ask whether the executive figure is a faithful aggregation or a flattering subset, and who — if anyone — audits that roll-up. A good answer shows that reporting layers were designed deliberately with agreed definitions and owners, identifies at least one point where the aggregation could mask a problem, and names the balancing measure or drill-down that keeps the top view truthful. Honesty here means admitting where the roll-up is currently taken on trust rather than checked (see Topic 10.4 ). In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system (ICS) launches a digital referral service that lets GPs refer directly into community musculoskeletal (MSK) physiotherapy, replacing a paper and fax process. The programme board's instinct is to report two KPIs: number of digital referrals received, and system uptime. Within three months both are strongly green — thousands of referrals, 99.9% uptime — and the board is ready to declare success. The clinical director is uneasy and asks the analytics team (working with the pattern in Topic 4.5 ) to rebuild the KPI set around outcomes. They land on a balanced handful: time from referral to first contact (access, shown as an SPC chart), the proportion of referrals returned or rejected as incomplete (a leading quality signal), a patient-reported outcome score at discharge (outcome), a short experience measure (did you feel involved in decisions?), and change-failure rate for the service's releases (delivery stability). Every access and outcome measure is segmented by deprivation decile and by whether the patient needed digital support. The rebuilt view tells a very different story. Uptime is genuinely fine, but the return-to-referrer rate is 22% — one in five referrals bounces because the digital form makes a free-text history mandatory, so GPs game it by typing "see attached" and the triage team rejects them. The SPC chart shows access time is stable but sitting well above target with no improvement trend. And segmentation reveals that patients in the two most deprived deciles are half as likely to complete the self-referral route that the service was quietly nudging people towards, widening a gap the programme had assumed it was closing. None of this was visible in the original two green numbers. The board redesigns the form, adds an assisted-referral pathway, and keeps the balanced, segmented, SPC-based KPI set as its standing view — with the raw referral count demoted to a supporting metric where it belongs. Sector lenses # Startup # A digital-health startup lives or dies by a few actionable metrics, so the discipline is ruthless focus and honesty. x: Topic 10.2 — Quality Improvement & Improvement Science Quality improvement gives frontline teams a disciplined, data-driven way to make care measurably better through small tests of change — and when you connect it to your digital tools, you turn dashboards and automation into engines of continuous learning rather than static reporting. Why this matters in health and care # Quality improvement (QI) is the dominant improvement discipline across the National Health Service (NHS) and much of global health and care. It is taught in trusts, embedded in ward-level huddles, and championed by national bodies. If you lead digital delivery, you are not working alongside QI — you are working inside a system that already thinks in aims, measures, and tests of change. Ignoring that language isolates your team; speaking it fluently makes your digital work legible to clinicians, managers, and boards who already trust it. The deeper reason matters more. In health and care, variation in how work is done is not a cosmetic problem. Unwarranted variation means some patients wait longer, some receive unsafe care, and some are excluded entirely. Improvement science exists precisely because good intentions and heroic effort do not reliably produce better outcomes — systems do. A digital service that shaves minutes off a clinical workflow, closes a safety gap, or removes a step that disproportionately excludes people with low digital confidence is doing improvement work, whether or not you call it that. QI also protects you from a common digital failure: shipping a change and assuming it worked. Improvement science is built around a single humbling insight — most changes are not improvements, and you cannot tell which are without measurement over time. Adopting that discipline keeps your team honest, keeps your claims defensible to boards and regulators, and keeps your users safer. This topic shows you how to run QI properly, how it differs from project delivery and research, and how to fuse it with the digital tooling you already own. Core concepts # Quality management in health and care draws on a lineage that runs from manufacturing to the bedside. The intellectual root is the work of W. Edwards Deming , the statistician who taught that quality comes from understanding and reducing variation in systems, not from exhorting individuals to try harder. Deming's thinking, together with Walter Shewhart's, produced the PDCA / Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle — the iterative Plan-Do-Study-Act loop that sits at the heart of modern healthcare QI. Most NHS teams run PDSA inside the Model for Improvement , a framework popularized by the Institute for Healthcare Improvement (IHI) that pairs the cycle with three questions: What are we trying to accomplish? How will we know that a change is an improvement? What change can we make that will result in improvement? The first question is answered with an aim statement (specific, measurable, time-bound). The third is often mapped with a driver diagram , which links your aim to the primary and secondary drivers you believe influence it, and then to concrete change ideas. QI is one member of a family of improvement approaches that share the continual improvement process philosophy. Two siblings you will meet constantly are Lean , derived from the Toyota Production System and focused on removing waste and improving flow, and Six Sigma , which uses statistical methods to reduce defects and variation. In healthcare these are frequently blended as "Lean Six Sigma". Measurement for improvement relies on seeing data over time rather than in snapshots. The two workhorse tools are the run chart — observed data plotted in time sequence against a median — and the control chart , a run chart with statistically derived limits, which underpins statistical process control (SPC). SPC lets you distinguish common-cause variation (the ordinary noise of a stable system) from special-cause variation (a signal that something has genuinely changed). In the NHS this is taught as the "Making Data Count" approach. None of this works without psychological safety : the shared belief that people can raise problems, admit that a test failed, and challenge the status quo without being punished. Improvement is impossible where staff hide defects, and it is the precondition for everything else in this topic. Best practices # Start with an aim statement, not a solution. Before you design anything, write down what you are trying to accomplish, for whom, by how much, and by when — for example, "reduce the median time from referral to first digital triage from 9 days to 3 days by March." A numeric, time-bound aim forces clarity and gives you something to measure against. Teams that skip this step end up debating features instead of outcomes, and can never tell whether they succeeded. This connects directly to Topic 10.0 — Objectives & Key Results (OKRs), but note that a QI aim is narrower and more testable than a typical objective. Use a driver diagram to expose your theory of change. Map your aim to the primary drivers that most influence it, then to secondary drivers, then to specific change ideas. This makes your assumptions visible and debatable, and it stops teams from betting everything on a single intervention. It also helps you sequence tests: you can attack the highest-leverage driver first. Keep the diagram on the wall (physical or virtual) and revise it as you learn — it is a living hypothesis, not a one-off artefact. Run small, fast PDSA cycles rather than big-bang launches. Test a change on one clinic, one ward, or one cohort before scaling. Predict what will happen, run the test, study the data against your prediction, and decide whether to adopt, adapt, or abandon. Small tests reduce risk, surface problems early, and build the evidence and confidence you need to spread. This is a fundamentally different rhythm from a fixed-scope project plan, and it is where digital teams most often need to unlearn habits. Measure over time with run charts and SPC, not before-and-after snapshots. A single pair of numbers cannot tell you whether a change caused an improvement or whether you caught random variation. Plot your measure as a run chart or control chart so you can see trends, shifts, and special-cause signals. Adopt the NHS "Making Data Count" conventions so your charts are consistent and readable to others. This discipline also protects you from claiming credit for noise, which erodes trust with boards and regulators. Balance your measures. Every improvement has the potential to make something else worse. Alongside your outcome measure, track process measures (is the change actually happening?) and balancing measures (is anything deteriorating as a side effect — safety, staff workload, equity of access?). A digital triage tool that speeds throughput but quietly excludes people without smartphones has not improved care. Balancing measures are your early-warning system for exactly this kind of harm. Give frontline teams genuine permission and capability to improve. Improvement that is mandated top-down and executed by a central team rarely sticks. Invest in QI training, coaching, and protected time so the people doing the work can run their own tests. Build the infrastructure — a QI faculty, a measurement function, accessible data — that the IHI and mature NHS trusts describe as the backbone of a trust-wide programme. Your digital team's job is often to remove the data and tooling friction that stops frontline improvement. Design for spread and sustainability from the start. A one-off gain on one ward that evaporates in six months is a common and demoralizing outcome. Plan how a successful change will be standardized, embedded in workflow, and monitored so it holds — and how it will spread to comparable settings without simply copy-pasting. Digital tools help enormously here: automation and defaults can lock in an improved process far more reliably than a laminated poster. This is where QI meets Topic 8.1 — Change Management. Fuse QI with your digital data and dashboards. Improvement science is starved without timely data, and most NHS QI historically ran on hand-counted samples. If your team can surface near-real-time run charts and SPC charts from existing systems, you dramatically shorten the learning loop. Treat dashboards, automated data pipelines, and self-service analytics as improvement infrastructure, not just reporting. This is one of the clearest, highest-value contributions a digital function can make to clinical quality. Questions to discuss with your team # Are we running quality improvement, project delivery, or research — and do we know the difference? These three modes are routinely confused, and the confusion is expensive. Project delivery aims to deliver a defined scope on time and budget; research aims to produce generalizable knowledge with rigorous controls and ethics approval; QI aims to make a local system better through iterative small tests of change. Measurement for improvement is deliberately lighter than measurement for research — you want just enough data to guide the next cycle, not a publishable study. Applying research-grade rigour to a QI test paralyses the team; applying QI informality to something that is really research risks ethical and safety failures. Talk through where each of your current initiatives genuinely sits, and whether you have the right governance for each. Getting this wrong is a frequent reason digital improvement work stalls or draws unwarranted scrutiny. How will we know a change is an improvement, and not just noise or wishful thinking? This is the second question of the Model for Improvement, and it is where most teams are weakest. Decide now what your outcome, process, and balancing measures are, how often you will collect them, and how you will display them over time. Commit to run charts or SPC before you launch, so you are not tempted to cherry-pick a favourable before-and-after comparison afterwards. Discuss what a "special-cause signal" would look like for each measure, and who is empowered to call it. Be honest about the uncomfortable corollary: you must be willing to see that a change you invested in did not work. Link this to Topic 1.3 — Evidence-Driven Decisions, because the same intellectual honesty underpins both. Do our frontline teams actually have permission, time, and data to improve — or only pressure to deliver? Improvement capability is not a slogan; it requires protected time, coaching, psychological safety, and accessible data. Ask candidly whether staff feel safe reporting that a test failed, or whether they expect blame. Ask whether the data they need arrives in days and weeks rather than months, and whether your digital systems help or hinder. Consider whether your organization has genuine QI infrastructure — a faculty, a method, a measurement function — or whether improvement depends on a few enthusiasts. Discuss what your digital team could remove from the frontline's path: manual data collection, brittle spreadsheets, delayed reports. The answer usually reveals more about your culture than your technology, and it directly shapes what Topic 10.4 — Visibility for the CEO & Senior Leaders should surface to the board. When a change works, how will we make it hold and spread — and how will we know it has not quietly reverted? The most demoralizing QI outcome is a genuine local gain that fades within months once attention moves on, and the second most demoralizing is a success that never spreads beyond the ward that pioneered it. Discuss concretely how a proven change will be standardized and embedded — ideally in the tooling itself, through defaults and automation, rather than a laminated poster or individual goodwill that decays. Decide who owns the measure after the improvement project closes, and whether your run chart or SPC chart will keep running so a reversion shows up as a special-cause signal rather than a surprise a year later. Talk about spread as a deliberate act of adaptation, not copy-paste: what worked in one clinic must be re-tested, not merely rolled out, in settings with different staff, patients, and systems. Be honest about whether your organization actually resources sustainability and spread, or treats "closed" as "done". This is where QI meets Topic 8.1 — Change Management, and where digital defaults are your strongest lever. Are our improvements narrowing or widening inequity — and would our balancing measures actually catch it? Digital improvements are especially prone to lifting the average while leaving some groups behind, because the people a new online route serves least well are often the least visible in aggregate data. Decide now whether you will disaggregate your measures by the dimensions that matter — age, deprivation, language, digital confidence, disability — rather than reporting a single headline number that can hide harm. Discuss what an equity balancing measure looks like for this specific change, and who is accountable for acting when it moves the wrong way. Be candid about the trade-off: maintaining a phone route alongside a self-referral form costs money and staff, and the pressure to decommission the "old" channel once digital uptake climbs is exactly how exclusion creeps in. An honest answer names the groups most at risk for this change, states how you would detect harm early, and commits to keeping the non-digital path open until the data says it is safe to change. This connects directly to the equity duties discussed elsewhere in this book and to your obligations as a public service. What is our digital function's specific, highest-value contribution to improvement here — and where are we over-building? It is tempting for a digital team to answer every quality problem with new software, but the biggest contribution is often industrializing measurement: turning hand-counted samples into trustworthy, near-real-time run charts and SPC charts drawn from live systems, so the learning loop shortens from months to days. Discuss where automated measurement and sensible defaults genuinely lock in improvement, versus where you would be gold-plating a problem that a simple process change already solved. Be wary of rebuilding a tool — the online form in this topic's example — before the driver diagram has shown the tool is actually the bottleneck. Ask whether your effort is removing friction from the frontline's improvement work or adding a shiny artefact that nobody asked for. The honest answer distinguishes the one or two moves that measurably accelerate learning from the features that merely look like progress, and it keeps your team's scarce capacity pointed at the highest-leverage driver. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care board (ICB) is worried about its community physiotherapy service. Patients referred from primary care wait a median of 21 days for first contact, complaints are rising, and a new online self-referral form has not obviously helped. The digital team's instinct is to rebuild the form. Instead, the service's clinical lead and the digital product manager decide to run this as a quality improvement project. They write an aim statement: reduce median time from referral to first meaningful contact from 21 days to 7 days within four months, without increasing the did-not-attend rate or reducing access for patients who cannot use online tools. They build a driver diagram. The primary drivers turn out to be referral quality, triage speed, and appointment availability — not, as first assumed, the form itself. The biggest bottleneck is triage: referrals sit in a shared inbox for days before a clinician reviews them. They start small. In one PDSA cycle, a single physiotherapist trials same-day triage for one GP practice's referrals, using a simple digital worklist the team stands up in a week from existing data. They predict triage time will fall to under a day; the study phase confirms it, and reveals a surprise — a third of referrals lack the information needed to triage safely, forcing rework. The next cycle tests a structured referral template. Throughout, the digital team surfaces a run chart of daily triage times and an SPC chart of the median wait, following "Making Data Count" conventions, so the whole service can see progress in near-real time rather than waiting for a monthly report. Crucially, they track a balancing measure: the proportion of referrals arriving by phone versus the online form, disaggregated by patient age and deprivation. When online self-referral climbs, they notice it is not reaching older patients in the most deprived neighbourhoods, so they keep the phone route fully staffed. By month four the median wait sits stable at six days — a genuine shift on the control chart, not a lucky month — and the improvement holds because the structured template and triage worklist are now the default workflow, embedded in the tooling rather than dependent on goodwill. Sector lenses # Startup # A health-tech startup rarely has a formal QI programme, and does not need one — but the core discipline is directly applicable and often neglected. The Model for Improvement maps naturally onto product experimentation: an aim statement is a hypothesis, a PDSA cycle is a build-measure-learn loop, and balancing measures guard against the classic startup failure of optimizing one metric while quietly harming clinical safety or equity. The main risk is speed without measurement over time — shipping fast and declaring victory on a single week's uplift. Adopt run-chart thinking early; it is cheap and it makes your outcome claims credible to the NHS buyers and clinical partners you will eventually need. Treat psychological safety inside your small team as a competitive asset: honest reporting of failed tests is how you avoid building the wrong thing at scale. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home, a domiciliary-care provider, or a single-site clinic — has real patients and ongoing operations but rarely any dedicated QI or analytics capability, and cash is tight. The good news is that the Model for Improvement scales down honestly: a practice manager and a clinician can write one aim statement, run a small PDSA cycle, and keep a simple run chart on a whiteboard or spreadsheet without buying anything. The discipline to protect is measurement over time — resist the urge to judge a change on last week's numbers, and pick two or three measures (including a balancing measure such as access for patients who cannot use online tools) that you can actually collect within the working day. Lean on what your existing clinical system already records rather than building bespoke dashboards you cannot maintain, and where a national approach like "Making Data Count" offers free conventions and templates, adopt them rather than reinventing. Your constraint is not ambition but time, so keep tests genuinely small and let a proven change become the standing workflow so it holds without ongoing effort. Enterprise # A large provider or supplier usually has an established QI infrastructure — a faculty, trained coaches, an improvement method, and a measurement function — sometimes running to hundreds of concurrent projects. The enterprise risk is the opposite of the startup's: bureaucratic QI that becomes a compliance ritual, with driver diagrams produced for governance rather than genuine tests of change. Your digital function's highest-value move is to industrialize measurement for improvement — automated, trustworthy, near-real-time SPC charts drawn from live systems — so improvement teams stop hand-counting and start learning faster. Guard against the enterprise habit of confusing a large transformation programme with improvement; the two need different governance, as Topic 5.2 — Programme-Led Work makes clear. Sustainability and spread are your hardest problem
