x: Topic 10.3 — Knowledge Management & Documentation In one sentence: In a safety-critical service, what your teams know but have never written down is a clinical risk, not just an inconvenience — so treat documentation as a first-class deliverable and knowledge continuity as a duty, not a nicety. Why this matters in health and care # Digital health teams are small, specialized, and often stitched together from permanent staff, contractors, and supplier engineers. The person who understands why the pathology interface retries three times before failing, or which flag in the electronic patient record suppresses a duplicate-allergy alert, is frequently one individual — and that individual moves on, retires, or is off sick the week the integration breaks at 2am. When the knowledge leaves with them, the system does not become merely harder to maintain; it becomes harder to operate safely . An undocumented workaround that a clinician relied on can silently disappear, and nobody left knows it was load-bearing. The stakes are specific to the sector. A misunderstood configuration can produce a wrong-patient record, a missed alert, or a broken referral — harms measured in patient outcomes, not downtime tickets. Public bodies also carry statutory obligations: health records must be retained for defined periods, and decisions about care and about public money must be auditable years later and findable when a coroner, a regulator, or a Freedom of Information request comes calling. Good knowledge management is therefore part clinical safety, part governance, and part respect for the next person who has to keep the service running. It is inseparable from how you run live operations (see Topic 3.8 — Service Management & Live Operations) and how you design teams (see Topic 7.0 — Team Structures, Roles & Responsibilities). Core concepts # Knowledge management as a discipline. Knowledge management is the set of practices by which an organization creates, captures, shares, and reuses what it knows. It balances three components — people and culture, processes and structure, and technology — and fails whenever leaders treat it as a tool-purchase rather than a habit. The "knowledge" ranges from how a clinical pathway actually works in a given trust to how a specific integration engine is configured. Tacit versus explicit knowledge. Tacit knowledge is what lives in people's heads and hands — the judgement, intuition, and hard-won "you have to know that this trust codes discharge differently" that is hard to write down. Explicit knowledge is what has been articulated and codified into documents, diagrams, and runbooks. Most of the knowledge that keeps a service safe starts tacit; the work of knowledge management is to convert enough of it to explicit form that the service does not depend on any one head. The SECI knowledge-conversion model. The SECI model (Socialization, Externalization, Combination, Internalization), from Nonaka and Takeuchi, describes how knowledge moves between tacit and explicit forms: sharing by working alongside each other (socialization), writing tacit knowledge down (externalization), combining explicit pieces into larger documents (combination), and absorbing documented knowledge back into fluent practice (internalization). It is useful because it reminds you that documentation alone is not enough — pairing, shadowing, and communities matter just as much as the wiki. Key-person dependency and the bus factor. The bus factor is the number of people who would have to be lost before a service stalls for lack of anyone who understands it. A bus factor of one is the default state of most small digital teams and a serious operational risk in a service people's health depends on. High staff turnover, heavy contractor use, and single-supplier lock-in all push the number down; deliberate documentation, cross-training, and pairing push it back up. Documentation as a first-class deliverable. Treat documents as products, not by-products. A service manual describes what the service is and how it behaves; a runbook (or playbook) gives step-by-step procedures for starting, stopping, and recovering it; an architecture decision record (ADR) captures why a significant choice was made, so future maintainers do not unpick it without knowing the reasons. A single source of truth means each fact is mastered in exactly one place, so people are not chasing contradictory copies of "the current architecture". Docs-as-code. Keeping documentation in the same version-controlled repository as the work — written in plain text or Markdown, reviewed like code, published automatically — keeps docs close to the thing they describe and far more likely to stay current. When the diagram lives next to the code and changes in the same pull request, it rots more slowly. Communities of practice. A community of practice (sometimes called a guild) is a cross-team group that shares a craft — clinical safety officers, front-end engineers, information governance leads — and improves it together. Communities spread tacit knowledge horizontally across an organization that vertical team boundaries would otherwise trap. Records management and retention. Records management governs information through its lifecycle, including how long it must be kept and when it may be destroyed. In health this is partly statutory: clinical records carry defined retention periods under the NHS Records Management Code of Practice. This is distinct from team documentation, and conflating the two causes real errors — a point we return to below. Information architecture and findability. Information architecture is the structural design of an information space so that people can find what they need. A wiki with ten thousand pages and no structure is not documentation; it is a landfill. Findability is the difference between knowledge that exists and knowledge that is used. Best practices # Make documentation a definition-of-done, not an afterthought. A feature, integration, or configuration change is not "done" until its runbook entry, its ADR (if a significant decision was made), and its service-manual update exist. Bake this into your ways of working so it is written while the knowledge is fresh, by the person who has it. Retro-documenting a system six months later, from memory, is where inaccuracies and dangerous gaps are born. Keep a single source of truth and link outward from it. Decide, per domain, where the authoritative version of each fact lives — the architecture, the on-call rota, the data-flow diagram — and make everything else point to it rather than copy it. Duplicated documentation drifts, and in a clinical context a stale copy that says "the allergy check is on" when it is off is worse than no document at all. Ruthlessly delete or redirect the stale duplicates you already have. Adopt docs-as-code and keep documentation next to the work. Store runbooks, ADRs, and service manuals in version control alongside the systems they describe, review documentation changes in the same pull request as the code change, and publish automatically. This makes updates cheap, changes reviewable, and history auditable — and it means the person changing the system is nudged to change the docs in the same breath. Write runbooks a stressed stranger could follow at 3am. A runbook should assume the reader is tired, unfamiliar with the system, and under pressure — because during a major incident they will be. Use numbered, literal steps, name the exact screens and commands, and state the expected result of each step and what to do if it fails. Test them by having someone who did not write them execute a recovery in a drill. Capture the "why", not just the "what", with architecture decision records. A short ADR — context, decision, consequences — preserves the reasoning behind significant choices so that future maintainers do not reverse a decision without understanding the constraint that drove it. In health this matters acutely: a configuration that looks odd may exist because of a clinical-safety hazard analysis or an information-governance ruling. Recording the reason prevents a well-meaning "clean-up" from reintroducing a known risk. Deliberately raise the bus factor on every critical system. Identify the systems with a bus factor of one and treat that as a risk on your register with a named owner and a plan. Pair people, rotate on-call knowledge, run "teach-back" sessions where the expert documents while a colleague follows along, and forbid any single person being the only one who can deploy or recover a safety-critical service. This is cheaper than discovering the gap during an outage. Run post-incident reviews that change practice, not blame people. After any significant incident, run a blameless post-incident review that produces documented, owned, time-bound actions — and then actually close them. Lessons-learned that are filed and never revisited are theatre; the test of the process is whether a later incident of the same shape is prevented. Feed the findings straight back into runbooks and the clinical-safety case (see Topic 3.8 — Service Management & Live Operations). Invest in information architecture and findability. Structure your knowledge base so a new joiner can find the on-call runbook in under a minute, and prune aggressively — an out-of-date page is a liability, not an asset. Agree naming conventions, a clear hierarchy, and an owner for each area, and put a "last reviewed" date on pages that matter so readers can judge freshness. Search is not a substitute for structure; it is a complement to it. Grow communities of practice to spread tacit knowledge. Stand up cross-team guilds for the crafts that matter — clinical safety, security, front-end, data engineering — with a light remit: share what you are learning, agree common patterns, mentor newcomers. These forums move the tacit knowledge that no document captures, and they reduce duplicated mistakes across teams (see Topic 7.5 — People & Organizational Development). Give them time in the working week, or they wither. Separate team documentation from statutory records — and manage both. Be explicit about what is team knowledge (runbooks, ADRs, wikis) versus what is a record subject to legal retention (clinical records, care decisions, financial approvals, information-governance decisions). Apply the NHS Records Management Code of Practice retention schedules to the latter, and do not let casual wiki deletion destroy something you were legally required to keep. Equally, do not hoard everything forever "to be safe" — over-retention is its own governance and data-protection risk. Make onboarding a test of your documentation. Treat every onboarding as a live audit: if a competent new engineer or clinician cannot get productive from your written material plus a little pairing, your documentation has failed, and the gaps they hit are your backlog. Ask new joiners to fix the first thing that confused them as their first contribution. This turns onboarding from a one-way cost into a continuous improvement loop for knowledge continuity. Questions to discuss with your team # If the one person who understands our most critical integration left tomorrow, how long until we were exposed — and what specifically would we not know? This turns the abstract idea of a bus factor into a concrete stress test of your most important systems. Work through a real example — the pathology feed, the single-sign-on configuration, the shared care record's matching logic — and ask honestly who else could operate, change, and recover it without that person. The tension to surface is that the deepest knowledge usually sits with your busiest, most trusted individual, and the pressures of delivery make it rational for them never to stop and write it down. Distinguish knowledge that is genuinely tacit and hard to codify from knowledge that simply has never been captured because nobody made time. A good, honest answer names your bus-factor-one systems out loud, admits which gaps are real, and produces a costed plan — pairing, documentation sprints, cross-training — rather than a vague reassurance that "it's all in people's heads and that's fine". If the conversation is comfortable, you have not been specific enough. When we write something down, how do we know anyone will ever find it, trust it, and keep it current — and where is our documentation already lying to us? Documentation that is out of date is not neutral; in a safety-critical setting it actively misleads a stressed operator into the wrong action. The discussion should confront the difference between having documents and having documents people can find, trust, and act on — a question of information architecture, ownership, and freshness, not volume. Debate whether your knowledge base has a real structure or has become a sprawl nobody navigates, and whether docs live close enough to the work (docs-as-code) to stay current or drift in a separate tool nobody updates. Ask each person when they last relied on an internal document and found it wrong, and what that cost. A strong answer identifies specific pages you know to be stale, assigns owners and review dates, and agrees a single source of truth for the facts that matter most — and it is willing to delete more than it adds. After our last serious incident, what actually changed in how we work — and if the answer is "not much", why do we keep running reviews? Post-incident reviews are common; reviews that change practice are rare, and the gap between the two is where the same failures recur. This tests whether your lessons-learned process is a genuine feedback loop or a ritual that produces a document and no change. Explore the cultural conditions honestly: reviews only surface the truth if they are blameless, and people will hide the real cause if the process punishes them, so psychological safety is a precondition, not a nicety (see Topic 8.1 — Change Management). Look at your last few incidents and trace each action to whether it was completed and whether it prevented recurrence. A good answer can point to a concrete change — a rewritten runbook, a new alert, a design fix — that a past review produced, and is candid about actions that were logged and quietly abandoned, with a plan to close that loop. Which of the things we hold are statutory records we are legally obliged to keep, which are working notes we manage for currency — and are we confident we are not deleting the first or hoarding the second? Health and care organizations carry retention duties that most digital teams handle by instinct rather than by rule, and both directions of error are real: casually deleting a wiki page that turned out to document a care decision, or hoarding everything forever "to be safe" and creating a data-protection and findability liability. The discussion should force a clear line between a record subject to the NHS Records Management Code of Practice — clinical records, care and funding decisions, information-governance rulings — and team knowledge like runbooks and ADRs that you manage for freshness, not for legal retention. Surface the awkward middle cases, such as an ADR that documents why a clinical-safety hazard was accepted, which may be both. The tension is that engineers optimize for tidy, current documentation while governance optimizes for defensible retention, and the two instincts pull in opposite directions. An honest answer can say who owns the retention schedule, where the boundary is drawn, and what would happen to a specific record if it were requested by a coroner, a regulator, or a Freedom of Information request years from now. What in our ways of working actually causes documentation to get written while the knowledge is fresh — and where are we still relying on goodwill and good intentions? Every team agrees documentation matters; far fewer have a mechanism that makes it happen by default rather than by heroics. This question probes whether writing things down is engineered into the flow of work — a definition-of-done that blocks "done" without a runbook entry or ADR, documentation reviewed in the same pull request as the change, docs-as-code so the diagram lives next to the thing it describes — or whether it depends on individuals choosing to stop and write when delivery pressure says ship. Examine the incentives honestly: retro-documenting a system from memory six months later is where dangerous inaccuracies are born, so the value is almost entirely in capturing it in the moment. Look at your last few changes and ask whether the documentation was written by the person who held the knowledge, at the time, or bolted on later by someone reconstructing it. A strong answer points to concrete mechanisms already in place and names the gaps where the process still leans on memory and willpower, with a plan to close them. How do we move the knowledge that no document will ever capture — the judgement and the "you have to know this trust codes discharge differently" — and does that get harder every time a contractor's contract ends? Much of what keeps a service safe is tacit: intuition, pattern recognition, and hard-won context that resists being written down, and the SECI model is a reminder that documentation alone never fully externalizes it. This question asks how deliberately you spread that knowledge through pairing, shadowing, teach-back sessions, and communities of practice, rather than assuming the wiki does the job. The tension is sharpest where you rely on contractors and multiple suppliers, because their deepest knowledge walks out of the door at the end of every engagement unless capture is a contractual and cultural expectation, not a favour asked in the final week. Discuss whether your crafts — clinical safety, integration, data engineering — have living guilds with protected time, or whether cross-team learning happens only by accident. An honest answer distinguishes knowledge that is genuinely tacit and needs person-to-person transfer from knowledge that is merely uncaptured, and can point to real practices — a pairing rota, a knowledge-continuity plan for departing contractors, an active community of practice — rather than an aspiration. In practice: a health & care example # An integrated care system (ICS) runs a shared care record that pulls data from three acute trusts, community services, and a social-care case-management system. The integration was built two years ago largely by one contract engineer, "Dev", who understood every quirk of the matching logic that decides when two records refer to the same person. Dev's contract ends in six weeks. There is a wiki, but it was last meaningfully updated during the build. The delivery lead treats this as a bus-factor-one risk and puts it on the programme risk register with her own name against it. Over the six weeks, she funds a small "knowledge continuity" effort: Dev pairs each morning with two permanent engineers, and instead of a farewell brain-dump they externalize as they go — writing runbooks for the failure modes Dev knows by heart, and ADRs explaining why the matching logic tolerates certain mismatches (it turns out one apparently sloppy rule exists to avoid a known patient-safety hazard flagged in the original clinical-safety case). The docs go into the same Git repository as the integration code, reviewed in pull requests, so they are versioned and current. Two months after Dev leaves, the feed from one acute trust starts producing duplicate patient records overnight. The on-call engineer — who never met Dev — opens the runbook, follows the numbered steps, confirms the expected result at each stage, and restores correct matching within the hour. In the blameless post-incident review the team finds the trigger (an upstream change to how the trust codes NHS numbers) and turns it into a monitoring alert and a runbook update. x: Topic 10.4 — Visibility for the CEO & Senior Leaders In one sentence: Executives and boards do not need more reports — they need a trustworthy, layered line of sight from strategic outcome to delivery reality, built on a single source of truth and honest confidence assessments that surface bad news early enough to act. Why this matters in health and care # A chief executive of an NHS trust or the accountable officer of an integrated care board (ICB) is answerable — to a public board, to regulators, to Parliament, and ultimately to patients — for outcomes they cannot personally observe. Between the boardroom and the ward, or between the strategy and the codebase, sit many layers, each with an incentive to round up. If visibility is poor, leaders learn of a failing digital programme only when it has already consumed the money and missed the window; if visibility is dishonest, they learn even later. The stakes are specific to this sector. Digital programmes here carry clinical-safety risk, statutory data-protection duties, and large sums of public money whose misdirection is a matter of public record. Boards operate within corporate governance frameworks that demand documented assurance, not vibes. Good executive visibility is therefore not a nicety of management style; it is how a board discharges its legal duty of oversight and how a system avoids the failures that follow when confident reporting masks quiet collapse. Core concepts # What leaders actually need to see. Not activity logs, but a small, stable set: strategic outcomes (are we achieving the change we promised — see Topic 10.0 — Objectives & Key Results (OKRs)); delivery confidence (will the things in flight land, and how sure are we); risks and issues (what could stop us, ranked by impact); spend and benefits (are we on budget and is the investment paying back); and safety and compliance (are we within our clinical-safety and information-governance obligations). Everything else is detail available on request. Reporting layers. Visibility is layered, not flat. A board sees a portfolio-level view (a page per programme, exceptions only); an executive team sees a programme-level view; a delivery lead sees the team-level view. Each layer is a summarization of the one below, and the discipline is that they must reconcile — the board's green must be the same green the team would recognize. This is the reporting expression of enterprise portfolio and programme management (see Topic 5.3 — Enterprise Portfolio & Programme Management). Single source of truth. The numbers a leader sees should derive from one authoritative dataset — a single source of truth — not from a slide deck someone re-typed. When finance, delivery, and benefits each maintain their own version, board discussions collapse into arguments about whose figure is right. A single source of truth means the dashboard, the finance system, and the risk register draw from the same underlying records. Delivery Confidence Assessment (DCA). The UK Infrastructure and Projects Authority (IPA) uses a Delivery Confidence Assessment — a rated judgement (typically a red/amber/green (RAG) scale ) of a project's likelihood of achieving its objectives at a point in time. Crucially, it is an assessment , not a calculation: a reviewer weighs multiple factors rather than averaging individual RAG scores. It is a professional opinion about the future, made explicit. Watermelon reporting. The characteristic failure of RAG reporting: green on the outside, red on the inside. A status turns green at each layer as it rises, because reporting red is career-risky, until the board sees an all-green portfolio over a programme that is actually failing. Defeating the watermelon is the central problem of executive visibility. Best practices # Report exceptions, not everything. A board's attention is the scarcest resource in the organization. Give it a portfolio on a page where healthy programmes are a single green line and the discussion time goes to the exceptions — the ambers and reds — with a clear ask for each. Comprehensiveness is the enemy of attention. Build on a single source of truth. Invest in one authoritative data layer from which every reporting view is generated, so finance, delivery, benefits, and risk cannot diverge. When a leader asks "where does this number come from?", there should be one answer. This also makes self-serve possible (see practice 8). Use structured delivery confidence assessments, not just RAG dots. Adopt an IPA-style DCA for each major programme: a rated, narrated judgement of the likelihood of success, refreshed on a cadence and at gateways. Require the narrative — the why behind the colour — because a colour with no reasoning is exactly what the watermelon exploits. Engineer honesty into the reporting culture. The watermelon is a cultural artefact, not a formatting problem. Make it safe — indeed expected — to report amber and red early; treat a programme that goes red as a request for help, not a confession of failure. Independent assurance reviews (the IPA model) and rotating challenge break the incentive to round up. A leader who shoots the messenger will be the last to know. Anchor everything to a board assurance framework. NHS boards use a Board Assurance Framework (BAF) — a close cousin of the project risk register — to map principal risks to the controls and assurances that manage them, with RAG-rated confidence in each. Tie digital and delivery reporting into the BAF so the board sees strategic risk, the controls in place, and the gaps in one governance instrument, satisfying its assurance duty rather than running a parallel unofficial view. Define escalation paths and thresholds in advance. Decide, before the crisis, what conditions force a programme onto the board's agenda between scheduled meetings (a red DCA, a budget breach beyond tolerance, a clinical-safety incident, a slipped critical milestone). Pre-agreed thresholds turn escalation from a judgement call — which the watermelon suppresses — into a rule. Set a governance rhythm and hold it. Match reporting cadence to decision cadence: a weekly delivery signal, a monthly programme review, a bi-monthly or monthly board. Stale reporting is worse than none because it invites decisions on old reality. The rhythm should feed, and be fed by, the OKR check-in cadence of Topic 10.0 . Offer self-serve alongside curated views. Give leaders and non-executive directors a live dashboard they can interrogate themselves, so they are not wholly dependent on the story a report tells. Balance it with a curated narrative for the board pack — self-serve answers "what is happening?", curation answers "what does it mean and what should we do?". Both are needed; neither alone suffices. Tell the story with the data, honestly. A number on a slide changes no decision; a leader needs the interpretation — trend, comparison, and the "so what". Use statistical process control (see Topic 10.0 ) rather than month-on-month arrows so the board reacts to signal, not noise, and pair every reassuring figure with the risk it does not capture. Storytelling with data is not spin; it is making a true situation legible. Questions to discuss with your team # Where in our reporting chain is a watermelon most likely forming right now — and what would make it safe for the layer below to tell us the truth earlier? The watermelon — green on the outside, red within, ripening upward as each layer softens the status because reporting red is career-risky — is the central failure of executive visibility, and the honest version of this question names the specific programme where you suspect it rather than discussing it in the abstract. In a health and care setting the cost is not just a missed deadline but public money already spent and a clinical or access benefit that never materialized, discovered too late to redirect. The tension to debate is that culture, not format, drives the watermelon: a leader who has ever shot the messenger has taught every layer beneath to round up, and no dashboard redesign will undo that lesson. Concrete angles include whether your recent red or amber statuses arrived early enough to act, whether independent assurance or rotating challenge exists to break the incentive to soften, and whether a team lead genuinely believes an early amber will be met with help rather than blame. A good answer is uncomfortable — it identifies a real candidate watermelon, admits where the culture punishes bad news, and commits to a specific change (a safe-to-escalate norm, an independent reviewer, a pre-agreed threshold) rather than a platitude about openness. When a leader asks "where does this number come from?", can we give one answer — and where do our finance, delivery, and benefits figures currently diverge? A single source of truth is what stops board discussions collapsing into arguments about whose spreadsheet is right, yet most organizations discover on inspection that the "beds saved" or "savings realized" figure on the board slide was re-typed from a deck and no longer reconciles with the finance ledger or the delivery tracker. The exercise is to trace one or two of your most consequential board numbers back to their origin and see whether every reporting view genuinely draws from the same underlying records or from parallel, quietly diverging copies. The trade-off worth debating is the real cost of building that authoritative data layer against the recurring cost of boards litigating data provenance instead of making decisions — and whether "good enough for now" reconciliation is masking a figure that can be re-spun at will. Consider who owns each number today, how often the versions are checked against each other, and what a leader currently does when two sources disagree. A strong answer locates at least one number that cannot yet be traced to a single origin, names the divergence, and decides who is accountable for closing it so that self-serve and curated views can safely share one foundation. Does every RAG rating we report carry the reasoning behind its colour, and have we agreed in advance what forces a programme onto the board's agenda between meetings? A colour with no narrative is unfalsifiable and is precisely the habitat the watermelon thrives in; an IPA-style Delivery Confidence Assessment is valuable because it is a rated professional judgement with its rationale made explicit , not an average of sub-scores that hides the reasoning. Test your current reporting: could a non-executive interrogate the "why" behind an amber, or does the colour arrive naked and unchallengeable? The second half matters just as much — deciding before the crisis what conditions (a red DCA, a budget breach beyond tolerance, a clinical-safety incident, a slipped critical milestone) trigger escalation turns raising the alarm from a judgement call the watermelon suppresses into a rule that fires automatically. The tension is that narrated assessments and pre-agreed thresholds feel like bureaucratic overhead until the month a programme fails quietly for want of them, and busy reviewers resent writing the rationale. Concrete evidence to bring includes a recent status that changed with no explanation, and any past escalation that happened too late because it depended on someone's discretion. A good answer commits to requiring the narrative behind every rating and to a written set of escalation thresholds the board has actually endorsed, so bad news reaches decision-makers while there is still time to act. Do our reporting layers actually reconcile — would the board's green be recognized as green by the team doing the work — and is our board pack short enough to command attention? Visibility is layered rather than flat: the board sees a portfolio-on-a-page, the executive a programme view, the delivery lead a team view, and the whole edifice only works if each layer is a faithful summarization of the one beneath it. The discipline this question tests is reconciliation — whether the confident green a board reads is the same reality a ward manager or an engineer would recognize, or whether meaning has quietly leaked out at each hand-off. Alongside fidelity sits the scarcity of board attention: a wall of sixty undifferentiated metrics buries the two that matter, so exception-based reporting that shows healthy programmes as a single line and spends discussion time on the ambers and reds is not laziness but focus. The tension is real — summarizing for the board risks smoothing over the texture that would reveal trouble, yet refusing to summarize drowns the board in detail it cannot act on. Concrete angles include picking one recent green status and walking it down to the delivery team to see if it survives, and counting how many metrics your last board pack actually carried. A good answer commits to a layered structure that reconciles top to bottom and to a board pack disciplined enough that exceptions stand out rather than hiding in the noise. Are our non-executives and senior leaders able to interrogate the data themselves, and do we present signal rather than month-on-month noise? A board that can only see the story a report chooses to tell is captive to the narrator, which is why live self-serve dashboards for non-executive directors matter — they let independent challenge probe beneath the curated narrative rather than accepting it whole. But self-serve alone is not enough: raw numbers without interpretation change no decision, and a leader confronted with a month-on-month arrow will react to noise as if it were a trend, chasing a single bad month or celebrating a single good one. This is where statistical process control earns its place, distinguishing a genuine shift from ordinary variation so the board reacts to signal, and where honest storytelling with data — trend, comparison, and the "so what" — makes a true situation legible without spinning it. The tension worth surfacing is that self-serve access can expose leaders to unmediated numbers they misread, while over-curation slides into spin; both a live view and a curated narrative are needed, and neither alone suffices. Consider whether your non-executives have ever found something the executive did not flag, and whether your board reacts to variation as if every wobble were meaningful. A good answer gives independent access real teeth while pairing it with interpretation that separates signal from noise. Do the metrics we put in front of the board measure outcomes — including benefits realized, safety and compliance — or do they flatter us with activity counts? The vanity trap is reporting what is easy to count ("users onboarded", "systems deployed") instead of the strategic outcome the investment was meant to buy ("beds saved", "admissions avoided", "waits shortened"), and in health and care that gap is not cosmetic because public money is justified by patient benefit, not by activity. This question also forces the two dimensions boards most often under-report to the surface: whether the promised benefits are actually being realized against the business case, and whether the programme remains within its clinical-safety and information-governance obligations — a green delivery status over a live safety or data-protection risk is its own kind of watermelon. The trade-off to debate is that outcome and benefit measures are slower, noisier and harder to attribute than activity counts, so teams gravitate to the easy number precisely when the hard one matters most. Concrete angles include auditing your current board metrics to see how many are activity versus outcome, checking whether benefits are tracked past go-live or quietly abandoned, and confirming safety and compliance appear on the board's line of sight rather than only in a separate committee. A good answer re-anchors every board metric to a strategic outcome, keeps benefits realization visible after delivery, and ensures safety and compliance are reported to the board rather than assumed. In practice: a health & care example # An ICB is investing £14m over three years in a virtual-ward programme to move eligible patients from hospital beds to monitored care at home. The board has been receiving a monthly slide: three programmes, all green, a headline of "beds saved". For fourteen months it is reassured. At month fifteen the programme misses its bed-reduction target badly, and it emerges the amber had been known at team level for two quarters — the community-nursing capacity to staff the wards was never secured, but each layer softened the status upward. Classic watermelon. The new chief digital officer rebuilds visibility. A single source of truth links the delivery tracker, the finance ledger, and the benefits model, so "beds saved" is computed once and cannot be re-spun in a deck. Each programme carries an IPA-style Delivery Confidence Assessment with a written rationale, refreshed monthly and challenged quarterly by an independent reviewer. The board pack becomes a portfolio-on-a-page: two greens shown as one line each, the virtual-ward programme in amber with a specific ask — fund the nursing gap or rescope. Escalation thresholds are agreed: any red DCA or any staffing shortfall beyond 10% comes to the board within a week, not at the next monthly cycle. Benefits are plotted on an SPC chart so a single good month is not mistaken for recovery. Non-executive directors get a live self-serve dashboard for their own probing, and the curated narrative explains what the numbers mean. The programme does not instantly succeed — but the board now sees the truth early enough to redirect money and demand the staffing fix while it still matters. Sector lenses # Startup # In a digital-health startup the "board" is a founder, a handful of investors, and a monthly update, so the visibility problem is inverted: the danger is not layers of watermelon but a single optimistic narrator with no independent check. Keep one honest dashboard — runway, active users, uptime, open safety issues — drawn from a single source of truth rather than a hand-built board deck, and report amber early to investors because a seed-stage company that hides a slipping metric simply runs out of cash in the dark. A lightweight delivery-confidence line ("will we hit the pilot by Q3, and how sure are we") is enough; a full IPA-style DCA would be theatre at this scale. The cultural work is making it safe for a five-person team to tell its backers bad news while there is still time to pivot. Small business # An established small provider — a GP practice, a community pharmacy, a care home or domiciliary-care service, a single-site clinic, or a small health-tech supplier past the startup stage — has real patients and ongoing operations but little or no dedicated IT capability and tight cash, so executive visibility falls to a practice manager or registered manager as one job among many. The point is not a layered board apparatus, which there is no one to staff, but a single honest weekly glance at the few things that can hurt patients or the business: open safety and information-governance issues, whether a supplier's system is actually delivering, and whether a funded digital change is on track or quietly stalling. Because the practice carries the same clinical-safety and data-protection duties as a large trust with none of the assurance machinery, the discipline is to write down a short escalation rule — what forces a problem to the partners or the owner this week rather than at the next quarterly review. A cheap dashboard drawn straight from the clinical or operational system, rather than a hand-typed spreadsheet, keeps the one source of truth honest without a reporting team. The cultural work is making it safe for a receptionist or a care worker to flag a slipping problem early, because in a small team the person who sees it first is often the only one who will. A # Accessibility — Designing services so people with disabilities can use them; in UK public services, measured against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) and a legal duty. See Topics 1.9 , 3.0 . ADKAR — Prosci's individual change model: Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement. A people-centred complement to organizational change models. See Topic 8.1 . Agile — A family of iterative, incremental ways of working that deliver value in small increments and adapt to feedback. See Agile software development . See Topics 1.0 , 3.5 . Alert fatigue — Desensitization caused by too many low-value safety alerts, so clinicians begin to override important and trivial warnings alike. See Alarm fatigue . See Topics 4.7 , 4.8 . Alpha — The lifecycle phase where a team tests solutions to the problems found in discovery, usually with throwaway prototypes. See Topic 3.5 . Arden syntax — A standard for encoding shareable medical knowledge as executable rules (Medical Logic Modules) for clinical decision support. See Arden syntax . See Topic 4.7 . Architecture decision record (ADR) — A short document capturing one significant design decision, its context and its consequences, kept close to the code. See Topic 10.3 . Artificial intelligence (AI) — Computer systems performing tasks that normally require human intelligence; in health, increasingly delivered through machine learning. See Artificial intelligence . See Topic 8.4 . Assisted digital — Support for people who cannot use a digital service independently, so they are not excluded. See Topic 1.9 . Asynchronous consultation (e-consultation) — Store-and-forward clinical contact where patient and clinician are not present at the same time. See Topic 3.11 . Autoscaling — Automatic adjustment of cloud capacity to match demand, a core lever for cutting idle spend. See Autoscaling . See Topic 6.5 . Airlock (output checking) — In a Secure Data Environment, the holding area and human review gate through which analytical results pass, checked for disclosure risk, before release. See Topic 4.10 . B # Budget impact analysis — An estimate of the total cash cost of adopting an intervention across a health system; something can be cost-effective yet unaffordable in-year. See Topic 6.1 . Behaviour Change Wheel / COM-B — A framework explaining behaviour through Capability, Opportunity and Motivation, used to design adoption interventions. See Topic 8.3 . Big bang adoption — Switching an organization onto a new system on a single cut-over date, with no parallel-running period. See Big bang adoption . See Topic 4.6 . Business continuity — Keeping critical services running, and recovering them, through disruption. See Business continuity planning . See Topic 3.9 . Business intelligence — Tools and practices that turn data into reporting and insight for decisions. See Business intelligence . See Topic 4.5 . Balanced scorecard — A strategic performance framework balancing financial, customer, internal-process, and learning-and-growth measures. See Balanced scorecard . See Topic 10.0 . Benefits realization — The discipline of identifying, planning, measuring and actually achieving the benefits a change is meant to deliver. See Benefits realisation management . See Topics 5.2 , 5.3 , 8.1 . Beta — The lifecycle phase where a team builds and iterates a working service with real users, first privately then publicly. See Topic 3.5 . Bus factor — The number of people who would have to be lost before a system or service could no longer be run or understood; a measure of key-person risk. See Bus factor . See Topic 10.3 . Business case — The justification for an investment, in the UK public sector usually the Five Case Model (strategic, economic, commercial, financial, management). See Topics 6.0 , 9.1 . Bioinformatics — The computational pipelines that turn raw genomic sequence into interpreted, clinically actionable variants. See Bioinformatics . See Topic 4.11 . C # Cost–benefit analysis (CBA) — An economic evaluation that expresses both costs and health benefits in monetary terms. See Cost–benefit analysis . See Topic 6.1 . Care Quality Commission (CQC) — The independent regulator of health and adult social care in England, whose remit includes digitally-enabled and well-led care. See Topic 1.5 . Chargeback — Recovering technology cost from the consuming team's own budget, as opposed to showback, which only reports it. See Cost allocation . See Topic 6.5 . Chief Clinical Information Officer (CCIO) — A senior clinician accountable for the clinical design, safety and adoption of an organization's IT; with the Chief Nursing Information Officer (CNIO), leads clinical informatics. See Chief medical informatics officer . See Topics 4.6 , 4.7 . Clinical decision support (CDS / CDSS) — Health IT that delivers person-specific, filtered knowledge to a clinician at the point of care to improve a decision. See Clinical decision support system . See Topic 4.7 . Clinical engineering — The discipline (also biomedical engineering) that manages medical devices across their lifecycle — inventory, maintenance, safety and decommissioning. See Topic 4.4 . Clinical informatics — The discipline joining clinical practice, information and technology; the professional home of the CCIO and CNIO. See Health informatics . See Topic 4.7 . Closed-loop medication administration — An unbroken electronic chain from prescribing to dispensing to barcode-verified bedside administration, enforcing the "five rights" of medication. See Topic 4.8 . Committed-use / reserved capacity — Discounted cloud pricing exchanged for a one- or three-year commitment to a baseline level of usage. See Topic 6.5 . Computerized physician order entry (CPOE) — Electronic entry of clinical orders (tests, drugs, referrals) by the ordering clinician; also called order communications. See Computerized physician order entry . See Topics 4.6 , 4.7 . Content design — Designing the words, structure and formats that help people complete a task, in plain language and accessible forms. See Topic 3.1 . Cloud computing — Delivering computing services over the internet on a public or hybrid basis. See Cloud computing . See Topic 4.0 . Caldicott Guardian — A senior person responsible for protecting the confidentiality of health and care information and enabling appropriate sharing. See Caldicott Guardian . See Topic 1.7 . Change management — The structured approach to moving people and organizations from a current to a future state. See Change management . See Topic 8.1 . Clinical safety (DCB0129/DCB0160) — Mandatory NHS standards for managing clinical risk in the manufacture (DCB0129) and deployment (DCB0160) of health IT, overseen by a Clinical Safety Officer. See Topic 1.6 . Continuous delivery / integration — Engineering practices for releasing software frequently and safely. See Continuous delivery and Continuous integration . See Topic 3.5 . Conway's law — The observation that a system's design mirrors the communication structure of the organization that builds it. See Conway's law . See Topic 7.0 . Cost-effectiveness analysis — Comparing the cost of interventions against a common health outcome (often the QALY) to judge value for money. See Cost-effectiveness analysis . See Topic 6.1 . Cost of delay — The economic cost of not having something finished yet; the numerator in prioritization methods such as WSJF. See Cost of delay . See Topic 2.2 . Cyber security — Protecting systems, networks and data from digital attack; in the NHS, guided by the NCSC and the Data Security and Protection Toolkit. See Computer security . See Topic 1.7 . Cynefin — A sense-making framework distinguishing clear, complicated, complex and chaotic contexts to match the response to the situation. See Cynefin framework . See Topics 1.3 , 2.1 . Concentration risk — The exposure created by depending too heavily on a single supplier, platform or region. See Concentration risk . See Topic 6.6 . D # Digital public infrastructure — Shared, reusable digital platforms and services (identity, data exchange, national APIs) that many organizations build on. See Topic 4.1 . Design system — A single source of truth of reusable, accessible interface components, patterns and guidance (e.g. the NHS and GOV.UK design systems). See Topic 3.2 . Digital social care record (DSCR) — A digital replacement for paper care records in adult social care, supplied from an assured list. See Topic 9.3 . DevOps — A culture and set of practices uniting development and operations to release software frequently and safely. See DevOps . See Topic 3.6 . Digital literacy — The capability of the whole workforce (not just specialists) to use digital tools confidently and safely. See Topic 7.4 . Data cleansing — Detecting and correcting or removing inaccurate, corrupt or duplicate records. See Data cleansing . See Topic 4.9 . Data ethics — Doing the right thing with data beyond legal compliance; social licence and public trust. See Big data ethics . See Topic 1.8 . Data migration — The one-off transfer of historical records from a legacy system into a new one; technically routine but clinically high-risk. See Data migration . See Topic 4.6 . Data profiling — Examining existing data to measure its actual condition before cleansing, migration or reporting. See Data profiling . See Topic 4.9 . Data quality — Fitness of data for use, judged across dimensions such as accuracy, completeness, timeliness, validity, consistency and uniqueness; in care, poor quality is a clinical-safety hazard. See Data quality . See Topic 4.9 . Data Quality Maturity Index (DQMI) — NHS England's measure of the quality of the data organizations submit in national datasets. See Topic 4.9 . Data steward — The named role accountable for the quality and fitness of a defined data domain. See Data steward . See Topic 4.9 . Digital strategy — A statement of digital vision, priorities and roadmap aligned to organizational and clinical strategy. See Topic 1.2 . Disaster recovery — The technical recovery of systems and data after a major failure, measured by RTO and RPO. See IT disaster recovery . See Topic 3.9 . Dictionary of medicines and devices (dm+d) — The NHS standard terminology giving every medicine and device a unique code for unambiguous recording and interoperability. See Topic 4.8 . Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT) — The annual self-assessment NHS and social-care organizations complete to show they meet data-security and information-governance standards. See Topic 1.7 . Demand management — Capturing, understanding and shaping the flow of incoming requests so supply can meet it. See Topics 2.0 , 5.3 . Diffusion of innovations — Rogers' theory of how new ideas and technology spread through a population over time. See Diffusion of innovations . See Topic 8.0 . Digital inclusion / exclusion — Whether people can access and use digital services; exclusion (the digital divide ) maps closely onto health inequalities. See Topics 1.9 , 3.11 . Discovery — The first lifecycle phase: understanding users and the problem before committing to a solution. See Topic 3.4 . DORA metrics — Four key measures of software delivery performance (deployment frequency, lead time, change-fail rate, time to restore). See DevOps . See Topics 3.8 , 10.0 . Double Diamond — The Design Council's model of divergent-then-convergent thinking across "discover/define" and "develop/deliver". See Double Diamond . See Topics 3.0 , 3.4 . DTAC — The NHS Digital Technology Assessment Criteria: a baseline for clinical safety, data protection, security, interoperability and usability of digital health products. See Topics 1.6 , 8.4 . Data re-identification — Matching supposedly anonymous data against other datasets to reveal who someone is; genomic data is inherently re-identifiable. See Data re-identification . See Topics 4.10 , 4.11 . Dynamic consent — A digital, ongoing consent model letting people see and change how their data or samples are used over time. See Dynamic consent . See Topic 4.11 . E # Externality — A cost or benefit of a treatment falling on people not party to it, such as herd immunity from vaccination. See Externality . See Topic 6.1 . E-iatrogenesis — Patient harm caused or enabled by health IT, such as a pick-list or default-dose error. See Iatrogenesis . See Topic 4.8 . Electronic patient record (EPR) — A provider's core clinical system: the digital patient record plus the tools clinicians use to order, document and review at the point of care (also EHR/EMR). See Electronic health record . See Topic 4.6 . Electronic prescribing & medicines administration (ePMA) — A hospital system, usually an EPR module, managing the whole inpatient medicines process from prescribing to recorded administration. See Electronic prescribing . See Topic 4.8 . Electronic Prescription Service (EPS) — The NHS England service that sends prescriptions electronically from prescriber to pharmacy. See NHS Electronic Prescription Service . See Topic 4.8 . Enterprise architecture — A disciplined view of an organization's business, data, application and technology layers to guide change. See Enterprise architecture . See Topic 4.0 . Equality, Diversity & Inclusion (EDI) — Fair treatment, representation and belonging in the workforce, underpinned by the Equality Act 2010 and duties such as WRES and WDES. See Topic 7.6 . Enterprise Project Portfolio Management (EPPM) — Managing the entire portfolio of change initiatives as one coordinated whole. See Project portfolio management . See Topic 5.3 . Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) — Integrated software for finance, HR, payroll, procurement and supply chain that acts as an organization's system of record. See Enterprise resource planning . See Topic 5.4 . Evidence hierarchy — A ranking of evidence types by susceptibility to bias, from expert opinion up to systematic reviews of randomized trials. See Hierarchy of evidence . See Topic 1.3 . Experience-level agreement (XLA) — A commitment measuring the outcome a user actually experiences, complementing component-level SLAs. See Topic 6.6 . F # FHIR — Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources, the HL7 standard for exchanging health data. See Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources . See Topic 4.3 . FinOps (cloud financial operations) — An operating discipline uniting engineering, finance and business/clinical teams to manage cloud cost as a shared, data-driven responsibility across an Inform/Optimize/Operate lifecycle. See Topic 6.5 . Five Case Model — The HM Treasury / UK government standard structure for a business case. See Topics 6.0 , 9.1 . Five rights of CDS — The quality frame for decision support: the right information, to the right person, in the right format, through the right channel, at the right time. See Topic 4.7 . Frontline digitization — NHS England's national programme setting a core electronic patient record as the baseline for every provider and tying capital funding to digital maturity. See Topic 4.6 . Federated analytics / federated learning — Running queries or training models across separate data holdings so insight is combined without the raw data being pooled. See Federated learning . See Topic 4.10 . Five Safes — A framework structuring safe data access across safe people, projects, settings, data and outputs. See Five Safes . See Topic 4.10 . G # GDPR — The General Data Protection Regulation (and UK GDPR): the legal framework for processing personal data. See Topic 1.7 . Golden record — A single reconciled, trusted version of an entity (such as a patient) assembled from multiple source systems. See Topic 4.9 . Goodhart's law — "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." See Goodhart's law . See Topic 10.0 . Greener NHS / net zero — The NHS programme and commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions across its own footprint and wider supply chain. See Topic 8.5 . Green Book — HM Treasury guidance on appraising and evaluating public spending. See Topics 6.0 , 6.1 , 9.1 . GA4GH (Global Alliance for Genomics and Health) — The international standards body for responsible genomic data sharing. See Global Alliance for Genomics and Health . See Topic 4.11 . Genomics — The study of the whole genome and its use in care; genomic data is large, lifelong, familial and uniquely identifying. See Genomics . See Topic 4.11 . Genomics England / 100,000 Genomes Project — The government-owned company and programme that sequenced 100,000 genomes and curates the National Genomic Research Library. See Genomics England . See Topic 4.11 . H # Hazard ratio (HR) — The ratio of the event rate in a treatment group to a control group over time, from survival analysis; often misread because it averages over follow-up and does not translate simply into absolute risk or life-years. See Hazard ratio . See Topic 1.4 . Health literacy — People's ability to find, understand and use health information and services; low health literacy widens inequalities. See Health literacy . See Topic 3.1 . Health Research Authority (HRA) — The body overseeing research ethics and governance for health and social care research in the UK. See Topic 8.6 . Hazard log — The living register of clinical hazards, their risk ratings and controls that sits at the heart of a clinical safety case. See Topic 1.6 . Health economics — The study of how to allocate scarce resources to maximize health, using tools such as cost-effectiveness analysis and the QALY. See Health economics . See Topic 6.1 . Health inequalities — Unfair and avoidable differences in health across the population; digital exclusion can widen them. See Health equity . See Topic 1.9 . HIMSS EMRAM — The HIMSS Electronic Medical Record Adoption Model, a 0–7 international benchmark of a provider's clinical-system digital maturity. See Healthcare Information and Management Systems Society . See Topic 4.6 . Hospital-at-home / virtual ward — Delivering hospital-level acute care to patients in their own homes with daily clinical review and rapid escalation. See Hospital-at-home . See Topic 3.11 . I # Information asymmetry — The imbalance where clinicians hold far more information about treatment than patients, one reason the healthcare market cannot be left to itself. See Information asymmetry . See Topic 6.1 . Identity & access management (IAM) — Controlling who can access what: authentication, authorization, role-based access control and least privilege. See Topic 4.2 . Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) — Connected medical devices and sensors that generate and exchange data; a major clinical and security surface. See Topic 4.4 . ICER (incremental cost-effectiveness ratio) — The extra cost per extra unit of health (e.g. per QALY) of one option versus another; compared against a threshold to judge value. See Topic 6.1 . Incident management — The service-management practice of restoring normal service as quickly as possible after disruption, with major-incident and business-continuity procedures for the most serious. See Incident management . See Topic 3.8 . Information governance — The rules and accountability for handling information legally, securely and ethically. See Topic 1.7 . Integrated Care System (ICS) — A partnership of NHS and local-government organizations planning and delivering joined-up health and care in an area of England. See Integrated care system . See Topics 5.2 , 9.0 . Interoperability — The ability of systems to exchange and use information, at technical and semantic levels. See Interoperability . See Topic 4.3 . ITIL — A framework for IT service management, including incident, problem, change and service-request management. See ITIL . See Topic 3.8 . Incide

x: Specification — Ways of Working for Digital Health & Care Status: Authoritative source of truth. This document governs the book. Where a topic, the README, the style guide, or any generated content disagrees with this spec, this spec wins — fix the artifact, or change the spec deliberately and then bring the artifacts into line. Purpose: Enough here for any author or agent to (a) understand what the book is, (b) build or regenerate any single topic to a consistent standard, and (c) verify the result against a checklist — without reading the other 72 files first. 1. Product definition # A practical handbook of best practices for leading and running digital delivery in health and social care organizations. Working title: Ways of Working for Digital Health & Care Subtitle: A practical handbook of best practices for delivering digital services in health and social care organizations Format: A set of Markdown files, one per topic, stitched by README.md (the table of contents) plus reference matter ( GLOSSARY.md , INDEX.md ). Premise (the book's spine): In health and care, how you work is a clinical-safety, equity, and public-trust issue — not merely an efficiency one. Every topic must ultimately serve this thesis. Centre of gravity: UK NHS and social care, with principles that transfer to any publicly-accountable, safety-critical, partnership-dependent health organization internationally. Audience # Chief executives and senior leaders; directors of digital and transformation; product, delivery, programme, and portfolio leads; clinical and care professionals moving into digital roles; and the operational managers who run services daily. Write for a busy director who wants to act . 2. Repository layout # Path Role README.md Reader-facing front door in English (en-gb): premise, audience, table of contents linking to locales/en-gb/ . STYLE_GUIDE.md The prose/formatting contract every topic author follows. Subordinate to this spec. locales/<locale>/ One directory per locale (15: ar-001, bn-001, cy-001, cy-gb, de-001, en-001, en-gb, en-gb-oxendict, en-us, es-001, fr-001, hi-001, ja-001, ru-001, zh-001). Every locale directory is named <language>-<region> (e.g. en-gb , cy-001 ); two-letter language-only directories such as locales/en/ are not allowed. Registry: spec/locales-for-global-sharing-with-svelte/locales.tsv ; routing (two-letter aliases, language detection on / ) is specified in spec/locales-for-global-sharing-with-svelte/index.md . locales/<locale>/index.md The locale's home page and table of contents ( README.md is a symlink to it); see spec/contents-for-global-sharing-with-svelte/ . locales/<locale>/<topics-dir>/PP-CC-slug/index.md The 73 topics plus the preface ( 00-01-… ), one folder each. Both the topics directory and the slug are translated per locale (e.g. es-001/temas/01-00-introducción/ ); English locales use topics/ and English slugs. The leading PP-CC- (two-digit part, dash, two-digit within-part number, dash) is identical in every locale and is what ties translations together, so a plain lexical sort lists topics in reading order. README.md in each folder is a symlink to index.md . locales/<locale>/.locale-peer-id A 32-character hexadecimal id, byte-identical across every locale's version of the same page. GLOSSARY.md A–Z definitions of key terms, Wikipedia-linked, each pointing to its home topic. Shared by every locale. INDEX.md A–Z concepts/frameworks → topic numbers (numbers are topic numbers, not pages ). Shared. _sources/ Raw source material used for grounding (e.g. workforce-strategy text). Not shipped as topics. digital-health-guide.github.io/ The SvelteKit site (adapter-static, Lily Design System, pnpm) that renders the book; deployed by .github/workflows/deploy-site.yml . spec/index.md This file — the source of truth. spec/contents-for-global-sharing-with-svelte/ , spec/locales-for-global-sharing-with-svelte/ , spec/search/ , spec/sitemap/ Cross-site specs shared with the other *.github.io sites. spec/oxford-spelling.md The spelling standard (Oxford spelling, en-GB-oxendict ) and its URL/citation-protection rules. spec/README.md Symlink to this file. AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md , AGENTS/ Working instructions for AI agents (CLAUDE.md imports AGENTS.md; AGENTS/ holds task-focused guides). The site also serves generated /llms.txt and /llms.json ( digital-health-guide.github.io/scripts/build-llms.mjs ). 3. Topic template (canonical structure) # Every topic uses these headings, in this order. This is the contract the maturity model, checklist, and reviews are verified against. # Topic N — Title In one sentence — a single bold sentence stating the topic's thesis. (No heading; it's the first line of body.) ## Why this matters in health and care — the domain-specific stakes: safety, equity, statutory duties, public money. ## Core concepts — definitions and mental models. First mention of each key named concept is hyperlinked to its English Wikipedia article. ## Best practices — numbered ; each item a bold lead-in + 2–4 sentences. This is the heart of the topic. ## Questions to discuss with your team — exactly six numbered, open (non-yes/no) questions, each in bold , each followed by a 4–8 sentence briefing that names the real tensions, concrete angles, and what an honest answer looks like. Placed before the worked example. Must be workshop-ready. ## In practice: a health & care example — one concrete, realistic, fictional worked scenario (e.g. an ICS rolling out a shared care record). ## Sector lenses — the same topic across four ### subsections in this order : ### Startup , ### Small business , ### Enterprise , ### Government . Each 3–6 sentences, showing how the practice changes with scale, funding model, risk appetite, and accountability. Startup = a pre-revenue or early-stage digital-health company; Small business = an established small or independent provider/SME (e.g. a GP practice, a care home, a single-site provider, or a small health-tech supplier past the startup stage); Enterprise = a large, complex organization (NHS trust, ICS, big supplier); Government = a national or local public body. ## Common failure modes — anti-patterns and how to avoid them. ## Maturity model — a 5-level table with columns Initiate / Develop / Standardize / Manage / Orchestrate and 3–5 rows of observable characteristics. (Levels progress from ad hoc Initiate , through Develop and Standardize , to measured/governed Manage and continuously-optimizing Orchestrate .) ## Checklist — 6–12 actionable - [ ] items. ## Key sources — bulleted, real and verifiable; cite frameworks by name. ## References — a numbered list combining (a) Wikipedia articles for the key concepts named in the topic and (b) authoritative sources. Format each: title — publisher/author — URL . 4. Topic manifest # 73 topics in 10 parts, numbered by part and within-part (section.topic, e.g. 1.0 , 1.1 ), plus front and reference matter. Each topic is a folder named PP-CC-slug (sortable zero-padded decimals: two-digit part, dash, two-digit within-part, dash, slug) holding an index.md ; the slugs below are the English ones ( locales/en-*/topics/<slug>/ ), and translated locales keep the PP-CC- prefix with a translated slug (two-digit part, dash, two-digit within-part, dash, slug), so files sort in reading order; the heading and table of contents use the natural form ( Topic 1.0 , Topic 3.10 ). Voice, style & formatting rules # Voice: authoritative, practical, calm. No hype. Name trade-offs honestly; evidence over assertion. Person: second person ("you", "your organization") for guidance; third person when describing practice. Acronyms: expand every acronym on first use in each topic . Spelling: Oxford spelling ( en-GB-oxendict ) — British English with -ize / -ization endings for the Greek-derived family (organize, prioritize, standardize, realize, optimize, digitize, recognize). Keep every other British form: -our (behaviour, colour), -re (centre, theatre), -yse (analyse, paralyse — not analyze), doubled l (modelling, labelled), licence / defence nouns, programme (use "program" only for a computer program), and -ae/-oe (paediatric). The full rules, exceptions, and the URL/citation-protection mechanics live in spec/oxford-spelling.md — follow it exactly. Be consistent within a topic. Paragraphs: 2–4 sentences. Markdown only. Use tables for comparisons and maturity models. Length: target ~3,000–3,500 words of substantive prose per topic (most run ~3,000–4,000 words including tables and references). Deepen rather than pad; never invent filler. No topic should fall below ~3,000 words. Cross-references: reference sibling topics by number and title — e.g. "(see Topic 8.1 — Change Management)". Always include the title, not just the number, so references survive renumbering. 6. Grounding & citation rules (non-negotiable) # Real, checkable sources only. Never invent citations, URLs, statistics, or quotations. If unsure of a figure, describe the pattern qualitatively. Wikipedia linking: on first mention of a key named concept/framework/method, hyperlink it to its canonical English Wikipedia article, e.g. [Cost of delay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cost_of_delay) . Verify each article exists before linking; never invent a slug. Aim for 5–12 Wikipedia links per topic. Every inline Wikipedia link must also appear in ## References . Favoured bodies of knowledge (use where they fit): NHS Digital Service Standard & Service Manual; GOV.UK Service Manual (GDS); NICE Evidence Standards Framework for Digital Health Technologies; MHRA; DTAC; HM Treasury Green Book / Five Case Model; Team Topologies; SAFe; PRINCE2; MSP; Management of Portfolios (MoP); Kotter's 8 steps; ADKAR (Prosci); OKRs (Doerr); Lean/Toyota; Cynefin (Snowden); Double Diamond (Design Council); Topol Review; Caldicott principles; clinical safety standards DCB0129/0160. 7. Cross-artifact consistency rules # When a topic is added, renamed, renumbered, or its concepts change, update all of these in the same change so the book stays coherent: README.md table of contents (number, title, filename, part). This manifest (§4) if structure changed. GLOSSARY.md — every newly-introduced key term gets an entry pointing to its home topic. INDEX.md — every key concept maps to the topic numbers that cover it. Inbound/outbound cross-references in sibling topics. 8. Definition of done (per topic) # A topic is complete when all are true: Filename and # Topic N — Title match the manifest (§4) exactly. All 13 template sections (§3) present, correctly ordered and named. Opens with a single bold one-sentence thesis. ## Best practices is numbered with bold lead-ins. Exactly six open discussion questions, each with a 4–8 sentence briefing, placed before the worked example. Four sector lenses in order: Startup, Small business, Enterprise, Government. Maturity model is a 5-level table (Initiate / Develop / Standardize / Manage / Orchestrate). Checklist has 6–12 - [ ] items. 5–12 verified Wikipedia links; every inline link also in ## References . Every citation is real and checkable; no invented facts, URLs, or numbers. UK spelling; acronyms expanded on first use; ~2,500–3,500 words. README.md , GLOSSARY.md , and INDEX.md updated for any new terms/structure (§7). 9. How to author or regenerate a topic # A topic can be written from scratch, regenerated, or deepened by a human or an agent using only this spec plus the topic's manifest entry. The workflow: Fix the scope. Read the manifest (§4) entry — number, title, filename, part — and the neighbouring topics so you know where the boundaries lie and what to cross-reference rather than repeat. A topic earns its place by covering what no other topic owns; if it overlaps a sibling, narrow it or deepen the sibling instead (§13). Research and verify sources first. Gather real, current sources and verify every Wikipedia article exists before you link it (a quick check per slug). Never link a guessed slug; if no good article exists, name the concept in plain text and cite an authoritative source in ## References instead. Draft to the template. Follow §3 exactly — all thirteen sections, in order, with the correct headings. Open with the bold one-sentence thesis; make ## Best practices the substantive heart; write exactly six workshop-ready questions before the worked example; give the four sector lenses in the fixed order. Hit the length by depth. Reach the §5 length target by adding real substance — more best practices, richer core concepts, a fuller worked example — never filler. If a topic is short, add practices and concepts a practitioner would actually use. Self-check against the definition of done (§8) and update the reference matter (§7) for any new terms or structure. Authoring at scale. When many topics are created or renumbered at once, one writer per topic — each editing a distinct file — is safe and fast; never let two writers touch the same file concurrently. Give every writer the full final manifest so cross-references resolve to the right numbers, and complete any renumbering before writing new topics so numbers are final when authors cite them. Transient failures happen: check what actually reached disk and re-run only what is genuinely missing, rather than blindly repeating work. 10. Review & quality gates # Before a topic or a change is considered complete, it passes four gates. Automate them wherever possible; a failure in any gate blocks "done". Structural gate. Thirteen sections present and correctly named; a bold one-sentence thesis; numbered best practices with bold lead-ins; exactly six discussion questions before the example; four sector lenses in the order Startup, Small business, Enterprise, Government; a five-column maturity table (Initiate / Develop / Standardize / Manage / Orchestrate); a checklist of 6–12 - [ ] items. Link gate. Every inline Wikipedia link resolves to a real article and also appears in ## References ; no invented or guessed slugs; 5–12 links per topic. Source gate. No invented citations, URLs, statistics, or quotations. Figures are either real and checkable or described qualitatively. Consistency gate. The # Topic N — Title heading matches the filename and the manifest; every Topic N — Title cross-reference names the topic that actually holds that number; UK spelling; acronyms expanded o
